regions.label: Bresse, Dombes, Bugey and the Pays de Gex - the Ain
regions.sub: Bourg-en-Bresse, Belley, Gex, Nantua, Trévoux (Dombes), Ferney

eras.polity: Lothar I's kingdom after the Treaty of Verdun; local lords
eras.note: Before registers. The Treaty of Verdun in 843 assigned this area to Lothar I's kingdom.

eras.polity: County, then Duchy, of Savoy - Bresse (from 1272) and Bugey
eras.note: Bresse joined the House of Savoy's domains in 1272 through a marriage.

eras.polity: French conquest of the Duchy of Savoy
eras.note: Francis I conquered the Duchy of Savoy in 1536, and the territory was restored after the treaty of 1559.

eras.polity: Duchy of Savoy - Bresse, Bugey, Valromey and Gex
eras.note: The Savoy period ended with the Franco-Savoyard War of 1600-1601.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - government of Burgundy (Bresse, Bugey, Valromey, Gex); Dombes separate to 1762
eras.note: By the Treaty of Lyon of 17 January 1601 Savoy gave France Bugey, Valromey, Gex and Bresse, and Bresse was attached to the military government of Burgundy. Dombes stayed separate until the Count of Eu ceded it to Louis XV on 28 March 1762, so Dombes parishes were under a different sovereign until then.
The department of Ain was created in 1790 from Bresse, Dombes, Bugey and the Pays de Gex. Secular civil registration by the municipalities dates from the decree of 20 September 1792.
After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 seven communes of the Pays de Gex went to Geneva, so some Gex families appear in Genevan, not French, records after that date.

regions.label: Dauphiné - Isère and Drôme
regions.sub: Grenoble, Vienne, Valence, Montélimar, Romans, Die

eras.polity: Dauphiné of Viennois, a lordship of the Dauphins
eras.note: Before registers. Humbert II was the last lord before the sale to the French crown.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - province of Dauphiné
eras.note: Humbert II's lordship was sold to Philip VI under a treaty of Romans in 1349, after which the French heir carried the title Dauphin. Under Louis XI the Conseil Delphinal became the third Parlement of France.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - province of Dauphiné, boundaries changed in 1713
eras.note: Under the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the province gained Barcelonnette and lost most of the Briançonnais, so the upper Alpine valleys changed sovereign.

eras.polity: France - departments of Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes
eras.note: In 1790 Dauphiné was divided into three departments: Isère, Drôme and Hautes-Alpes. A Dauphiné family can therefore have records in three departmental archives.

eras.polity: France - departments of Isère and Drôme
eras.note: Civil registration passed to the municipalities with the decree of 20 September 1792.

regions.label: Hautes-Alpes - the Briançonnais, Embrunais and Gapençais
regions.sub: Gap, Briançon, Embrun, Queyras, La Grave

eras.polity: Dauphiné of Viennois; Briançon chartered 1244, Escartons grand charter 1343
eras.note: Before registers. Guigues VII granted Briançon a charter of liberty in 1244, and on 29 May 1343 Humbert II confirmed a grand charter with 18 representatives of the Alpine valleys.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Dauphiné, the five Escartons of the Briançonnais
eras.note: The Dauphiné passed to the French crown in 1349. The Briançonnais valleys (Briançonnais, Oulx, Casteldelfino, Val Chisone and Queyras) kept their charter privileges.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Briançon and Queyras after the Treaty of Utrecht
eras.note: The Treaty of Utrecht of 1713 gave most of the Briançonnais valleys to Savoy; some accounts say Oulx, Val Chisone and Casteldelfino were separated and Briançon and Queyras stayed French. The privileges ended on 4 August 1789.
The department was one of the original 83 created on 4 March 1790, from the south-east of Dauphiné and the north of Provence. Lay civil registers date from the decree of 20 September 1792.

eras.polity: France under Austrian and Piedmontese occupation
eras.note: Austrian and Piedmontese troops occupied the department from 1815 to 1818.
Italy occupied the department from November 1942 to September 1943.

regions.label: Vivarais - Ardèche
regions.sub: Privas, Annonay, Aubenas, Tournon, Largentière

eras.polity: Vivarais, in the Holy Roman Empire with its bishop as count
eras.note: Before registers. The bishop was count.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Vivarais in the province of Languedoc
eras.note: In 1309 the Vivarais became a Capetian territory and was included in the province of Languedoc. Eight pitched battles of the Wars of Religion were fought here between 1562 and 1595.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Vivarais after the Edict of Nantes
eras.note: The Edict of Nantes in 1598 ended the fighting; over 75 Protestant churches are recorded around that date. In 1629 the forces of Louis XIII burned Privas to the ground during a Protestant revolt, and about one-fifth of the Vivarais Protestant population then emigrated.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Vivarais after the Revocation
eras.note: The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 was followed by the Camisard revolt; peace was restored only in 1715.

The department of Ardèche was created on 4 March 1790 as one of the original 83 and corresponds to the former Vivarais. Civil registration by the municipalities followed from the decree of 20 September 1792.

regions.label: Savoy - Savoie, Chambéry, Maurienne and Tarentaise
regions.sub: Chambéry, Aix-les-Bains, Albertville, Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne, Moûtiers

eras.note: Before registers. The House of Savoy ruled the region from 1032.
The Holy Roman Emperor Sigismund made the County of Savoy an independent duchy on 19 February 1416.

eras.polity: French conquest of the Duchy of Savoy
eras.note: Francis I conquered the Duchy of Savoy in 1536, and it was restored after the treaty of 1559.
The capital moved from Chambéry to Turin in 1563 under Emmanuel Philibert.
The Savoyard states became the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1720, so this period is catalogued with the Sardinian monarchy, not France.

eras.polity: French occupation - department of Mont-Blanc (capital Chambéry)
eras.note: The department of Mont-Blanc was created by the decree of 27 November 1792 that joined Savoy to France. Parish registers were handed to the priests after this period under a Sardinian decree of 22 December 1815.

Two-thirds of Savoy was restored in 1814 and the rest after Waterloo in 1815. Copies of the Catholic registers of 1816-1860 went to lay courts and bishoprics, and extracts, then certified copies, of acts from 1828 to 1860 were given to the mairies after 1861.

The Treaty of Turin was signed on 24 March 1860, the plebiscite held on 22-23 April and the annexation promulgated on 14 June. Mayors took over civil registration on 1 January 1861, and the Archbishop of Chambéry deposited a very large part of the diocese's parish registers at the departmental archives in 1972.

regions.label: Upper Savoy - Haute-Savoie, Annecy, Chablais and Faucigny
regions.sub: Annecy, Thonon-les-Bains, Annemasse, Chamonix, Évian

eras.note: Before registers. The House of Savoy ruled the region from 1032 to 1860.
Savoy became a duchy on 19 February 1416.

eras.polity: French conquest of the Duchy of Savoy
eras.note: Francis I conquered the Duchy of Savoy in 1536; it was restored after the treaty of 1559.
The Savoyard states became the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1720.

eras.polity: French occupation - departments of Mont-Blanc and Léman
eras.note: The department of Mont-Blanc was created on 27 November 1792. In 1798, after the French took Geneva, the northern part of Mont-Blanc went to Léman, and on 17 February 1800 the cantons of Chamonix, Saint-Gervais, Megève, Flumet and Sallanches were transferred to Léman.
Parish registers had been handed back to the priests under a Sardinian decree of 22 December 1815, and the Catholic registers of 1816-1860 were also copied to lay courts and bishoprics.
France annexed the region under the Treaty of Turin of 24 March 1860; mayors took over civil registration on 1 January 1861. Italy occupied the department from November 1942 to September 1943.

regions.label: Comtat Venaissin, Avignon and the Principality of Orange - Vaucluse
regions.sub: Avignon, Carpentras, Orange, Cavaillon, Apt, Valréas

eras.polity: Lands later held by the Holy See and the Princes of Orange
eras.note: Before registers. Alphonse, Count of Poitiers, died on 21 August 1271 and the lands of the Comtat were bequeathed to the Holy See.

eras.polity: Papal Comtat Venaissin and Avignon; Orange a separate principality
eras.note: The Comtat became a papal territory in 1274, and the papacy bought Avignon from Joanna I in 1348; the capital moved from Venasque to Carpentras in 1320. Orange was a separate sovereign principality of the Holy Roman Empire from 1163, passing to William the Silent in 1544; French forces captured it in 1672 and 1682.

eras.polity: Papal Comtat and Avignon; Orange French from 1713
eras.note: Orange was ceded to France under the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, while the Comtat and Avignon stayed papal, so two neighbouring towns can have French and papal records for the same decades. French troops also occupied the Comtat in 1663, 1668 and 1768-1774.
The Comtat was incorporated into France on 14 September 1791 after an unauthorised plebiscite. Orange had been absorbed into the Drôme in 1790, later moving to Bouches-du-Rhône and then Vaucluse.
The department of Vaucluse was created in 1793 (25 June or 12 August depending on the source). The Valréas exclave still lies inside the Drôme.

regions.label: Lower Provence - Marseille, Aix and Arles (Bouches-du-Rhône)
regions.sub: Marseille, Aix-en-Provence, Arles, Tarascon, Salon, Camargue

eras.polity: Kingdom of Arles - Count Boson of Arles invested with Provence in 947
eras.note: Before registers. Boson, Count of Arles, was invested with Provence in 947.

eras.polity: County of Provence, a fief of the Holy Roman Empire
eras.note: The Kingdom of Arles passed to the Holy Roman Empire in 1032. The Treaty of Paris in 1229 transferred the part of Provence west of the Rhône to France.
The Angevin dynasty began to rule Provence in 1246.

eras.polity: County of Provence united with the French crown
eras.note: Charles III died on 11 December 1481, a day after his will named Louis XI heir; the Estates acknowledged the will in 1482, Charles VIII proclaimed the union in 1486, and the Estates received the decree in April 1487. It remained a personal union of crowns until the provincial institutions were dissolved in 1790.
Provence was divided into departments in 1790; lay civil registers by the municipalities date from 20 September 1792.

regions.label: Eastern Provence - Toulon, the Var and the Riviera to the Var river
regions.sub: Toulon, Hyères, Fréjus, Draguignan, Grasse, Cannes, Antibes

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: County of Provence, a fief of the Empire

eras.note: In 1388 the area east of the Var, including Nice, submitted to Savoy, so the Var river became the frontier.

eras.polity: County of Provence united with the French crown
eras.note: The union with the French crown followed the will of Charles III in 1481; Provence's own institutions were dissolved in 1790.

eras.polity: France - department of Var, including the Grasse district
eras.note: Grasse was part of Var, not of the 1793 Alpes-Maritimes, and moved to Alpes-Maritimes only in 1860, so its earlier records may be filed under either department.

eras.polity: France - Var; the Grasse district joined Alpes-Maritimes
eras.note: The new Alpes-Maritimes of 1860 combined the former County of Nice with the Grasse arrondissement taken from Var.

regions.label: Upper Provence - Digne, Sisteron, Manosque and Barcelonnette
regions.sub: Digne, Sisteron, Manosque, Forcalquier, Barcelonnette, Castellane

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: County of Provence, a fief of the Empire
County of Provence united with the French crown
eras.note: The county passed to the French crown after the death of Charles III in 1481; the union was proclaimed in 1486.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France - Provence and the Barcelonnette valley
eras.note: France annexed the Barcelonnette region under the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713, so the Barcelonnette valley's records before 1713 were made under a different sovereign.
Provence was divided into departments in 1790.

regions.label: County of Nice - Nice, Menton, Tende and the Alpes-Maritimes
regions.sub: Nice, Menton, Villefranche, Sospel, Tende, Puget-Théniers

eras.polity: County of Provence - the area east of the Var
eras.note: Before registers. The area east of the Var was part of Provence until 1388.

eras.polity: Savoy - the dedication of Nice, 28 September 1388; County of Nice
eras.note: Nice became part of Savoy's domains on 28 September 1388, and the County of Nice was formed in 1526. French forces occupied it in 1691-1697 and 1707-1713.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia - County of Nice
eras.note: Savoy's states became the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1720, so these records belong to the Sardinian crown, not to Provence or France.
The French army entered Nice on 29 September 1792, and the department of Alpes-Maritimes was ordered on 31 January 1793 with boundaries different from today's; it included Monaco but not Grasse.
The county returned to Sardinia on 23 April 1814. Menton and Roquebrune were under Monaco until 1848, then free cities, and part of the County of Nice until 1860.
The Treaty of Turin was signed on 24 March 1860 and a referendum held on 15 and 16 April 1860. The department combined the former County of Nice with the Grasse arrondissement of Var.

eras.polity: France - Alpes-Maritimes with Tende and La Brigue
eras.note: Tende, La Brigue and parts of the Vésubie and Tinée valley communes were attached in 1947 after the Treaty of Paris and a referendum; they had not been ceded in 1860.

regions.label: Corsica
regions.sub: Ajaccio, Bastia, Corte, Calvi, Bonifacio, Sartène

eras.polity: Republic of Genoa (the Bank of Saint George from 1450 or 1453)
eras.note: Genoa took Corsica in 1284; administration passed to the Bank of Saint George in 1450 (1453 in another account). The oldest surviving parish registers begin in 1548 and are very rare, with more from the later sixteenth century; they cover baptisms and marriages first and burials from the early seventeenth century, written in Latin or mostly Italian, never Corsican.

eras.polity: Corsican Republic under Pasquale Paoli; Genoa ceded its claim to France in 1768
eras.note: The republic was proclaimed in 1755 and lasted until the French conquest of 1769. Registers are patchy for 1730-1768, the years of the uprising against Genoa and Paoli's rule.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France, then Revolutionary Republic
eras.note: The Treaty of Versailles of 1768 had ceded the island. The royal edict of July 1770 required two registers in each parish, one to the royal jurisdiction, so two copies often survive for 1770-1794. In 1793 the island was divided into Golo and Liamone (1 July or 11 August 1793 depending on the source).

Paoli invited British forces in 1794; Britain withdrew in 1796. The decree of 20 September 1792 secularising civil registration reached Corsica but was not applied during this period, and registers are scarce.

eras.polity: France - Golo and Liamone, one department of Corsica from 1811
eras.note: Civil registration took effect more than a year after the British left in August 1796, and some communes have lay registers from the start of year VI (September 1797). The tables décennales begin only in 1803 (year XI). Registers stayed in Italian in many communes until between 1820 and 1850. Golo was abolished in 1811 (24 April by one account, 19 April by another).

Germany arranged for Italy to occupy Corsica in November 1942; Germany formally took over on 9 September 1943, and the Germans evacuated Bastia by 4 October 1943. Most of the Bastia arrondissement's court copies of registers were destroyed in the war.

eras.polity: France - Haute-Corse and Corse-du-Sud since January 1976
eras.note: Since the two-department split in January 1976, the registers of the arrondissements of Bastia and Corte are at the archives of Haute-Corse and those of Ajaccio and Sartène at the archives of Corse-du-Sud. The two merged into a single territorial collectivity on 1 January 2018.

regions.label: Réunion (Île Bourbon)
regions.sub: Saint-Denis, Saint-Pierre, Saint-Paul, Saint-Louis, Le Tampon

eras.note: Before settlement. The island was uninhabited when Jacques Pronis claimed it for France in 1642; it was named Île Bourbon in 1649.

eras.polity: French East India Company - Île Bourbon
eras.note: Colonisation began in 1665 with settlers sent by the French East India Company. Censuses of Île Bourbon from 1708 to 1779 (except the general census of 1774) are digitised by the departmental archives; the archives' registers fill gaps in the overseas archives' holdings, notably for slave registers.

eras.polity: French Republic and Empire - La Réunion, then Isle Bonaparte
eras.note: The National Convention renamed the island La Réunion in March 1793 (19 or 23 March by different accounts) and General Decaen renamed it Isle Bonaparte in 1806.
British forces invaded in July 1810 and restored the name Isle Bourbon; the island returned to France under the Treaty of Paris in 1814.

eras.polity: France - Île Bourbon, a slave colony
eras.note: Emancipation registers of 1832 are digitised by the Archives départementales.

The name La Réunion was restored in 1848 and slavery abolished with effect from 20 December 1848. The special registers of 1848 are digitised. Indentured workers (engagés), many from South India, were brought in between 1848 and 1864.
Réunion became an overseas department on 19 March 1946 and an overseas region as well in 1982.

regions.label: Cres and Lošinj, the northern Kvarner islands
regions.sub: Cres, Mali Lošinj, Veli Lošinj, Osor, Beli

eras.note: Cres and Lošinj are described as Venetian until 1797; the start of Venetian rule is dated differently by source (1409 is the date given for neighbouring Rab).
The Treaty of Campo Formio (1797) gave Lošinj to Austria as part of the province of Istria.

eras.polity: French rule, then the Illyrian Provinces
eras.note: Istria is dated to the Napoleonic period 1805-1814, with the Illyrian Provinces from 1809; the islands are described as French after Austria's defeat in 1809.

eras.polity: Austria, then Austria-Hungary: Istria and the Austrian Littoral
eras.note: Austria regained Istria in 1814. Istria lay in the Kingdom of Illyria from 1816 to 1849 and then in the Austrian Littoral (Küstenland), which excluded Trieste.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy: Cres and Lošinj
eras.note: The transfer to Italy is dated 1919 (Saint-Germain) or 12 November 1920 (Treaty of Rapallo, which named Cres, Lošinj and Lastovo) depending on the source. Rab, nearby, was ceded to Yugoslavia in 1921, so neighbouring islands fall under different states. Italy lost Cres and Lošinj after the German and Croatian occupation of 1943 and ceded them by the 1947 peace treaty.

A 1946 state law moved the keeping of parish registers from religious communities to state services, and an order of 13 May 1949 required registers made before 1860 to be delivered to the State Archives in Zagreb. Cres and Lošinj were handed to Yugoslavia in 1947.

regions.label: Rab, Pag and the Zadar archipelago
regions.sub: Rab, Novalja, Ugljan, Pašman, Dugi Otok, Silba

eras.polity: Republic of Venice: Rab, Pag and the Zadar islands
eras.note: Rab submitted to Venice in 1000 and was held by it continuously from 1409. Pag is dated to Venice from 1409, after Louis I sold his Dalmatian claims in 1403. Venetian Dalmatia ended with the fall of the Republic in 1797.

eras.polity: First Austrian rule: Dalmatia administered from Zadar
eras.note: Under the Treaty of Campo Formio the Habsburgs took Dalmatia and ran it from Zadar, keeping most of the Venetian system.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy, then the Illyrian Provinces
eras.note: Dalmatia passed to France at the Peace of Pressburg (1805) and was linked to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and later the Illyrian Provinces.

Austrian forces retook Dalmatia in 1813-14 and the Congress of Vienna created the Kingdom of Dalmatia in 1815, with Zadar as capital; Rab is described as annexed by the Habsburgs in 1815. Islands, mainland coast and Zadar all sat in the one crown land.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: Rab was ceded to Yugoslavia in 1921. Zadar itself became an Italian semi-enclave under the Treaty of Rapallo (12 November 1920), so a town record and an island record of the same family can lie in two different states' archives.

eras.polity: Italian annexation: Governorate of Dalmatia and Province of Fiume
eras.note: From 1941 the islands in front of Zadar belonged to the Governorate of Dalmatia (Province of Zara), and Rab was joined to the Province of Fiume. Fascist Italy ran the Rab concentration camp at Kampor; its memorial dates from 1953.

Badoglio cancelled the Governorate administratively on 19 August 1943; German forces took over and the territory was absorbed into the Independent State of Croatia. Parish registers were kept by religious communities until 1946; the State Archives in Zadar has a branch at Novalja.

regions.label: Labin and eastern Istria
regions.sub: Labin, Barban, Skitača, Sv. Lucija

eras.polity: Patriarchate of Aquileia, with a period under the dukes of Pazin
eras.note: Before registers.

Labin was Venetian from 1420 to 1797. Coastal towns of Istria had been falling to Venice since 1267 while inland districts stayed under Aquileia and then the Habsburgs (the Pazin area from the 14th century), so a parish near Pazin can be Habsburg in the same years.

eras.polity: Austria, after the Treaty of Campo Formio
eras.note: The Venetian parts of Istria passed to the Habsburg monarchy in 1797.
Istria was combined with neighbouring lands in the Illyrian Provinces after 1809.
Istria was part of the Kingdom of Illyria from 1816 to 1849 and of the Austrian Littoral afterwards.

Labin was annexed to Italy in 1918. A miners' strike in March and April 1921 grew into an anti-fascist rebellion, the short-lived Labin Republic. The town passed to Yugoslavia after the 1947 peace treaty.
The coal mine in the centre of Labin closed in 1989.

regions.label: Kastav, Opatija and the Liburnian coast
regions.sub: Opatija, Lovran, Kastav, Klana, Gradin

eras.polity: Lords of Walsee at Kastav; estates of the Patriarchs of Aquileia on the coast
eras.note: Before registers. Kastav passed from the counts of Duino to the Walsee family around 1400; the Kastav Statute is dated 1400 or 1490 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Habsburg lordship of Kastav; Habsburg Istria
eras.note: Kastav and its district came into Habsburg possession in 1465 or 1466 depending on the source. In the Istrian peninsula the Pazin (Mitterburg) area had been Habsburg since the 14th century.
Istria and neighbouring lands were combined in the Illyrian Provinces after 1809.

After a railway branch to Rijeka opened in 1873, Opatija (Abbazia) grew as a resort and was declared the first climatic seaside resort on the Austrian Riviera in 1889. Istria formed the Austrian Littoral after 1849.
The Treaty of Rapallo (12 November 1920) gave Italy Istria and the lands north of it, and Opatija was assigned to Italy in 1920. Fiume stayed a separate free state until Italy annexed it in 1924.

Most of Istria went to Yugoslavia under the peace treaty of 10 February 1947; Zone B of the Free Territory of Trieste was under Yugoslav administration until 1954 and the 1975 Treaty of Osimo formalised the division. Most of Opatija's Italian-speaking population emigrated.
The Croatia-Slovenia line is an international boundary across former Istria, and some border points remain disputed. Opatija stands on the Istrian peninsula but is not in Istria County.

regions.label: Gorski Kotar: Brod na Kupi and Kuželj
regions.sub: Brod na Kupi, Kuželj, Delnice, Vrbovsko

eras.note: Before registers. The Frankopan family ruled much of the region from the 12th century; Ottoman incursions in the 15th century brought new settlement, and Orthodox Vlach refugees settled along the border from the late 16th century. The Zrinski controlled the iron mines around Čabar in the 17th century.

eras.polity: Habsburg Croatia: estates divided after the Zrinski-Frankopan plot
eras.note: Petar Zrinski and Fran Krsto Frankopan were executed on 30 April 1671 and the emperor confiscated their lands, which were given to other nobles. The Karolina road (1732) between Karlovac and Bakar began the most intense period of settlement.
By decree of 1777 Maria Theresa incorporated the whole region into the county of Severin.
The French built the Lujziana road between Karlovac and Rijeka (1803-1809), and Delnice became the region's most developed centre.
The first railway was built in 1873. In 1886 the whole region was placed under Rijeka county.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: In the Second World War the region was divided between Italy and the Independent State of Croatia.

regions.label: Hvar and Vis, the outer Adriatic islands
regions.sub: Hvar, Vis, Komiža

eras.polity: Republic of Venice: Hvar and Vis
eras.note: Hvar passed to Hungary in 1358 and was held briefly by Bosnia in 1390 before Venice became its long-term owner in 1409. The Hvar Rebellion belongs to the 16th century. Vis was Venetian until 1797.

eras.polity: Austria, after the Treaty of Campo Formio
eras.note: The Habsburg monarchy annexed the islands in 1797 when the Venetian Republic fell.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy, then the Illyrian Provinces
eras.note: Vis is described as part of Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy from 1805 and the Illyrian Provinces from 1809; French forces seized Hvar in 1806.

eras.polity: British naval occupation: Vis from 1811, Hvar from 1813
eras.note: The Royal Navy secured Vis after the Battle of Lissa on 13 March 1811, and British marines and sailors took Hvar from the French in 1813. The Congress of Vienna gave the islands to Austria in 1815.
The Austrian fleet under Tegetthoff defeated a larger Italian fleet north of Vis in the Battle of Vis on 20 July 1866.

Italian forces occupied Hvar and Vis from 1918 to 1921. In 1941-43 Vis was part of the Italian province of Spalato, while Hvar was occupied but not formally annexed. Vis was Tito's headquarters in 1944, and the Yugoslav army kept it as a closed naval base until 1989.

regions.label: The Republic of Ragusa: Dubrovnik, Konavle, Mljet and Lastovo
regions.sub: Dubrovnik, Cavtat, Lopud, Koločep, Mljet, Lastovo

eras.note: Venice gave up its Dalmatian claims in the Treaty of Zadar (1358). Ragusa took in the Primorje in 1399 and Konavle in 1419-26, and held Pelješac, Mljet, Lastovo (which joined in 1252) and the smaller islands. It paid tribute to the Ottoman sultan from 1458 and accepted Habsburg sovereignty in 1684 while still recognising the Ottomans.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Italy, then the Illyrian Provinces
eras.note: Marshal Marmont abolished the republic in 1808 and merged it into the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy; in 1810 it became part of the Illyrian Provinces. British forces captured Lastovo in January-February 1813, and a popular uprising backed by the British navy removed the French garrison from Ragusa in early 1814.

eras.polity: Austria: Kingdom of Dalmatia, Dubrovnik county
eras.note: Austrian troops took control in 1814 and the Congress of Vienna placed the former republic in the Kingdom of Dalmatia; Lastovo became part of Dubrovnik county in 1815. Italian troops took possession of Lastovo on 11 November 1918.
The Treaty of Rapallo (12 November 1920) gave Lastovo to Italy, which held it until the Partisans took the island on 8 September 1943, while Dubrovnik and Konavle were in Yugoslavia.
Lastovo became part of the People's Republic of Croatia in 1945, and foreign tourists were barred from it until 1988.

Yugoslav Army forces occupied Konavle from October 1991 to May 1992, and the last army bases on Lastovo closed in July 1992. The State Archives in Dubrovnik has branches at Metković and Žrnovo (Korčula).

regions.label: Boka Kotorska and Budva
regions.sub: Kotor, Herceg Novi, Tivat, Budva

eras.note: Budva and the Kotor area were Venetian from 1420 to 1797. Herceg Novi was not: it was Ottoman from 1481 or 1482 to 1687, with a Spanish interval in 1538-39, and Venetian from 1687.

eras.polity: Austria, after the Treaty of Campo Formio
eras.note: The bay came under the Habsburgs in 1797; the date for Herceg Novi is given as 1797 or 24 August 1798 within the same source.

eras.polity: Russian occupation, French Kingdom of Italy and Illyrian Provinces, Montenegrin-held bay
eras.note: Herceg Novi was Russian from 28 February 1806 to 12 August 1807, then French, and was annexed to the Illyrian Provinces on 14 October 1809. In 1813 Montenegrin forces took the bay and a government at Dobrota ran it from 11 September 1813 to 10 June 1814.

Montenegro handed the bay to Austria on 11 June 1814, and the 1815 Congress of Vienna placed it in the Kingdom of Dalmatia, which was extended to Sutomore. Budva was historically counted as part of Boka.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: The Serbian army entered the bay on 7 November 1918. In 1922 the bay was reorganised into smaller districts under the Oblast of Cetinje, and in 1929 it joined the Zeta Banovina.
Italy annexed Kotor, Perast and Herceg Novi in 1941 as the Province of Cattaro; Yugoslav Partisans retook Herceg Novi on 10 September 1943.
Montenegro became one of Yugoslavia's six republics in 1945 and in April 1992 voted to join Serbia in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.
Independence was declared on 3 June 2006 after the referendum of 21 May.

regions.label: Cetinje, Podgorica and the Zeta plain, Bar and Ulcinj
regions.sub: Cetinje, Podgorica, Nikšić, Bar, Ulcinj, Kolašin

eras.note: The prince-bishopric dates from 1516, as an Ottoman vassal until 1697 and independent from 1697 under the Petrović-Njegoš family; the Brda, including the Bjelopavlići and Piperi, joined in 1796. Podgorica, Nikšić, Bar and Ulcinj lay outside it under the Ottomans (Ulcinj from 1571 after Venetian rule).

On 13 March 1852 Prince-Bishop Danilo II gave up his church office and became Prince Danilo I, secularising the state. Bar, Podgorica, Spuž and Žabljak were still Ottoman, in the Vilayet of Scutari formed in 1867.

eras.polity: Principality, from 28 August 1910 the Kingdom of Montenegro
eras.note: The 1878 settlement raised Montenegro's area from 4,405 to 9,475 km2 and added Nikšić, Kolašin, Spuž, Podgorica, Žabljak and Bar. Ulcinj followed after the naval demonstration of 1880 (some sources date its transfer to 1878 or 1881). The Central Powers occupied Montenegro after the 1916 invasion.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: The Podgorica Assembly voted for union with Serbia, effective 1 December 1918. In 1922 the area became the Zeta region with Cetinje as its administrative seat, and in 1929 the Zeta Banovina.

eras.polity: Italian occupation and puppet Kingdom of Montenegro, German occupation from 1943
eras.note: Italy occupied Montenegro in 1941 and Germany replaced it in 1943. Ulcinj was under Albanian administration from 1941 to 1944. Partisans entered Podgorica on 19 December 1944.
Podgorica was renamed Titograd in 1947 and replaced Cetinje as the capital.

regions.label: Northern Montenegro: Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane and Plav
regions.sub: Pljevlja, Žabljak, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Plav, Rožaje

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Sanjak of Novi Pazar and neighbouring districts
eras.note: The Sanjak of Novi Pazar was created in 1865 and the Sanjak of Pljevlja split from it in 1880. Austria-Hungary could station garrisons there from the 1878 Congress of Berlin until 1908, when they were withdrawn. The line between the land Montenegro gained in 1878 and the part it took in 1912-13 runs through this area, so the pre-1912 sovereign has to be checked district by district.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Montenegro: its share of the Sanjak
eras.note: After the First Balkan War the Treaty of London (1913) divided the sanjak: Pljevlja went to Montenegro and Sjenica and Novi Pazar to Serbia. The Central Powers occupied Montenegro after the 1916 invasion.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, then Yugoslavia
eras.note: The Podgorica Assembly's union with Serbia took effect on 1 December 1918, and a royalist rising followed in January 1919.
Italy occupied Montenegro in 1941; fighting among Chetniks, Partisans and others followed until Germany replaced Italy in 1943.
Montenegro was a constituent republic from 1945 to 1992.

regions.label: Northern Albania: Shkodër, Lezhë, Kukës and Dibër
regions.sub: Shkodër, Lezhë, Kukës, Peshkopi

eras.note: The Ottomans took Shkodër from Venice in 1479 after a siege, and the city became the centre of the Sanjak of Scutari. Control was strongest in towns and valleys and weak in the mountains, where highlanders followed customary law.

eras.polity: Pashalik of Scutari under the Bushati family
eras.note: From 1757 to 1831 the Bushati family ran a semi-autonomous pashalik centred on Shkodër.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Vilayet of Scutari from 1867
eras.note: In 1867 the Sanjak of Scutari was merged with the Sanjak of Skopje as the Vilayet of Scutari (sanjaks Scutari, Prizren and Dibra); in 1877 Prizren went to the Kosovo Vilayet and Dibra to the Monastir Vilayet. Ottoman population (nüfus) registers date from the 1830s.

Independence was declared at Vlorë on 28 November 1912 and the powers recognised a neutral principality on 29 July 1913; the Balkan League states occupied Albania soon after the declaration. The 1923 census, the first official one, was a population count only.

eras.polity: Italian invasion (7 April 1939) and personal union under Victor Emmanuel III
eras.note: The Albanian Kingdom of this period was a puppet state of Fascist Italy.

eras.polity: German occupation after the Italian capitulation, then the provisional government
eras.note: Germany occupied Albania after Italy's capitulation of 8 September 1943, until the end of the war.

eras.polity: People's Republic, from 1976 People's Socialist Republic of Albania
eras.note: The 1945 census was meant to found the civil population registry. In 1967 the state declared itself atheist.
The Republic of Albania was proclaimed on 29 April 1991.

regions.label: Central Albania: Durrës, Tirana, Elbasan, Berat and Fier
regions.sub: Durrës, Tirana, Elbasan, Berat, Fier

eras.polity: Ottoman Sanjak of Albania and its successors
eras.note: The Ottomans established the Sanjak of Albania in 1415, with Gjirokastër as its centre from 1419. Durrës, held by Venice, fell to the Ottomans in 1501.

eras.polity: Ottoman vilayets of Janina (Berat), Scutari (Durrës) and Monastir (Elbasan)
eras.note: Berat belonged to the Vilayet of Janina, created in 1867. Durrës became its own sanjak within the Vilayet of Scutari in 1877. Elbasan, Gramsh and Peqin formed the Sanjak of Elbasan in the Vilayet of Monastir (1874-1912).
The northern part of the Vilayet of Janina, including Berat, went to Albania in 1913 under the Treaty of Bucharest, and the southern part, including Ioannina, to Greece.

eras.polity: German occupation, then the provisional government
People's Republic, from 1976 People's Socialist Republic of Albania
eras.note: The state existed from 11 January 1946 to 29 April 1991.

regions.label: Southern Albania: Vlorë, Gjirokastër, Sarandë and Korçë
regions.sub: Vlorë, Gjirokastër, Sarandë, Korçë

eras.polity: Ottoman Sanjak of Albania, centred on Gjirokastër
eras.note: Gjirokastër became the administrative centre of the Sanjak of Albania in 1419.

eras.polity: Ottoman vilayets of Janina (Gjirokastër, Berat) and Monastir (Korçë)
eras.note: The Vilayet of Janina, created in 1867, held the Ergiri (Gjirokastër) and Berat sanjaks. Korçë (Görice), with Pogradec and Ersekë, lay in the Sanjak of Görice in the Vilayet of Monastir until 1912.

eras.polity: Albanian independence declared at Vlorë; Greek army in the south
eras.note: The Greek army took the region in the First Balkan War. The Protocol of Florence assigned it to Albania, local Greeks rejected this, and an Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus was declared at Gjirokastër on 28 February 1914. The Protocol of Corfu (17 May 1914) recognised autonomy under nominal Albanian sovereignty but was never fully implemented.

eras.polity: Greek, Italian and French zones: Greek annexation (1916) and the French-run Korçë
eras.note: Greek forces reoccupied the area in October 1914 and Greece formally annexed it in 1916; Italian forces occupied much of it in September 1916. French troops entered Korçë on 29 November 1916 and stayed until 15 June 1920. The region was ceded to Albania in 1921.
Albania's borders were fixed in 1925, and Greece dropped its claims.

eras.polity: German occupation, then the provisional government
People's Republic, from 1976 People's Socialist Republic of Albania

regions.label: Oltenia (Little Wallachia)
regions.sub: Craiova, Târgu Jiu, Râmnicu Vâlcea, Slatina, Drobeta-Turnu Severin

eras.polity: Banate of Severin (Hungary) in the west; the Wallachian principality east of it
eras.note: Before registers. Hungary formed the Banate of Severin in the western part in 1233; by about 1330 the rule of Basarab I covered both sides of the Olt.

eras.polity: Principality of Wallachia under Ottoman suzerainty
eras.note: Wallachia first accepted Ottoman suzerainty in 1417. Târgoviște was the capital from 1418 to 1659 and Bucharest after.

eras.polity: Habsburg monarchy — the Banat of Craiova (Oltenia)
eras.note: The Treaty of Passarowitz (1718) gave Oltenia to the Habsburgs, who held it de facto from 1716, as the Banat of Craiova. It went back to Wallachia in 1739 (Treaty of Belgrade); one account dates the return 1737.

eras.polity: Principality of Wallachia — Phanariot princes to 1821, Russian protectorate from 1829
eras.note: The residence of the Bans of Oltenia moved from Craiova to Bucharest in 1761 and stayed there until 1832. Tudor Vladimirescu's rising of 1821 was centred on Oltenia and Gorj.

Civil status registers on the French model began in 1865, moving registration from parishes to town-hall offices; registers more than 100 years old are normally deposited in the county archive. A law of 1925 organised the country into 71 counties.

regions.label: Muntenia — Bucharest and eastern Wallachia
regions.sub: Bucharest, Ploiești, Buzău, Brăila, Giurgiu, Târgoviște

eras.note: Before registers. Basarab I's victory at Posada led to a principality covering both sides of the Olt by about 1330.

eras.polity: Principality of Wallachia under Ottoman suzerainty — Phanariot princes 1715–1821
eras.note: Târgoviște was the capital from 1418 to 1659, Bucharest after. Brăila, Giurgiu and Turnu Măgurele were held by the Ottomans, with brief interruptions, until the Treaty of Adrianople (1829) returned them to Wallachia.

eras.polity: Wallachia under Russian military rule — a de facto protectorate 1829–1854
eras.note: The Organic Regulation (Regulamentul Organic) dates from 1834–1835.
Civil status registers began in 1865. The 1925 law created 71 counties; a reform of 1938 replaced them with ten ținuturi that did not last, so a county named in a document may not be the present one.

regions.label: Moldavia west of the Prut — Iași, Bacău, Botoșani
regions.sub: Iași, Botoșani, Piatra Neamț, Bacău, Vaslui, Focșani, Galați

eras.polity: Principality of Moldavia (Bogdan I took control in 1359)
eras.note: Before registers. The capital was Suceava from 1388 to 1564 and Iași after.

eras.polity: Principality of Moldavia under Ottoman suzerainty (dated from 1498, with interruptions)
Principality of Moldavia — Phanariot princes from 1711
eras.note: Bukovina went to the Habsburgs in 1775 (Convention of Pera). In 1812 the eastern half, Bessarabia, was ceded to Russia; this region is the western half that remained Moldavian, and Bessarabia is a separate record region.

eras.polity: Moldavia (west of the Prut) — Russian protectorate 1829–1856
eras.note: The Iași archives were constituted on 1 January 1832; they hold parish-drafted civil-status registers for 1832–1865, of which only a small part has been inventoried.

eras.polity: United Principalities (union 1859, Cuza elected at Iași), Romania (1866), Kingdom (1881)
eras.note: Civil registers from 1865: those of Iași county are in the Iași archives; the rest of Moldavia is in the county-centre archives (Suceava, Botoșani, Piatra Neamț, Bacău, Vaslui, Galați, Focșani). Registers are consulted in the reading room, not online.
Civil-status documents less than 100 years old are not open to public research.

regions.label: Dobruja — Constanța, Tulcea, Silistra, Dobrich
regions.sub: Constanța, Tulcea, Mangalia, Silistra, Dobrich, Balchik

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — Silistra sanjak, then Silistra Eyalet; in the Vilayet of the Danube from 1864
eras.note: The region was annexed by the Ottomans in 1420. Crimean Tatars settled here from 1512–1514, and an estimated 200,000 more arrived between 1770 and 1784; at the start of the 1877–1878 war most of the population was Tatar and Turkish.

eras.polity: Northern Dobruja in Romania; Southern Dobruja in the Principality of Bulgaria
eras.note: After the war of 1877–1878 Northern Dobruja went to Romania (a strip around Mangalia included); Silistra stayed Bulgarian. The Bulgarian regional state archives hold civil registers for 1893–1912.
The Saint Petersburg Conference of May 1913 awarded Silistra and a 3 km radius to Romania; the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) gave Romania all of Southern Dobruja (about 286,000 people).

eras.polity: Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria (Treaty of Craiova, September 1940); Northern Dobruja in Romania
eras.note: Romanians were forced out of the south and the Bulgarian minority in the north was expelled, in a population exchange. The Paris Peace Treaties of 1947 reaffirmed the 1940 border.

eras.polity: Romanian People's Republic in the north; People's Republic of Bulgaria in the south (from 15 September 1946)
Romania (north); Republic of Bulgaria (south, renamed 15 November 1990)

regions.label: Banat Mountains — Caraș-Severin
regions.sub: Reșița, Caransebeș, Oravița, Bocșa

eras.note: The Eyalet of Temeşvar existed from 1552 to 1716; the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) recognised Ottoman sovereignty over the region with the fortress of Temeşvar.

eras.polity: Habsburg monarchy — the Banat of Temeswar
eras.note: Prince Eugene conquered the Banat in 1716–1718 and the Banat of Temeswar was established on 12 July 1718. In 1751 civil administration was introduced in the north and the Banatian Military Frontier was created in the south, so check whether a parish lay under the civil Banat or the Frontier.
The Banat province was abolished on 6 June 1778 and incorporated into Hungary on 23 April 1779, divided into the Torontál, Temes and Krassó counties.

eras.polity: Voivodeship of Serbia and Banat of Temeschwar
eras.note: The Banat was revived as a Habsburg crown land in 1849. In 1860 the arrangement was abolished and the counties were merged back into Hungary.
The southern part of the Banat stayed in the Military Frontier until 1873.
The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) assigned Transylvania, the Banat and Partium to Romania; a border exchange with the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes followed in 1923.

regions.label: Székely Land — Covasna (Háromszék)
regions.sub: Sfântu Gheorghe, Târgu Secuiesc, Háromszék

eras.polity: Székely seat of Háromszék (Sepsi, Kézdi and Orbai seats merged), in Hungary and the Principality of Transylvania
eras.note: The Székelys probably settled in Transylvania in the twelfth century. The date of the merger into Háromszék is uncertain.

eras.polity: Principality of Transylvania under Habsburg rule
eras.note: Transylvania came under Habsburg rule in the late seventeenth century, with imperial governors.
Transylvania was reunited with Hungary in 1867. A reform of 1876 abolished the autonomy of the Székely seats and created Háromszék county (with Udvarhely, Csík and Maros-Torda).

eras.polity: Kingdom of Romania — Northern Transylvania to Hungary 1940–1944
eras.note: The Treaty of Trianon (1920) ceded Transylvania to Romania. The Second Vienna Award of 1940 returned Northern Transylvania, including most Székely areas, to Hungary; the armistice of 12 September 1944 voided it and the Paris Peace Treaties (1947) confirmed the return to Romania.

eras.polity: Romanian People's Republic — Magyar Autonomous Region 1952–1968
eras.note: The Magyar Autonomous Region was created in 1952, renamed the Mureș-Magyar Autonomous Region in 1960 and abolished in 1968, when the county system returned.

regions.label: Szatmár — Satu Mare
regions.sub: Satu Mare, Negrești-Oaș, Sighetu Marmației

eras.note: Before registers. The county was formed in the eleventh century, centred on Szatmárnémeti (Satu Mare).

eras.polity: Eastern Hungarian Kingdom, then Hungarian and Transylvanian administration by turns
eras.note: The county was part of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom in 1526–1570 and then changed between Hungarian and Transylvanian administration several times up to 1645.
In 1876 part of the former Kővár (Chioar) district was added to the county.
The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) assigned most of the county to Romania.

eras.polity: Hungary — Szatmár county enlarged by the Second Vienna Award
eras.note: After the Second Vienna Award in 1940 the county was expanded with its Romanian part.

eras.polity: Romania — administration restored 1945; People's Republic from 30 December 1947
eras.note: The Romanian part returned to Romania after the Second World War.

regions.label: Danubian Bulgaria — Vidin, Pleven, Ruse, Veliko Tarnovo, Varna
regions.sub: Vidin, Pleven, Ruse, Veliko Tarnovo, Gabrovo, Varna

eras.note: The Ottoman conquest of 1396 ended the Second Bulgarian Empire. The Bulgarian Exarchate was created by firman on 12 March 1870 and declared schismatic by the Patriarchate of Constantinople in September 1872, so the church a family belonged to is the first thing to establish.

eras.polity: Principality of Bulgaria, tributary to the Ottoman Empire (Treaty of Berlin, 13 July 1878)
eras.note: The Tarnovo Constitution was adopted on 28 April 1879. The regional state archives hold civil registers for 1893–1912, church registers and censuses.

eras.polity: Kingdom (Tsardom) of Bulgaria — independence declared 5 October 1908
eras.note: Bulgaria signed the Tripartite Pact and joined the Axis on 1 March 1941.
The Fatherland Front took power in a communist-led coup on 9 September 1944; the monarchy was abolished by plebiscite in 1946.

eras.polity: Republic of Bulgaria (renamed 15 November 1990; constitution of 12 July 1991)

regions.label: Sofia, Kyustendil and Pirin Macedonia
regions.sub: Sofia, Pernik, Kyustendil, Blagoevgrad, Bansko

eras.note: The Bulgarian Exarchate's bishoprics included Sofia, Kyustendil and Nevrokop (the Pirin diocese); a diocese seat is not a civil district.

eras.polity: Principality of Bulgaria (Sofia area); Pirin Macedonia still Ottoman
eras.note: Sofia was the capital of the Principality from 1878. Pirin Macedonia (Blagoevgrad) was assigned to Bulgaria only after the Balkan Wars.

eras.polity: Kingdom (Tsardom) of Bulgaria — Pirin Macedonia added
eras.note: The Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) gave Bulgaria Pirin Macedonia. The Treaty of Neuilly (1919) removed the Exarchate's dioceses in Macedonia and Aegean Thrace.
The regional state archives hold civil registers for 1893–1912.

regions.label: Eastern Rumelia and the Rhodopes — Plovdiv, Stara Zagora, Burgas
regions.sub: Plovdiv, Pazardzhik, Stara Zagora, Sliven, Yambol, Burgas, Haskovo, Smolyan

eras.note: Ottoman rule dates from the conquest of 1396.

eras.polity: Eastern Rumelia — an autonomous Ottoman province (Treaty of Berlin, 13 July 1878)
eras.note: THE TRAP. The Organic Statute of 14 April 1879 governed Eastern Rumelia until 1885, so for these years the region was not in the Principality of Bulgaria north of the Balkan range.

eras.polity: Principality of Bulgaria — Eastern Rumelia annexed 6 September 1885
eras.note: The Tophane Agreement (24 March 1886) recognised the union under nominal Ottoman suzerainty and returned the Kardzhali canton to the Ottoman Empire. Ferdinand was governor-general of Eastern Rumelia from 1887 to 1908.

eras.polity: Kingdom (Tsardom) of Bulgaria — independence declared 5 October 1908
eras.note: The Treaty of Neuilly (1919) removed the Exarchate's dioceses in Aegean Thrace. The regional state archives hold civil registers for 1893–1912.

regions.label: Macedonia (Greek) — Thessaloniki, Kozani, Florina, Mount Athos
regions.sub: Thessaloniki, Veria, Kozani, Florina, Kastoria, Mount Athos

eras.note: Serres held out until 1383 and Thessaloniki until 1387.
Thessaloniki returned to Ottoman control in 1430 after a Byzantine interval.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — Salonica and Monastir Vilayets
eras.note: Mount Athos kept a degree of autonomy under Ottoman rule. The Macedonian Struggle ran from 1904 to the Young Turk Revolution of 1908.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Greece (gains confirmed by the Treaty of Bucharest, 10 August 1913)
eras.note: Thessaloniki's incorporation was secured by international recognition in November 1913. Greece organised civil registration systematically only from 1925; Athens and Thessaloniki town halls hold older records that are not open to researchers.

eras.polity: German occupation (western and central Macedonia); Bulgarian annexation of the east
eras.note: Germany took western and central Macedonia, including Thessaloniki; Bulgaria occupied and annexed eastern Macedonia.

regions.label: Eastern Macedonia and Western Thrace
regions.sub: Kavala, Drama, Xanthi, Komotini, Alexandroupoli, Thasos

eras.polity: Eastern Macedonia up to Kavala to Greece; Western Thrace to Bulgaria (Treaty of Bucharest, 10 August 1913)
eras.note: Greece gained eastern Macedonia from Bulgaria up to Kavala; Bulgaria received Western Thrace and a stretch of Aegean coast with Dedeagach as its only port.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Greece — Western Thrace annexed by the Treaty of Neuilly (27 November 1919)
eras.note: Systematic civil registration dates from 1925 across Greece.

eras.polity: Bulgarian occupation and annexation of eastern Macedonia
eras.note: Bulgaria occupied and annexed eastern Macedonia during the Axis occupation.

regions.label: Epirus — Ioannina, Arta, Preveza
regions.sub: Ioannina, Arta, Preveza, Igoumenitsa, Parga

eras.note: Ioannina was the seat of the Ioannina Eyalet until 1867.

eras.polity: Ali Pasha's territory centred on Ioannina
eras.note: Ali Pasha ruled from Ioannina from 1788 until he was assassinated in 1822.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire (Ioannina); the Arta district in Greece from 1881
eras.note: The Convention of Constantinople (2 July 1881) added Thessaly and the Arta region to Greece. Ioannina was incorporated into Greece on 21 February 1913 after the Battle of Bizani.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Greece — Northern Epirus to Albania
eras.note: The Treaty of Florence (17 December 1913) assigned Northern Epirus to Albania, so historic Epirus is divided by the Greek–Albanian border. Greek civil registration is systematic only from 1925.
On 25 March 1944, 1,870 of Ioannina's Jews were deported; almost all were murdered at Auschwitz-Birkenau.

regions.label: Thessaly — Larissa, Volos, Trikala
regions.sub: Larissa, Volos, Trikala, Karditsa, Skiathos

eras.note: Larissa fell to the Ottomans about 1392–1393. The population fell to about 200,000 by 1820 after heavy taxation and a plague in 1813.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Greece (Convention of Constantinople, 2 July 1881); the Elassona area Ottoman until 1912
eras.note: Ottoman forces briefly captured parts of Thessaly in the war of 1897.
The Muslim population was sent to Turkey under the 1923 exchange. Systematic civil registration dates from 1925.

regions.label: Attica and Central Greece — Athens, Thebes, Lamia, Euboea
regions.sub: Athens, Piraeus, Thebes, Chalcis, Lamia, Livadeia

eras.note: Athens was captured from its Latin overlord in 1458; the fall of the Despotate of the Morea in 1460 completed the conquest of mainland Greece.

eras.polity: Greek revolution (from 25 March 1821) and the new Greek state
eras.note: The protocol of 1830 set the northern border on the Acheloos and Spercheios rivers and put Euboea and the Sporades inside Greece; the settlement of 1832 moved it to the Arta–Volos line.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Greece (Convention of 11 May 1832; Otto the first king)

eras.note: Civil registration was organised systematically only from 1925. Athens town hall holds older records that are not open to researchers.

regions.label: Peloponnese and Western Greece — Patras, Corinth, Sparta, Messolonghi
regions.sub: Patras, Corinth, Nafplio, Tripoli, Kalamata, Messolonghi

eras.note: The Despotate of the Morea fell to the Ottomans in 1460.

Francesco Morosini landed in 1685 and the Morea was formally established as a Venetian territory in 1688. Venetian registers record 97,118 inhabitants in 1691 and 176,844 in 1700; the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) left the Morea to Venice.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — the Morea reconquered in 1715
eras.note: The Ottomans reconquered the Morea between June and September 1715.

eras.polity: Greek revolution (from 25 March 1821, proclaimed by Bishop Germanos of Patras)

eras.note: Civil registration was organised systematically only from 1925.

regions.label: Ionian Islands — Corfu, Lefkada, Kefalonia, Zakynthos
regions.sub: Corfu, Lefkada, Kefalonia, Zakynthos, Paxos, Ithaca

eras.note: Venetian rule ended with the fall of the Republic in 1797. Lefkada (Santa Maura) was seized from the Ottomans in 1684.
French rule ended when Russo-Ottoman forces took Corfu on 4 March 1799.

eras.polity: Septinsular Republic under Ottoman suzerainty and Russian protection (established 1800)
eras.note: The Septinsular Republic was founded under the Treaty of Constantinople in 1800, with Corfu as its capital.

eras.polity: French Empire (ceded by the Treaty of Tilsit, 20 August 1807)
eras.note: The French annexed the islands on 1 September 1807.

eras.polity: British protectorate — United States of the Ionian Islands (established 9 November 1815)
eras.note: Corfu's vital records start in 1841 and are held by the General State Archives of Corfu; registry-office archives were also given to the General State Archives in Kefalonia and Lefkada.
The sources give different days in 1864 for the union with Greece.
Systematic civil registration across Greece dates from 1925.

regions.label: Crete
regions.sub: Heraklion, Chania, Rethymno, Agios Nikolaos, Sitia

eras.note: The last Venetian outpost, Spinalonga, fell in 1718, after Candia in 1669.

eras.polity: Egyptian administration under Muhammad Ali (Convention of Kütahya, 1833)
eras.note: Direct Ottoman rule was restored by the Convention of London on 3 July 1840.
The Pact of Halepa was adopted in 1878.
Prince George was replaced by Alexandros Zaimis in 1906. Cretan deputies declared union with Greece in 1908; the Treaty of London (1913) recognised it.
The exchange of populations took place in 1923 under the Treaty of Lausanne. Systematic civil registration dates from 1925.

regions.label: Aegean islands — Cyclades, Dodecanese, Lesbos, Chios, Samos
regions.sub: Syros, Naxos, Rhodes, Kos, Lesbos, Chios, Samos

eras.polity: Duchy of the Archipelago in the Cyclades; Knights Hospitaller in the Dodecanese
eras.note: Most inhabitants of the Cyclades stayed Greek Orthodox under Latin lords, and the Latin Church restricted Orthodox clergy. The Knights held Rhodes until 1522.
Rhodes fell in 1522. The Duchy of the Archipelago became an Ottoman tributary in 1537, its last duke was deposed in 1566 and it was annexed in 1579; Tinos stayed Venetian until 1714–1715.

eras.polity: Cyclades in the Kingdom of Greece; Dodecanese, Lesbos and Chios Ottoman; Samos an autonomous principality (1834–1912)
eras.note: The protocol of 1829 placed the Cyclades inside the new Greek state. The Principality of Samos was a tributary state under a Christian prince nominated by the Ottoman government.

eras.polity: Greece (Protocol of Florence, 13 February 1914); Dodecanese Italian from 1912
eras.note: Italy occupied most of the Dodecanese in 1912 (Kastellorizo in 1921). Samos declared union with Greece in November 1912, with the official union dated 2 March 1913 in one account. Registry-office archives of Samos have been given to the General State Archives there.

eras.polity: Greece — Dodecanese united by the 1947 treaty with Italy
eras.note: A German garrison surrendered to the British on Rhodes on 8 May 1945, and the islands were under British administration until the union.

regions.label: Skopje, Kumanovo and Polog
regions.sub: Skopje, Kumanovo, Tetovo, Gostivar, Kriva Palanka, Kratovo

eras.note: The region was conquered by the Ottoman army at the end of the fourteenth century.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — Manastir, Kosovo and Salonica Vilayets
eras.note: The Rumelia Eyalet was abolished in 1867. The Bulgarian Exarchate (firman of 12 March 1870) had bishoprics at Skopje and Veles.
Serbia captured the region in the First Balkan War, and the Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) gave it central Vardar Macedonia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia) — South Serbia, then the Vardar Banovina
eras.note: The area was part of 'South Serbia' in 1919–1922 and of the Vardar Banovina from 1929.

eras.polity: Bulgarian occupation; the Albanian-populated west annexed by Italian-ruled Albania
eras.note: Bulgaria occupied the remainder of the Vardar Banovina, while Italian-ruled Albania annexed the Albanian-populated western regions.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia — People's Republic (1946) then Socialist Republic (1963) of Macedonia
eras.note: Democratic Federal Macedonia was proclaimed in August 1944.

eras.polity: Republic of Macedonia, North Macedonia since 2019
eras.note: Independence was voted in a referendum on 8 September 1991. The country was renamed North Macedonia under the Prespa Agreement (June 2018), in force 12 February 2019.

regions.label: Pelagonia, Ohrid and Debar
regions.sub: Bitola, Prilep, Ohrid, Struga, Kichevo, Debar, Krushevo

eras.note: The region was conquered by the Ottomans at the end of the fourteenth century.
The Kruševo Republic was proclaimed in 1903 by rebels of the Ilinden–Preobrazhenie Uprising. The Bulgarian Exarchate had bishoprics at Ohrid, Debar and Bitola.
The Treaty of Bucharest (10 August 1913) gave Serbia Ohrid and Monastir (Bitola), which Bulgaria had wanted.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia) — Vardar Banovina from 1929
Bulgarian occupation; the Albanian-populated west annexed by Italian-ruled Albania
eras.note: Italian-ruled Albania annexed the Albanian-populated western regions, so records for 1941–1944 in the west may be Albanian.

regions.label: Veles, Štip, Strumica and Gevgelija
regions.sub: Veles, Štip, Kočani, Strumica, Kavadarci, Gevgelija

eras.note: The region was conquered by the Ottomans at the end of the fourteenth century.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire — Salonica, Manastir and Kosovo Vilayets
eras.note: The Bulgarian Exarchate had bishoprics at Veles and Strumica.
Strumica was part of Bulgaria from 1912 to 1919; the Treaty of Bucharest (1913) had given Bulgaria Pirin Macedonia including Strumica.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia) — Vardar Banovina from 1929

regions.label: Thrace, Istanbul and the Marmara
regions.sub: Istanbul, Edirne, Bursa, İzmit (Kocaeli), Çanakkale, Balıkesir

eras.polity: Byzantine Thrace and Marmara; the Karasi beylik at Balıkesir
eras.note: Before registers. The Karasi beylik, based at Balıkesir, is dated 1296-1357, and the Byzantine Empire still held Constantinople until 1453.

eras.polity: Ottoman beylik and sultanate - capitals at Bursa and Edirne
eras.note: The Ottomans held Çimpe Castle from 1352, their first land in Europe, began advancing into Rumelia in 1354 and annexed Karasi, whose end is dated 1357. Edirne (Adrianople) was the capital before Constantinople.
Constantinople fell on 29 May 1453 and replaced Adrianople as the Ottoman capital. Provinces were eyalets until the Vilayet Law of 1867 (the Danube Vilayet of 1864 was the trial).

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - vilayets, then the Balkan Wars
eras.note: Ottoman population registration (nüfus) is dated from 1837 in one guide. For Eastern Thrace just before the Balkan Wars there are two separate counts: the Ottoman official statistics of 1910 and the Ecumenical Patriarchate's own figures of 1912.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Eastern Thrace on the 1913 frontier; Constantinople under Allied occupation
eras.note: The Treaty of Constantinople of 1913 set the present Thracian border, which the Treaty of Lausanne confirmed in 1923. Allied forces occupied Constantinople after the Armistice of Mudros (30 October 1918).

The Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923. The Greek-Turkish exchange of 1923-24 exempted the Greeks of Istanbul and of Imbros (Gökçeada) and Tenedos (Bozcaada). Surnames became compulsory under the Surname Law of 21 June 1934, in force from 1 January 1935; detailed vital records are dated from 1925 or 1926 depending on the source.

regions.label: Aegean Turkey - İzmir, Aydın, Muğla and Antalya
regions.sub: İzmir, Manisa, Aydın, Denizli, Muğla, Antalya, Isparta

eras.polity: Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, then the Aegean beyliks
eras.note: Before registers. After the Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 local beys declared themselves sovereign: the Aydınids (Birgi), Menteşe (Milas), Saruhan (Manisa), Germiyan (Kütahya) and Teke (Antalya, later Korkuteli). The Aydınid beylik is dated 1300-1425.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - eyalets of western Anatolia
eras.note: After the Ottoman defeat at Ankara in 1402, Mehmed I and Murad II reincorporated most of the beyliks within about 25 years. Provincial government ran through eyalets until the vilayet reform of the 1860s.
The vilayet system, introduced by the Vilayet Law of 1867, was not fully applied until 1884; the hierarchy below the vilayet ran sanjak, kaza, nahiye and village.

eras.polity: Greek occupation of Smyrna and western Anatolia
eras.note: Twenty thousand Greek soldiers landed at Smyrna (İzmir) on 15 May 1919, and in the summer of 1920 the zone of occupation was extended over all of western and most of north-western Anatolia. The war ended on 14 October 1922 with the Armistice of Mudanya after the Turkish counter-attack of August 1922.

eras.polity: Turkey - Ankara government, then the Republic from 1923
eras.note: The Convention on the exchange of populations was signed at Lausanne on 30 January 1923 and the compulsory exchange began on 1 May 1923; most Greeks had already left Anatolia in 1922. About 1,221,489 Greek Orthodox people left Turkey; property left behind was to be listed for reimbursement, with a commission set up to handle movable and immovable property.

regions.label: Cilicia and Hatay - Adana, Mersin, Antakya, Maraş
regions.sub: Adana, Mersin, Tarsus, Antakya (Hatay), Kahramanmaraş, Osmaniye

eras.polity: Armenian Principality and Kingdom of Cilicia
eras.note: Ruben I founded the principality in 1080; Levon II was crowned king at Tarsus on 6 January 1198 and the capital moved from Tarsus to Sis (Kozan). The kingdom ended when the Mamluks took Sis on 13 April 1375.

eras.polity: Ramadan beylik at Adana and Dulkadir beylik at Elbistan and Maraş
eras.note: The Ramadan beylik was based at Adana (dated 1352-1608) and the Dulkadir beylik at Elbistan, later Maraş (dated 1348-1522). Selim I took their territory in 1515, so the end dates are contested.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Adana and the Aleppo province
eras.note: Ottoman rule in Cilicia dates from the 16th century. Syria was first one province centred on Damascus; Aleppo was split off in 1534 and Adana later appears as a province of its own.
Provinces were reorganised as vilayets under the law of 1867, each divided into sanjaks, kazas and nahiyes.

French troops landed at Mersin on 17 November 1918 and took Antep, Maraş and Urfa from the British at the end of 1919. The Battle of Maraş ran from 20 January to 10 February 1920; the Treaty of Ankara was signed on 20 October 1921 and the French left Cilicia between 3 and 7 January 1922.

eras.polity: Turkey - Cilicia; Hatay still under the French mandate for Syria
eras.note: The Sanjak of Alexandretta (Antakya, Hatay) stayed under the French mandate for Syria. Hatay State existed from 2 September 1938 to 29 June 1939, and Turkey created Hatay Province in July 1939; many Arabs and Armenians then left for Syria.

Hatay's records before July 1939 date from the French mandate period and are separate from Turkey's. The 1936 population of the sanjak was about 220,000, with Turks the largest single group at 39% but Arabic speakers collectively more numerous.

regions.label: Central Anatolia - Ankara, Konya and Kayseri
regions.sub: Ankara, Konya, Kayseri, Eskişehir, Aksaray, Niğde

eras.polity: Seljuk Sultanate of Rum - capital Konya
eras.note: Before registers. The sultanate (dated 1077-1307 or 1308) had Nicaea as capital to 1097 and Konya after; after Köse Dağ in 1243 it was a Mongol, then Ilkhanid, vassal.

The Karaman beylik (Larende, Konya area) is dated 1250-1487 and the Eretna beylik (Sivas, later Kayseri) 1335-1390. The beylik ended with Mehmed II's conquest of its lands; 1487 is its given end date.
Süleyman's campaign of 1534 more or less completed the unification of the territory of present-day Turkey; provinces were eyalets until the Vilayet Law of 1867.
Ottoman population registration (nüfus) is dated from 1837 in one guide.

eras.polity: Turkish National Movement - the government at Ankara
eras.note: The nationalist government formed at Ankara during the war and was recognised as the legitimate government; the Greek advance toward Ankara was halted at the Battle of Sakarya. The Republic was declared on 29 October 1923.

The vilayets were renamed il in the late 1920s and the 1927 census lists 63 of them. Surnames were made compulsory by the Surname Law of 21 June 1934 (in force 1 January 1935). Detailed vital records are dated from 1925 in one guide, and the Civil Code was enacted on 17 February 1926.

regions.label: Black Sea Turkey - Samsun, Trabzon, Sinop and Zonguldak
regions.sub: Samsun, Trabzon, Sinop, Kastamonu, Zonguldak, Rize, Artvin

eras.polity: Byzantine Black Sea coast after Manzikert
eras.note: Before registers. The Seljuk victory at Manzikert in 1071 opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

eras.polity: Empire of Trebizond (Komnenoi); Candar beylik in the west
eras.note: Alexios Komnenos was proclaimed emperor at Trebizond in April 1204 and Mehmed II took the city on 15 August 1461. The empire held the coast from the Yeşilırmak east, and the dioceses of Trebizond, Cerasous and Rizaion survived the conquest into the 17th century. The Candar beylik (Kastamonu, last at Sinop) is dated 1291-1461.
Trebizond fell to Mehmed II in 1461, the year the Candar beylik is dated to end.
Provinces were reorganised as vilayets from 1867.

eras.polity: Republic of Turkey - after the exchange
eras.note: Greek Orthodox Christians of Pontus were among the roughly 1.2 million who left Turkey under the exchange agreed on 30 January 1923, which followed the Ottoman millet classification of religion. Detailed Turkish vital records are dated from 1925 or 1926 depending on the source.
The Surname Law took effect on 1 January 1935, and many Armenian, Jewish, Assyrian and Kurdish families then changed their names.

regions.label: Kars, Erzurum and Ardahan
regions.sub: Kars, Erzurum, Ardahan, Iğdır, Ağrı

eras.note: Before registers. Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

Chaldiran on 23 August 1514 was the first Ottoman expansion into Eastern Anatolia; Ottoman control was not secure until the Peace of Amasya (1555), and the Safavids ceded the territory permanently at Zuhab in 1639.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Kars, Çıldır and Erzurum
eras.note: The Ottoman Kars, Çıldır and Erzurum provinces were dissolved when Russia took Kars after the war of 1877-78.

The oblast, capital Kars, had four okrugs: Ardahan, Kagizman, Kars and Olti, and covered only parts of today's Erzurum province. The 1897 count was 50.18% Muslim, 24.47% Armenian Apostolic and 16.96% Eastern Orthodox. Erzurum, in the Ottoman Erzurum vilayet, was one of the places named in the 23 May 1915 deportation order.

The Treaty of Brest-Litovsk ceded the oblast to the Ottomans on 3 March 1918; the South-West Caucasus Republic held it briefly until Armenian and British forces ended it in April 1919. Turkish forces returned in 1920, the Treaty of Alexandropol was signed on 3 December 1920, and the treaties of Kars and Moscow confirmed Turkey's hold in 1921.
Kars and Ardahan have been Turkish since the 1921 treaties. The Surname Law took effect on 1 January 1935.

regions.label: Lake Van and Hakkâri - Van, Bitlis, Muş and Siirt
regions.sub: Van, Bitlis, Hakkâri, Muş, Siirt, Şırnak

eras.note: Before registers. Manzikert (1071) opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement.

After Chaldiran (23 August 1514) Kurdish chiefs switched allegiance from the Safavids to the Ottomans, though Kurdish tribes fought on both sides; the Peace of Amasya (1555) ended forty-one years of war.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - provincial government by eyalet
eras.note: The Safavids ceded these territories permanently at the Treaty of Zuhab in 1639.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Van and Bitlis vilayets
eras.note: Van and Bitlis were two of the six vilayets where most Armenian villages stood; the Armenian Patriarchate counted 2,925 Armenian towns and villages empire-wide in 1913-14.

Arrests of Armenian leaders began on the night of 23-24 April 1915, and an order of 23 May 1915 directed deportations from Van, Bitlis and Erzurum. By early 1916 about 500,000 deportees were alive in Syria and Mesopotamia.
The Surname Law took effect on 1 January 1935 and forbade non-Turkish affixes such as the Armenian -ian; Armenian, Assyrian and Kurdish families often changed names.

regions.label: Sivas, Malatya, Diyarbakır and Urfa
regions.sub: Sivas, Malatya, Elazığ, Diyarbakır, Mardin, Şanlıurfa, Gaziantep

eras.polity: Seljuks of Rum and the Eretna beylik
eras.note: Before registers. Sivas was a capital of the Sultanate of Rum from 1211 to 1220, and the Eretna beylik (Sivas, later Kayseri) is dated 1335-1390.

Chaldiran (23 August 1514) gave the Ottomans Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia from the Safavids; Selim I took the Ramadan and Dulkadir territories in 1515. The Safavids ceded the lands permanently at Zuhab in 1639.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - provincial government by eyalet
eras.note: Provinces were eyalets until the Vilayet Law of 1867 replaced them with vilayets.
Sivas, Diyarbekir and Harput (Mamuret-ul-Aziz) were three of the six vilayets where most Armenian villages stood.
Deportations began after the arrests of 23-24 April 1915. More than 200,000 Armenians were killed between March and October 1916, leaving about 200,000 deportees alive at the end of that year.

eras.polity: French occupation of Antep and Urfa
eras.note: The French took over Antep and Urfa from the British at the end of 1919. The Battle of Urfa ran from 9 February to 11 April 1920 and Antep held out until 9 February 1921; the Treaty of Ankara followed on 20 October 1921.
The Republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, and the Surname Law took effect on 1 January 1935.

regions.label: Iranian Azerbaijan, Kurdistan and the western Zagros
regions.sub: Tabriz, Urmia, Ardabil, Zanjan, Hamadan, Kermanshah, Sanandaj

eras.polity: Safavid Iran - Tabriz, Qazvin, then Isfahan
eras.note: The Safavid state was established on 22 December 1501 with Tabriz as capital until 1555; Qazvin followed to 1598 and Isfahan to 1736. The Ottomans briefly occupied Tabriz after Chaldiran in September 1514.
Nader Shah was crowned on 8 March 1736, the day the Safavid state was disestablished. The Zand dynasty ruled 1751-1794.

Tehran became the capital. The Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) ceded the South Caucasus and the Erivan area to Russia. The Qajar provinces numbered about 20 in 1847, 39 in 1886 and 18 in 1906; the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 divided Iran into spheres of influence.

The Majlis declared Reza Shah on 12 December 1925. A Civil Registry Office was set up by a Cabinet decision of 12 December 1918 and the first identity record was issued on 25 December 1918; from March 1925 the identity booklet was compulsory where a registry office existed.

eras.polity: Iran under Anglo-Soviet occupation; the Azerbaijan and Mahabad states
eras.note: British and Soviet troops occupied Iran in August 1941, and Reza Shah abdicated on 16 September 1941. The Azerbaijan People's Government (Tabriz) ran from 20 November 1945 to 12 December 1946 and the Kurdish Republic of Mahabad from 22 January to 15 December 1946.
Mohammad Reza Shah reigned until deposed on 11 February 1979.
The Pahlavi monarchy ended in February 1979 and a referendum followed in March 1979.

regions.label: Tehran, the Caspian coast and Khorasan
regions.sub: Tehran, Rasht, Sari, Gorgan, Mashhad, Qazvin, Qom, Semnan

eras.note: Qazvin was the Safavid capital from 1555 to 1598, then Isfahan until 1736.
Nader Shah was crowned on 8 March 1736; the Zand dynasty is dated 1751-1794.
Agha Mohammad Khan was crowned in 1796 and made Tehran his capital. Russian officers founded the Persian Cossack Brigade in 1879, and the Constitutional Revolution is dated from 5 August 1906.

eras.polity: Gilan: the Persian Socialist Soviet Republic (Rasht); the rest still Qajar Iran
eras.note: The Soviet Caspian fleet entered Anzali in May 1920 and the republic is dated to May or June 1920. After the Russo-Persian treaty of February 1921 Soviet forces withdrew, and the republic ended in September 1921.
The Majlis deposed Ahmad Shah in October 1925 and Reza Khan was proclaimed monarch.
Reza Shah's reign began on 15 December 1925. The identity booklet (shenasnameh) became compulsory in March 1925, but only where a registry office existed.
British and Soviet troops entered in August 1941, and the Soviets held the north until 1946. The shah was deposed on 11 February 1979.
The monarchy ended in 1979, with a referendum in March of that year.

regions.label: Isfahan, Fars and Khuzestan
regions.sub: Isfahan, Shiraz, Yazd, Ahvaz, Bushehr, Abadan

eras.polity: Safavid Iran - Isfahan the capital from 1598
eras.note: Isfahan was the capital from 1598. It fell to the Afghan Hotaks in 1722; some historians date the end of the dynasty to then, others to 1736.
Nader Shah's reconquest ran 1726-1729 and he was crowned on 8 March 1736; the Zand dynasty is dated 1751-1794.

eras.polity: Qajar Iran - with the autonomous emirate of Arabistan in western Khuzestan
eras.note: In the two decades before 1925 western Khuzestan acted as an autonomous emirate called Arabistan (the Emirate of Muhammara). Commercial oil production began in 1908 at Masjed Soleyman, and the provincial capital moved from Shushtar to Ahvaz in 1924.
The rebellion of the Sheikh of Mohammerah was put down in late 1924 and early 1925 and the emirate dissolved; the name Khuzestan was applied to the whole territory by 1936.
Reza Shah abdicated on 16 September 1941 and his son reigned until 11 February 1979.
Iraq invaded Khuzestan in 1980, and the Battle of Khorramshahr in May 1982 was a turning point; the city was almost wholly destroyed.

regions.label: Kerman, Hormozgan and Baluchestan
regions.sub: Kerman, Bandar Abbas, Zahedan, Chabahar, Zabol

eras.note: Ismail I conquered Sistan in 1508; the Safavid state is dated 1501-1736, or to 1722 when Isfahan fell.

eras.polity: After Nader Shah - the Khanate of Kalat in Baluchistan
eras.note: After Nader Shah's assassination in 1747 the Sistan and Baluchestan area became part of the Brahui Khanate of Kalat, which ruled it until 1896.
The Sistan and Baluchestan area became part of Qajar Iran from 1896.
The identity booklet was compulsory from March 1925 only where a Civil Registry Office had been established, so early coverage varies by district. The shah was deposed on 11 February 1979.
The monarchy gave way to the Islamic Republic in 1979.

regions.label: The Gaza Strip
regions.sub: Gaza City, Khan Yunis, Rafah, Deir al-Balah

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Gaza within Ottoman Syria
eras.note: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and took Egypt in 1517; Gaza has been under Ottoman control since the 16th century.

The mutasarrifate of 1872-1917 reported directly to Constantinople and covered Jerusalem, Hebron, Jaffa, Gaza and Beersheba. Most surviving Ottoman registers of the Palestine area are in the Israel State Archives, microfilmed in 1964 and 1969.

eras.polity: British occupation and the Mandate for Palestine
eras.note: The military Occupied Enemy Territory Administration ran until July 1920. The mandate was assigned on 25 April 1920, Britain assumed control on 29 September 1923, and the mandate ended at midnight on 14-15 May 1948.

The All-Palestine Government was proclaimed in Gaza City on 22 September 1948; the Israel-Egypt armistice followed on 24 February 1949. It was dissolved in 1959 and Egypt ruled through a military governor until June 1967.
The IDF captured Gaza in June 1967.
A phased transfer of authority to the Palestinians began in May 1994 under the Gaza-Jericho Agreement.

eras.polity: Gaza Strip - after the Israeli withdrawal
eras.note: Israel withdrew from Gaza in 2005; by 14 June 2007 Hamas fully controlled the Strip.

regions.label: Jerusalem and the West Bank
regions.sub: Jerusalem, Hebron, Bethlehem, Ramallah, Nablus, Jericho

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire - Jerusalem within the Damascus province
eras.note: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and took Egypt in 1517, and made Syria a single province centred on Damascus.
Jerusalem was separated from the Damascus province and placed directly under Constantinople in 1841; another account has it a sanjak of the Syria Vilayet until 1872.

Created in 1872 as an independent province under Constantinople. Nablus and Acre were first combined with it and within two months moved to the Vilayet of Beirut, so Nablus lay outside the mutasarrifate. Surviving Ottoman registers for the area are mostly in the Israel State Archives and many are organised by religious community; some list males only.

eras.polity: British occupation and the Mandate for Palestine
eras.note: The mandate was assigned on 25 April 1920 and Britain assumed control on 29 September 1923; the 1922 census counted 757,182. The UN partition resolution was adopted on 29 November 1947 and the mandate ended on 14-15 May 1948.

eras.polity: Jordan - the West Bank and East Jerusalem
eras.note: The Jericho Conference of December 1948 accepted Jordanian rule, the Israel-Jordan armistice was signed on 3 April 1949, and the West Bank was formally annexed on 24 April 1950.
Israel occupied the West Bank in the Six-Day War of 5-10 June 1967. Jordan severed its legal and administrative ties to the West Bank on 31 July 1988.

eras.polity: Palestinian Authority in Areas A and B; Israeli control in Area C
