eras.note: The Palestinian Authority was created by the Gaza-Jericho Agreement of 1994; Oslo II (28 September 1995) divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C, with Area C, about 60% of the territory, under exclusive Israeli control. Israel withdrew from about 80% of Hebron in January 1997.

regions.label: Orkney Islands
regions.sub: Kirkwall, Stromness, Hoy, Westray, South Ronaldsay

eras.note: Before registers. The Norse jarldom is dated to c. 892, with Sigurd Eysteinsson as its first holder; the Norse line of earls ended in 1230.

eras.polity: Earldom of Orkney under the Norwegian crown
eras.note: Before registers. The Treaty of Perth (2 July 1266) left Orkney and Shetland with Norway while the Hebrides and Man passed to Scotland. Henry Sinclair was granted the jarldom on 2 August 1379.

eras.polity: Scotland — after the forfeiture of the earldom
eras.note: Before registers. Christian I could not pay the dowry of Margaret of Denmark on her marriage to James III and pledged the islands as security; the Sinclair earl gave up his rights in 1470 and in 1472 James declared the islands forfeit.

The Old Parish Registers run from 1553 to 1854, but the standard of keeping varied from parish to parish and year to year and about 3,500 volumes survive. One catalogue reports that Orkney's registers are held by Orkney Archives, with microfilm copies at National Records of Scotland in Edinburgh.

Statutory registration of births, deaths and marriages began in Scotland on 1 January 1855 and records far more than the parish registers did; some 1855 and later entries also appear in the Old Parish Registers, and a few are in only one of the two.

regions.label: Shetland Islands
regions.sub: Lerwick, Unst, Yell, Fetlar, Dunrossness

eras.note: Before registers. The Treaty of Perth (2 July 1266) confirmed Norwegian sovereignty over Shetland and Orkney; Scotland's annual payment to Norway under that treaty was cancelled in 1469 in the marriage agreement of James III and Margaret of Denmark.

eras.polity: Shetland pledged to the Scottish crown
eras.note: Before registers. Christian I pledged Orkney and Shetland as security for the unpaid dowry of his daughter Margaret; in 1470 the Sinclair earl quitclaimed his rights over both.
Before registers. In 1472 James III declared Orkney and Shetland forfeit and gave up the dowry.

Shetland's pre-1855 parish registers are the Church of Scotland Old Parish Registers, held in the care of the Registrar General for Scotland and searchable on ScotlandsPeople. Coverage is uneven: the registers survive in about 3,500 volumes nationally and are far from complete.
Civil registration began in Scotland on 1 January 1855. The statutory registers hold much more detail than the parish books.

regions.label: Outer Hebrides — Lewis, Harris, the Uists, Barra
regions.sub: Stornoway area, Harris, North Uist, South Uist, Barra

eras.note: Before registers. The Kingdom of the Isles is dated 849 to 1265; in 1098 Magnus Bareleg made a treaty with Edgar of Scotland by which Magnus kept the Isles. The Treaty of Perth (2 July 1266) recognised Scottish sovereignty over the Hebrides.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Lordship of the Isles (Clan Donald)
eras.note: Before registers. The Lords of the Isles were of Clan Donald. In 1462 John MacDonald II signed a treaty with Edward IV of England, and James IV of Scotland seized his lands and titles in 1493 after it was discovered.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Crown after the forfeiture
eras.note: Before registers. Two Clan Donald claimants, Aonghas Óg and Dómhnall Dubh, contested the lordship after 1493; Dubh's Rebellion is one example.

The Statutes of Iona (1609) required chiefs to send their heirs to Lowland schools; among the clans named in connection with them, the MacLeods of Harris adopted the Protestant religion and the Clanranald MacDonalds remained Roman Catholic. The Old Parish Registers cover 1553 to 1854, far from completely.
Statutory registers of births, deaths and marriages start on 1 January 1855 and hold more information than the older parish books.

regions.label: Inner Hebrides and Kintyre — Skye (Duirinish), Small Isles, Coll, Tiree, Colonsay, Islay, Gigha, Kintyre
regions.sub: Campbeltown, Islay, Colonsay, Tiree, Coll

eras.note: Before registers. Somerled began taking the Isles in 1135 and died in 1164; Islay, Jura, Kintyre and Knapdale passed to Donald, son of Ranald, from whom Clan Donald takes its name. The Treaty of Perth (2 July 1266) ended Norway's claim to the Hebrides.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Lordship of the Isles
eras.note: Before registers. The seat of the Lords of the Isles was Finlaggan on Islay, until James IV took the lordship's lands and titles in 1493.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Crown after the forfeiture
eras.note: Before registers. The Lordship of the Isles was treated as extinct after 1493; the title has been reserved since 1540 for the eldest son of the reigning monarch.

Under the Statutes of Iona (1609) some clans, among them the MacDonalds of Sleat, adopted the Protestant religion while others, among them the MacLeans of Mull, remained Roman Catholic. Parish registers survive in about 3,500 volumes for 1553–1854, far from complete.
Scottish civil registration began on 1 January 1855; the statutory entries say far more than the parish registers before them.

regions.label: Galloway — Wigtownshire (the Rhins and the Machars)
regions.sub: Stranraer, Wigtown, Whithorn, Portpatrick, Ballantrae

eras.polity: Lordship of Galloway — Fergus and Alan
eras.note: Before registers. Galloway takes its name from the Gall-Gàidheil, a mixed Gaelic and Norse people who seem to have settled there in the 10th century; Fergus established himself in the mid-12th century. Alan died in 1234, and the revolt of 1234–35 against Alexander II ended in the partition of Galloway.
Before registers. After the partition the bishopric and the Justiciar of Galloway survived.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Douglas lordship; Shire of Wigtown
eras.note: Before registers. Archibald the Grim received the land east of the Cree in 1369, which became the Stewartry of Kirkcudbright, and the western part the next year, which became the Shire of Wigtown. The two later became separate counties.
Irish cattle were exported to England through Galloway, up to 10,000 head in 1667, the year England banned their import. The Old Parish Registers cover 1553–1854 and are far from complete.
Statutory registers of births, deaths and marriages in Scotland began on 1 January 1855.

regions.label: Anglesey and the Menai coast of Gwynedd
regions.sub: Beaumaris, Holyhead, Llangefni, Aberffraw, Menai Bridge

eras.polity: Kingdom of Gwynedd — the House of Aberffraw
eras.note: Before registers. Rhodri Mawr built a royal palace at Aberffraw in 873, and it remained the capital until the 13th century. The House of Aberffraw ended its rule of Gwynedd in 1283.

eras.polity: England — Edward I's conquest; Anglesey a county
eras.note: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd was killed on 11 December 1282 and the conquest of Gwynedd was completed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) made Anglesey a county, and Beaumaris Castle was begun after Madog ap Llywelyn's revolt of 1294.

eras.polity: England and Wales — the Laws in Wales Acts
eras.note: The Laws in Wales Acts (royal assent 14 April 1536 and 12 May 1543) incorporated Wales into England; English law and English-language courts replaced Welsh law, though Welsh stayed the majority language until the later 19th century.

Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths began on 1 July 1837 (the Act's own commencement is given as 1 March 1837), and parents were made responsible for registering births from 1875. The GRO index gives a reference; the certificate itself is ordered separately.

eras.polity: United Kingdom — Anglesey a district of Gwynedd
eras.note: In 1974 Anglesey became a district of Gwynedd, so council papers of these years may be filed under Gwynedd rather than under Anglesey.

eras.polity: United Kingdom — Isle of Anglesey County Council
eras.note: Anglesey became a unitary authority under the Isle of Anglesey County Council on 1 April 1996.

regions.label: The Ards Peninsula, County Down
regions.sub: Newtownards, Donaghadee, Portaferry, Ballywalter, Kircubbin

eras.polity: Uí Echach Arda; the Earldom of Ulster; the Savage and Clannaboy lordships
eras.note: Before registers. The peninsula was held by the Gaelic Uí Echach Arda until Anglo-Normans under John de Courcy conquered it in the late 12th century, and the Earldom of Ulster later collapsed. The Savage family held the Upper (Little) Ards for about three centuries and the Lower (Great) Ards fell into the Gaelic territory of Clannaboy.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Ireland — the Hamilton and Montgomery settlements
eras.note: The grant of the Clandeboye and Ards lands to the Scots James Hamilton and Hugh Montgomery is dated 1605 or 1606 depending on the source, and the first Lowland settlers arrived in May 1606, mainly at Donaghadee. Church records of the period are held at PRONI, listed by civil parish and denomination, and the Church of Ireland was the established church until 1871.

eras.polity: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
eras.note: The Acts of Union took effect on 1 January 1801. Civil registration of non-Catholic marriages began in 1845 and of all births, deaths and marriages in 1864.

The Government of Ireland Act took effect on 3 May 1921, creating Northern Ireland; the Irish Free State followed on 6 December 1922. Records after partition divide between PRONI in Belfast and the repositories in Dublin.

regions.label: Buchan coast — Peterhead
regions.sub: Peterhead, Boddam, Longside, Cruden Bay

eras.note: In 1560 Mary, Queen of Scots granted the lands of Peterugie (Inverugie of St Peter) to Robert Keith, 1st Lord Altrie. The earliest surviving entry in any Scottish Old Parish Register is a baptism of 27 December 1553.

eras.polity: Scotland — the Barony of Keith Insche, Peterhead
eras.note: George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal, founded the town in 1593 with its harbour, under the name 'Harbour and Barony of Keith Insche commonly called Peterhead'.
The Keith estate was forfeited in 1716 for Jacobite loyalty after the 1715 rising. Whaling began in 1788, and registered vessels rose from 72 in 1815 to over 400 by 1850 as herring fishing grew.
Scottish statutory registration began on 1 January 1855. The convict prison opened in 1888, and Peterhead became a head port.

regions.label: Iceland
regions.sub: Reykjavik, Akureyri, Isafjordur, Egilsstadir, Selfoss

eras.note: Before registers. Settlement is traditionally dated to c. 874 and the Althing was established in 930.
Before registers. Icelandic chieftains signed the Old Covenant in 1262–64 accepting Norwegian rule; the end of the Commonwealth is dated either to that or to the adoption of Jónsbók in 1281.

eras.polity: Kalmar Union — Iceland under the joint crown
eras.note: Before registers. The Kalmar Union was formed in 1397 and is dated 1397–1523.

eras.polity: Denmark–Norway — Iceland under the Danish crown
eras.note: Iceland was barred from trade with countries other than Denmark from 1602 until the 1780s (1786 in one account). Clergy were required to record baptisms, confirmations, marriages and burials from 1685, and the 1703 census names every Icelander. The registers are held by the National Archives of Iceland.

eras.polity: Denmark — Iceland after the Treaty of Kiel
eras.note: The Treaty of Kiel (1814) separated Denmark and Norway and Denmark kept Iceland. A constitution and limited home rule came in 1874 and were expanded in 1904. Complete census returns survive for 1801, 1835, 1845, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1901 and 1910.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Iceland — in personal union with Denmark
eras.note: The Act of Union recognised the Kingdom of Iceland as a sovereign state in personal union with Denmark on 1 December 1918.

Iceland became a republic on 17 June 1944. The Íslendingabók database is open only to those with an Icelandic national ID number (family abroad may search through a relative), and its coverage before 1650 is only about 10 percent of the population.

regions.label: South and west Norway — Agder, Rogaland, Vestland
regions.sub: Kristiansand, Stavanger, Bergen, Haugesund, Arendal

eras.polity: Kalmar Union — Norway under the joint crown
eras.note: Before registers. The Kalmar Union linked Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1397.

Denmark and Norway formed a union in 1536–37 that lasted to 1814. The first national census of 1801 is based on complete lists of individuals; an earlier census of males was taken in 1663–66 but excluded townspeople.

eras.polity: Norway in personal union with Sweden
eras.note: The Treaty of Kiel (1814) ceded Norway to Sweden; Norway declared independence, resisted, and then entered a personal union with Sweden. The 1865 census, taken on 31 December 1865, introduced self-counting and recorded birthplace and religious affiliation; the 1875 census added nationality.
The union with Sweden was dissolved peacefully in 1905. The 1900 census reintroduced building lists; its agricultural data were lost in a 1939 fire.

regions.label: Troms — the north Norwegian coast
regions.sub: Tromsø, Harstad, Lyngen, Skjervøy, Finnsnes

eras.polity: Hålogaland — Norse chieftains and the Sámi
eras.note: Before registers. The Sámi were the first of the current ethnic groups to settle the county, and Norse settlement spread north from the 10th century; south and mid Troms was a petty kingdom within Hålogaland.

eras.polity: Kalmar Union — Norway under the joint crown
eras.note: Before registers. Norway was linked to Denmark and Sweden by the Kalmar Union from 1397.

Tromsø received town status in 1794. Kven residents are largely descended from Finnish immigrants who arrived before the 19th century and settled mainly in the north-east, including Skjervøy, and some reached Lyngen.

eras.polity: Norway in personal union with Sweden — Tromsø amt
eras.note: Troms was established as a county in 1866, succeeding Finnmarkens amt, and was called Tromsø amt until 1919. The 1865 census recorded ethnicity so as to identify Sámi people and people of Finnish descent.

Troms was merged with Finnmark as Troms og Finnmark from January 2020 to December 2023 and re-established on 1 January 2024, so a current county search may not match the county named in an older record.

regions.label: Western Finland — Satakunta and Southwest Finland
regions.sub: Pori, Rauma, Turku, Uusikaupunki, Naantali

eras.note: Before registers. Swedish rule in Satakunta was consolidated in the 13th century and Rauma was established in 1442.

eras.polity: Sweden — Pori founded; the counties introduced
eras.note: Pori was founded on the coast in 1558 by Johan III, Grand Duke of Finland; counties were introduced in 1634.

In 1649 Satakunta was merged with Southwest Finland into Turku and Pori County. The church law of 1686 required parish registers in every parish; a few parish registers survive from as early as 1667 in 14 parishes in south-western Finland, and many parishes began keeping them only in the 1720s (sources differ).

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Finland under the Russian crown
eras.note: The Treaty of Fredrikshamn (17 September 1809) ceded Finland to Russia and it became an autonomous Grand Duchy. The 1686 church law remained in force in Finland until the Church Law of 1869 (1870 in some accounts).

Parish registers continued as the civil record; their keeping is reported to have ended in 1962, when a card-based system replaced them. The Genealogical Society of Finland's HisKi project transcribes parish records into a free database.

regions.label: Copenhagen and north-east Zealand — the Capital Region
regions.sub: Copenhagen, Frederiksberg, Lyngby, Hillerød

eras.note: Before registers. The Kalmar Union linked Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1397.
Before registers. Denmark and Norway formed a union in 1536–37; the union became an absolute monarchy by 1660.

Danish parish registers are dated from an ordinance of 1645–46, and some parishes have earlier books. After the Treaty of Roskilde (1658) Charles X Gustav attacked Copenhagen in 1659 and was forced to withdraw.
From 1812–14 pastors kept two copies of each register, the second held by the parish clerk. Danish censuses were taken in 1787, 1801, 1834, 1840 and later; sources list the later dates differently.

regions.label: Skåne on the Sound (Øresund coast)
regions.sub: Malmö, Landskrona, Helsingborg, Lund

eras.note: Before registers. Scania came under Harald Bluetooth in the mid-10th century, and Lund became the archbishopric for all Scandinavia in 1103.
Scania's Danish-period parish books fall in this short window after the 1645–46 ordinance that began Danish register-keeping.

The Treaty of Roskilde (26 February or 8 March 1658) ceded Scania to Sweden. Denmark occupied parts of it in 1676–79 and 1710, and the province was divided into Kristianstad and Malmöhus counties in 1719 and confirmed Swedish by peace in 1720.
Scania was administered like the rest of Sweden through its two counties.
Skåne County became operative on 1 January 1997; Region Skåne dates from 1997 or 1999 depending on the source.

regions.label: Baden-Württemberg — Heidelberg, Stuttgart, the Neckar and Swabia
regions.sub: Heidelberg, Schwetzingen, Karlsruhe, Stuttgart, Ulm

eras.polity: Holy Roman Empire — Electoral Palatinate (Heidelberg, Schwetzingen), Württemberg and other imperial states
eras.note: The north of this ring belonged to the Electoral Palatinate, whose capital moved from Heidelberg to Mannheim in 1720; French forces destroyed Heidelberg Castle in 1689. The right-bank Palatine lands went to Baden in 1803.

eras.polity: Electorate of Baden (from 27 April 1803) and Württemberg
eras.note: Baden was raised to an electorate on 27 April 1803 and took the Prince-Bishopric of Constance and part of the Rhenish Palatinate. Records of the same village can therefore sit in Palatine, Constance or Baden files depending on the year.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Baden (from 24 Oct 1806) and Kingdom of Württemberg
eras.note: Württemberg became a kingdom on 1 January or 26 December 1806 depending on the source; both states belonged to the Confederation of the Rhine 1806-1813 and the German Confederation from 1815. The Hohenzollern principalities in the south existed until 1850.

eras.polity: German Empire — Grand Duchy of Baden and Kingdom of Württemberg
eras.note: Civil registers (Standesamt) began in Baden on 1 February 1870 and Reich-wide on 1 January 1876. The Grand Duke of Baden abdicated on 22 November 1918 and King William II of Württemberg on 30 November 1918.

eras.polity: Republic of Baden (from 14 Nov 1918) and Free People's State of Württemberg
eras.note: Both monarchies were replaced in November 1918.

eras.polity: Post-war states of Baden and Württemberg
eras.note: The present state was created only in 1952, so records of these years may sit under the older state boundaries.
Baden, Württemberg and the Hohenzollern lands were merged into one state in 1952.

regions.label: Bavaria — Munich, Franconia and Swabia
regions.sub: Munich, Nuremberg, Würzburg, Augsburg, Regensburg

eras.polity: Electorate of Bavaria (1623-1806) and the imperial states of Franconia and Swabia
eras.note: Bavaria was an electorate from 1623 until 1806. Franconia and Swabia were split among many separate rulers until the nineteenth century, so ancestors there are filed under the local sovereign, not under Munich.

The kingdom was proclaimed on 1 January 1806 (26 December 1806 depending on the source) after Bavaria left the Empire for the Confederation of the Rhine on 1 August 1806. Franconia was annexed in 1815 and the circles were renamed in 1838, including Swabia and Neuburg.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Bavaria within the German Empire
eras.note: Civil registration (Standesamt) became Reich-wide on 1 January 1876; before that, church books are the main source. Louis III left Munich on 7 November 1918 and issued the Anif declaration on 12 November.
The monarchy ended with the Anif declaration of November 1918.

regions.label: Saxony and Thuringia — Dresden, Leipzig, Weimar, Erfurt
regions.sub: Dresden, Leipzig, Weimar, Gotha, Erfurt

eras.polity: Electorate of Saxony and the Ernestine duchies of Thuringia
eras.note: After the Ernestine line lost the electorate (c. 1547) its Thuringian lands were split into small Ernestine duchies. Thuringian records are therefore filed duchy by duchy (Weimar, Gotha, Meiningen, Altenburg and others).
The Electorate joined the Confederation of the Rhine on 11 December 1806 and became a kingdom on 20 December. On 9 June 1815 it lost about 60 percent of its land to Prussia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Saxony and the Thuringian duchies (German Confederation)
eras.note: Land north of this ring that Saxony lost in 1815 became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony, a different record set.

eras.polity: German Empire — Kingdom of Saxony and the Thuringian states
eras.note: Civil registration (Standesamt) became Reich-wide on 1 January 1876. King Frederick Augustus III of Saxony abdicated on 13 November 1918.

eras.polity: Free State of Saxony; State of Thuringia (from 1920)
eras.note: The Kingdom of Saxony became the Free State of Saxony on 1 November 1920. In 1920 the small Thuringian states merged into one state with Weimar as capital; Saxe-Coburg voted to join Bavaria instead.
In July 1945 Thuringia gained Erfurt, Mühlhausen and Nordhausen from the Prussian Province of Saxony. In 1952 East Germany replaced the states with districts.

eras.polity: Free State of Thuringia and Free State of Saxony
eras.note: Thuringia was re-established in 1990 with slightly altered borders.

regions.label: Prussian Saxony — Magdeburg, Halberstadt and the Altmark
regions.sub: Magdeburg, Halberstadt, Stendal, Wittenberg, Wernigerode

eras.polity: Duchy of Magdeburg, Principality of Halberstadt, the Altmark and neighbouring territories
eras.note: The Prussian Province of Saxony of 1816 was assembled from the Duchy of Magdeburg, the Principality of Halberstadt, the Altmark and other territories, so earlier records sit under those names, not under "Saxony".
Control of these lands shifted repeatedly in 1806-1815; the Napoleonic Kingdom of Westphalia was founded in 1807 and ended in 1813.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia — Province of Saxony (capital Magdeburg)
eras.note: The province was created from lands returned or given to Prussia in 1815 (including the northern parts of the former Kingdom of Saxony). Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Province of Saxony (split in 1944)
eras.note: On 1 July 1944 the province was divided along its district lines: Magdeburg and Merseburg became separate provinces and Erfurt went to Thuringia.

eras.polity: Soviet zone — Saxony-Anhalt (1945) and East German districts
eras.note: In 1945 the Soviet zone formed Saxony-Anhalt from the Prussian province and neighbouring lands. East Germany replaced its states with districts in 1952.
The East German states were re-established in 1990.

regions.label: Mecklenburg — Schwerin, Rostock, Wismar
regions.sub: Schwerin, Rostock, Wismar, Güstrow, Neubrandenburg

eras.polity: Duchies of Mecklenburg (Schwerin and Strelitz lines) under the House of Mecklenburg
eras.note: Henry the Lion held the region in the late twelfth century. The land was later divided into Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz, which became grand duchies in 1815.

eras.polity: Grand Duchies of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz
eras.note: Both duchies became grand duchies in 1815; the monarchy ended in the revolution of 1918. Reich-wide civil registration (Standesamt) began on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free States of Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklenburg-Strelitz (united 1934)
eras.note: The two free states were united in 1934.
After the war the Soviet authorities merged Mecklenburg with Western Pomerania into Mecklenburg-Vorpommern; East Germany abolished the state in 1952.
The state was revived during reunification in 1990.

regions.label: Brandenburg, Berlin and the Neumark (Lubusz)
regions.sub: Berlin, Potsdam, Frankfurt (Oder), Cottbus, Gorzów Wielkopolski

eras.polity: Margraviate (Electorate) of Brandenburg, including the Neumark east of the Oder
eras.note: The Province of Brandenburg was created in 1815 and lasted until 1947. Cottbus was ceded to Saxony on 9 July 1807.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia — Province of Brandenburg
eras.note: From 1822 the province was split into the Potsdam and Frankfurt governorates; Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Province of Brandenburg; Greater Berlin from 1920
eras.note: The 1920 Greater Berlin Act took Berlin out of the province.

eras.polity: Soviet zone — State of Brandenburg (to 1952); the Neumark under Poland
eras.note: The Neumark east of the Oder was ceded to Poland in 1945, so records of its towns are now in Polish archives. The remaining state of Brandenburg was dissolved in 1952.

eras.polity: State of Brandenburg and the city-state of Berlin; Lubusz in Poland
eras.note: Brandenburg was re-established after German reunification in 1990.

regions.label: Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg
regions.sub: Kiel, Lübeck, Hamburg, Schleswig, Itzehoe

eras.polity: Duchies of Schleswig and Holstein under the Danish crown
eras.note: From 1460 the Danish king ruled Schleswig and Holstein together as duke, while Holstein stayed in the Holy Roman Empire; all Schleswig was united as one duchy under the Danish king in 1721.

eras.polity: Prussian-Austrian rule, then Prussian Province of Schleswig-Holstein
eras.note: After the Second Schleswig War the 1864 Treaty of Vienna ceded the duchies; the 1865 Gastein Convention gave Schleswig to Prussia and Holstein to Austria, and the 1866 Peace of Prague gave Holstein to Prussia. The province dates from 1867 or 1868 depending on the passage.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Province of Schleswig-Holstein
eras.note: After plebiscites on 10 February and 14 March 1920, North Schleswig returned to Denmark on 15 June 1920. The 1937 Greater Hamburg Act redrew the borders around Hamburg and Lübeck.
The British military government made the province a separate state on 23 August 1946.

regions.label: Hanover and Lower Saxony
regions.sub: Hanover, Göttingen, Osnabrück, Celle, Lüneburg

eras.polity: Electorate of Hanover (in personal union with Great Britain from 1714)
eras.note: Hanover was raised to an electorate in 1708; George Louis became George I of Great Britain in 1714.

eras.polity: French and Prussian occupation; Kingdom of Westphalia (1807-1813)
eras.note: Hanover was conquered in 1803, and from 1807 part of it lay in the Napoleonic Kingdom of Westphalia.
The kingdom was constituted on 12 October 1814. The personal union with Britain ended in 1837.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia — Province of Hanover
eras.note: Prussia annexed the kingdom on 20 September 1866. Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Province of Hanover
eras.note: The Hanover province continued within Prussia until 1946.
The State of Hanover was created in 1946 and became part of Lower Saxony.

regions.label: Rhine Province — Cologne, Koblenz, Trier
regions.sub: Cologne, Koblenz, Trier, Bonn, Bacharach

eras.polity: Holy Roman Empire — the Lower Rhine and Jülich-Cleves-Berg territories and the Rhenish prince-bishoprics
eras.note: The Rhine Province was a Prussian creation of 1822, so earlier records of these places are filed under the separate lordships and prince-bishoprics that preceded it.

eras.polity: French occupation and annexation of the left bank
eras.note: Civil registers were introduced in the French-occupied Rhineland between 1792 and 1808.
Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Rhine Province
eras.note: Allied forces occupied the area after the First World War until 1930; Eupen-Malmedy went to Belgium and Wetzlar was transferred to Hesse-Nassau in 1932. The province was abolished in August 1946.
The northern part of the former province joined North Rhine-Westphalia and the southern part Rhineland-Palatinate.

regions.label: Westphalia — Münster, Minden, Paderborn, Arnsberg
regions.sub: Münster, Minden, Paderborn, Bielefeld, Dortmund

eras.polity: Prince-bishoprics and other territories of Westphalia
eras.note: These lands were not yet one unit; the Prussian province of 1815 later joined them, so older records are filed under the local lordship.
The Kingdom of Westphalia was founded in 1807; the region was reconquered in 1813.

eras.polity: General Government between Weser and Rhine, then Prussian Province of Westphalia (1815)
eras.note: The province was formed in 1815, and the Duchy of Westphalia came under Prussia in 1816. Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Free State of Prussia — Province of Westphalia
eras.note: The province was dissolved in 1946.
The province was dissolved in 1946 and its lands became part of the new state.

regions.label: Hesse-Kassel (Electoral Hesse) — Kassel, Marburg, Hersfeld
regions.sub: Kassel, Marburg, Hersfeld, Eschwege, Korbach

eras.note: Hesse-Kassel was a landgraviate until it became an electorate in 1803.
The electorate dates from 1803.
The French annexed the territory into the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807; the Congress of Vienna restored the electorate in 1814.

eras.polity: Electorate of Hesse (the German Confederation's only electorate)
eras.note: A constitution dates from 1831; it was abolished in 1852 and reinstated in 1862.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia — Province of Hesse-Nassau (decree of 7 Dec 1868; capital Kassel)
eras.note: Prussia took the electorate in 1866. Waldeck joined the province in 1929.

eras.polity: Kurhessen, then the state of Hesse
eras.note: The province was split into Kurhessen and Nassau in 1944, and Greater Hesse was formed in 1945-1946.

regions.label: French-speaking Switzerland — Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel, Valais, Jura
regions.sub: Geneva, Lausanne, Neuchâtel, Sion, Delémont

eras.polity: Holy Roman Empire — counts, bishops and the Duchy of Savoy in the Romandy lands
eras.note: Records before the cantons took shape are filed under the local count, bishop or house, not under a Swiss state.

eras.polity: Old Swiss Confederacy — Bern's Vaud, the Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva as allies and subjects
eras.note: Reformed parish registers in Switzerland start in the sixteenth century and Catholic ones about fifty years later.

eras.polity: Helvetic Republic (1798-1803), Mediation (1803) and French annexations
eras.note: The Helvetic Republic lasted 1798-1803 and the Act of Mediation followed in 1803. Geneva's civil registration system dates from 1798; Vaud's dates from 1800 or 1821 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Restored Confederation — Valais, Neuchâtel and Geneva join in 1815
eras.note: The Jura lands passed to the Canton of Bern in 1815. The Sonderbund war followed in 1847.
The federal constitution dates from 1848. Federal civil registers began on 1 January 1876 under a law of 24 December 1874.

eras.polity: Swiss Confederation — Canton of Jura (from 23 June 1979)
eras.note: The Canton of Jura was created on 23 June 1979. Moutier moves from Bern to Jura as of 1 January 2026.

regions.label: Bern, Lucerne and central Switzerland
regions.sub: Bern, Lucerne, Aarau, Solothurn, Basel

eras.polity: Old Swiss Confederacy — Bern, Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden
eras.note: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden allied in 1291 and the Confederacy grew to eight cantons by 1353. Reformed registers start in the sixteenth century and Catholic ones about fifty years later.
The Helvetic Republic of 1798-1803 replaced the old cantons with a single state.
The Act of Mediation of 1803 restored the cantons. The Sonderbund of 1847 preceded the 1848 constitution.
Federal civil registers began on 1 January 1876 under a law of 24 December 1874.

regions.label: Eastern Switzerland — Zürich, St. Gallen, Thurgau
regions.sub: Zürich, St. Gallen, Winterthur, Frauenfeld, Schaffhausen

eras.polity: Old Swiss Confederacy — Zürich, the Abbey of St. Gall and subject lands
eras.note: Zwingli's Reformation began in Zürich in 1523. The Abbey of St. Gall was a separate ecclesiastical territory.

eras.polity: Helvetic Republic — Säntis and Linth cantons
eras.note: The abbey was secularised on 17 September 1798, and the Helvetic Republic created the Säntis and Linth cantons from the area.
The Act of Mediation of 1803 restored cantonal government; St. Gallen became a canton in 1803.
Federal civil registers began on 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Graubünden — Chur, Davos, the Engadine
regions.sub: Chur, Davos, St. Moritz, Disentis, Poschiavo

eras.polity: Free State of the Three Leagues
eras.note: The Three Leagues were allied with the Swiss Confederacy but were not a full canton. The Valtellina was lost in 1797.
The Helvetic Republic of 1798-1803 took in the Three Leagues.

eras.polity: Canton of Graubünden in the Swiss Confederation
eras.note: Graubünden became a canton in 1803. Federal civil registers began on 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Ticino — Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno
regions.sub: Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno, Mendrisio, Chiasso

eras.note: The Ticino valleys were held by Milan before the Swiss cantons took them.

eras.polity: Swiss bailiwicks of the Old Confederacy (1512-1798)
eras.note: The Swiss cantons ruled the area as common bailiwicks from 1512 until 1798.

eras.polity: Helvetic Republic — cantons of Lugano and Bellinzona
eras.note: The Helvetic Republic of 1798-1803 organised the area as cantons.
Ticino became a canton in 1803. Federal civil registers began on 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Tyrol and Vorarlberg — Innsbruck, Bregenz
regions.sub: Innsbruck, Bregenz, Kufstein, Landeck, Feldkirch

eras.polity: County of Tyrol under the House of Habsburg
eras.note: Tyrol passed to the Habsburgs in 1363. Church books also served as civil registers in Austria from 1784.
Tyrol and Vorarlberg were under Bavaria for about nine years before returning to Austria.

eras.polity: Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary — County of Tyrol and Vorarlberg
eras.note: Tyrol and Vorarlberg returned to Habsburg rule in 1814.

eras.polity: Republic of Austria — Tyrol and Vorarlberg
eras.note: The republic followed the Empire's collapse; civil registration offices replaced parish books in 1938-1939.

regions.label: Salzburg and Upper Austria — Salzburg, Linz
regions.sub: Salzburg, Linz, Wels, Steyr, Braunau

eras.polity: Archduchy of Austria above the Enns and the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg
eras.note: Salzburg was ruled by its prince-archbishops until the secularisation of 1803, while the Upper Austrian lands belonged to the Habsburgs.
The archbishopric was secularised in 1803 and the area changed hands during the Napoleonic wars.
Church books served as civil registers in Austria from 1784 to 1938.

eras.polity: Republic of Austria — Salzburg and Upper Austria
eras.note: The republic was proclaimed after the First World War.

eras.polity: Nazi Germany — Reichsgau Oberdonau and Salzburg
eras.note: Austria was annexed in 1938, and civil registration offices replaced church-book registers in 1938-1939.
Salzburg and Upper Austria are federal states of the Second Republic.

regions.label: Styria — Graz, Leoben, Maribor border
regions.sub: Graz, Leoben, Bruck an der Mur, Judenburg, Fürstenfeld

eras.polity: Duchy of Styria within the Holy Roman Empire
eras.note: Styria became a duchy in 1180 and passed to the Habsburgs in 1278.

eras.polity: Duchy of Styria under the Habsburgs
eras.note: The Habsburgs held Styria from 1278.

eras.polity: Austrian Empire and Austria-Hungary — Duchy of Styria
eras.note: Southern Styria was divided between Austria and Yugoslavia after 1918 and 1919.
Church books also served as civil registers until 1938, when civil offices took over.

regions.label: Upper Hungary — Slovakia (Bratislava, Košice, Banská Bystrica)
regions.sub: Bratislava, Košice, Prešov, Banská Bystrica, Nitra

eras.note: The area that is now Slovakia was the northern part of the Kingdom of Hungary, called Upper Hungary.

eras.polity: Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary — Upper Hungary
eras.note: Hungarian-kingdom records of these places are mostly filed under Hungarian place names.
Upper Hungary became part of Czechoslovakia after the First World War.
The wartime Slovak state existed from 1939 to 1945.
Czechoslovakia was restored in 1945 and divided at the end of 1992.
The Slovak Republic became independent on 1 January 1993.

regions.label: Zakarpattia (Carpathian Ruthenia) — Uzhhorod, Mukachevo
regions.sub: Uzhhorod, Mukachevo, Berehove, Khust, Rakhiv

eras.note: The region was part of the Kingdom of Hungary until 1918-1919.
The region joined Czechoslovakia after the First World War.
Hungary re-annexed the region in 1939.
The region was ceded to the Soviet Union by a treaty of 29 June 1945, and the oblast was formed on 22 January 1946.
The oblast has been part of independent Ukraine since 1991.

regions.label: Lithuania — Vilnius, Kaunas, Suwałki
regions.sub: Vilnius, Kaunas, Marijampolė, Alytus, Suwałki

eras.note: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania was a separate state before the union with Poland.
Lithuania and Poland were joined in the Commonwealth from 1569 until the partitions of 1795.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Vilna, Kovno and Suwałki governorates
eras.note: The area was divided among the Vilna and Suwałki governorates and neighbouring ones, so archive holdings follow the governorate.
Vilnius was held by the Republic of Central Lithuania and then Poland from 1920 to 1939.
The Soviet occupation began in 1940.
Lithuania restored its independence in 1990-1991.

regions.label: Courland — Liepāja (Latvia)
regions.sub: Liepāja, Kuldīga, Ventspils

eras.polity: Duchy of Courland and Semigallia under Polish-Lithuanian suzerainty
eras.note: The duchy existed from 1561 and ended with the partition of 1795.
Courland was annexed by Russia in 1795.
Latvia proclaimed independence on 18 November 1918; the Treaty of Riga with Soviet Russia was signed on 11 August 1920.
The Soviet occupation began in 1940.
Latvia restored its independence in 1991.

regions.label: Southern Warmia and Masuria (Poland)
regions.sub: Olsztyn, Mrągowo, Ełk

eras.polity: Royal Prussia and Warmia under the Polish crown
eras.note: Warmia was under Polish suzerainty after the Second Peace of Thorn of 1466.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia — Province of East Prussia
eras.note: Warmia passed to Prussia in the First Partition of 1772.

eras.polity: German Empire and Weimar Germany — East Prussia
eras.note: Prussian civil registers began on 1 October 1874 and Reich-wide registration on 1 January 1876.
The area came under Poland after the Second World War.

regions.label: Western Luxembourg and the 1839 border (Redange)
regions.sub: Redange, Arlon border, Martelange

eras.polity: Duchy of Luxembourg under the Habsburgs (Burgundian rule ended 1477)
eras.note: The country passed to the Habsburgs in 1477. Louis XIV invaded in 1684 and the Treaty of Ryswick (1697) returned the duchy to the Habsburgs.
Austrian rule lasted 1714-1795; the Treaty of Utrecht in 1715 confirmed Habsburg rule.
France annexed Luxembourg in 1795 as the Département des Forêts.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in personal union with the Netherlands
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna created the Grand Duchy in 1815 under William I. In 1830-1839 most of it was treated as a Belgian province.
The Treaty of London in 1839 ceded the predominantly French-speaking western part to Belgium. This ring lies along that border, so records of border villages may be in Luxembourg or Belgian archives.

regions.label: Komi Republic and Nenets — Syktyvkar, Ukhta, Naryan-Mar
regions.sub: Syktyvkar, Ukhta, Vorkuta, Naryan-Mar, Pechora

eras.note: Muscovy's control grew in the area by 1499, and Pustozyorsk became its administrative hub.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Komi AO (1921), Komi ASSR (1936), Nenets National Okrug (1929)
eras.note: The Komi Autonomous Oblast was created on 22 August 1921 and became an ASSR on 5 December 1936. The Nenets okrug was created on 15 July 1929, and Vorkuta moved to Komi on 23 November 1959.

eras.polity: Russian Federation — Komi Republic and Nenets Autonomous Okrug
eras.note: The Komi constitution dates from 17 February 1994.

regions.label: Yamalo-Nenets — Salekhard, Novy Urengoy
regions.sub: Salekhard, Novy Urengoy, Nadym

eras.note: Records of the Russian state apply here; the Yamalo-Nenets National Okrug was formed on 10 December 1930.
The okrug was formed in 1930.
The okrug remains an autonomous okrug of Russia.

regions.label: Galicia — A Coruña, Lugo, Santiago de Compostela
regions.sub: A Coruña, Lugo, Santiago, Ferrol

eras.polity: Kingdom of Galicia within the Crown of Castile
eras.note: The Kingdom of Galicia formed in 910 and came under the Crown of Castile in 1230 with Ferdinand III's accession; it was administered within Castile in 1490-1715.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Galicia within the Crown of Spain
eras.note: Galicia was administered within the Crown of Spain from 1715 until the kingdom was dissolved in 1833 (1834 depending on the source).

eras.polity: Spain — Galician provinces (A Coruña, Lugo, Ourense, Pontevedra)
eras.note: The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Western Castile and León — León, Zamora, Salamanca
regions.sub: León, Zamora, Salamanca, Astorga

eras.polity: Kingdom of León, permanently united with Castile on 10 Dec 1230
eras.note: The Kingdom of León was founded in 910 and permanently united with Castile on 10 December 1230; a brief reunion also occurred in 1301.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of León, Zamora and Salamanca (1833)
eras.note: The 1833 division created the modern provinces of León, Zamora and Salamanca. The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Extremadura — Cáceres, Badajoz, Mérida
regions.sub: Cáceres, Badajoz, Mérida, Plasencia

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — military orders hold about half the land
eras.note: Alfonso IX of León took Alcántara in 1214, Cáceres in 1227-1229, and Mérida and Badajoz in 1230; Trujillo fell in 1232 and Medellín in 1234, and the last fortresses in Lower Extremadura were taken by 1248. The Orders of Santiago and Alcántara held about half the territory by the late Middle Ages.

eras.polity: Spain — border region during the Portuguese Restoration War (1640-1668)
eras.note: The region suffered pillage, raids and destruction along the border in 1640-1668.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Cáceres and Badajoz; autonomous community (Statute dated 26 Feb 1983)
eras.note: The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Aragon — Zaragoza, Huesca, Teruel
regions.sub: Zaragoza, Huesca, Teruel, Calatayud

eras.note: The County of Aragon was linked to the Kingdom of Pamplona until 1035.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon (union with the County of Barcelona)
eras.note: The dynastic union with the County of Barcelona in 1137 gave rise to the Crown of Aragon.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon after the marriage of Ferdinand II and Isabella I (1469)
eras.note: The marriage of Ferdinand II and Isabella I in 1469 led to the union of the crowns.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Nueva Planta decrees abolish the fueros
eras.note: The Nueva Planta decrees dated 1707 abolished the fueros; Aragon and Valencia are dated to 1707 or 1712 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Huesca, Zaragoza and Teruel; autonomous community (1982)
eras.note: The 1833 provincial division created the three provinces. The Statute of Autonomy dates from August 1982 (10 or 16 August depending on the source). The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Córdoba and Jaén — Andalucía
regions.sub: Córdoba, Jaén, Úbeda, Baeza

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — conquest of Úbeda (1233) and Córdoba (1236)
eras.note: Ferdinand III took Úbeda in 1233 and the Córdoba medina in 1236.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Kingdoms of Córdoba and Jaén
eras.note: Jaén was taken in 1246; Ferdinand III used the royal title King of Córdoba from 1237 and King of Jaén from 1246.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Córdoba (royal decree of 30 Nov 1833) and Jaén
eras.note: The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Albacete and Alicante — Murcia and Valencia borderlands
regions.sub: Albacete, Alicante, Elche, Villena, Chinchilla

eras.polity: Castile (Albacete, 1240) and Aragon (Valencia) divided at Almizra
eras.note: Albacete capitulated to Ferdinand III in 1240. The Treaty of Almizra set the southern limit of Valencia with Castile, and the 1304-1305 agreements at Torrellas and Elche fixed the final border.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Valencia (Alicante, Crown of Aragon) and Kingdom of Murcia (Albacete, Crown of Castile)
eras.note: The Kingdom of Valencia lasted 1238-1707. The Kingdom of Murcia (1266-1833) belonged to the Crown of Castile and included parts of Albacete province, Villena and Sax.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Spain — Valencia ended in 1707 after Almansa
eras.note: The Kingdom of Valencia ended as a legal and political entity in 1707 after the Battle of Almansa.

eras.polity: Spain — provinces of Albacete and Alicante (1833)
eras.note: Albacete became a provincial capital in 1833. The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.

regions.label: Ceuta (autonomous city)
regions.sub: Ceuta

eras.note: Portugal conquered Ceuta in August 1415 (14 or 21 August depending on the passage) and the Treaties of Alcáçovas (1479) and Tordesillas (1494) recognised it as Portuguese.
Ceuta was integrated into the Hispanic Monarchy in 1580; after the Iberian union ended in 1640 it chose to stay under Spanish authority. The Treaty of Lisbon ceded it to Spain on 1 January 1668.
Ceuta remained Spanish after 1668. The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.
Ceuta became an autonomous city in 1995 (14 March).

regions.label: Melilla (autonomous city)
regions.sub: Melilla

eras.polity: Occupied for the Crown on 17 Sep 1497; administered with the Duke of Medina Sidonia
eras.note: Melilla was occupied on 17 September 1497 and initially administered jointly by the Duke's house and the Crown.

eras.polity: Spain — military garrison from 7 June 1556, in the province of Málaga
eras.note: The Duke gave up the garrison on 7 June 1556. Melilla was a municipality of the province of Málaga until 1995. The civil register law of 20 June 1870 took effect on 1 January 1871; earlier baptisms, marriages and burials are in parish books.
Melilla became an autonomous city with its Statute of Autonomy in 1995 (14 March).

regions.label: Central Sicily — Enna (Castrogiovanni)
regions.sub: Enna, Piazza Armerina, Leonforte

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily, later the Two Sicilies
eras.note: The Normans took Enna in 1087, and the town was called Castrogiovanni until it was renamed Enna in 1926 or 1927 depending on the passage. Sicilian civil registers date from 1820.
The town appears in records as Castrogiovanni in this period.
Mussolini ordered the renaming to Enna in 1927 (1926 depending on the source).

regions.label: Friuli and Gorizia — Udine, Pordenone, Gorizia
regions.sub: Udine, Pordenone, Gorizia, Trieste

eras.polity: Patriarchate of Aquileia and the County of Gorizia
eras.note: The Holy Roman Emperor recognised the territorial powers of the Patriarchate of Aquileia in 1077, and by the twelfth century the County of Gorizia was independent.

eras.polity: Venetian Friuli (Gorizia and Trieste remain Habsburg)
eras.note: Friuli became Venetian in 1420. Gorizia came under Habsburg dominance in 1500, and Trieste had done so in 1382.
The Treaty of Campo Formio ended Venetian rule and gave Friuli to the Habsburg Monarchy.
The Peace of Pressburg in 1805 transferred Friuli to the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy.

eras.polity: Austrian Empire — Lombardy-Venetia and the Austrian Littoral
eras.note: Austria held the region until the war of 1866.

eras.polity: Italy (western Friuli from 1866; Gorizia and Trieste later)
eras.note: The Treaty of Vienna of 3 October 1866 gave only western Friuli to Italy, so the eastern part of this ring stayed Austrian longer.

regions.label: Massa and Carrara — Lunigiana
regions.sub: Massa, Carrara, Pontremoli

eras.polity: Lordships of Massa and Carrara (united 1473), later Cybo-Malaspina
eras.note: The Lordship of Massa acquired Carrara on 22 February 1473, and in 1568 Maximilian II made Massa a marquisate and Carrara a principality.

eras.polity: Duchy of Massa and Carrara (from 1664), Este influence from 1741
eras.note: Leopold I raised Massa to a duchy on 22 February 1664.

eras.polity: French rule, then Lucca and Piombino (1806)
eras.note: French troops took the territory in May 1796, and in 1806 Napoleon assigned it to the Principality of Lucca and Piombino.

eras.polity: Este Duchy of Modena and Reggio
eras.note: Maria Beatrice d'Este regained the duchy in 1814-1815, and her son annexed it to Modena in 1829.
After Francis V was deposed, the Modena territories including Massa and Carrara were annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1859-1860.

regions.label: Rieti and the Sabina
regions.sub: Rieti, Antrodoco, Poggio Mirteto

eras.note: Rieti became a free commune in 1198; after the papacy moved to Avignon the King of Naples conquered it, and Cardinal Albornoz won it back in 1354.
Rieti was the Papal States' province capital in 1816-1860.
After unification Rieti was initially part of Umbria.
Rieti was annexed to Lazio in 1923 and became provincial capital on 2 January 1927.

regions.label: Salerno and the Cilento
regions.sub: Salerno, Vallo della Lucania, Eboli

eras.polity: Norman and later Neapolitan kingdom — Principato Citeriore
eras.note: Salerno declared independence from Benevento in 839 and fell to the Normans after 1077. Charles I of Anjou granted the Principality of Salerno in 1272, and the city was capital of the Principato Citeriore from the thirteenth to the nineteenth century.
Joseph Bonaparte and then Joachim Murat ruled Naples; Antenati dates the mainland civil registers from 1809.
Many Salernitans joined Garibaldi in 1861.
Operation Avalanche landed near Salerno in September 1943.

regions.label: The Senj and Vinodol coast
regions.sub: Senj, Novi Vinodolski, Crikvenica, Kraljevica, Bakar, Vinodol

eras.polity: Frankopan counts of Krk (Vinodol, Senj), later Zrinski lords at Bakar; Senj captaincy from 1469
eras.note: The Vinodol Statute was drawn up in 1288 at Novi (Novigrad) for the Frankopan counts of Krk, who made Novi the centre of Vinodol. Vinodol was split in 1577: the north around Bakar went to the Zrinski and the south around Bribir stayed Frankopan; Novi returned to the Frankopan line in 1580. Senj passed from the Templars to the Frankopans in 1269-71, was taken by Matthias Corvinus's forces in 1469 and became the seat of the Senj captaincy, and was held by the Uskoks from 1537 to 1618.

eras.polity: Habsburg crown lands; Senj under the Military Frontier (Otočac regiment)
eras.note: After the Zrinski-Frankopan conspiracy (executions 30 April 1671) their estates were confiscated; Bakar passed to the Court Chamber. Senj's Primorska krajina was abolished in 1746 and Senj went to the Otočac regiment, so its records follow the Military Frontier, not a county. The coast's status moved repeatedly and the sources disagree on the dates: Austrian Littoral from 1749 (Bakar) or 1754 (Vinodol), Bakar back to Croatia in 1777 and a free royal city in 1779, the Vinodol coast under Hungarian administration at Rijeka in 1786. The Kotor-Crikvenica parish register was kept 1735-1793.

eras.polity: French Empire, Illyrian Provinces (Civil and Military Croatia)
eras.note: The Treaty of Schönbrunn (14 October 1809) gave France the Croatian lands south-west of the Sava, which became the Illyrian Provinces; Senj and Vinodol are described as under French rule 1809-1813, which ruined Bakar's maritime trade. Austrian forces retook the region in 1813.

eras.polity: Austrian Empire: the Littoral under the ban from 1822; Senj in the Otočac regiment
eras.note: Rijeka and Civil Croatia were restored to the Kingdom of Croatia in 1822; Bakar was placed under the ban that year, and Vinodol was attached to the Rijeka governorate, with Croatian state authority there dated to 1848 after Jelačić took charge of Rijeka. Senj stayed in the Otočac regiment of the Military Frontier. Records of this period are largely in Latin, German and Italian, and German, Hungarian and Croatian in the second half of the century.

eras.polity: Croatia-Slavonia within the Hungarian crown; Modruš-Rijeka and Lika-Krbava counties
eras.note: The 1868 Croatian-Hungarian Settlement created the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. Senj came out of the Military Frontier in 1871 (1881 in some sources, when the Frontier was dissolved as a whole) and was placed in Lika-Krbava county. The 1886 county reform put Crikvenica, Bakar and Novi in Modruš-Rijeka county (seat Ogulin). Fiume itself was a separate Hungarian corpus separatum.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes; Kingdom of Yugoslavia (Primorje-Krajina oblast, Sava and Croatian banovinas)
eras.note: The Treaty of Rapallo (12 November 1920) left Sušak with the Kingdom across the Rječina from the Free State of Fiume, and Fiume went to Italy in 1924; Bakar and the coast east of the river stayed Yugoslav. The coast was in the Primorje-Krajina oblast (seat Karlovac) from 1922, the Sava Banovina 1929-31 and the Banovina of Croatia from 1939 (dated by source).

eras.polity: Independent State of Croatia under Italian zones; Bakar in the Italian Province of Fiume
eras.note: By the Treaties of Rome (18 May 1941) Italy annexed Sušak and Bakar to the Province of Fiume (Bakar as Buccari). The NDH formed the great county of Podgorje, seated at Senj, although Italy effectively controlled the area; Italian forces took over civil and military administration of the coastal Zone II on 7 September 1941. After the 1943 Italian armistice German forces occupied the Province of Fiume, and Partisans took control of Senj in 1943.

eras.polity: Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, SR Croatia
eras.note: Universal civil registration by civil authorities began in Croatia in May 1946, so earlier vital records are the Church registers; registers over 100 years old were passed to archives from 1957. Sušak and Rijeka merged in 1948, and Bakar later became part of Rijeka municipality. The Senj-Modruš diocese merged into the Rijeka archdiocese in 1969.

eras.polity: Republic of Croatia (Primorje-Gorski Kotar and Lika-Senj counties)
eras.note: The Državni arhiv u Rijeci covers Primorje-Gorski Kotar county and the city of Senj, although Senj lies in Lika-Senj county; Bakar, Crikvenica, Kraljevica, Novi Vinodolski, Senj and Vinodol municipality are among its listed record creators. Bakar and Kostrena became separate municipalities in 1992. Senj's diocese is Gospić-Senj since 2000; many registers remain with the parishes and the Archdiocese of Rijeka.

regions.label: The Galápagos Islands
regions.sub: Puerto Ayora, Puerto Baquerizo Moreno, Puerto Villamil, Floreana, Isabela

eras.note: The islands were found on 10 March 1535 when the ship of the bishop Tomás de Berlanga drifted off course in a calm; the ship left them unclaimed and unsettled.

eras.polity: Ecuador - Floreana settlement, penal colony and the first colonies
eras.note: Ecuador formally claimed the islands on 12 February 1832, with an annexation ceremony on Floreana; José de Villamil's settlement there reached about 120 people by October 1832 and he became the first governor. The islands were named a penal colony in March 1833; a colony of 21 was founded on Santa Cruz in 1837, an uprising in 1841 sent most settlers back to the mainland, and Villamil abandoned his rebuilding attempt in 1848.

eras.polity: Ecuador - civil registration and the wartime airfield
eras.note: Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths began in Ecuador in 1900; the books are held by the municipal civil-registration office, with copies at the Dirección General del Registro Civil in Quito. In the 1930s the United States built the islands' first airport (Seymour) as a base protecting the western approaches to the Panama Canal, and its facilities passed to Ecuador after the Second World War.
The Galápagos became a province of Ecuador on 18 February 1973. The islands have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1978.

regions.label: San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina
regions.sub: San Andrés, Providencia, Santa Catalina, Old Providence

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - claimed 1510, Captaincy General of Guatemala from 1544
eras.note: Spain formally claimed the archipelago in 1510 and in 1544 placed it under the Captaincy General of Guatemala.

eras.polity: English Puritan colony of Providence Island (Providence Island Company)
eras.note: English Puritans settled Providence Island in 1630 under the Providence Island Company; the colony ran plantations worked by enslaved people and engaged in privateering. Spanish and Portuguese forces conquered it in May 1641.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Captaincy General of Guatemala
eras.note: The islands returned to Spanish control. Henry Morgan's English buccaneers held them from 1670 to 1672 and used them as a base to attack Panama.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Viceroyalty of New Granada, administered from Cartagena
eras.note: In 1803 Spain assigned the islands to the Viceroyalty of New Granada, administered from Cartagena. Louis-Michel Aury captured Old Providence and Santa Catalina on 4 July 1818.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia, then Colombia - Magdalena Department
eras.note: The islands voluntarily joined Gran Colombia in 1822 and were placed under the Magdalena Department; Gran Colombia dissolved on 19 November 1831. Before 1960 the population was almost entirely Raizal, speaking San Andrés-Providencia Creole, with a minority of English-speaking white Protestants of British descent.

eras.polity: Colombia - Intendencia of San Andrés and Providencia
eras.note: Colombia established an intendencia in the islands in 1912. The Esguerra-Bárcenas treaty of 1928, finally ratified in 1930, gave Colombia control of the islands in agreement with Nicaragua; Nicaragua later repudiated it.

eras.polity: Colombia - Department of San Andrés, Providencia and Santa Catalina
eras.note: The archipelago became a department in July 1991 (4 July in one entry). The International Court of Justice ruled on 13 December 2007, and again on 19 November 2012, that the islands are Colombian territory; Raizals were about 30% of the 60,000 or more inhabitants in 2005.

regions.label: Darién and the Emberá-Wounaan comarca
regions.sub: Darién, Pinogana, Yaviza, Embera lands

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Tierra Firme and the Darién coast
eras.note: Santa María la Antigua del Darién was founded in September 1510 west of the Gulf of Urabá, the first city founded on Tierra Firme. Balboa sighted the South Sea from the isthmus on 25 September 1513.

eras.polity: Scottish colony of New Caledonia (the Darien scheme)
eras.note: The first Scottish expedition left Leith on 14 July 1698, landed on 30 October 1698 and founded New Caledonia at Acla; disease forced its abandonment in June 1699. A second expedition arrived on 30 November 1699, and on 28 March 1700 the colonists asked the Spanish commander for surrender terms.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Panama within the Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: The Viceroyalty of New Granada was created on 27 May 1717, suspended in 1723 and re-established on 20 August 1739, when Panama was incorporated into it. Panama gained independence from Spain on 28 November 1821.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia, then Colombia - Department of the Isthmus, State of Panama, Panama Department
eras.note: Panama joined Gran Colombia in 1821; under centralism it was the Department of the Isthmus, under federalism the State of Panama, and from 1886 the Panama Department of Colombia. A short-lived independent republic existed in 1840-41, and Darién Province is listed as founded in 1822.

Panama declared independence from Colombia on 3 November 1903, and Colombia recognised it on 7 January 1909. Civil registration began on 15 April 1914, kept at first by district mayors; the Dirección Nacional del Registro Civil under the Tribunal Electoral was created in 1974.

eras.polity: Republic of Panama - Emberá-Wounaan comarca and Darién Province
eras.note: The Emberá-Wounaan comarca was established out of Darién Province on 8 November 1983; the Guna de Wargandí comarca followed in 2000 inside Pinogana District.

regions.label: Nunavut and the Arctic islands
regions.sub: Iqaluit, Rankin Inlet, Cambridge Bay, Pond Inlet, Resolute, Grise Fiord

eras.note: Martin Frobisher's 1576 account is the earliest written record of the area. The Thule people began migrating in the 11th century, and by 1300 their settlement included most of modern Nunavut.

eras.polity: Rupert's Land - Hudson's Bay Company (Hudson Bay drainage)
eras.note: Charles II's charter of 1670 gave the Hudson's Bay Company trading rights over the Hudson Bay drainage basin, known as Rupert's Land. The Company surrendered its charter on 19 November 1869 and Canada assumed control on 15 July 1870.

eras.polity: Canada - Northwest Territories (districts of Keewatin, Franklin and Mackenzie)
eras.note: Before 1999 the area lay in the Northwest Territories districts of Franklin, Keewatin and Mackenzie; in 1912 territory around Hudson Bay passed from Keewatin to Manitoba and Ontario. From the 1940s Inuit were tracked by identification-disc numbers carrying a letter for region (E for the Eastern Arctic, W for the Western), and in 1953-55 the federal government relocated Inuit from Nunavik to Resolute and Grise Fiord.

eras.polity: Canada - Northwest Territories, Project Surname and the division plebiscite
eras.note: Project Surname (1968-71), led by Abe Okpik, visited 55 settlements to record family surnames; Inuit had not used family surnames before it, and surnames eventually replaced disc numbers. A plebiscite on dividing the territory was held on 14 April 1982, the Nunavut land claims agreement was ratified in September 1992, and Parliament passed the Nunavut Act on 9 July 1993.
Nunavut was separated from the Northwest Territories on 1 April 1999. A devolution agreement giving the territory control of its lands and resources was signed on 18 January 2024.

regions.label: Nord-du-Québec - James Bay, Nunavik and the north shore interior
regions.sub: Radisson, Chisasibi, Kuujjuaq, Inukjuak, Schefferville

eras.note: England claimed the territory in 1670 as Rupert's Land, which the Hudson's Bay Company held under its charter. Its Indigenous peoples are the Cree, Montagnais, Naskapi and Inuit.
Canada took control of Rupert's Land on 15 July 1870. The northernmost part of this region was the Ungava District of the North-West Territories until 1912.

eras.polity: Canada - North-West Territories, Quebec's boundaries first extended
eras.note: The Quebec Boundary Extension Act, 1898 gave Quebec its first enlargement into the North-West Territories; the Ungava district was still outside the province.

eras.polity: Canada - Province of Quebec (Ungava added in 1912)
eras.note: The Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1 April 1912 moved Quebec's northern boundary to its present line and transferred the Ungava district (bounded by the Eastmain River, the Labrador coast and Hudson and Ungava Bays), but not the offshore islands. Inuit in Nunavik were given family surnames under Project Surname in 1968-71, and in 1953-55 families were relocated from Nunavik to Resolute and Grise Fiord.

eras.polity: Canada - Quebec, the James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement territory
eras.note: The James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement of 1975 covers the Cree territory (Eeyou Istchee) and Kativik (Nunavik, north of the 55th parallel, predominantly Inuit). The administrative region was called Nouveau-Québec until 1987.

regions.label: Mimaropa - Mindoro, Palawan and Romblon
regions.sub: Calapan, San Jose, Puerto Princesa, Coron, Romblon

eras.polity: Before registers. Pre-Spanish Mindoro and Palawan
eras.note: Antonio Pigafetta recorded Palawan as 'Pulaoan' in 1521, during Magellan's expedition. A Chinese record of 972 mentions Mindoro (Ma-i) as a trading state, and Brunei had Moro settlements on Mindoro before the Spanish arrived.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines - missions and garrisons against Moro raids
eras.note: Spanish friars began missions at Cuyo, Agutaya, Taytay and Cagayancillo in the early 17th century, and churches enclosed by garrisons were built at Cuyo, Taytay, Linapacan and Balabac against Moro raids. Mindoro, which the Spanish called Mina de Oro, lost much of its population to Moro-Spanish wars, and most residents fled to Batangas.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines - Calamianes, Isla de Paragua and Mindoro
eras.note: In 1749 the Sultanate of Brunei ceded southern Palawan to Spain. The Spanish census of 1818 recorded Palawan as the Isla de Paragua under the Calamianes jurisdiction, with Taytay as the capital of the Province of Calamianes, and recorded 47 Spanish-Filipino families on Mindoro.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines - Castilla and Asturias, Mindoro
eras.note: In 1858 Palawan was split into Castilla in the north (capital Taytay) and Asturias in the south (capital Puerto Princesa). In 1889 the Spanish government created the Central Office of Statistics and parish priests had to submit lists of births, marriages and deaths; most vital records from before 1889 come from Catholic parish and diocesan archives.

eras.polity: American Philippines - Palawan, Mindoro and Romblon
eras.note: After the 1898 Revolution church and state were separated and civil registration officials were appointed in each municipality; registration became mandatory in 1930, but most births were recorded only from 1940. The United States set up civil rule in northern Palawan in 1902, Act No. 1363 of 1905 renamed the province Palawan with Puerto Princesa as capital, and Mindoro was a single province, with Calapan as capital, from 1920 to 1950. About 150 prisoners of war were killed at Puerto Princesa on 14 December 1944, and Palawan was liberated between 28 February and 22 April 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of the Philippines - Occidental and Oriental Mindoro, Palawan, Romblon
eras.note: Mindoro was divided into Occidental and Oriental Mindoro by Republic Act No. 505 (dated 13 June 1950), and Presidential Decree No. 1 of 1972 moved Romblon from Western Visayas to Southern Tagalog. Executive Order No. 103 of 17 May 2002 created Region IV-B (Mimaropa); Palawan was moved to Western Visayas by Executive Order 429 on 23 May 2005, which was put in abeyance on 19 August 2005, and Republic Act No. 10879 of 17 July 2016 established the Mimaropa Region with no boundary changes.

regions.label: The Argentine Gran Chaco - Chaco, Formosa and the north of Santa Fe
regions.sub: Resistencia, Formosa, Clorinda, Presidencia Roque Sáenz Peña

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - the Chaco frontier and Concepción del Bermejo
eras.note: In 1585 Alonso de Vera y Aragón founded Concepción de Nuestra Señora (Concepción del Bermejo), the first European settlement, abandoned in 1632; a Jesuit mission, San Fernando del Río Negro, was founded near modern Resistencia in the 17th century and abandoned fifteen years later. The Pilagá, Wichí and Toba peoples are recorded as the native inhabitants of Formosa.
After Argentine and Paraguayan independence in the 1810s the area was disputed between the two countries, a dispute settled only after the War of the Triple Alliance (1865-70).

eras.polity: Argentina - Territorio Nacional del Gran Chaco
eras.note: The Territorio Nacional del Gran Chaco was established in 1872. San Fernando was re-established as a military outpost named Resistencia in 1876 (1878 in some accounts), and Luis Jorge Fontana founded Formosa in 1879.

eras.polity: Argentina - national territories of Chaco and Formosa
eras.note: The Territorio Nacional del Chaco replaced the Gran Chaco territory in 1884, and Formosa gained territorial status the same year. Argentine civil registration began in 1886 and was running in most provinces by 1900; the original books stay in the local civil-registration office, with duplicates in the provincial or judicial archive. In 1947 the Gendarmería carried out the Rincón Bomba massacre of nomadic Indigenous people in Formosa.

eras.polity: Argentina - provinces of Chaco and Formosa
eras.note: Chaco became a province on 8 August 1951 as Presidente Perón and took the name Chaco again in 1955; Formosa became a province by decree in 1955. The southern strip of this ring is the north of Santa Fe province, covered under the Santa Fe region.

regions.label: Northern La Pampa - the Pampa frontier
regions.sub: Santa Rosa, General Pico, Realicó, Victorica

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Pampa frontier, Indigenous land
eras.note: Hernando Arias de Saavedra reached the area in 1604 and Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera explored it in 1662; Spanish colonists made no permanent settlements until the 18th century.

Resistance by the local Indigenous people limited expansion until the government of Juan Manuel de Rosas, and continued until Julio Roca's campaign in the 19th century. The territory was then divided among officers, who founded the first Argentine settlements.

eras.polity: Argentina - Territorio Nacional de La Pampa Central
eras.note: The Territorio Nacional de La Pampa Central, established in 1884, included present-day Río Negro Province and parts of surrounding provinces, with about 25,000 inhabitants rising to about 110,000 by 1915.

A provincial constitution was written in 1952 and the province was renamed after Eva Perón until 1955, when it reverted to La Pampa. Provincial status is dated 1945 in one source, so the date it became a province is contested.

regions.label: Orinoquia - Arauca, Vichada, Guainía and Venezuela's Amazonas
regions.sub: Arauca, Puerto Carreño, Inírida, Puerto Ayacucho, San Fernando de Atabapo

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - the llanos and the Orinoco missions
eras.note: Nikolaus Federmann is the first conquistador recorded in the Arauca area, in 1539, and Catholic missions founded settlements among the Guahibo, U'wa and other peoples from 1659. On the Venezuelan side Ignacio Fiol established the locality of Atures in 1682; some chronicles date the discovery of the Casiquiare to 1639.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Viceroyalty of New Granada and Captaincy General of Venezuela
eras.note: The Venezuelan provinces were separated from New Granada into the Captaincy General of Venezuela on 8 September 1777. After the Jesuits left, Augustinian Recollects founded five catechism centres including San Fernando de Arauca; Arauca joined the new province of Casanare in 1810 and was provisional capital of the Republic in 1818.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia - Casanare and the Orinoco
eras.note: Gran Colombia was proclaimed at Angostura on 17 December 1819 and its constitution adopted at Cúcuta on 30 August 1821; in 1819 Casanare, with Arauca, became part of the Department of Cundinamarca. Gran Colombia dissolved on 19 November 1831, and Arauca remained in the province of Casanare.

eras.polity: Colombia and Venezuela, now separate - Arauca in Boyacá, Venezuela's Territory Amazonas
eras.note: Arauca became part of the Department of Boyacá in 1886. In Venezuela the district of Río Negro was created on 20 August 1841, the name Amazonas was assigned on 2 June 1856, it became a federal territory in 1864, was divided in 1881 and reunited in 1893. Colombian civil registration began in 1865 and was fully adopted by 1888; Venezuela's civil registers are dated 1865 or 1873 depending on the source, and before 1873 only the Church recorded baptisms, marriages and burials.

eras.polity: Colombia - commissaries of Arauca, Vichada and Guainía; Venezuela's Territorio Amazonas
eras.note: Colombia created a Special Commissioner of Arauca in 1911 and the commissary of Vichada in 1913, and Guainía was separated from Vaupés as a commissary in 1963. Venezuela moved the capital of Amazonas to Puerto Ayacucho in 1928, and Colombian law 92 of 1938 made civil registration an exclusive State responsibility.

eras.polity: Colombia - departments of Arauca and Vichada; Venezuela's Amazonas State
eras.note: Arauca and Vichada became departments under the Constitution of 5 July 1991. Venezuela's Amazonas became a state in 1992, although one entry gives 1994.

regions.label: Colombian Amazonia - Caquetá, Putumayo, Vaupés and Amazonas
regions.sub: Florencia, Mocoa, Mitú, Leticia, Puerto Leguízamo

eras.note: The Spanish invaded the Putumayo area in 1542, and Catholic missions began administering it in 1547. During Spanish colonisation and the early republic the territory formed part of the Province of Popayán.

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Viceroyalty of New Granada
eras.note: The Viceroyalty of New Granada was suspended on 5 November 1723 and re-established on 20 August 1739, with the territory still part of the Province of Popayán.

eras.polity: Gran Colombia, then Colombia - Popayán, Caquetá territory and Cauca
eras.note: From 1831 the area appears under Popayán Province and under the National Territory of Caquetá (1831-57); in 1857 it passed to the Federal State (Sovereign State) of Cauca and in 1886 to the Department of Cauca. The rubber industry brought colonisers who altered, and in some cases wiped out, most of the Indigenous population of the Vaupés.

The Intendencia del Putumayo dates from 1905 and the Intendencia del Caquetá from 1909 (the Caquetá entry gives 1905, so the dates conflict); the Vaupés was organised as commissaries in 1910 with Calamar as first capital, and the Comisaría Especial del Putumayo followed in 1912. The Salomón-Lozano treaty of 24 March 1922 transferred the Leticia district to Colombia, and Amazonas was an intendancy from 1931.

eras.polity: Colombia - the Leticia Incident and war with Peru
eras.note: A civilian takeover of Leticia on 1 September 1932 led to an undeclared war between Colombia and Peru that lasted until 24 May 1933, with a League of Nations commission taking Leticia over. The Rio de Janeiro Protocol, signed in 1934, reaffirmed the Salomón-Lozano treaty.

The Comisaría Especial del Putumayo was restored in 1957 and became an Intendencia Especial in 1968. After La Violencia (1948-58) migrants settled the unclaimed lands of Caquetá, which became a department in 1981; Law 92 of 1938 had made civil registration an exclusive State responsibility.

eras.polity: Colombia - departments of Putumayo, Amazonas, Vaupés and Caquetá
eras.note: Vaupés was established as a department on 4 July 1991 under the 1991 Constitution; Putumayo and Amazonas are also listed as departments from 1991, and Caquetá had been one since 1981.

regions.label: Peruvian Amazonia - Loreto and Ucayali
regions.sub: Iquitos, Pucallpa, Yurimaguas, Requena, Contamana

eras.polity: Spanish Empire - Maynas missions, Audiencia of Quito
eras.note: Jesuit, Dominican and Franciscan missionaries worked in the area from Moyobamba, and Iquitos is said to have been founded in the 1750s.

eras.polity: Spanish Peru, then Peru - General Command of Maynas and Quixos
eras.note: A royal decree of 1802 created the General Command of Maynas and Quixos, separating the territory from the Audiencia of Quito and returning it to Peru.

The Department of Loreto was created on 7 September 1866 with its capital at Moyobamba, and the late 19th-century rubber boom made Iquitos a major latex export centre. Most Peruvian municipalities began recording deaths in 1857 and births and marriages in 1886, the 1892 Civil Law made registration mandatory, and the Supreme Court in Lima holds duplicates.
Ecuadorian claims led to a full-scale war in 1941 over the region. The Peru-Ecuador dispute is recorded as ending in 1999.

The province of Coronel Portillo was separated from Loreto in 1980 to form the Department of Ucayali (another entry gives an establishment date of 18 June 1890), so Ucayali places before that belong to Loreto.

regions.label: Madre de Dios and Pando - the rubber frontier
regions.sub: Puerto Maldonado, Cobija, Salvación, Iberia, Manu

eras.note: Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald (1862-1897), a rubber baron from Iquitos, is the figure associated with the Madre de Dios basin; the Isthmus of Fitzcarrald, a low range, separates the Madre de Dios River from the Urubamba and Ucayali basins. In the late 19th century an estimated 15,000 to 60,000 settlers, mostly Brazilian, moved into neighbouring Acre as rubber prices rose.

Bolivia set up a customs post at Puerto Alonso on 2 January 1899, which provoked the Acre revolts, and on 11 June 1901 it leased Acre to the Bolivian Syndicate. A Bolivian force under President Pando took the confluence where the Manuripe and Tahuamanu rivers meet to form the Orton.

eras.polity: Bolivia and Peru after the Treaty of Petrópolis
eras.note: Under the Treaty of Petrópolis (17 November 1903 in one account; a ratification date of 11 November is also given, so the dates conflict) Bolivia ceded Acre to Brazil in return for Brazilian territory, a payment of £2 million and a railway promise. Puerto Maldonado is recorded as founded in 1902.

eras.polity: Peru - Department of Madre de Dios; Bolivia - Acre remnant
eras.note: Peru created the Department of Madre de Dios by law on 26 December 1912, with Puerto Maldonado as capital; in 1915 it produced 23% of Peru's rubber, and workers left in thousands when the boom collapsed. Peruvian municipal civil registration began in 1886 for births and marriages.

eras.polity: Peru - Madre de Dios; Bolivia - Pando Department
eras.note: Bolivia's Pando Department, named for President José Manuel Pando, has an establishment date of 24 September 1938 and was organised from what remained of the Acre Territory, with Cobija as capital. In Madre de Dios, gold mining along the Inambari and Madre de Dios rivers is the main industry after the rubber collapse.

regions.label: Manchuria: Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang
regions.sub: Shenyang, Harbin, Changchun, Dalian, Jilin

eras.polity: Later Jin, the Manchu state, which became the Qing
eras.note: Nurhaci founded the Later Jin in 1616; it was later known as the Qing, and the Qing began to rule all China in 1644.
The Willow Palisade, built in 1681, was meant to restrict Han migration into the homeland.

eras.polity: Qing: the three eastern provinces (Fengtian, Jilin, Heilongjiang)
eras.note: Jilin and Heilongjiang were separated in 1683 and, with Fengtian, formed the three eastern provinces. The Treaty of Aigun (1858) and the Treaty of Peking (1860) moved the Russian frontier, so places on the Amur and Ussuri sides now lie in Russia.
