eras.polity: Qing: Russian and Japanese influence in the three eastern provinces
eras.note: Russia gained the right to build the Chinese Eastern Railway in 1896, and Japan replaced Russian influence in southern Manchuria after the war of 1904-1905. Jilin and Heilongjiang gained full provincial status in 1907.
The Republic was proclaimed on 1 January 1912. Zhang Zuolin was assassinated in 1928 and Japan staged the Mukden incident in 1931.
Manchukuo was founded in 1932 under Puyi as emperor. Soviet forces invaded in August 1945 and left in spring 1946.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Soviet withdrawal and civil war
eras.note: Fighting between the Nationalists and the Communists resumed in 1946 and the Communists won in 1949.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang
eras.note: The People's Republic was proclaimed on 1 October 1949.

regions.label: Northern China: Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei, Shanxi and Inner Mongolia
regions.sub: Beijing, Tianjin, Shijiazhuang, Taiyuan, Hohhot

eras.note: Beiping was renamed Beijing in 1403 and the Yongle Emperor moved the capital there from Nanjing in 1421. The surrounding region was known as Beizhili (North Zhili).

eras.polity: Qing: Zhili ("directly ruled") and the Mongol banners
eras.note: North Zhili became simply Zhili in 1644. A household law of 1644 had each household keep a board listing its members, and a regulation of 1758 required a yearly door sign with the owner's name, age, occupation and household size. Inner Mongolia was organised into six leagues and the Chahar Mongols were placed under direct imperial control as the Eight Banners of Chahar after the revolt of 1675.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Beiyang government at Beijing
eras.note: The Beiyang government in Beijing was the internationally recognised government until 1928. The Republic reorganised Inner Mongolia into the provinces of Rehe, Chahar and Suiyuan.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Nanjing government; Zhili becomes Hebei
eras.note: When Nanjing became the capital in 1928, Zhili province was abolished and renamed Hebei; Beijing had been part of the province until then. Rehe was incorporated into Manchukuo in 1933.

eras.polity: Second Sino-Japanese War: Japanese occupation and Mengjiang
eras.note: Full-scale war began in 1937. On 8 December 1937 Demchugdongrub declared Mengjiang, covering the provinces of Suiyuan and Chahar.
The Inner Mongolian People's Republic existed from 9 September to 6 November 1945, and the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region was established in 1947.

Rehe province was dissolved in 1955 and parts of it joined Hebei; Tianjin was part of Hebei from 1954 to 1967. Much of Inner Mongolia was divided among neighbouring provinces in 1969, a division reversed in 1979. The household register (hukou) in its present form dates from the 1958 regulation and records births, deaths, marriages, divorces and moves.

regions.label: Shandong and Henan: the Yellow River plain
regions.sub: Jinan, Qingdao, Zhengzhou, Kaifeng, Luoyang

eras.polity: Late Ming and early Qing: the wars in Henan
eras.note: The wars of the late Ming and early Qing years devastated Henan; the span is given as about 1630 to 1662.
In Shandong, the Yellow River has reached the sea on the northern coast since 1855. In Henan, a dike breach near Zhengzhou in 1887 caused a flood disaster.

eras.polity: Qing: German leasehold at Jiaozhou Bay and British Weihaiwei
eras.note: Germany leased Jiaozhou Bay and Qingdao after 1898 and Britain received Weihaiwei in 1898. The Boxer uprising began in Shandong, and Yuan Shikai was appointed governor in 1899 to suppress it.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Shandong and Henan
eras.note: Japan took the German holdings in Shandong during the First World War, and China regained Weihaiwei in 1930. The Huji Law of 1911 was the first formal codification of household registration.

Japan invaded again in 1937 and its forces crossed the Yellow River into Shandong. In Henan, Japanese forces captured Kaifeng in 1938; the Huayuankou dam was breached to slow them, flooding Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu, and famine followed in 1942-1943.
The People's Liberation Army entered Qingdao on 2 June 1949 and the Communists controlled all Shandong by August 1949.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Shandong and Henan
eras.note: Pingyuan province, which had included northern Henan, was abolished in 1952, and Henan's capital moved from Kaifeng to Zhengzhou in 1954.

regions.label: Jiangnan: Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang
regions.sub: Nanjing, Shanghai, Hangzhou, Suzhou, Ningbo, Hefei

eras.note: The Qing renamed the former Nanzhili as Jiangnan province.

Jiangsu and Anhui were separated into distinct provinces in 1666. Printed clan genealogies (jiapu, zupu) survive in public collections in mainland China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Japan and the United States; many were destroyed in the Cultural Revolution.

eras.polity: Qing: treaty ports and the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
eras.note: The Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842) opened Shanghai and Ningbo among five treaty ports. The Taiping rebellion lasted from 1851 to 1864 and by 1853 the Taipings had made Nanjing their capital, Tianjing.
The Republic was established on 1 January 1912, and the Beiyang government in Beijing held until 1928.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Nanjing as the capital
eras.note: Chiang Kai-shek set up a government in Nanjing in April 1927, and it was the capital of the Republic. Shanghai was split off from Jiangsu as a separate municipality in 1927.

eras.polity: Republic of China: war with Japan and civil war
eras.note: The government moved inland after the full-scale war began in 1937. Henan, Anhui and Jiangsu were flooded in 1938 after the Huayuankou dam was breached.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Jiangsu, Anhui, Shanghai and Zhejiang
eras.note: The People's Republic was proclaimed on 1 October 1949.

regions.label: The Middle Yangtze: Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi
regions.sub: Wuhan, Changsha, Nanchang, Yichang, Jiujiang

eras.polity: Qing: Hubei and Hunan (formerly Huguang) and Jiangxi
eras.note: The Qing took control in 1644 and Huguang was soon split into Hubei and Hunan; the year of the split is uncertain.

eras.polity: Wuchang Uprising and the early Republic
eras.note: The Wuchang Uprising of 1911 in present-day Wuhan began the Xinhai Revolution. Hankou was part of Hubei until 1927. The Old Guangxi clique later overran Hunan and Guangdong.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Wuhan and the Nationalist government
eras.note: In 1927 Wuhan became the seat of a left-wing Kuomintang government.
After the full-scale war with Japan began in 1937, the government moved inland, first to Wuhan and then to Chongqing.
Japan surrendered in 1945 and the Nationalists and the Communists fought a renewed civil war from 1946.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Hubei, Hunan and Jiangxi
eras.note: The People's Republic was proclaimed on 1 October 1949.

regions.label: The South-East Coast: Fujian, Guangdong and Hainan
regions.sub: Guangzhou, Fuzhou, Xiamen, Shantou, Haikou, Macau and Hong Kong

eras.polity: Ming: Fujian and Guangdong provinces; Hainan under Guangdong
eras.note: Fujian became a province with Fuzhou as its seat after the Ming was founded, and Hainan was placed under Guangdong administration in the Ming period.

eras.polity: Ming: Macau, the first European settlement in the province
eras.note: Macau became the first European settlement in Guangdong in 1557.

eras.polity: Qing: the sea trade ban and Koxinga
eras.note: The early Qing imposed a sea trade ban of about twenty years under the Kangxi Emperor to cut off Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga), whose regime was based in Taiwan.
The Qing took Taiwan in 1683 and placed it under Fujian as Taiwan Prefecture; Fujian and Taiwan were separated into two provinces in 1885-1887.

eras.polity: Qing: treaty ports and Hong Kong
eras.note: The Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842) ceded Hong Kong Island to Britain and opened Canton, Xiamen and Fuzhou among five ports; Kowloon was added in 1860 and the New Territories were leased in 1898. Hong Kong birth and death registration began in 1842 but was required by law only from 1883.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Guangdong as the Kuomintang base
eras.note: Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit within Guangdong in 1912. A short-lived Fujian People's Government existed in 1933-1934, and Japan attacked Hainan in 1939 and held part of it until 1945.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Fujian, Guangdong and Hainan
eras.note: The People's Republic took most of Fujian on 17 August 1949, while Kinmen and Matsu remained under the Republic of China. Hainan was taken in April-May 1950 and became a separate province on 26 April 1988.

regions.label: The Southwest: Yunnan, Guizhou and Guangxi
regions.sub: Kunming, Guiyang, Nanning, Guilin, Dali

eras.note: The Ming conquest of Yunnan took place in 1381-1382.
Guizhou was formally made a province in 1413. Large areas of Yunnan were governed through native chieftains in the Ming and Qing periods, and Guilin was the capital of Guangxi under both dynasties.
The governor-general Ortai abolished the tusi system of indirect rule, which prompted rebellions by displaced chieftains. Miao rebellions occurred in 1735-1736 and 1795-1806.

eras.polity: Qing: the Taiping rising, the Miao rebellion and the French frontier
eras.note: The Jintian Uprising of January 1851 in Guangxi began the Taiping rebellion, and the Miao rebellion in Guizhou ran from 1854 to 1873. Guangxi seceded from the Qing on 6 November 1911. The Guangxi Army fought the French in 1884-1885, and the French built the railway from Hanoi to Kunming in 1904-1909.
In Yunnan, Cai E opposed Yuan Shikai's monarchy in 1915 and Long Yun took control of the clique in 1927. Guiyang was established as a city in 1941.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Yunnan, Guizhou and the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region
eras.note: The PLA took Guiyang on 15 November 1949, Yunnan's governor defected on 9 December 1949, and Guangxi became an autonomous region in 1958.

regions.label: Sichuan and Chongqing
regions.sub: Chengdu, Chongqing, Luzhou, Yibin, Mianyang

eras.polity: Mid-17th century: Zhang Xianzhong and the Daxi
eras.note: Zhang Xianzhong's rebels conquered Sichuan and declared the Daxi dynasty in the mid-17th century. The population fell sharply in the late 17th century and the Qing later resettled people from Huguang and other provinces.

eras.polity: Qing: Sichuan grouped with Shaanxi and Shanxi
eras.note: Sichuan was grouped with Shaanxi and Shanxi as "Shenzhuan" in 1680-1731 and 1735-1748.
Sichuan's present borders were set in the early 18th century, including the area that is now Chongqing.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Sichuan and the Chuanbian district
eras.note: The Chuanbian Special Administrative District was created west of the Sichuan Basin in the early 20th century and later became Xikang province.

eras.polity: Chongqing, the wartime stronghold of the Nationalist government
eras.note: Chongqing was the Kuomintang's wartime stronghold from 1938 to 1945 and was heavily bombed.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Sichuan including Chongqing
eras.note: Sichuan was reconstituted in 1952 and Xikang was split between Tibet and Sichuan.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Sichuan and the Chongqing municipality
eras.note: Chongqing was split off as a municipality in 1997.

regions.label: The Northwest: Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia and Qinghai
regions.sub: Xi'an, Lanzhou, Yinchuan, Xining, Yan'an

eras.polity: Ming: the Shaanxi Provincial Administration Commission
eras.note: The commission founded in 1376 covered what is now Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia and part of Qinghai.

eras.polity: Qing: Shaanxi and Gansu under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan
eras.note: Gansu was split off from Shaanxi after the Qing founding but both provinces were governed under the Viceroy of Shaan-Gan.
The Dungan Revolt ran from 1862 to 1877 and a second revolt followed in 1895-1896.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Gansu including Ningxia
eras.note: A great earthquake at Haiyuan in 1920 killed around 180,000 people, mostly in present-day Ningxia. Ningxia remained part of Gansu until 1929.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Ningxia separate; the Communist base at Yan'an
eras.note: Yan'an was the Communist base from late 1935 to early 1947, within the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Shaanxi, Gansu, Ningxia and Qinghai
eras.note: The People's Government of Shaanxi was established at Xi'an on 10 January 1950. Ningxia was again part of Gansu from 1954 to 1958.

regions.label: Tibet
regions.sub: Lhasa, Shigatse, Gyantse, Chamdo

eras.note: Before Qing rule.
Qing forces expelled the Dzungars in 1720. Imperial residents called ambans were stationed in Lhasa with over 2,000 troops and reported to the Lifan Yuan.

eras.polity: Tibet after the fall of the Qing
eras.note: The Qing fell in 1912. Accounts differ on how to describe the years to 1951, which some call de facto independence.

eras.polity: Agreement of 1951 and the People's Republic
eras.note: The Agreement on Measures for the Peaceful Liberation of Tibet was ratified by the Dalai Lama in 1951. Xikang was split between Tibet and Sichuan in 1952.
The Tibet Autonomous Region was established in 1965.

regions.label: Xinjiang
regions.sub: Urumqi, Kashgar, Ili (Yining), Turpan, Hotan

eras.note: The Qing suppressed the Revolt of the Altishahr Khojas in 1759.
The Qing established Xinjiang as a province in 1884.
The First East Turkestan Republic was declared at Kashgar on 12 November 1933 and had collapsed by April 1934. Sheng Shicai's tenure is dated 1933 or 1934 to 1944 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Second East Turkestan Republic at Ghulja
eras.note: The Second East Turkestan Republic was established at Ghulja on 12 November 1944; its end is dated 1946 or 1949 depending on the source.
The People's Republic took over Xinjiang in 1949.
Xinjiang became an autonomous region in 1955.

regions.label: Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh
regions.sub: Srinagar, Jammu, Leh, Kargil, Anantnag

eras.note: Mughal rule is dated from 1586 to about 1751; Afghan (Durrani) rule is dated from 1747 or 1752 depending on the source.
The Sikh kingdom of Punjab took the region from the Durrani empire in 1819.
The British annexed the Kashmir Valley from the Sikhs on 9 March 1846 as a war indemnity after the First Anglo-Sikh War.

eras.polity: Princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under the Dogra Maharajas
eras.note: The valley was sold to Gulab Singh, Raja of Jammu, on 16 March 1846; Hari Singh was the last Maharaja (1925-1947). The 1941 census listed Ladakh as a wazarat with the tehsils of Leh, Skardu and Kargil.

eras.polity: Accession to India and the ceasefire line
eras.note: Hari Singh's accession to India is dated 26 or 27 October 1947 depending on the source. A ceasefire line was set with United Nations intercession.

eras.polity: Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and of Ladakh
eras.note: The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 created the two union territories from 31 October 2019.

regions.label: Sikkim
regions.sub: Gangtok, Namchi, Gyalshing, Mangan

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sikkim: the Namgyal dynasty
eras.note: Phuntsog Namgyal was consecrated as the first Chogyal in 1642.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sikkim and the Treaty of Titalia
eras.note: The Treaty of Titalia between Sikkim and British India was signed in 1817.
The Treaty of Tumlong of 1861 made Sikkim a British protectorate. A Qing-era protectorate of Tibet over Sikkim is listed as ending in 1890.
Sikkim became an Indian protectorate in 1950.
Sikkim became an Indian state on 16 May 1975.

regions.label: The North-East: Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh
regions.sub: Guwahati, Shillong, Imphal, Aizawl, Agartala, Kohima

eras.note: The Ahom kingdom is dated 1228-1826 in the timeline of Assam's history.

eras.polity: East India Company: annexation of Assam
eras.note: The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) left the British in control of the Brahmaputra Valley. The Kachari kingdom was annexed in 1832, Jaintia in 1835, Upper Assam in 1838, the Matak country and Sadiya in 1842 and the North Cachar Hills in 1854.

eras.polity: British Raj: Assam within the Bengal Presidency
eras.note: Crown rule replaced the East India Company under the Government of India Act of 1858. Assam was separated from the Bengal Presidency in 1874.
Assam became a Chief Commissioner's Province in 1874 with Sylhet added. In 1906 Eastern Bengal and Assam were placed under a Lieutenant-Governor, and the partition of Bengal was annulled in 1911.

The Chief Commissioner's Province (Assam plus Sylhet) was reinstated in 1912 with a Legislative Council. Sylhet voted by referendum in July 1947 to join East Pakistan, and the Radcliffe Line left mainly Karimganj in India.

eras.polity: Independent India: Assam and its hill districts
eras.note: Nagaland became a state in 1963.
Meghalaya, split from Assam, and Manipur and Tripura became states in 1972 (one source gives 1971 for Tripura). Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh became states on 20 February 1987.

regions.label: Andhra and Telangana: the Northern Circars and Hyderabad
regions.sub: Hyderabad, Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Warangal, Kakinada

eras.polity: Mughal Empire and the Asaf Jahi state
eras.note: Aurangzeb conquered Golconda in 1687 and the Northern Circars were annexed to the Mughal Empire. Asaf Jah I established the state of Hyderabad on 31 July 1724.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Northern Circars; Hyderabad under the Nizam
eras.note: The British took Masulipatnam from the French in 1759, Robert Clive obtained a grant of the five Circars in 1765, and the Treaty of Masulipatnam of 1768 transferred them from the Nizam to the Company. In 1798 Nizam Ali Khan placed Hyderabad under British protection.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Madras Presidency and Hyderabad
eras.note: The Company bought the Nizam's claims over the Circars in 1823, making them a British possession. Berar was under the Nizam from 1853.

eras.polity: British Raj: Madras Presidency and the princely state of Hyderabad
eras.note: Berar remained within the Nizam's dominions until 1903.

eras.polity: Madras State, Andhra State and Hyderabad State
eras.note: The Circars became part of Madras State in 1947 and the Telugu-speaking north formed Andhra State in 1953. Indian forces began the invasion of Hyderabad, Operation Polo, on 13 September 1948.
Andhra State merged with the Telugu-speaking parts of Hyderabad State to form Andhra Pradesh in 1956; the rest of Hyderabad State was divided with Bombay State and Mysore.
Telangana was formed from Andhra Pradesh on 2 June 2014, with Hyderabad as its capital.

regions.label: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands
regions.sub: Port Blair, Car Nicobar, Nancowry, Diglipur

eras.note: Danish East India Company settlers arrived on the Nicobar Islands on 12 December 1755 and the islands became a Danish colony on 1 January 1756. The British colonised the Andamans from 1789 to 1796; the penal colony on Chatham Island was abandoned in 1796.
The British re-established a colony at Port Blair in 1858 and convicts arrived on Ross Island that March. The Danes sold their Nicobar rights to the British on 16 October 1868.

eras.polity: British India: Andaman and Nicobar Islands
eras.note: The Nicobars became part of British India in 1869 and the two groups were united under one command at Port Blair in 1872. Church records for the Andamans mainly appear in the Bengal Presidency records, with a few in the Madras Presidency records.
Japan captured Port Blair on 23 March 1942 and occupied the islands until the 1945 surrender.
The islands were part of British India until independence in 1947.
The islands became part of the Dominion of India in 1947.

eras.polity: Union Territory of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
eras.note: The islands became a union territory on 1 November 1956.

regions.label: Lakshadweep
regions.sub: Kavaratti, Agatti, Minicoy, Amini

eras.note: Portuguese control began in the late 15th century and the islanders expelled the Portuguese in 1545.
In the mid-16th century the Chirakkal (Kolathiri) family granted the inhabited islands as a jagir to the Arakkal family of Kannur.
Tipu Sultan of Mysore took control of the Aminidivi islands in 1787.
The British annexed the Aminidivi islands in 1799 after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War; the rest remained under Arakkal suzerainty and paid tribute to the British.

eras.polity: British Raj: Aminidivi islands and the Arakkal islands
eras.note: Crown rule replaced the East India Company in 1858.
The British took over administration in 1908 and attached the islands to the Madras Presidency.
The islands became part of the Dominion of India in 1947 and came under Madras State in 1950.
The islands were organised as a union territory on 1 November 1956 and renamed Lakshadweep on 1 November 1973.

regions.label: Dadra, Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu
regions.sub: Daman, Silvassa, Dadra, Nagar Haveli

eras.note: Daman and Diu were Portuguese colonies from the 1520s.

eras.polity: Portuguese Daman, Diu, Dadra and Nagar Haveli
eras.note: Dadra and Nagar Haveli were Portuguese territories from 1779. Indian forces annexed Dadra and Nagar Haveli on 11 August 1961 and Daman and Diu on 19 December 1961.

eras.polity: India: Daman and Diu within Goa
eras.note: Daman and Diu were administered within Goa, Daman and Diu from 1962 to 1987. Portugal recognised Indian sovereignty in 1974.

eras.polity: Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and of Daman and Diu
eras.note: Daman and Diu became a separate union territory in 1987 when Goa became a state.

eras.polity: Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
eras.note: The two union territories merged on 26 January 2020, with Daman as the capital.

regions.label: South-West Ceylon: Colombo, Galle and the maritime provinces
regions.sub: Colombo, Galle, Matara, Kurunegala, Ratnapura

eras.note: The Portuguese arrived on the island in 1505. Dharmapala of Kotte bequeathed the Kingdom of Kotte to the Portuguese monarch in 1580.
Portuguese rule began after Dharmapala died on 27 May 1597, with local resistance; Jeronimo de Azevedo was the first captain-general (1597-1614).

Dutch forces stormed Galle on 13 March 1640, and the capital moved to Colombo in 1658. The National Archives of Sri Lanka hold about 310 metres of VOC records from Ceylon, including the thombos (land and population registers); the Dutch Reformed Church's registers are held separately at Wolvendaal in Colombo.

eras.polity: British Ceylon: Madras then Crown colony
eras.note: Dutch forces surrendered on 14 February 1796 (some accounts give 16 February). The British ran the territory under a dual administration from 1798 and made it a Crown colony in 1802.

The territories came under unified administration in 1833. Civil registration of births, marriages and deaths began in 1867 for Europeans and Sri Lankans; the originals are with the Registrar General's office and regional registration offices.
Ceylon became independent on 4 February 1948.

eras.polity: Sri Lanka: Western, Southern, North Western and Sabaragamuwa provinces
eras.note: Ceylon became a republic in 1972.

regions.label: The Kandyan Highlands: Central, Uva and North Central
regions.sub: Kandy, Nuwara Eliya, Badulla, Anuradhapura, Matale

eras.note: The kingdom was founded in 1469 with Senkadagalapura (Kandy) as capital; the city may have existed from the mid-14th century.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kandy: Vimaladharmasuriya I and his successors
eras.note: Vimaladharmasuriya I took the throne in 1592. The Luso-Kandyan Treaty was made in 1633 and a treaty with the Dutch was signed at Batticaloa in 1638.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kandy: the Nayak dynasty
eras.note: Sri Vijaya Rajasinha was crowned in 1739, beginning Nayakkar rule.

British forces seized Kandy on 14 February 1815 and the Kandyan Convention of 2 March 1815 ended native rule. A rebellion began in 1817 and the Kandyan territory was annexed to British Ceylon in 1817.

eras.polity: British Ceylon: Central, Uva and North Central
eras.note: The Kandyan territories came under unified administration with the rest of the colony in 1833. The civil registers of 1867 cover the highlands as well as the coast.
Ceylon became independent on 4 February 1948.

eras.polity: Sri Lanka: Central, Uva and North Central provinces
eras.note: Ceylon became a republic in 1972.

regions.label: The North: Jaffna, Mannar and the Vanni
regions.sub: Jaffna, Mannar, Vavuniya, Kilinochchi, Mullaitivu

eras.note: Before registers.
The Portuguese conquest of the north is dated within the range 1560-1621 depending on the account. Jaffna fell to the Dutch in June 1658.
The National Archives of Sri Lanka hold the VOC records of coastal Ceylon, which the Nationaal Archief catalogues as the central government archive of coastal Ceylon, 1640-1796.
The British abolished caste-based slavery in Jaffna by Ordinance 20 of 1844.
The Northern and Eastern provinces were temporarily merged into the North-East Province between 1989 and 2006.

regions.label: The East: Trincomalee, Batticaloa and Ampara
regions.sub: Trincomalee, Batticaloa, Ampara, Kalmunai

eras.note: The Portuguese arrived on the island in 1505.
The Dutch took the Batticaloa fort from the Portuguese on 18 May 1638, and the Kandyan treaty with the Dutch was signed at Batticaloa the same year.
Dutch forces surrendered to the British in February 1796.
Ceylon became independent on 4 February 1948 and a republic in 1972.
For these years the Eastern Province was merged with the Northern Province.
The temporary merger of the Northern and Eastern provinces ended in 2006.

regions.label: Northern Sumatra - Aceh to Riau and Jambi
regions.sub: Banda Aceh, Medan, Padang, Pekanbaru, Batam, Jambi

eras.polity: Sultanate of Aceh and the other Sumatran kingdoms
eras.note: Before registers. The Aceh Sultanate is dated from 1480 and fought the Portuguese in 1519-1639. In the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 17 March 1824 Britain ceded its Sumatran possessions to the Netherlands, with transfers scheduled for 1 March 1825.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - Sumatra outside Aceh
eras.note: Under the 1824 treaty Britain agreed to open no offices on Sumatra and to make no treaties with its rulers. Civil registration of Europeans in the Indies began in October 1828, with the registers in Indonesia and FamilySearch microfilm copies.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - the Aceh War
eras.note: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of Sumatra of 1871 gave the Dutch control of Sumatra and the Aceh War began in 1873; the Dutch took the palace on 31 January 1874. The sultan surrendered in 1903 and the sultanate was dissolved in 1904, though resistance lasted to about 1912 (the war is dated to 1914 in one source).
Japan occupied the Indies from 1942 to 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: Independence was declared on 17 August 1945. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949 (27 December in one dating).

regions.label: Southern Sumatra - Bengkulu to Lampung and Bangka
regions.sub: Palembang, Bengkulu, Bandar Lampung, Pangkal Pinang

eras.polity: Sumatran kingdoms, with the British factory at Bencoolen
eras.note: Before registers. The British held Fort Marlborough at Bencoolen (Bengkulu) until the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 17 March 1824 ceded it and all other British Sumatran possessions to the Netherlands, with transfers scheduled for 1 March 1825.

Bengkulu changed from British to Dutch administration in 1825, so its earliest records are British, not VOC. Civil registers for Europeans start in October 1828 and are held in Indonesia, with FamilySearch microfilm.
Japan held the Indies from 1942 to 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: The republic was proclaimed on 17 August 1945. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949 (27 December in one dating).

regions.label: West Java - Banten, Batavia and the Priangan
regions.sub: Jakarta, Bandung, Serang, Bogor, Cirebon

eras.note: Before registers. Syarif Hidayatullah took Banten in 1526, Sunda Kelapa (later Jayakarta) fell in 1527 and the sultanate was founded under Hasanuddin; it became independent of Cirebon in 1552.

eras.polity: VOC - Batavia, with Banten a client state
eras.note: The Dutch founded Batavia after the fall of Jayakarta in 1619. Banten came under VOC control after the civil war of 1682 (a client state from 1683 by one dating); Mataram handed over Priangan after the 1680 settlement and Cirebon in 1705. The VOC archive (1602-1811) is in the Nationaal Archief, and part of the colonial correspondence can be reconstructed from the Arsip Nasional in Jakarta.

eras.polity: Dutch state rule after the Company
eras.note: Direct Dutch control is dated from 31 December 1799 (the Company is also said to have been dissolved in 1800). On 22 November 1808 Daendels declared the Banten sultanate absorbed into the Dutch East Indies.
British forces occupied Java in 1811 and Dutch control was restored in 1816. The Banten sultanate ended in 1813 when Raffles forced the sultan to give up his throne.
Java was returned to the Netherlands. Civil registers did not yet exist: they begin in October 1828.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - residencies of Java
eras.note: Civil registration (burgerlijke stand) began in October 1828 for Europeans only; Chinese were included from 1919 and Indonesians a few years later. The originals are in the Arsip Nasional in Jakarta, microfilmed by FamilySearch, while the Indische Almanak (1815-1942) printed registration notices in the Netherlands, with registration dates that can differ from the event. The Cultivation System of 1830-1870 applied here on land the colonial government controlled directly.
Japan invaded on 10 January 1942 and the colonial army on Java surrendered on 8 March 1942. In 1943-1945 a new population registration also recorded Chinese inhabitants in Chinese characters.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: Independence was declared on 17 August 1945, two days after Japan surrendered. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949 (27 December in one dating).
The Dutch-era civil registers remain in Indonesia, not in the Netherlands.

regions.label: Central and East Java - Mataram and the north coast
regions.sub: Semarang, Surakarta, Yogyakarta, Surabaya, Malang

eras.note: Before registers. Mataram gained independence from Pajang in 1584 and moved its capital to Kartasura in 1680 after the VOC helped restore Amangkurat II. Semarang was promised to the VOC in 1677-80, and in 1705 Mataram ceded Cirebon and eastern Madura and gave the VOC Semarang as its headquarters.

eras.polity: VOC - north coast, with the courts of Surakarta and Yogyakarta
eras.note: After the Chinese War of 1741-43 Mataram ceded the northern coast (Pasisir) to the VOC; in 1749 its ruler ceded sovereignty. The Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 split the realm into the Surakarta Sunanate and the Yogyakarta Sultanate, and the Mangkunegaran house was settled at Solo in 1757.

eras.polity: Dutch state rule after the Company
eras.note: The Company's rule is dated to end in 1799 or 1800 depending on the source, with direct Dutch control from 31 December 1799.
British forces occupied Java in 1811, the Anglo-Dutch Treaty was signed on 13 August 1814, and independent Dutch control returned in 1816.
Dutch rule resumed. Civil registers for Europeans start only in October 1828.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - residencies of Central and East Java
eras.note: From 1830 to 1870 the Cultivation System applied on Dutch-governed land, while the princely states (Surakarta, Yogyakarta) and private domains were exempt. Civil registration for Europeans began in October 1828; the registers are in Indonesia, with FamilySearch microfilm copies.
Japanese forces landed in January 1942 and the Dutch army on Java surrendered on 8 March 1942; the occupation ended in 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: In September 1945 the Sultan of Yogyakarta and the Duke of Pakualaman wrote to Sukarno backing the republic. Yogyakarta was the republic's capital from January 1946 until the capital moved to Bukittinggi on 19 December 1948.
Yogyakarta received special administrative status in 1950.

regions.label: Bali and the Lesser Sundas - Lombok to West Timor
regions.sub: Denpasar, Mataram, Labuan Bajo, Waingapu, Kupang

eras.polity: Portuguese posts on Solor, Flores and Timor
eras.note: Portuguese first landed on Timor in 1515, Dominican friars set up Lifau in 1556, and the first Portuguese settlement on nearby Solor dates from the 1560s. Bali and Lombok were under their own kings; the first Dutch expedition reached Bali in 1597.

eras.polity: VOC and Dutch state - Kupang and western Timor
eras.note: The Dutch took western Timor in 1613 and retook Kupang in 1652. Bali and Lombok kept their own rulers until the Dutch interventions of 1846-1849.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - conquest of Bali and Lombok
eras.note: Northern Bali came under Dutch control in 1849; Portugal gave up its claims on Flores and Solor in the Treaty of Lisbon of 1859; the Dutch took Lombok and Karangasem in 1894, Badung in 1906 and Klungkung in 1908. Civil registration of Europeans in the Indies began in October 1828, with the registers in Indonesia and FamilySearch microfilm.
The Dutch-Portuguese border on Timor was settled by a treaty in 1904, an arbitration award of 1914 and ratification in 1916; western Timor stayed Dutch.
Japan occupied Bali in 1942 and held the Indies until 1945.

eras.polity: Indonesian independence declared; Bali a district of the Dutch-made State of East Indonesia
eras.note: Independence was declared on 17 August 1945, and in 1946 the Dutch made Bali one of 13 districts of the State of East Indonesia. The Netherlands recognised Indonesian independence in December 1949.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia - Bali and Nusa Tenggara
eras.note: In 1958 the former Lesser Sunda province was split into Bali, West Nusa Tenggara and East Nusa Tenggara.

regions.label: Kalimantan - Indonesian Borneo
regions.sub: Pontianak, Banjarmasin, Balikpapan, Samarinda, Palangka Raya

eras.note: Before registers. Brunei's sultanate ruled most of coastal Borneo between the 15th and 17th centuries, and Portuguese trade with Brunei began in 1530.
The British traded with Sambas from 1609 and the Dutch began trading in southern Borneo in 1644. In 1812 the sultan of southern Borneo ceded forts to the British East India Company.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - residencies of Borneo
eras.note: The Dutch posted residents to Banjarmasin, Pontianak and Sambas in 1815, and the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 set the spheres of influence; Sarawak, North Borneo and Brunei became British protectorates in 1888. Civil registration of Europeans in the Indies began in October 1828, with the registers in Indonesia and FamilySearch microfilm.
Japan occupied most of Borneo between 1941 and 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: Independence was declared on 17 August 1945. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949 (27 December in one dating).
Sabah and Sarawak joined Malaysia on 16 September 1963, which fixed the northern border as an international one.

regions.label: Sulawesi - Makassar to Minahasa
regions.sub: Makassar, Manado, Palu, Kendari, Gorontalo

eras.polity: Gowa-Tallo sultanate and the Bugis and Minahasa lands
eras.note: Before registers. Gowa is dated from about 1320 and adopted Islam, traditionally on 22 September 1605. The VOC fought Gowa in 1666-69; the Treaty of Bungaya was signed on 18 November 1667 and the main fortress at Somba Opu fell on 12 June 1669.

After the war the VOC built Fort Rotterdam on the site of Somba Opu in 1673 as its Sulawesi headquarters, and the city of Makassar grew around it. The Company's archive (1602-1811) is in the Nationaal Archief.

Gowa kept its independence until the Dutch campaigns that began in 1904. Civil registration of Europeans in the Indies began in October 1828, with the registers in Indonesia and FamilySearch microfilm.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - Celebes after the South Sulawesi campaigns
eras.note: The Dutch campaigned against the South Sulawesi kingdoms from 1904 to 1906; in one account Gowa lost its independence in 1911 and became a Dutch regency.
Japan occupied the Indies from 1942 to 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia proclaimed; Dutch recognition came in December 1949
eras.note: Independence was declared on 17 August 1945. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949 (27 December in one dating).
The sultanate of Gowa was dissolved in 1957 and became Gowa Regency.

regions.label: Maluku - the Spice Islands
regions.sub: Ambon, Ternate, Tidore, Banda, Halmahera

eras.polity: Portuguese in Ambon and the spice islands, with the sultanates of Ternate and Tidore
eras.note: Portuguese presence began in 1512-13, when Francisco Serrao was shipwrecked on Hitu and the first Portuguese landed on Ambon; Portuguese-backed missionary work from 1546 established lasting Christian communities.

eras.polity: VOC - Ambon, Banda, Ternate and Tidore
eras.note: In 1605 the Dutch and the sultan of Ternate took Ambon and Tidore and expelled the Portuguese; the Dutch conquered the Banda Islands in 1621, the English on Ambon were eliminated in 1623, and Ternate and Tidore came under Dutch control in the 1650s. The Nuku Rebellion of 1780-1810 spread across Maluku and Papua.
The British captured the islands in 1796 and held them until 1817.
Civil registration of Europeans in the Indies began in October 1828, with the registers in Indonesia and FamilySearch microfilm.
Japan occupied the Indies from 1942 to 1945.

eras.polity: Maluku one of Indonesia's first provinces; Republic of South Maluku declared in 1950
eras.note: Maluku was proclaimed one of Indonesia's first provinces in 1945; in 1950 the Republic of South Maluku was declared and was defeated by the Indonesian army. Dutch recognition of Indonesian sovereignty came in December 1949.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia - Maluku and North Maluku
eras.note: North Maluku split off as a separate province in 1999, the year religious and ethnic conflict erupted in Maluku.

regions.label: Western New Guinea - Papua
regions.sub: Jayapura, Merauke, Sorong, Manokwari, Biak, Timika

eras.polity: Papuan peoples, with Ternate and Tidore claiming tribute
eras.note: Before registers. The Dutch claim of 1848 rested on the Sultanate of Ternate's claimed tributary ties to Papua, and Dutch sovereignty was later recognised through Tidore.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - claimed, not administered
eras.note: The Netherlands claimed western New Guinea in 1848.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies - Netherlands New Guinea
eras.note: Administrative posts were set up at Fakfak and Manokwari in 1898, and Merauke was founded in 1902 as capital of the southern division; the territory's eastern frontier is the 141st meridian.
Japan occupied the Netherlands East Indies from 1942 to 1945.
The Netherlands kept the territory when the rest of the Indies became independent on 27 December 1949, made it an overseas territory in 1954, and seated a New Guinea Council on 5 April 1961.

eras.polity: UN administration from 1 October 1962, then Indonesia from 1 May 1963
eras.note: The New York Agreement of 15 August 1962 put the territory under United Nations administration on 1 October 1962; it passed to Indonesia on 1 May 1963. The Act of Free Choice followed in 1969, and its fairness is disputed.

eras.polity: Republic of Indonesia - Irian Jaya, now the Papua provinces
eras.note: The territory was administered as Irian Jaya until 2003 and now forms the Papua region.

regions.label: Papua - British New Guinea and the Territory of Papua
regions.sub: Port Moresby, Daru, Kerema, Popondetta

eras.note: Before registers.

Britain proclaimed a protectorate on 6 November 1884 and annexed it, with some adjacent islands, as British New Guinea on 4 September 1888. The National Archives of Australia describes records of this administration for 1884-1906 and keeps a microfilm set, the originals having been returned to Papua New Guinea.

eras.polity: Commonwealth of Australia - Territory of Papua
eras.note: Letters patent of 18 March 1902 placed the possession under the authority of Australia, and the Territory of Papua was formally constituted on 1 September 1906 under the Papua Act 1905, with Port Moresby as capital. The territory was administered separately from the mandated Territory of New Guinea to the north until 1949.

eras.polity: Territory of Papua and New Guinea
eras.note: On 1 July 1949 Papua and New Guinea were merged administratively into the Territory of Papua and New Guinea.

eras.polity: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
eras.note: Papua New Guinea became independent on 15 September 1975 (16 September in some accounts).

regions.label: New Guinea mainland and Highlands - German New Guinea and the Mandated Territory
regions.sub: Lae, Madang, Wewak, Mount Hagen, Goroka, Vanimo

eras.note: Before registers.

Germany raised its flag on the mainland on 3 November 1884 under the New Guinea Company and took over direct imperial rule on 12 February 1899; the capital moved from Finschhafen to Friedrich-Wilhelmshafen in 1891. The National Archives of Australia describes German New Guinea and military administration records for 1885-1921, which stayed in Australia after Australia took the colony in 1914.
Australian forces seized German New Guinea in September-October 1914 and the territory remained under Australian military control until 1921.

Australia assumed the League of Nations Class C mandate on 17 December 1920; the capital was Rabaul until 1937, then Lae. Before 1949 Papua and New Guinea were separate territories, so a locality near the old boundary may have records in either series; patrols reached the Wahgi Valley and the Mount Hagen area in 1933, and a 1934 airstrip became the Mount Hagen town site.
Lae was destroyed in a Japanese air raid on 20 January 1942 and Rabaul was overwhelmed on 22-23 January; the administration's capital fell back to Wau.

eras.polity: Territory of Papua and New Guinea
eras.note: The two territories were united as the Territory of Papua and New Guinea on 1 July 1949 under the Papua and New Guinea Act 1949.

eras.polity: Independent State of Papua New Guinea
eras.note: Hela and Jiwaka provinces were created on 17 May 2012, split from Southern Highlands and Western Highlands.

regions.label: Bismarck Archipelago and Bougainville
regions.sub: Rabaul, Kavieng, Lorengau, Kokopo, Buka, Arawa

eras.note: Before registers. A French expedition made the first European contact with Bougainville in 1768.

eras.polity: German New Guinea - Bismarck Archipelago and the North Solomons
eras.note: The Bismarck Archipelago and the North Solomon Islands became a German protectorate in 1885 (Bougainville is dated to 1899 in another account), with direct imperial control from 12 February 1899. The capital moved to Herbertshoehe in 1899 and to Simpsonhafen (Rabaul) in 1910.
Australian forces occupied the territory in 1914 and it stayed under military control until 1921.
Bougainville became part of Australia's Territory of New Guinea under the League of Nations mandate in 1920; Rabaul was the territory's capital from 1914 to 1937.
Rabaul was overwhelmed on 22-23 January 1942; Japan seized Bougainville in 1942 and Allied forces began to retake it in 1943.

eras.polity: Territory of Papua and New Guinea
eras.note: The mandate territory merged with Papua on 1 July 1949.

Bougainville declared itself the Republic of the North Solomons in September 1975 and was absorbed back into Papua New Guinea; a civil war ran from 1988 to 1998 and a 2001 agreement led to autonomy. A 2019 non-binding referendum recorded 98.31 percent for independence.

regions.label: Samoa - Upolu and Savai'i
regions.sub: Apia, Salelologa, Mulifanua, Falealili

eras.note: Before registers. The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen was the first European to sight the islands in 1722, and Bougainville named them the Navigator Islands in 1768.

eras.polity: Samoan chiefly rule under mission and trading influence
eras.note: London Missionary Society missionaries arrived about 1830 and the Godeffroy firm expanded its trade into the islands in 1855. The First Samoan Civil War ran 1886-1894, and in March 1889 a storm wrecked the warships of three powers at Apia.

The Tripartite Convention of 1899 partitioned the islands between Germany and the United States, and the US flag was raised at Fagatogo in 1900 over the eastern islands. The Mau movement began in 1908-1909 and its chiefs were exiled to Saipan.

eras.polity: New Zealand occupation, mandate and trusteeship
eras.note: New Zealand occupied German Samoa in 1914 without fighting, and Germany gave up its claims in 1919. Archives New Zealand holds the New Zealand Samoan Administration series (1915-1938 in one guide) and the British Consul series from 1920, and the records of the military occupation are divided between Archives New Zealand and the Samoan Archives.

Samoa became independent as Western Samoa on 1 January 1962 and dropped "Western" in 1997. Births, deaths and marriages are now registered under the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Act 2002, which replaced the 1961 ordinances.

regions.label: Fiji - Viti Levu, Vanua Levu and Rotuma
regions.sub: Suva, Nadi, Lautoka, Levuka, Labasa, Rotuma

eras.note: Before registers. Abel Tasman sighted Vanua Levu in 1643, and Pacific Islander labourers were recruited to work abroad, often by deception or force, from 1865 until it was banned in 1911.
Cakobau of Bau was declared monarch of the Kingdom of Fiji in 1871.

Cakobau and other chiefs signed the Deed of Cession on 10 October 1874, founding the Colony of Fiji. Indian indentured labourers were brought in from 1879 to 1916, and Rotuma was ceded to the United Kingdom on 13 May 1881.
Fiji became independent on 10 October 1970, and Rotuma became independent as part of Fiji.
A series of coups in 1987 led to a republic being declared that year.

regions.label: Vanuatu - the New Hebrides
regions.sub: Port Vila, Luganville, Lenakel, Sola, Lakatoro

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Island societies, with European explorers, traders and missionaries
eras.note: Queiros made the first recorded European contact in 1606, and Cook named the islands the New Hebrides in 1774. Sandalwood trading boomed on Erromango in 1825-1830, and the blackbirding labour trade of the 1860s took more than half the adult men from some islands.
A Joint Naval Commission was set up in 1887 to protect British and French citizens, and Franceville (now Port Vila) declared independence in 1889.

eras.polity: Anglo-French Condominium of the New Hebrides
eras.note: Britain and France agreed a joint Condominium in 1906, with separate administrations and a shared court. Annamese workers from Vietnam began arriving on five-year contracts in 1921.
The Republic of Vanuatu was created on 30 July 1980.

regions.label: Gilbert Islands - Tarawa, Butaritari and Abemama
regions.sub: Tarawa, Betio, Abemama, Butaritari, Tabiteuea

eras.note: Before registers. Queiros sighted Butaritari and Makin in 1606, Thomas Gilbert crossed the islands in 1788, and the name Gilbert Islands was applied in 1820.
Britain proclaimed a protectorate in 1892.
The Gilberts became part of the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916.
Japan occupied the islands in December 1941, American forces raided Makin in 1942, and in November 1943 they landed at Makin and Tarawa.
The Ellice Islands separated and became Tuvalu in 1978.
The Gilberts became the independent state of Kiribati on 12 July 1979.

regions.label: Chatham Islands
regions.sub: Waitangi, Kaingaroa, Pitt Island

eras.note: Before registers. Polynesian settlers, the ancestors of the Moriori, probably arrived from mainland New Zealand in the 15th century.

eras.polity: Moriori, with British sealers and whalers
eras.note: The crew of HMS Chatham landed on 29 November 1791 and claimed the islands for Great Britain; sealers and whalers used the islands as a base in the early 1800s.

eras.polity: Moriori and Maori of Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama
eras.note: In 1835 about 900 Maori of Ngati Mutunga and Ngati Tama arrived from the Wellington area and enslaved the surviving Moriori. A 1841 New Zealand Company agreement to sell the islands to Germany fell through.

eras.polity: Colony and Dominion of New Zealand
eras.note: The islands officially became part of the Colony of New Zealand in 1842 and German Lutheran missionaries arrived in 1843. Moriori slavery was abolished by proclamation in 1863, and Maori prisoners including Te Kooti were exiled to the islands in 1865-1868.

regions.label: Hokkaido and Ezo
regions.sub: Sapporo, Hakodate, Asahikawa, Nemuro, Wakkanai

eras.polity: Ainu lands; Japanese settlement at the southern tip
eras.note: Before registers. The Ainu were the main inhabitants; Japanese settlement on the southern tip began in the 16th century.

In 1604 the Tokugawa granted the Matsumae clan exclusive trading rights with the Ainu. The southern Oshima Peninsula was the Wajinchi (Japanese territory) and the rest the Ezochi. Shakushain's revolt of 1669-1672 was the last large Ainu uprising.

eras.polity: Shogunate control of Ezo; Republic of Ezo
eras.note: The shogunate took control of most of the island in 1855-1858. After the Boshin War a Tokugawa loyalist group held the island until its defeat in May 1869. The Matsumae domain name was reinstated on 24 June 1869.
The government annexed the island in 1869, renamed it Hokkaido and set up the Development Commission, which ran settlement until 1882. Settlement dispossessed the Ainu of land and resources.
The Commission was abolished in 1882 and replaced by three prefectures, Hakodate, Sapporo and Nemuro, not by one Hokkaido prefecture.
The three prefectures were folded into a single Hokkaido Agency in 1886. The Hokkaido Former Aborigines Protection Act followed in 1899. Hokkaido was not a standard prefecture until 1947.
Hokkaido became a standard prefecture in 1947; the Hokkaido Development Agency existed from 1949 and was absorbed into a national ministry in 2001.

regions.label: Tohoku
regions.sub: Sendai, Aomori, Morioka, Akita, Yamagata, Fukushima

eras.note: Before registers.
Edo-period shumon registers list household and temple but not samurai, court nobles or surnames, so a family can drop out of them.

eras.polity: Boshin War; Mutsu and Dewa divided
eras.note: Mutsu Province was divided on 19 January 1869 into Iwashiro, Iwaki, Rikuzen, Rikuchu and Rikuo (Rikuo is roughly today's Aomori); Dewa was divided into Uzen and Ugo the same year. Records of 1869-1871 use these names, not the single Mutsu.
In August 1871 the 261 surviving domains were reorganised into three urban prefectures and 302 prefectures, cut to 72 later that year.
Koseki are usually kept in the village or city where the family originated. Local government laws of 1888-1890 subdivided the prefectures into cities, districts, towns and villages.

Copies of a koseki can be requested only for direct ancestors, from the prefecture or village office where the family lived. Village offices keep paper records only for a set number of years, and wars and disasters destroyed some.

regions.label: Kanto
regions.sub: Tokyo, Yokohama, Chiba, Saitama, Mito, Utsunomiya, Maebashi

eras.note: Before registers.
Ieyasu took up residence in Edo in 1590 and founded the shogunate in 1603. Edo became the de facto capital while Kyoto stayed the de jure capital.

Temple affiliation became compulsory in 1638 after the Shimabara Rebellion; nationwide shumon registers began in 1665 and the format was fixed in 1671 and unchanged to 1870. Shogunate records of the period are in the Naikaku Bunko collection of the National Archives of Japan.

eras.polity: Meiji - Tokyo and the new prefectures
eras.note: Edo was renamed Tokyo in 1868 and the capital moved there in 1868-1869. The first urban (fu) and rural (ken) prefectures were created in 1868; the domains became prefectures in 1871.

eras.polity: Empire of Japan - Tokyo-fu, Kanagawa, Chiba, Saitama, Ibaraki, Tochigi, Gunma
eras.note: The family registration law of 1871 took effect in 1872. From 1898 the registered domicile (honseki) is separate from where a person lived, so the koseki of a Kanto resident may sit in the municipality the family came from. The earthquake of 1 September 1923 devastated Tokyo, Yokohama, Kanagawa and Chiba; estimates of the dead run from 105,000 to 140,000. Tokyo-fu became Tokyo-to in 1943.

eras.polity: Japan - Tokyo Metropolis and the Kanto prefectures
eras.note: The Family Register Act of 1947, in force from 1948, centres the koseki on a married couple and their children. A closed register (joseki) is kept for 150 years.

regions.label: Chubu
regions.sub: Niigata, Kanazawa, Nagano, Nagoya, Shizuoka, Gifu, Fukui, Kofu

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Tokugawa shogunate - the Chubu domains and shogunal lands
eras.note: Temple death registers (kakocho) give a person's Buddhist name and date of death and sometimes family ties, but were not made as genealogies and cannot be requested like a koseki.
The abolition of the domains in 1871 produced over 300 prefectures at first, reduced to 72 later that year.

Koseki date from 1872. The prefecture count fell from 72 to 47 in 1888, so an 1870s-1880s record can sit under a different prefecture from today's. Shizuoka and Yamanashi were among the seven prefectures hit by the earthquake of 1 September 1923.
Computerised processing of the koseki was authorised in 1994 and later adopted by every municipality.

regions.label: Kinki (Kansai)
regions.sub: Kyoto, Osaka, Kobe, Nara, Otsu, Wakayama, Tsu

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Tokugawa shogunate - Kyoto, Osaka and the Kinki domains
eras.note: Kyoto remained the de jure capital while Edo was the de facto capital. The earliest temple registers, dated 1638-1640, are mostly from Kyoto and Kyushu.
The capital moved from Kyoto to Tokyo in 1868 or 1869 depending on the source.

Awaji Island, now in Hyogo, was part of Myodo Prefecture (with Tokushima and Kagawa) from 1873 and joined Hyogo Prefecture on 21 August 1876, so earlier Awaji records are filed with Tokushima. Koseki date from 1872.

regions.label: Chugoku
regions.sub: Okayama, Hiroshima, Matsue, Tottori, Yamaguchi, Hagi

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Tokugawa shogunate - Choshu and the Chugoku domains
eras.note: After Sekigahara the Mori clan fell from 1,200,000 to 369,000 koku and moved from Aki to Nagato. Hagi was the Choshu domain seat until the move to Yamaguchi in 1862 (1863 in another account).
Choshu allied with Satsuma and fought in the Boshin War. The domain was abolished in 1871 and its territory became part of Yamaguchi Prefecture.
The unified family register began in 1872, based at first on actual residence.

regions.label: Shikoku
regions.sub: Matsuyama, Takamatsu, Tokushima, Kochi, Imabari

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Tokugawa shogunate - the four provinces of Shikoku
eras.note: The island is named for its four old provinces: Awa, Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo.
The domains were abolished in 1871 and became prefectures.

eras.polity: Empire of Japan - Shikoku prefectures merged and split
eras.note: Sanuki became Kagawa Prefecture in 1872 and was merged with Tokushima and Awaji into Myodo Prefecture the next year; Kagawa was separated in 1875 and merged into Ehime on 21 August 1876, leaving it again on 3 December 1888. Awa was tied to Kochi Prefecture from 1876 until Tokushima Prefecture was inaugurated on 2 March 1880; accounts of this step differ.
From 1898 the registered domicile (honseki) is separate from where a person lived.

regions.label: Kyushu
regions.sub: Fukuoka, Nagasaki, Kumamoto, Oita, Miyazaki, Kagoshima, Saga

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Tokugawa shogunate - Satsuma and the Kyushu domains
eras.note: Satsuma Domain (the Shimazu) existed from 1600 to 1871. Dejima, an artificial island off Nagasaki, was built in 1634-1636.

Temple affiliation became compulsory in 1638 after the Shimabara Rebellion, and the earliest registers (1638-1640) are mostly from Kyoto and Kyushu. Dejima held the Portuguese until their expulsion in 1639 and the Dutch from 1641 until the 1858 treaty. Satsuma invaded the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1609 and held it as a vassal.
Satsuma Domain was abolished in 1871 and became Kagoshima Prefecture.
Saigo Takamori led the Satsuma Rebellion against the government in 1877.

regions.label: Ryukyu and Okinawa
regions.sub: Naha, Shuri, Ishigaki, Miyakojima, Amami

eras.note: Sho Hashi of Chuzan took Nanzan Castle in 1429, united Okinawa for the first time and moved the capital to Shuri. Ming tributary relations dated from 1372.

Satsuma invaded on 5 April 1609 and the kingdom owed allegiance to both Japan and China. The Amami and Tokara islands were annexed by Satsuma and remain in Kagoshima Prefecture, not Okinawa. Qing tributary status ran 1646-1872.
The Meiji government declared the kingdom a domain in 1872, with the last king as domain head. It was abolished and Okinawa Prefecture created in 1879 (27 March or 4 April, depending on the source).
Amami remained part of Kagoshima Prefecture, not Okinawa Prefecture.

eras.polity: United States Military Government, then Civil Administration of the Ryukyu Islands
eras.note: American military control began in 1945 and became the Civil Administration in 1950. Under the 1952 San Francisco treaty the United States held administrative rights south of 29 degrees N; Tokara returned in February 1952 and Amami on 25 December 1953.
Administrative rights reverted to Japan in 1972 under the 1971 reversion agreement.

regions.label: Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi
regions.sub: Seoul, Incheon, Suwon, Paju, Yeoju, Ganghwa

eras.note: Yi Seong-gye chose Hanyang as capital in September 1394, and the Eight Provinces date from 1413. Household registers (hojeok) were meant to be revised every three years, and a Goryeo law of 1390 already required upper-class members to submit copies every third year. Many jokbo claim Goryeo origins, but few families keep complete copies after wars and the Japanese occupation.

Gojong proclaimed the empire in October 1897. The Eulsa treaty of November 1905 made Korea a Japanese protectorate and Gojong was forced to abdicate on 19 July 1907. The minjeok household register system dates from 1909. Annexation was signed on 22 August 1910 and announced on 29 August.

eras.polity: Japanese rule - Government-General of Chosen; Seoul as Gyeongseong
eras.note: Seoul became Gyeongseong (Keijo) and, from 1 October 1910, an ordinary city within Gyeonggi; Yeongdeungpo was added on 1 April 1936. The hojeok came into use in 1922. An order of 10 November 1939 in effect banned Korean names.

eras.polity: US Army Military Government in Korea (south of the 38th parallel)
eras.note: US forces landed at Incheon on 8 September 1945 and the parallel divided Gyeonggi. The Charter of the City of Seoul of 1945-1946 made Seoul the official name.

eras.polity: Republic of Korea - Seoul, Incheon and Gyeonggi
eras.note: Seoul fell on 28 June 1950 and changed hands four times in the Korean War; the capital sat temporarily in Busan in 1950-1951. The Hojeok Act dates from 1960; the Constitutional Court found the hoju system unconstitutional on 3 February 2005 and a Civil Code reform replaced it in 2008 with the family relations register.

regions.label: Gangwon
regions.sub: Chuncheon, Wonju, Gangneung, Sokcho, Samcheok

eras.note: The Eight Provinces of Joseon were established in 1413; in 1895 districts replaced them and in 1896 thirteen provinces.
The 13 provinces stayed largely unchanged under Japanese rule, with Japanese readings of their names.

eras.polity: US Army Military Government in Korea (south of the 38th parallel)
eras.note: The 38th parallel split Gangwon, as it did Gyeonggi and Hwanghae; the southern half went to the US zone.

eras.polity: Republic of Korea - Gangwon, Korean War front
eras.note: The war ran from 25 June 1950 to the armistice of 27 July 1953.
The armistice created a demilitarized zone along the front, so today's border is the DMZ, not the 38th parallel.

regions.label: Chungcheong
regions.sub: Daejeon, Cheongju, Sejong, Gongju, Cheonan, Chungju

eras.note: The province was formed in 1356, in Goryeo, from the southern part of Yanggwang; its name comes from Chungju and Cheongju. Gongju was the provincial capital.

eras.polity: Joseon - Chungju, Gongju and Hongju districts
eras.note: The province was replaced in 1895 by the Chungju, Gongju and Hongju districts, which were reorganised in 1896 as North and South Chungcheong.

eras.polity: Korean Empire, then Japanese rule from 1910
US Army Military Government in Korea

regions.label: Honam (Jeolla)
regions.sub: Gwangju, Jeonju, Mokpo, Suncheon, Yeosu, Gunsan

eras.note: Jeolla was one of Joseon's Eight Provinces, with Jeonju as capital; the name Jeolla dates from 1018, and the area remained one province for nearly eight centuries. The province then also covered Jeju.

eras.polity: Joseon - Donghak Peasant Revolution and the 1896 division
eras.note: The Donghak Peasant Revolution of 1894-1895 began in Jeolla. On 4 August 1896 Jeolla was divided into North and South Jeolla.

eras.polity: Korean Empire, then Japanese rule from 1910
US Army Military Government in Korea
eras.note: Jeju separated from South Jeolla Province on 1 August 1946, so earlier records of the island are filed under Jeolla.

eras.polity: Republic of Korea - North and South Jeolla, Gwangju

regions.label: Jeju
regions.sub: Jeju City, Seogwipo, Chuja, Marado

eras.note: Before registers. Tamna's chief submitted to Goryeo in 938, and in 1105 Goryeo abolished the name Tamna and made the island a district (Tamna-gun).
The Mongol Empire used the island as a base and horse pasture from 1271 to 1356, and the Yuan set up a military governor in 1273.
The island became part of Joseon in 1392, was used for horse breeding and the exile of political prisoners, and was part of Jeolla Province. One revolt occurred in 1862.
Revolts occurred on the island in 1898 and 1901.
Haenyeo (women divers) led a protest in 1931-1932 against a Japanese-controlled divers' association, drawing about 17,000 participants.

eras.polity: US Army Military Government in Korea
eras.note: Jeju separated from South Jeolla Province on 1 August 1946 and became its own province.

eras.polity: Republic of Korea - the Jeju uprising
eras.note: The uprising began on 3 April 1948; it is dated to 13 May 1949 or to 21 September 1954 depending on the source. Estimates of the dead run from 14,000 to 30,000, about 230 of the island's 400 villages were burned, and about 40,000 people fled to Japan.
Jeju was designated a special self-governing province on 1 July 2006.

regions.label: Yeongnam (Gyeongsang)
regions.sub: Busan, Daegu, Ulsan, Gyeongju, Andong, Jinju, Ulleungdo

eras.note: Gyeongsang took its name in 1314 from Gyeongju and Sangju; Daegu was the provincial capital.

eras.polity: Joseon - Andong, Daegu, Jinju and Dongnae districts
eras.note: The province was replaced in 1895 by four districts, which in 1896 were merged into North and South Gyeongsang.

eras.polity: Korean Empire, then Japanese rule from 1910
US Army Military Government in Korea
eras.note: The Autumn Uprising of 1946 followed a general strike and a police shooting in Daegu.
By early August 1950 South Korean and UN forces held only the Pusan Perimeter in the southeast, and the capital sat temporarily in Busan in 1950-1951.

regions.label: Central Highlands — Imerina and the Betsileo
regions.sub: Antananarivo, Antsirabe, Fianarantsoa, Ambositra, Miarinarivo

eras.note: Before registers. Tradition dates the founding of Imerina to Andriamanelo, who reigned 1540-1575; the Betsileo kingdoms have oral traditions from the 17th century.

Andrianampoinimerina reunited Imerina from about 1787 (some sources give 1785) and had conquered the Bara and Betsileo by his death in 1810. Radama I made Fianarantsoa the administrative capital for the central and southern Betsileo.

eras.polity: Merina Kingdom under a French protectorate
eras.note: The treaty of 17 December 1885, signed by Ranavalona III, made Madagascar a French protectorate; other accounts date French protection to 1896. French forces took Antananarivo in September 1895.

France abolished slavery in 1896 and annexed the island that year; the colony is dated to 28 February 1897 in other accounts. Joseph Gallieni was Governor-General from 1897. French-period civil and parish records concerning Madagascar are held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.
Independence came in 1960, dated 26 June or 14 October depending on the source. Births are registered at the commune under Law 61.025.

regions.label: East Coast — Betsimisaraka and Lake Alaotra
regions.sub: Toamasina, Fenoarivo Atsinanana, Sainte-Marie, Mananjary, Manakara, Farafangana

eras.note: Before registers. Ratsimilaho took Fenerive in 1712, was elected king of the Betsimisaraka and ruled from Foulpointe; he died in 1754.

eras.polity: Betsimisaraka coast, French trading ports and Sainte-Marie
eras.note: Bety ceded Nosy Boraha (Île Sainte-Marie) to France in 1750, and French trading ports followed along the coast. The ANOM series 1Z at Aix-en-Provence is titled for Madagascar and the Sainte-Marie establishments, 1785-1889.

eras.polity: Merina Kingdom (French protectorate from the 1885 treaty); Sainte-Marie French
eras.note: Radama I took Toamasina in 1817 with an army of 25,000 and had defeated the Betsimisaraka by 1824; they rebelled unsuccessfully in 1825. Civil registration records of Sainte-Marie Island survive for 1820-1870.
Toamasina (Tamatave) was the island's main port.

regions.label: North — Diana, Sava and Sofia
regions.sub: Antsiranana (Diego Suarez), Nosy Be, Antalaha, Sambava, Vohemar

eras.polity: Sakalava kingdoms of the north-west; Betsimisaraka coast to the east
eras.note: Before registers. The first significant Sakalava kingdoms formed in the 1650s; the Betsimisaraka live along the east coast as far north as Antalaha.

eras.polity: Nosy Be a French protectorate; the mainland under local rulers and the Merina crown
eras.note: Nosy Be and Nosy Komba became a French protectorate in 1841.

eras.polity: Diego Suarez (Antsiranana) French; the rest under the Merina kingdom and French protectorate
eras.note: After the first Franco-Hova war (1883-85) Madagascar ceded Antsiranana (Diego Suarez) to France.

regions.label: West — the Sakalava kingdoms of Boina and Menabe
regions.sub: Mahajanga, Morondava, Maintirano, Maevatanana, Ambato-Boeni

eras.polity: Sakalava kingdom (Menabe, centred on Andakabe, now Morondava)
eras.note: Before registers. The first significant Sakalava kingdoms formed in the 1650s; Andriandahifotsy (c.1610-1658) extended Sakalava authority north past the Mangoky River.

eras.polity: Sakalava kingdoms of Menabe and Boina (Mahajanga)
eras.note: The kingdom split in two after the reign of Andriantonkafo (1712-1722) and reached its greatest extent between 1730 and 1760. Mahajanga, in the Tsongay region, was one of the largest slave-trade ports on Madagascar.

eras.polity: Merina garrison at Mahajanga; Menabe and the interior Sakalava lands outside Merina rule
eras.note: Radama I deposed Andriantsoly after the fall of Mahajanga in 1824. Sources differ on whether the Merina ever annexed Menabe or Boina.

regions.label: South — Antandroy, Mahafaly, Antanosy and Bara
regions.sub: Toliara, Tolagnaro (Fort-Dauphin), Ambovombe, Ihosy, Amboasary

eras.polity: French settlement at Fort-Dauphin (Tolagnaro), about thirty years to 1674
eras.note: The Antanosy massacred the settlers on Christmas night 1672 and a French ship rescued the survivors in 1674.

eras.polity: Tandroy confederation (Zafimanara dynasty), Mahafaly (Menarandra dynasty), Antanosy and Bara
eras.note: Before registers. Early in the 18th century the Zafimanara dynasty united the Tandroy between the Menarandra and Mendare rivers, and the Menarandra dynasty of the Mahafaly conquered the westernmost Tandroy lands.

eras.polity: Southern kingdoms outside the Merina crown; the Bara claimed by the Merina
eras.note: Tandroy power waned around 1790 after major flooding. The Tandroy were never part of the Merina Kingdom; Andrianampoinimerina had conquered the Bara by 1810.
The French struggled to exert authority over the Antandroy after colonization.

regions.label: Cabo Delgado and Niassa — the Niassa Company lands
regions.sub: Pemba, Montepuez, Mocímboa da Praia, Lichinga, Metangula

eras.polity: Coastal sultanates and inland chiefdoms; Portuguese claim
eras.note: Arab trading settlements and local sultans controlled the coast before the Portuguese came; Vasco da Gama reached the coast in 1498.

The company held the land from the Rovuma to the Lurio and from the Indian Ocean to Lake Niassa, and made Porto Amélia (now Pemba), founded in 1904, its headquarters. Portugal refused to extend the concession and the company was abolished on 27 October 1929.
The Arquivo Histórico de Moçambique in Maputo, created in 1934, is the national archive for 19th and 20th century documents.
The colonies were renamed Overseas Provinces in 1951. FRELIMO began its guerrilla campaign in September 1964.
Independence was on 25 June 1975. RENAMO's war against the government ran from 1977 to 1992.

regions.label: Nampula and the Island of Mozambique
regions.sub: Ilha de Moçambique, Nampula, Nacala, Angoche, Mossuril

eras.polity: Swahili coastal town on the Island of Mozambique
eras.note: Before registers. Pottery shows the town was founded no later than the 14th century, and its rulers had links with the rulers of Angoche and Quelimane.

eras.polity: Portuguese East Africa, capital on the Island of Mozambique
eras.note: The Portuguese set up a port and naval base in 1507, and in the 16th century the island became the capital of Portuguese East Africa; it withstood Dutch attacks in 1607 and 1608. Part of the pre-1834 administrative papers were sent to the Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino in Lisbon.

eras.polity: Portuguese Mozambique, capital moved to Lourenço Marques
eras.note: The capital moved to Lourenço Marques (now Maputo) in 1898. In the mid-20th century the port of Nacala took most of the island's remaining business.
A bridge connecting the island to the mainland was built in the 1960s.
The island was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991.

regions.label: Zambezia — Quelimane and the lower Zambezi
regions.sub: Quelimane, Mocuba, Pebane, Gurué, Milange

eras.note: Vasco da Gama landed at the site of Quelimane in 1498. Prazos were land grants leased for an annual fee, with residence required; the terms prazo and prazeiro appear only from the 18th century, earlier ones being foro and foreiro. Prazeiros could raise private armies, and a mid-19th-century reform failed.

eras.polity: Portuguese Mozambique — concession companies and the end of the prazos
eras.note: An attempt at reform in the 1890s failed, and concessionaire companies, the British Ultimatum of 1890 and the Colonial Act of 1930 all contributed to the end of the prazo system; sources give no single abolition date.
RENAMO attacked transport routes, schools and clinics during the war of 1977-1992.

regions.label: Tete and the middle Zambezi
regions.sub: Tete, Moatize, Zumbo, Songo, Angónia

eras.polity: Portuguese settlement at Tete and the Zambezi prazos
eras.note: The Portuguese founded a settlement at Tete in 1531, about 420 km up the Zambezi, after it had been a Swahili trade centre; the Swahili presence ended after a campaign of about 1,000 men in 1568. By the mid-17th century Tete was a market for ivory and gold.

eras.polity: Tete, a Portuguese town; prazos on the Zambezi
eras.note: Tete received a Portuguese town charter in 1761. In the 19th century 32 prazeiros owned 57 prazos in Tete Province.
The British Ultimatum of 1890 and an 1890s reform attempt belong to the decline of the prazo system.
Tete became a city of the Overseas Province in 1959.

regions.label: Manica and Sofala — Beira and the Company lands
regions.sub: Beira, Chimoio, Dondo, Sofala, Gorongosa

eras.polity: Portuguese Sofala and the Zambezi trade
eras.note: Portugal gained control of Sofala in the early 16th century.

eras.polity: Gaza Empire (Soshangane, then Mzila) inland; Portuguese on the coast
eras.note: Soshangane founded the Gaza Empire in 1824 and set his capital on the middle Sabi River; his sons Mawewe and Mzila fought for power after he died in 1856, and Mzila won in 1861 with Portuguese help.

eras.polity: Mozambique Company (Manica and Sofala), headquarters Beira
eras.note: The company held a 50-year concession from 11 February 1891 and ran the public administration from Beira, using forced labour; the Gaza ruler Gungunyana resisted until his defeat in 1895. Beira's founding is dated 1887 or 1890 depending on the source, and it became a city in 1907.
The concession was not renewed and the territory passed to Portuguese colonial authorities on 18 July 1942.

regions.label: Gaza and Inhambane
regions.sub: Inhambane, Xai-Xai, Chókwè, Vilankulo, Massinga

eras.note: The Portuguese set up a permanent trading post at Inhambane in 1534, and in 1560 it was chosen as the first Jesuit mission to south-east Africa. In the 18th century it was an ivory and slave port, largely under Indian trading control.

Soshangane destroyed Inhambane town in 1834, and Gaza at its height in the 1860s controlled the land between the Zambezi and the Limpopo. Gungunyana moved the capital closer to the Portuguese and was defeated in 1895 and exiled to the Azores.
The Berlin West Africa Conference of 1884-85 had placed the territory under Portuguese control. Inhambane's standing fell as Lourenço Marques became the main centre in the 20th century.

regions.label: Maputo and Delagoa Bay
regions.sub: Maputo (Lourenço Marques), Matola, Manhiça, Marracuene, Ponta do Ouro

eras.note: Before registers. The site was a Tsonga fishing village, named Lourenço Marques after a Portuguese navigator who explored the area in 1544.

eras.polity: Portuguese fort and trading town at Lourenço Marques
eras.note: The Portuguese fort is dated 1781 or 1787 depending on the source, and a town grew around it from about 1850. Britain claimed the southern part of the bay on the strength of Captain Owen's agreements of 1823.

eras.polity: Portuguese Lourenço Marques after the MacMahon award
eras.note: The President of France, Marshal MacMahon, decided the Delagoa Bay dispute for Portugal; the award is dated 24 July 1875 or 27 July depending on the source. The town was elevated in 1876 and became a city in 1887.

eras.polity: Portuguese Mozambique, capital at Lourenço Marques
eras.note: Lourenço Marques became the capital of Portuguese Mozambique in 1898, and its port and the railway to Pretoria drove growth.
The city was renamed Maputo in February 1976. Civil registration records are held by the Ministry of Justice in Maputo; the Arquivo Histórico de Moçambique, also in Maputo, was created in 1934.

regions.label: Barotseland and North-Western Rhodesia
regions.sub: Mongu, Kalabo, Senanga, Sesheke, Solwezi, Mwinilunga

eras.note: Before registers. The Lozi kingdom was likely founded in the 17th century and was ruled by the Litunga.
The Kololo, a Sotho group, conquered the Lozi kingdom around 1840; another account dates the conquest to 1838.
A rebellion led by Njekwa restored the kingdom in 1864 and installed Sipopa as Litunga.

Lewanika signed the Lochner Concession in 1890 and the Lawley Concession in 1898; the protectorate of Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia followed an Order in Council of 1899. It merged with North-Eastern Rhodesia on 17 August 1911.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company
eras.note: The kingdom was merged into Northern Rhodesia in 1911 and effectively became a province.
Administration passed from the Company to the British government on 1 April 1924.

eras.polity: Zambia — Barotse Province, from 1969 Western Province
eras.note: The Barotseland Agreement signed by Mwanawina III and Kenneth Kaunda shortly before independence gave the kingdom special status; the Zambian government revoked it in 1969 and renamed Barotse Province as Western Province.

regions.label: The Copperbelt, Kabwe and Lusaka
regions.sub: Lusaka, Kabwe, Ndola, Kitwe, Chingola, Mufulira

eras.polity: British South Africa Company sphere of influence
eras.note: Cecil Rhodes obtained mineral concessions in 1888 and the territory became a British sphere of influence. The Company ran two protectorates, North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia (created 29 January 1900), until they were merged on 17 August 1911.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company

eras.note: Large-scale Copperbelt mining began after 1924; the copper deposits are dated to 1928 in some accounts. Livingstone was the capital until 1935, when Lusaka replaced it, and major strikes took place on the Copperbelt in 1935 and 1940.

The Federation was dissolved on 31 December 1963 and Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia on 24 October 1964. Civil registration began under an act of 12 June 1898 for Europeans, aliens and coloured residents, with records from 1908, and was extended to all births and deaths by the 1973 Births and Deaths Registration Act; the Registrar General in Lusaka holds the records.

eras.polity: Republic of Zambia — one-party state from 1972
eras.note: A one-party state was declared in 1972 and a crash in world copper prices in 1973 hit the Copperbelt.
Frederick Chiluba's MMD won the multiparty elections of 1991.

regions.label: Southern Province — Tonga plateau and Livingstone
regions.sub: Livingstone, Choma, Mazabuka, Monze, Kalomo

eras.polity: Batoka (Tonga) and Tokaleya lands; Kololo conquest of the Lozi
eras.note: The Batoka, southern Tonga, were the predominant people near the river, and the Kololo placed Subiya chiefs over the Tokaleya. David Livingstone was the first European shown the Victoria Falls, in 1855.

A British settlement at the Old Drift crossing became the first municipality around 1897. The railway reached the Falls in 1904, Livingstone was founded in 1905, and the Company moved the territory's capital there in 1907.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company
eras.note: Livingstone was the capital of Northern Rhodesia from 1911 to 1935.
The capital moved from Livingstone to Lusaka in 1935.
Livingstone was provincial capital from 1907 until 2011, when Choma replaced it.

regions.label: Eastern Province — North-Eastern Rhodesia
regions.sub: Chipata (Fort Jameson), Petauke, Katete, Lundazi, Nyimba

eras.polity: British South Africa Company sphere of influence
eras.note: The area became a British sphere of influence after Rhodes obtained mineral concessions in 1888.

eras.polity: North-Eastern Rhodesia (British South Africa Company), capital Fort Jameson
eras.note: North-Eastern Rhodesia was created by Order in Council on 29 January 1900. The Company ran seven administrative districts from Fort Jameson (now Chipata), with Robert Codrington as Administrator 1900-1907 and Lawrence Wallace 1907-1909.
