eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company
eras.note: North-Eastern Rhodesia merged with Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia on 17 August 1911.

regions.label: Luapula — the Lunda kingdom of Kazembe
regions.sub: Mansa, Kawambwa, Mwense, Nchelenge, Samfya

eras.note: Before registers. Around 1740 Ng'anga Bilonda, the first Mwata, left the Luba-Lunda kingdom of Mwata Yamvo and migrated east; Francisco de Lacerda's Portuguese mission reached the kingdom in 1798 and he died within weeks.

eras.polity: Kazembe reduced by the Yeke kingdom of Msiri
eras.note: In the 1860s Msiri took over much of Kazembe's copper and ivory trade and reduced Kazembe to a small state until Msiri died in 1890.

eras.polity: British South Africa Company; the valley shared with the Congo Free State
eras.note: Britain and the Congo Free State divided the Luapula valley in 1894. British forces burned Mwata Kazembe X's capital in 1899 after he resisted tax collection, and he later returned and rebuilt at Mwansabombwe.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company

eras.note: The chieftainship continued after independence, and the Mutomboko festival, held at the end of July, began in 1971.

regions.label: Northern and Muchinga — Bemba country
regions.sub: Kasama, Mbala, Mpika, Chinsali, Mpulungu, Nakonde

eras.note: Before registers. The Bemba entered Zambia before 1740 and expanded by conquest in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, displacing the Lungu, Mambwe and Bisa.

eras.polity: British South Africa Company sphere; North-Eastern Rhodesia from 1900
eras.note: Rhodes obtained mineral concessions in 1888; North-Eastern Rhodesia was created by Order in Council in January 1900.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company

eras.note: Under the protectorate the Chitimukulu's role became more ceremonial than executive, and many Bemba moved to the Copperbelt in the 1930s for mining work.

regions.label: Liberia - Montserrado and the settler coast
regions.sub: Monrovia, Buchanan, Robertsport, Greenville, Harbel

eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese explorers made contact in 1462 and called it the Pepper Coast; the Dutch set up and abandoned trading posts in 1602 and 1663.

The American Colonization Society acquired Cape Mesurado, near Monrovia, in 1821. The Society's own records, including letters from Liberia for 1833-1917, passenger lists and land grants, are held by the Library of Congress and are largely un-indexed; they are the main source for the first settlers. Mississippi-in-Africa was settled at Sinoe in 1835 as a separate colony.

Separate colonies merged into the Commonwealth of Liberia, dated 1838 or 1839 depending on the source, with Monrovia as capital. Mississippi-in-Africa was annexed by Liberia in 1842. Montserrado and Grand Bassa counties date from 1839.

Independence was declared on 26 July 1847. Sinoe County dates from 1843 or 1847 and Grand Cape Mount from 1844, depending on the source. FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018; births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and marriage registers go to the Center for National Documents and Records in Monrovia.

eras.polity: Liberia - coup, civil wars and new counties
eras.note: Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. The first civil war began in December 1989 and the second ran 1999-2003. Bomi County was created in 1984, Margibi and Rivercess in 1985.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003 and UNMIL took over peacekeeping on 1 October 2003.

regions.label: Liberia - Maryland in Africa and the south-east
regions.sub: Harper (Cape Palmas), Pleebo, Barclayville, Fish Town, Zwedru

eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese contact dates from 1462.

The Maryland legislature funded the emigration of free Black Americans and former slaves in 1831, and settlement at Cape Palmas began on 12 February 1834 as Maryland in Africa. The colony was funded by the Maryland legislature, not by the American Colonization Society.

eras.polity: State of Maryland - an independent republic from 1854
eras.note: The colony declared statehood as the State of Maryland on 2 February 1841 and independence as Maryland in Liberia on 29 May 1854. The date it joined Liberia is 1857 on the Maryland page (18 March or 6 April depending on the passage) and 1854 on the general history of Liberia.

Maryland became a county of Liberia in 1857, and Grand Gedeh, formerly part of the interior provinces, became a county in 1964. Births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018.

eras.polity: Liberia - coup, civil wars and new counties
eras.note: Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. Grand Kru County was created in 1984 and River Gee in 2000. The first civil war began in December 1989 and the second ran 1999-2003.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003.

regions.label: Liberia - Lofa, Bong, Nimba and the interior
regions.sub: Gbarnga, Voinjama, Sanniquellie, Ganta, Kakata

eras.polity: Interior of the Pepper Coast - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. The American Colonization Society settlements of 1821-1847 lay on the coast.

eras.polity: Republic of Liberia - Central, Western and Eastern Provinces
eras.note: This ground was administered as the Central, Western and Eastern Provinces, not as counties, until 1964. A League of Nations report of 1930 criticised the government's treatment of indigenous people, and indigenous Liberians gained the vote in 1951.

eras.polity: Republic of Liberia - Lofa, Bong and Nimba counties
eras.note: Bong, Lofa, Nimba and Grand Gedeh were made counties in 1964. Births and deaths are registered with the Ministry of Health, and FamilySearch's Liberia vital records collection covers 1912-2018.

Samuel Doe seized power on 12 April 1980. The First Liberian Civil War began in December 1989, with Charles Taylor's forces invading from Cote d'Ivoire, and the second war ran 1999-2003. Gbarpolu County was created in 2001.
The Accra Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed on 18 August 2003.

regions.label: Sierra Leone - the Colony and the Protectorate
regions.sub: Freetown, Bo, Kenema, Makeni, Bonthe

eras.note: Before registers.

About 400 formerly enslaved Black Britons arrived on 15 May 1787 and settled Granville Town on land bought from King Tom and the regent Naimbanna II. King Jemmy burned it in 1789 and settlers regathered near Fourah Bay in 1791.

Nova Scotian settlers arrived in February-March 1792 and Freetown was named on 11 March. More than 500 Jamaican Maroons arrived in 1800, and their Maroon Town was founded on the land of the suppressed Nova Scotian rebels.

eras.polity: Crown Colony of Sierra Leone - Freetown and the Liberated Africans
eras.note: The Colony was a Crown colony from 1808 and the base of the Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron, whose rescued captives were called Liberated Africans or Recaptives. The Sierra Leone Public Archives in Freetown hold nineteenth-century Liberated African Department registers, including a series labelled 1808-1845, which have been scanned by the British Library's Endangered Archives Programme.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Sierra Leone
eras.note: A proclamation of 31 August 1896 declared the surrounding country a British Protectorate. The Colony stayed a separate political entity and the Protectorate was governed from it until the 1950s; the Hut Tax War of 1898 was fought in the Protectorate. The Colony and the Protectorate therefore have different legal and record histories.
Independence came on 27 April 1961. Today's divisions are the Eastern, Northern, North West, Southern and Western Area provinces.

regions.label: Ghana - Ashanti, Ahafo, Bono and the Western North
regions.sub: Kumasi, Sunyani, Techiman, Bibiani, Goaso

eras.note: Before registers.
Asante gained independence from Denkyira in 1701 and the Asante Union was founded; Bono was conquered in 1722. The first Anglo-Ashanti war was in 1823-24 and the second in 1863-64.

Britain burned Kumasi in the war of 1873-74 and the Asantehene signed a treaty in July 1874. The Gold Coast Colony was formally established on the coast on 24 July 1874, but Asante remained outside it.

eras.polity: Asante annexed - protectorate and the War of the Golden Stool
eras.note: Britain annexed Asante in January 1896 and proclaimed a protectorate; the War of the Golden Stool followed in March-September 1900.

eras.polity: Ashanti Colony, part of the Gold Coast
eras.note: The Ashanti Crown Colony was created on 26 September 1901 and joined the Gold Coast on 1 January 1902; some pages date this to 1901 and others to 1902. The Asante Confederacy was restored under colonial rule in 1935. The National Archives of Ghana in Accra holds births, marriages and deaths for Europeans and Africans from 1872.

Ghana became independent on 6 March 1957. In 2018 several new regions were created by splitting the Northern, Volta, Western and Brong-Ahafo regions; older records may sit under the former, larger region.

regions.label: Ghana - Volta and Oti, the Trans-Volta Togoland
regions.sub: Ho, Hohoe, Kpando, Nkwanta, Kete Krachi

eras.polity: Ewe, Guan and other states - before registers
eras.note: Before registers.
Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty with chief Mlapa III on 5 July 1884 and declared a German protectorate on the Slave Coast. The Reichskolonialamt files on Togo are in the Bundesarchiv (R 1001).

eras.polity: Anglo-French occupation and the British zone
eras.note: Anglo-French forces invaded in August 1914 and Togoland surrendered on 26 August 1914. On 27 December 1916 it was divided into British and French zones, and the British zone was run as part of the Gold Coast under the name Trans-Volta Togo.

eras.polity: British Togoland under League of Nations mandate
eras.note: Britain received a Class B mandate on 20 July 1922. The territory was administered as part of the Gold Coast.

The territory became a UN Trust Territory under British administration on 13 December 1946. A plebiscite on 9 May 1956 returned about 58 percent for integration with the Gold Coast, and it was annexed to Ghana on 6 March 1957 under the Ghana Independence Act.

Ho, the capital of British Togoland, is now the capital of the Volta Region, which includes much of the former mandate territory. In 2018 the Volta Region was one of four regions split to create new regions.

regions.label: Ghana - the Northern Territories
regions.sub: Tamale, Wa, Bolgatanga, Bawku, Damongo

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Dagomba, Mamprusi, Gonja and Wa states
eras.note: Dagomba was conquered by Asante in the early 1770s and began paying annual tribute.

eras.polity: British treaties and the Northern Territories district
eras.note: British treaties of 1896 with the chiefs of Bona, Dagarti, Wa and Mamprusi barred them from dealings with other powers. The area became a district in 1897.

A 1901 Order in Council made it a protectorate, dated 1 January 1902 or 1901 depending on the source. It was run by the Governor of the Gold Coast through a Chief Commissioner at Gambaga. The National Archives of Ghana in Accra holds births, marriages and deaths from 1872.
The territories joined Ghana on 6 March 1957. In 2018 the Northern Region was among four regions split to create new ones; a place's older records may sit under the former, larger region.

regions.label: Namibia - Windhoek, Walvis Bay and the central regions
regions.sub: Windhoek, Swakopmund, Walvis Bay, Gobabis, Otjiwarongo

eras.polity: Nama, Herero and Damara - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Herero herders moved into this country in the seventeenth century and missionaries arrived in the early 1800s.

eras.polity: Walvis Bay annexed to the Cape; Herero and Nama land inland
eras.note: Britain took Walvis Bay in 1878 (some sources give 1884). Inland the country remained Herero and Nama land.

Germany claimed the territory in 1884 after Adolf Lüderitz bought land at Angra Pequena. German forces carried out the Herero and Nama genocide in 1904-08. The Red Line of 1896, first a rinderpest cordon, became a political boundary in 1907, and police protection was limited to the areas where German economic interests were concentrated. The National Archives of Namibia in Windhoek hold the German colonial government records and the Bundesarchiv holds the Reichskolonialamt files; FamilySearch lists civil registration of marriages 1893-1930 and deaths 1894-1954 for South West Africa.
South African forces occupied the territory in 1915.

eras.polity: South West Africa under South African mandate
eras.note: South Africa governed under a League of Nations mandate from 1920, and the UN General Assembly ended the mandate in 1966. The Dutch Reformed Church registers of Namibia, 1904-2010, are on FamilySearch; the Windhoek archives hold South African administration records. Walvis Bay remained South African.

eras.polity: Independent Namibia; Walvis Bay still South African
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990, but Walvis Bay was transferred from South Africa only in 1994.

eras.polity: Namibia - Erongo, Khomas, Hardap, Omaheke and Otjozondjupa
eras.note: Walvis Bay was transferred to Namibia in 1994. The National Archives of Namibia is governed by the Archives Act 12 of 1992.

regions.label: Namibia - Ovamboland and the Kunene
regions.sub: Oshakati, Ondangwa, Opuwo, Ruacana, Outapi

eras.polity: Ovambo kingdoms and Herero herders - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Ovambo and Kavango farmers lived in the north, and Finnish Lutheran missionaries began work in Ovamboland in the 1870s.

eras.polity: German South West Africa - north of the Red Line
eras.note: The Red Line became a political boundary in 1907, and Oshana, Omusati and Kunene are among the regions listed north of it; the northern areas were largely governed indirectly through traditional authorities.

South Africa occupied the territory in 1915 and governed it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920. Finnish Lutheran missionaries were active from the 1870s and the Ovambo-Kavango Evangelical Lutheran Church was formed in 1954.

Ovamboland was set up as a Bantustan in 1968 under the Odendaal Plan and gained self-government in 1973. A Representative Authority replaced the Bantustan in 1980 and Ovamboland was abolished in May 1989.

eras.polity: Namibia - Kunene, Omusati, Oshana, Ohangwena and Oshikoto
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. The National Archives of Namibia in Windhoek hold records of the German and South African administrations.

regions.label: Namibia - Kavango and the Caprivi Strip
regions.sub: Rundu, Nkurenkuru, Katima Mulilo, Divundu

eras.polity: Kavango and Zambezi river peoples - before registers
eras.note: Before registers. Ovambo and Kavango farmers lived in the north of what is now Namibia.

eras.polity: German South West Africa - the Caprivi Strip and Kavango
eras.note: Germany acquired the Caprivi Strip through the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty with Britain in 1890, mainly for access to the Zambezi. The Kavango and Zambezi lay north of the Red Line, where rule was largely indirect through traditional authorities.

South Africa occupied the territory in 1915 and held it under a League of Nations mandate from 1920. The Ovambo-Kavango Evangelical Lutheran Church was formed in 1954. FamilySearch lists church records for Katima Mulilo.
South Africa created the Eastern Caprivi homeland in 1976 and transferred its administration to the South West African government in 1980.

eras.polity: Namibia - Kavango East, Kavango West and Zambezi
eras.note: Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990. In 1999 the International Court of Justice ruled that Kasikili/Sedudu Island belongs to Botswana.

regions.label: The Orange River borderland - Colesberg and Philippolis
regions.sub: Colesberg, Philippolis, Norvalspont

eras.polity: Griqua mission territory at Philippolis; Cape Colony at Colesberg
eras.note: The London Missionary Society founded Philippolis in 1823 for the Griqua, and Adam Kok II moved there in 1826. Colesberg was founded in 1830 and named for a governor of the Cape Colony.

eras.polity: Orange River Sovereignty north of the river
eras.note: Harry Smith proclaimed British sovereignty over the country between the Orange and Vaal rivers on 3 February 1848, with Bloemfontein as the capital.

eras.polity: Orange Free State; Cape Colony south of the river
eras.note: Britain renounced the Sovereignty and the Orange River Convention of 23 February 1854 recognised the Orange Free State. Britain annexed the diamond fields as Griqualand West in 1871, and the Cape gained responsible government in 1872. Orange Free State marriages are registered from 1848 and births and deaths from 1903; Cape births and deaths from 1895.

eras.polity: Orange River Colony and Cape Colony
eras.note: Britain annexed the Orange Free State as the Orange River Colony in 1900 and the Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 ended the republic's independence.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province and Orange Free State
eras.note: The Cape Colony and the Orange River Colony joined the Union in 1910, as the Cape Province and the Orange Free State province. Home Affairs civil registers have not been transferred to the National Archives.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Northern Cape and Free State
eras.note: Colesberg is now in the Northern Cape and Philippolis in the Free State, on opposite sides of the old Cape-Free State line.

regions.label: The Stormberg and the north-eastern Cape - Burgersdorp, Barkly East
regions.sub: Burgersdorp, Barkly East, Dordrecht, Lady Grey, Indwe

eras.note: Before registers.
The Anglo-Dutch treaty of 1814 confirmed British possession of the Cape, which Britain had re-occupied in 1806.

eras.polity: Cape Colony - Burgersdorp and the Stormberg
eras.note: Burgersdorp was established in 1846. Cape marriage registration is dated from 1700, with Dutch Reformed Church records preceding civil registration and matrimonial court records filling gaps where parish registers are missing.
The Cape gained responsible government in 1872. Civil registration of births and deaths in the Cape began in 1895.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Colony joined the Union in 1910 as the Cape Province. Home Affairs civil registers are held by Home Affairs, not by the National Archives.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Eastern Cape
eras.note: Burgersdorp lies in the Joe Gqabi District.

regions.label: British Kaffraria and the Border - East London, Stutterheim
regions.sub: East London, King William's Town, Stutterheim, Bhisho

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Queen Adelaide Province and Queen Adelaide Land
eras.note: Governor D'Urban annexed the area as Queen Adelaide Province in 1835 and London disapproved; it was disannexed and renamed the Queen Adelaide Land district, with Grahamstown as its capital, and indigenous rule largely returned.

Harry Smith annexed the territory as the British Kaffraria Colony in 1847, with King William's Town as capital, and it became a separate Crown Colony in 1860. German emigrants arrived in 1858-59 and 1877-78.
British Kaffraria was incorporated into the Cape Colony on 17 April 1866. Cape civil registration of births and deaths began in 1895.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: The Cape Colony joined the Union in 1910.
The area formed the basis of the Ciskei homeland, self-governing from 1972 and nominally independent from 4 December 1981, a status not recognised internationally. Its capital was Bisho.

eras.polity: Republic of South Africa - Eastern Cape
eras.note: Ciskei was reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994.

regions.label: Zona da Mata and the Caparaó foothills
regions.sub: Juiz de Fora, Muriaé, Cataguases, Carangola, Guaçuí

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Portugal — the Caminho Novo to the Minas gold fields
eras.note: The Caminho Novo road opened in the early 1700s, linking Rio de Janeiro with the gold district around Vila Rica. The forest of the Zona da Mata on either side stayed thinly settled, mostly by merchants and farmers serving travellers.

Minas Gerais was made a captaincy in 1720, split from São Paulo and Minas de Ouro. Part of this ring on the Espírito Santo and Rio de Janeiro sides lay in neighbouring captaincies, so a parish near the Itabapoana and Caparaó edges may be filed under another jurisdiction.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Minas Gerais
eras.note: Santo Antônio do Paraibuna became the city of Juiz de Fora on 30 May 1850. The Estrada União e Indústria replaced the Caminho Novo in 1861 and the Dom Pedro II railway reached the city in 1866. German immigrants arrived from about 1858.

Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s. The Marmelos Zero hydroelectric plant on the Paraibuna was built in 1889, and textile industry made Juiz de Fora one of Brazil's main industrial centres in the early 1900s.

regions.label: Serra da Mantiqueira and the upper Paraíba valley
regions.sub: Itajubá, Lorena, Cruzeiro, Cachoeira Paulista, Cambuí

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Captaincy of São Paulo and Minas de Ouro (named so from 1709)
eras.note: Lorena's growth began in the 1700s with the gold cycle, along the route of the Paraíba do Sul river.

eras.polity: Captaincies of São Paulo and Minas Gerais
eras.note: Minas Gerais and the remainder of the old São Vicente (São Paulo) were both set up as captaincies in 1720. This ring lies across their line, so a parish may be filed under São Paulo or Minas Gerais.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Provinces of São Paulo and Minas Gerais
eras.note: The valley's history is closely tied to the coffee cycle. Slavery ended nationwide on 13 May 1888 with the Golden Law.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro
eras.note: After the 1929 world economic crisis coffee declined and milk production expanded across the valley.

Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s. Industrialisation of the valley began in the 1940s under the Estado Novo, when a steel mill at Volta Redonda was built for the Allied war effort (inaugurated 1946).

regions.label: Jequitinhonha and Mucuri valleys
regions.sub: Teixeira de Freitas, Nanuque, Almenara, Barra de São Francisco, Taiobeiras

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Hereditary captaincies of Porto Seguro and Espírito Santo
eras.note: The coastal captaincies were granted from 1534: Porto Seguro to Pero Campos Tourinho and Espírito Santo to Vasco Fernandes Coutinho. Porto Seguro was one of only four private captaincies to survive beyond 1549.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Minas Gerais and the coastal captaincies
eras.note: Minas Gerais became a captaincy in 1720, split from São Paulo and Minas de Ouro. The last private captaincies reverted to the Crown in 1754.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Provinces of Minas Gerais, Bahia and Espírito Santo
eras.note: Filadélfia, now Teófilo Otoni, was founded in the Mucuri valley on 7 September 1853 and made a city on 9 November 1878; the municipality was installed on 25 March 1881.

eras.polity: Brazil — Minas Gerais, Bahia and Espírito Santo
eras.note: Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s. The ring crosses three state lines, so a family's records may be at the Arquivo Público Mineiro, the Fundação Pedro Calmon in Bahia or the Arquivo Público do Espírito Santo.

regions.label: Alto Paranaíba and the Paraná bank
regions.sub: Três Lagoas, Itumbiara, Paranaíba, Aparecida do Taboado, São Simão

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Captaincies of Goiás and Mato Grosso
eras.note: Goiás and Mato Grosso were both created in 1748, split from São Paulo. The Triângulo Mineiro, including Uberaba, belonged to Goiás until 1816; Uberaba began in 1810 as a settlement beside the road to Goiás.

eras.polity: Brazil — Minas Gerais (Triângulo from 1816), Goiás and Mato Grosso
eras.note: The Triângulo territory was incorporated into the Captaincy of Minas Gerais in 1816. Uberaba was made a parish in 1820 and a city in 1856; the Mogiana Railway reached it in 1889.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of Minas Gerais, Goiás and Mato Grosso
eras.note: Three Brazilian states meet on this ground, so the archive depends on the side of the Paranaíba and Paraná rivers: Minas Gerais, Goiás, or Mato Grosso.

eras.polity: Brazil — Mato Grosso do Sul, Goiás and Minas Gerais
eras.note: Mato Grosso do Sul was created on 11 October 1977 by splitting Mato Grosso, taking full effect on 1 January 1979. Records made at Três Lagoas, Paranaíba or Aparecida do Taboado before that were created under Mato Grosso.

regions.label: Pontal do Paranapanema and the Ivinhema bank
regions.sub: Teodoro Sampaio, Rosana, Cândido Mota, Batayporã

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Captaincies of São Paulo and Mato Grosso
eras.note: Mato Grosso was created as a captaincy in 1748, split from São Paulo; the Paraná river later became the line between the states of São Paulo and Mato Grosso do Sul.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Provinces of São Paulo and Mato Grosso
eras.note: The Guarani-Kaiowá, the first peoples of southern Mato Grosso do Sul, were first contacted by non-indigenous people in the 1800s.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of São Paulo and Mato Grosso
eras.note: The Estrada de Ferro Noroeste do Brasil links the centre-west of São Paulo with Corumbá.

eras.polity: Brazil — São Paulo and Mato Grosso do Sul
eras.note: Mato Grosso do Sul was created on 11 October 1977, effective 1 January 1979, so records from the Mato Grosso do Sul bank before 1979 were made under Mato Grosso. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: Rondônia — the Guaporé plateau
regions.sub: Rolim de Moura, São Francisco do Guaporé, Seringueiras

eras.note: Before registers.
Mato Grosso was created in 1748, split from São Paulo.
Rubber exploitation peaked near the end of the 19th century; rubber and Brazil nut gathering were the main activities for a long time afterwards.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of Amazonas and Mato Grosso
eras.note: The Treaty of Petrópolis of 1903 obliged Brazil to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway; building began in 1907 and the last section opened on 30 April 1912.

eras.polity: Federal Territory of Guaporé, renamed Rondônia in 1956
eras.note: Decree-Law 5812 of 13 September 1943 created the Federal Territory of Guaporé from parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso; a law of 17 February 1956 renamed it Rondônia. Records of earlier years may sit under Amazonas or Mato Grosso.

Rondônia became a state in 1982 (some sources say 1981), with 13 original municipalities. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Mamoré frontier — Riberalta, Guayaramerín and Guajará-Mirim
regions.sub: Riberalta, Guayaramerín, Guajará-Mirim

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Bolivia — the rubber frontier on the Beni
eras.note: Riberalta was named Barranca Colorada in 1880, La Cruz in 1884 and Ribera-Alta in 1885, and was founded as Villa Riberalta on 3 February 1894 (some sources give 1897).

eras.polity: Bolivia and Brazil — the Treaty of Petrópolis line
eras.note: By the Treaty of Petrópolis (17 November 1903) Bolivia gave Acre to Brazil and Brazil promised a railway round the Madeira rapids so that Bolivian rubber could reach the Amazon. Construction began in 1907; the last section opened on 30 April 1912.

eras.polity: Bolivia (Beni) and Brazil (Territory of Guaporé, then Rondônia)
eras.note: The Brazilian bank was in the Federal Territory of Guaporé from 13 September 1943, renamed Rondônia in 1956. The Madeira-Mamoré railway was abandoned in 1972 after the BR-364 highway was finished.
Guajará-Mirim was one of the 13 original municipalities of the State of Rondônia in 1982. Brazil nut gathering drives the economy of Riberalta.

regions.label: Acre
regions.sub: Xapuri, Brasiléia, Epitaciolândia, Assis Brasil

eras.note: Before registers.
Spanish colonisation brought the area into the Viceroyalty of Peru in the 1750s to 1820s; after the independence wars Peru and Bolivia both claimed it.

eras.polity: Bolivia (disputed with Peru) — the rubber boom
eras.note: The area belonged to the Peru-Bolivian Confederation in 1836-1839 and then mostly returned to Bolivian control; the Treaty of Ayacucho of 1867 addressed the boundary, though the sources describe its terms inconsistently. Rubber drew many migrants, mainly from north-eastern Brazil.

eras.polity: Bolivian Acre — the Acre War and the Independent State of Acre
eras.note: Bolivia set up an administrative post at Puerto Alonso in 1899. Rubber gatherers occupied Xapuri in August 1902, beginning the Acre War, and proclaimed the Independent State of Acre in February 1903.

By the Treaty of Petrópolis (17 November 1903) Bolivia ceded the territory for two million pounds sterling; its area is given as about 142,800 km2 by one account and 191,000 km2 by another. Brazil created the Territory of Acre in 1904; the Velarde-Río Branco Treaty of 1909 fixed the Peru-Brazil border, and from 1921 governors replaced appointed administrators.

Acre became a Brazilian state on 15 June 1962. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Upper Solimões — Tabatinga and the Three Frontiers
regions.sub: Tabatinga, Benjamin Constant, Atalaia do Norte, Ramón Castilla

eras.note: Before registers.
In the mid-1600s a Jesuit village is recorded near the mouth of the Solimões, undated.

A military post and a customs post were set up in 1766 by Fernando da Costa Ataíde Teives, who also placed guard posts along the Portuguese-Spanish line; the settlement of São Francisco Xavier de Tabatinga grew from them.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — municipality of São Paulo de Olivença
eras.note: Until the Brazil-Peru boundary marker was set near the settlement in 1866 (sources give 28 June or 28 July), the area belonged to the municipality of São Paulo de Olivença.

eras.polity: Empire and Republic of Brazil; Peruvian Loreto across the line
eras.note: Leticia was founded on 25 April 1867 by the Peruvian governor of Loreto and renamed on 15 December 1867. In 1898 Tabatinga became a subdistrict of the new municipality of Benjamin Constant, cut from São Paulo de Olivença.

eras.polity: Brazil — Amazonas; Peru and Colombia across the Amazon
eras.note: A 1922 agreement (ratified 1928) gave Leticia to Colombia in return for Peru's rights south of the Putumayo; Peruvians occupied Leticia in September 1932, and the League of Nations awarded the area to Colombia in June 1934.
The whole municipality of Benjamin Constant, which then included Tabatinga, was classed a National Security Area by federal law 5,449 on 4 June 1968.

eras.polity: Brazil — Tabatinga, Benjamin Constant, Atalaia do Norte
eras.note: Tabatinga became a municipality on 10 December 1981 and was installed on 1 January 1983 (one source gives 1 February). With Leticia in Colombia and Santa Rosa de Yavarí in Peru it forms one urban area of more than 120,000 people, so records are split across three countries.

regions.label: The Araguaia and Tocantins valleys
regions.sub: Dom Eliseu, Conceição do Araguaia, Carolina, São Geraldo do Araguaia, Itinga do Maranhão

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Portugal — Jesuit exploration of the Araguaia-Tocantins
eras.note: Portuguese Jesuit missionaries explored the area about 1625. Rivers navigable only in short stretches, and mountains, kept it isolated.
Goiás became a captaincy in 1748, split from São Paulo. After heavy mining taxes, local people began separatist agitation in 1809, and a minor revolt was quickly crushed.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of Goiás
eras.note: The 19th century saw several more failed uprisings in northern Goiás.

eras.polity: Brazil — States of Goiás, Pará and Maranhão
eras.note: The site of Brasília was chosen in the south of Goiás in 1956. From the 1970s people in northern Goiás lobbied for a separate state. The ring also crosses into Pará and Maranhão, so a place may be filed in any of three states.

The 1988 Constitution created Tocantins from the northern two-fifths of Goiás (sources differ; 1989 is also given), and building of the capital Palmas began in 1989. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Apodi and Jaguaribe borderland — Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte and Paraíba
regions.sub: Pau dos Ferros, Baraúna, Icapuí, Uiraúna

eras.note: Before registers.

Pero Coelho de Sousa founded a settlement near the mouth of the Ceará river in 1603 but left a year later because of drought. Martim Soares Moreno expelled the French in 1612; the Dutch held the area from 1637 until 1654.
Ceará was a dependency of Pernambuco from 1680; the captaincy became independent in 1799. This ring also holds ground in Rio Grande do Norte and Paraíba, which had different jurisdictions.
The captaincy of Ceará was independent of Pernambuco from 1799.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Provinces of Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte and Paraíba
eras.note: An 1824 revolution proclaimed a republic in Ceará before the province returned to the empire. The great drought of 1877-1880 destroyed nearly all the livestock and caused nearly half a million deaths. Ceará abolished slavery on 25 March 1884, the first Brazilian province to do so.

eras.polity: Brazil — Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte and Paraíba
eras.note: Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The lower São Francisco — Penedo and Traipu
regions.sub: Penedo, Piaçabuçu, Neópolis, Traipu, Gararu

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Portuguese Brazil — the São Francisco estuary
eras.note: Penedo was founded in 1614 and reached by sea from the São Francisco estuary. Its churches, including the Convent of São Francisco and Our Lady of the Angels, were built through the 18th century. The last private captaincies reverted to the Crown in 1754.

eras.polity: United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves
eras.note: In 1815 Brazil became a kingdom and all existing provinces and Crown captaincies became provinces of the United Kingdom.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Provinces of Alagoas and Sergipe
eras.note: The river separates Alagoas from Sergipe, so the two banks are filed in different provinces and later states. Penedo preserves Portuguese and Dutch colonial architecture.

Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Contestado — the Paraná and Santa Catarina border
regions.sub: Mafra, Canoinhas, Rio Negro, Três Barras, Itapoá

eras.note: Before registers.
The Captaincy of São Paulo was made in 1720 from the remainder of São Vicente.

eras.polity: Brazil — Provinces and States of Paraná and Santa Catarina
eras.note: The land between the two provinces was claimed by Paraná and Santa Catarina, and also by Argentina.

In 1908 President Afonso Pena commissioned a São Paulo-Rio Grande do Sul railway; its concession gave the Brazil Railway Company a strip 15 km wide on each side, displacing farmers. The Contestado War ran from October 1912 to August 1916.

The governors of Santa Catarina and Paraná signed a boundary agreement on 12 October 1916, and Campos do Irani was renamed Concórdia. Until then a place near the line could be recorded under either state. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Jaguarão and Chuí frontier
regions.sub: Jaguarão, Río Branco, Santa Vitória do Palmar, Pinheiro Machado

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Banda Oriental, with Portuguese claims
eras.note: The Treaty of Badajoz of 1801 made Colônia do Sacramento a Spanish possession.

eras.polity: Portuguese occupation of the Banda Oriental
eras.note: Portuguese forces invaded in 1816 and took Montevideo on 20 January 1817; Artigas was defeated at Tacuarembó in 1820.

On 31 July 1821 Montevideo's cabildo approved incorporation into the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves as the province of Cisplatina. The Cisplatine War ran from 10 December 1825 to 27 August 1828, with a garrison and camp at Jaguarão in 1827-1828.

eras.polity: Uruguay and the Empire of Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul)
eras.note: Under a preliminary peace convention of 27 August 1828 Cisplatina became the independent Oriental State of Uruguay. The Battle of Jaguarão was fought in 1865.

eras.polity: Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul) and Uruguay
eras.note: A bridge links Jaguarão with Río Branco across the border. Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: The Ribeira coast and the south-west of São Paulo
regions.sub: Cananéia, Itapeva, Taquarituba

eras.note: Before registers.

Cananéia was founded on 12 August 1531, about five months before São Vicente; some Portuguese and Spanish historians call it the oldest town in Brazil, though São Vicente is officially recognised as the oldest. The captaincy of São Vicente, granted to Martim Afonso de Sousa and Pero Lopes de Sousa, ran from Cananéia to Cabo Frio.
The Captaincy of São Paulo was made in 1720 from the remainder of São Vicente.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of São Paulo
eras.note: Cananéia's historic centre keeps buildings from the colonial period to the end of the 19th century.

Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: Manhattan and the Hudson Palisades — New Amsterdam
regions.sub: Lower Manhattan, Chinatown, Hell's Kitchen, Fort Lee, Palisades Park

eras.note: Before registers.

The Dutch settled Manhattan in 1624 (the city seal says 1625); Fort Amsterdam was begun in 1625-26, and the purchase of Manhattan is documented in a letter of 7 November 1626. New Amsterdam received municipal rights on 2 February 1653. The colony's administrative records survive largely untranslated and have been translated since the 1970s by the New Netherland Institute.
The English took the colony without a fight on 27 August 1664; the Articles of Surrender were signed on 6 September, and in June 1665 it was reincorporated as New York City.
The Dutch retook the colony on 9 August 1673 and renamed it New Orange. The Treaty of Westminster of February 1674 returned it to England, with the transfer taking effect on 10 November 1674.

eras.polity: United States — New York and New Jersey
eras.note: Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. The Hudson is the line between New York and New Jersey, so Hudson Palisades towns such as Fort Lee are in New Jersey records.
Brooklyn, which had annexed Gravesend and Coney Island in 1894, became part of New York City in 1898.

regions.label: Brooklyn's south shore — Gravesend to the Rockaways
regions.sub: Gravesend, Sheepshead Bay, Brighton Beach, Seaside, Belle Harbor

eras.note: Before registers.

Henry Hudson's Half Moon is believed to have made the first European landing at Coney Island in autumn 1609, and the Dutch claimed the land as New Netherland. Governor Kieft granted Lady Deborah Moody and English settlers a patent on 19 December 1645 (some sources give 1643); Gravesend was the only English-chartered town in what became Kings County. The town bought Coney Island from the Lenape in 1654.

eras.polity: United States — Town of Gravesend, Kings County
eras.note: British and German troops landed at Gravesend Bay in August 1776, leading to the Battle of Long Island. Gravesend Race Track opened on 26 August 1886, and Sheepshead Bay and Brighton Beach also had race tracks.
The City of Brooklyn annexed Gravesend and Coney Island in 1894.

eras.polity: City of New York — Brooklyn and Queens
eras.note: Brooklyn became part of New York City in 1898.

regions.label: The Delaware River shore — New Sweden to Philadelphia
regions.sub: Chester, Pennsville, Carneys Point, Torresdale, Claymont

eras.note: Before registers.

A Swedish expedition landed on 29 March 1638 and built Fort Christina, the first permanent European settlement in the Delaware Valley. New Sweden spread across the lower Delaware in what is now Delaware, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Maryland.
The Dutch conquered New Sweden, and Fort Christina surrendered on 15 September 1655.

eras.polity: English conquest and the Duke of York's colony
eras.note: The English conquest of 1664 ended Dutch rule, and Fort Casimir fell in October. The Revolt of the Long Swede in 1669 failed to restore Swedish rule. After the Dutch recapture of 1673 three courts were set up: Hoarkill, New Amstel and Upland.

eras.polity: Pennsylvania and Delaware under William Penn
eras.note: The former New Sweden area was divided into Delaware and Pennsylvania on 4 March 1681, and on 24 August 1682 the Duke of York transferred the western Delaware River region to William Penn. Swedish remained a church language into the 18th century, and Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church in Philadelphia was built about 1700 on the site of the 1669 blockhouse.

eras.polity: United States — Pennsylvania, Delaware and New Jersey
eras.note: The Delaware River is the line between New Jersey on the east bank and Pennsylvania and Delaware on the west, so a family on one bank is filed in a different state from one across the water.

regions.label: Northern Kentucky — Boone and neighbouring counties
regions.sub: Florence, Erlanger, Burlington, Edgewood, Elsmere

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Ohio Valley frontier — Big Bone Lick
eras.note: A Frenchman mapped the Big Bone Lick area in 1729. A Native American village at Petersburg shows habitation dating to about 1150 and 1400.
Boone County was created in 1798 from part of Campbell County, with Burlington as county seat. Ferries carried traffic across the Ohio River to Cincinnati.

eras.polity: United States — Boone, Kenton and Campbell counties
eras.note: Margaret Garner and her family escaped slavery in 1856 by crossing the frozen Ohio River near Covington.
The John A. Roebling Suspension Bridge, completed in 1866, replaced the ferries between Covington and Cincinnati.
Growth accelerated from the 1970s with the completion of I-75, new industrial parks and the Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport in Boone County.

regions.label: Cape Breton Island — Île Royale
regions.sub: Sydney, Glace Bay, New Waterford, Sydney Mines, North Sydney

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: French Acadia — Englishtown and St. Peter's
eras.note: The French established settlements at Englishtown and St. Peter's in 1629-30 after Scottish colonists had planted one at Baleine in 1627-29; the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye of 1632 gave the Scottish gains back to France. The settlements lapsed after Nicolas Denys left in 1659.

After the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 settlement was re-established, with Plaisance residents moved to Île Royale and a garrison at Sainte Anne before Louisbourg. New Englanders took Louisbourg in 1745, France got it back in 1748, and the British took it again in 1758 and demolished the fortress.

eras.polity: Nova Scotia (Cape Breton administered from Halifax)
eras.note: The Treaty of Paris of 1763 gave Île Royale to Britain and merged it with Nova Scotia. Acadians were allowed to resettle from 1764, Judique, settled in 1775, was the first permanent Scottish community, and coal mining at Sydney Mines was developed from 1777.
Britain made Cape Breton a separate colony with its capital at Sydney in 1784.
Cape Breton was merged with Nova Scotia again in 1820.
Nova Scotia joined Confederation on 1 July 1867. Glace Bay's last coal mine closed in the 1980s.

regions.label: The Detroit and St Clair River borderland
regions.sub: Leamington, Kingsville, Amherstburg, Sarnia, Tecumseh

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: New France — the Detroit River settlements
eras.note: The first permanent settlements began to appear about 1749 on the Canadian side of the river across from Fort Detroit. The "Assumption Settlement" took its name from its Catholic church.

eras.polity: British rule after the Seven Years' War
eras.note: The British took over French territory in the Detroit region after the Seven Years' War; the Treaty of Paris was signed in 1763.

Upper Canada was formed in 1791, and in 1792 it was divided into nineteen counties, of which Essex was the eighteenth. Britain gave up Fort Detroit under the Jay Treaty (signed 1794), and Amherstburg and Sandwich were both established in 1796. Fort Malden was built near Amherstburg. The War of 1812 ran from 1812 to 1815.

eras.polity: Upper Canada and the Province of Canada
eras.note: Black Americans reached Essex County by the Underground Railroad through Point Pelee, Gosfield (now Kingsville), Colchester, Sandwich and Windsor; Amherstburg and Windsor were the main settlement areas.

eras.polity: Canada — Ontario; Michigan across the river
eras.note: Confederation took effect on 1 July 1867. The river is the international border, so a family may appear in Ontario and in Michigan records.

regions.label: The western pampa — the Buenos Aires frontier
regions.sub: Junín, Nueve de Julio, Lincoln, General Villegas, Los Toldos

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Province of Buenos Aires — the Indigenous frontier
eras.note: An offensive by Juan Manuel de Rosas in 1833 achieved some success against the peoples of the pampa.

eras.polity: Province of Buenos Aires — Alsina's fortified line
eras.note: Calfucurá's raids of 1872 hit General Alvear, Veinticinco de Mayo and Nueve de Julio. Adolfo Alsina built the Zanja de Alsina, a 374 km trench three metres wide and two deep, with fortines along his route linked to Buenos Aires by telegraph.

eras.polity: Argentina — the Conquest of the Desert
eras.note: General Roca's sweeps began in late 1878 against the Ranqueles, Tehuelches and Pehuenches and their Mapuche allies; the last battle was on 18 October 1884.

regions.label: Formosa and the Bermejo-Pilcomayo Chaco
regions.sub: Formosa, La Leonesa

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Río de la Plata — Concepción del Bermejo
eras.note: The first European settlement, Concepción del Bermejo, was founded in 1585. Explorers had earlier sought a route from Peru to Asunción, but the shallow Pilcomayo and Bermejo rivers defeated them.
After independence the area was disputed between Argentina and Paraguay, a matter not settled until after the War of the Triple Alliance (1865-1870).
Commander Luis Jorge Fontana founded Formosa in 1879.
The area gained territorial status in 1884, and the population in 1914 was under 20,000. The Rincón Bomba massacre of nomadic Indigenous people by the Gendarmería took place in 1947.
Formosa became a province by decree of Juan Perón in 1955.

regions.label: The Murray River borderland
regions.sub: Wodonga, Mildura, Echuca, Swan Hill, Moama

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: New South Wales — the Hume and Hovell exploration
eras.note: Hume and Hovell set out to explore southward in October 1824.

eras.polity: Port Phillip District of New South Wales
eras.note: The Port Phillip District was formally established as an administrative division of New South Wales in September 1836.

eras.polity: Colony of Victoria and the Colony of New South Wales
eras.note: Victoria was formed on 1 July 1851 (some sources give 2 July). The border runs along the top of the southern (Victorian) bank of the Murray, so the whole river is in New South Wales: Echuca is in Victoria and Moama, across the water, in New South Wales.

eras.polity: Australia — Victoria and New South Wales
eras.note: Victoria became a state at the beginning of 1901. A 1980 High Court judgment settled which state had jurisdiction over a death on the Victorian side of the river's edge.

regions.label: The Northern Rivers and the Tweed border
regions.sub: Tweed Heads, Ballina, Byron Bay, Yamba, Woolgoolga

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: New South Wales — the Moreton Bay penal frontier
eras.note: The Moreton Bay penal settlement was founded in 1824, and convict transportation ended in 1839. The Northern Rivers are the country of the Bundjalung, Gumbaynggirr and Yaegl peoples.
Free settlement of the Moreton Bay district was permitted from 1842. Valuable red cedar drew early development to the river valleys.

eras.polity: New South Wales and the Colony of Queensland
eras.note: Queensland separated from New South Wales on 6 June 1859 and became a self-governing colony, so a family at Tweed Heads and one at Coolangatta fall under different colonies. The Big Scrub rainforest was largely cleared for timber and then dairying, and New Italy was settled in 1882.

eras.polity: Australia — New South Wales and Queensland
eras.note: Queensland and New South Wales became founding states of Australia on 1 January 1901. Dairying was extensive until the 1970s, and train services on the Murwillumbah line were suspended in 2004.

regions.label: The Táchira frontier — San Antonio, Rubio and Santa Ana
regions.sub: San Antonio del Táchira, Rubio, Santa Ana

eras.note: Before registers.

San Cristóbal was founded on 31 March 1561, and La Grita in 1576 became capital of the province of La Grita. Juan José García de Hevia led an insurrection against Spanish rule in 1781, and Bolívar invaded Venezuela through Táchira during his Admirable Campaign.
Congress created the Province of Táchira on 11 March 1856, and it became a state in 1863-1864; in 1867-1868 it was part of the State of Zulia.
In 1881 Táchira joined Trujillo and Mérida in the Great State of Los Andes.

The Great State of Los Andes was dissolved in 1899 and Táchira became an independent state again. Colombia's Norte de Santander borders it on the west and south, so many families have records on both sides.

regions.label: The Sonora-Arizona border — the Gadsden line
regions.sub: San Luis Río Colorado, San Luis, Sonoyta

eras.note: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War but left the border unsettled, including the Mesilla Valley.

eras.polity: Mexico (Sonora) and the United States (New Mexico Territory)
eras.note: James Gadsden and Santa Anna signed the treaty on 30 or 31 December 1853; the Senate approved it on 25 April 1854 and it took effect on 8 June 1854 (30 June by another account). The United States gained about 29,640 square miles of southern Arizona and south-western New Mexico for $10 million.
Arizona Territory was created in 1863 from the western half of New Mexico Territory. The Southern Pacific Railroad reached Yuma in 1877.
Arizona became a state on 14 February 1912. The border follows the Colorado River on part of its course, so San Luis, Arizona, and San Luis Río Colorado are in different countries.

regions.label: The Cayman Islands
regions.sub: George Town, West Bay, Bodden Town, Cayman Brac

eras.note: Columbus sighted the islands in 1503 and named them Las Tortugas for the sea turtles. Sir Francis Drake was the first recorded English visitor, in 1586.

eras.polity: England — Jamaica and the Treaty of Madrid
eras.note: England took formal control with Jamaica under the Treaty of Madrid in 1670. Isaac Bodden, born about 1700, is the first recorded permanent inhabitant.

Permanent settlement of Grand Cayman began in 1734; Cayman Brac and Little Cayman were not permanently settled until 1833. A legislative assembly was established in 1831. Slavery lasted from about 1734 to 1834.
Emancipation was declared in 1835 by Governor Sligo under the Slavery Abolition Act 1833.
The islands were officially a Jamaican dependency from 1863. The 1959 constitution gave women the vote and ended the Jamaica dependency.
After Jamaica's independence in 1962 the islands became a direct dependency of the Crown, and a governor replaced the administrator in 1971.

regions.label: Bermuda
regions.sub: Hamilton, St. George's, Southampton, Pembroke

eras.note: Juan de Bermúdez is the earliest recorded Spanish explorer associated with the island, which takes his name.
The Sea Venture was wrecked on a reef on 3 August 1609; its survivors stayed nine months, and Bermuda became a permanent part of the English colonial empire. St. George's was founded in 1612.
The Somers Isles Company took over the colony in 1615, and the House of Assembly held its first session in 1620.
The Somers Isles Company's charter was revoked in 1684 and Bermuda became a Crown colony. Hamilton became the seat of government in 1815.
Emancipation across the British Empire in 1834 followed an abolitionist push to which The History of Mary Prince contributed.
A formal constitution in 1968 strengthened internal self-government, and in 2002 Bermuda became a British Overseas Territory under the British Overseas Territories Act.

regions.label: Aruba
regions.sub: Oranjestad, Noord, San Nicolas, Santa Cruz

eras.note: The Arawakan-speaking Caquetío were the people of Aruba when Europeans arrived, and the Spanish disrupted them and depopulated the islands between 1513 and 1515.
The Dutch from Curaçao occupied Aruba and Bonaire in 1636.
The island was under British occupation from 1806 to 1816, during the Napoleonic Wars, and returned to Dutch rule under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814.

eras.polity: Dutch colony of Curaçao and Dependencies
eras.note: The Lago Oil and Transport Company, a Standard Oil subsidiary, built its refinery at San Nicolaas in 1924.
The Charter of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1954 created the Netherlands Antilles, uniting the Dutch Caribbean colonies.

eras.polity: Aruba — a country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands
eras.note: Aruba separated from the Netherlands Antilles on 1 January 1986 as a constituent country of the Kingdom.

regions.label: Curaçao
regions.sub: Willemstad, Bandabou, Sint Michiel

eras.polity: Spanish claim — the island of no use
eras.note: Alonso de Ojeda was the first European to visit, in 1499. By 1515 nearly all the Caquetío had been enslaved and taken to Hispaniola. The Spanish settled in 1527 and called the island an isla inutil.

The Company captured the island in 1634 and built Fort Amsterdam, around which Willemstad grew. Sephardic Jews arrived from Dutch Brazil, Curaçao became a free port in 1674 and a major slave-trading hub, and there were a French siege in 1713 and a slave revolt in 1716.

After the Company's bankruptcy in 1791 Curaçao became a Dutch colony. A slave revolt led by Tula took place in 1795, and the British occupied the island in 1800-1803 and 1807-1816, returning it under the 1815 Treaty of Paris. Slavery was abolished in 1863.

eras.polity: Dutch colony of Curaçao and Dependencies
eras.note: After oil was found in Venezuela in 1914 Shell built a refinery on the island. The British occupied it in 1940 and US troops arrived in 1941.
The island gained political autonomy in 1954 within the Netherlands Antilles. A workers' revolt on 30 May 1969 led to political reforms.

eras.polity: Curaçao — a country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands
eras.note: Curaçao became a constituent country on 10 October 2010.

regions.label: New Caledonia
regions.sub: Nouméa, Dumbéa, Païta, Bourail, Lifou

eras.note: Before registers.
France formally took possession in 1853 under Napoleon III, and founded Nouméa as Port-de-France in 1854.
The territory became a penal colony in 1864, the year nickel was discovered, and convict transportation continued until 1897. High Chief Ataï led a major Kanak uprising in 1878.
New Caledonia became an overseas territory in 1946. "The Events", a period of violence between the independence movement and the French government, ran from 1976 to 1988.

eras.polity: French sui generis collectivity — the Nouméa Accord
eras.note: The Nouméa Accord of 1998 set a 20-year transition toward greater self-governance. Independence referendums in 2018, 2020 and 2021 each voted to remain part of France.

regions.label: The Society Islands — Tahiti, Moorea and the Leeward Islands
regions.sub: Papeete, Faaa, Punaauia, Moorea, Raiatea, Bora Bora

eras.note: Before registers.
France established a protectorate over Tahiti in 1842 and annexed the islands in the late 1800s.
The territory became an overseas territory in 1946.
It was renamed French Polynesia in 1957. France conducted nuclear tests at Moruroa and Fangataufa until 1996.
French Polynesia became an overseas collectivity in 2003 and has 48 communes. The UN relisted it as a non-self-governing territory in 2013.

regions.label: The Solomon Islands
regions.sub: Honiara, Gizo, Noro, Auki

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish sighting; mission and labour trade
eras.note: Álvaro de Mendaña sighted the islands in 1568; later Spanish colonisation attempts failed, and missionaries arrived from the 1840s.
Britain declared a protectorate over the southern islands in 1893, partly to curb Queensland's recruitment of Pacific Islander labourers. Germany transferred several islands to Britain in 1900.
Japan occupied the north in 1942 and Allied forces landed on Guadalcanal and Tulagi that August; Honiara grew into a US logistics hub. A 1974 constitution set up Westminster-style government.
The country became independent on 7 July 1978. Land disputes and migration between Guadalcanal and Malaita led to armed conflict in 1998-2003, ended by an Australian-led regional mission in 2003.

regions.label: The Western Carolines — Palau and Yap
regions.sub: Koror, Colonia, Yap

eras.note: Before registers.

Diogo da Rocha, a Portuguese navigator, possibly made the first European contact with the Carolines in 1525, staying about four months at Ulithi and meeting Yap. Spain governed its islands in Micronesia from the Philippines.
Spain sold the Carolines, Marianas and other possessions to Germany by the treaty of 12 February 1899.

Japan seized the German islands by October 1914, and its League of Nations mandate dates from 1920. Koror was the seat of government, and the civilian Nan'yō-chō (South Seas Government) was established in March 1932.

eras.polity: US Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
eras.note: The United Nations placed the islands under US trusteeship on 18 July 1947. The Navy governed from Guam until 1951, when the Interior Department took over from Saipan.

eras.polity: Federated States of Micronesia (Yap) and Palau — free association
eras.note: The Security Council ended the trusteeship for most districts in 1990 and for Palau in 1994. Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia became independent states in free association with the United States.

regions.label: The Eastern Carolines — Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae
regions.sub: Weno, Kolonia, Palikir, Tofol

eras.note: Spain governed its Micronesian islands as part of the Spanish East Indies, from the Philippines. By the late 1890s, after the United States took Guam and the Philippines in 1898-1899, Spain was left with about 6,000 sparsely populated islands it could neither govern nor defend.
The German-Spanish treaty of 12 February 1899 transferred the Carolines to Germany.
Truk (Chuuk) and Ponape (Pohnpei) were two of the six administrative districts set up in 1922; the Japanese population of the mandate rose from under 4,000 in 1920 to about 70,000 in 1930.

eras.polity: US Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
eras.note: The islands became part of the Trust Territory on 18 July 1947, with six districts including Truk and Ponape.

eras.polity: Federated States of Micronesia — free association
eras.note: US administration ended in 1986 and the Security Council ended the trusteeship for most districts in 1990. The Federated States are an independent state in free association with the United States.

regions.label: The Marshall Islands
regions.sub: Majuro, Ebeye, Kwajalein, Jaluit

eras.note: Spanish expeditions sighted the islands from 1526, British ships visited in 1788, and American Protestant missionaries reached Ebon in 1855. German trading firms dominated the copra trade from the 1860s.

Germany declared a protectorate in October 1885 after a treaty of 1878 with the chief Kabua. The Jaluit Company administered the islands from 1888, and in 1906 Germany folded them into German New Guinea.
Japan seized the islands in 1914 and held a League of Nations mandate after the Treaty of Versailles. Jaluit was one of the mandate's six administrative districts.

eras.polity: US Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
eras.note: US forces invaded in January 1944, beginning with Majuro and Kwajalein. The islands passed to US trusteeship in 1947. The United States held 67 nuclear tests at the Pacific Proving Grounds between 1946 and 1958.

eras.polity: Republic of the Marshall Islands — free association
eras.note: The islands became self-governing in 1979, and the Compact of Free Association with the United States took effect in 1986.

regions.label: The Northern Mariana Islands
regions.sub: Saipan, Tinian, Rota

eras.note: Before registers.
Spain claimed the islands in 1521 after Magellan's expedition arrived.
Spain sold the Marianas other than Guam to Germany by the treaty of 12 February 1899.
Saipan was one of the mandate's six administrative districts, created in 1922.

eras.polity: US Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
eras.note: US forces captured Saipan in 1944. The Interior Department administered the Trust Territory from Saipan from 1951. Residents chose commonwealth status in a 1975 referendum.

eras.polity: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands
eras.note: The commonwealth government took effect in 1978, and residents became US citizens in 1986. Pagan has been largely uninhabited since an eruption in 1981.

regions.label: American Samoa — Tutuila and Manu'a
regions.sub: Pago Pago, Tāfuna, Ofu, Ta'ū

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Samoa — the Pago Pago coaling station
eras.note: A treaty of friendship in 1878 gave the United States rights to a naval coaling station at Pago Pago Bay.

The Tripartite Convention and Treaty of Berlin of 1899 divided Samoa between Germany and the United States. The United States formally occupied its part in 1900, when several Tutuila chiefs ceded the island.
Tui Manu'a Elisara signed the cession of Manu'a in 1904. Seventeen chiefs of the American Samoa Mau were arrested in 1921, and the United States ratified the cessions in 1929.
The territory's constitution took effect on 1 July 1967.

regions.label: Western Greenland — Nuuk and Sisimiut
regions.sub: Nuuk (Godthåb), Sisimiut

eras.note: Erik the Red reached the southwest coast in the 980s. The Eastern and Western Settlements lasted roughly 450 to 500 years, and the last written record is a marriage at Hvalsey Church in 1408. The ancestors of today's Greenlandic Inuit arrived about 1200 from northern Canada.
Before registers.
Denmark-Norway resumed contact in 1721 through Hans Egede's mission; trading colonies and a trade monopoly followed, and Nuuk (Godthåb) was founded in 1728.
In 1953 Greenland changed from a colony to a county of Denmark.
Greenland gained home rule in 1979, and self-government was expanded in 2008-2009.

regions.label: Easter Island (Rapa Nui)
regions.sub: Hanga Roa

eras.note: Before registers. Polynesians settled the island, with the current best estimate about the 12th century.
The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen arrived on Easter Sunday 1722 and named the island.

eras.polity: Rapa Nui — slave raids and depopulation
eras.note: Peruvian slave raids of 1862-63 captured about 1,500 people, and smallpox and other diseases spread after some returned. By 1877 only 111 native inhabitants remained.
Chile annexed the island in 1888.
Rapa Nui gained Chilean citizenship in 1966, and the island became a special territory in 2007. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 1995.

regions.label: The Missões frontier — São Borja
regions.sub: São Borja, Tiradentes do Sul

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Jesuit missions of the Uruguay river
eras.note: The Jesuits founded São Borja in 1682 as São Francisco de Borja, the first of the Seven Places of the Missions.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil — Province of São Pedro do Rio Grande do Sul
Empire of Brazil — Rio Grande do Sul
eras.note: São Borja is given as the oldest municipality in Rio Grande do Sul; its municipal founding is dated 11 March 1833.

eras.polity: Brazil — State of Rio Grande do Sul
eras.note: Civil registers are kept by each municipality's Cartório de Registro Civil; older books may have passed to a municipal, district or state archive. Compliance with civil registration was uneven, and some areas did not begin keeping civil records until the 1920s.

regions.label: West Kazakhstan: Ural, Mangyshlak and Aktobe
regions.sub: Oral, Aktobe, Atyrau, Aktau, Zhanaozen

eras.note: Before registers. The Kazakh Khanate is dated to 1465 in Kazakh historiography and to 1470-71 in Russian historiography. By the 17th century it had three zhuzes (Senior, Middle and Junior), each with its own territory.
Khan Abu'l Khayr of the Junior Zhuz swore fealty to the Russian empress Anna on 10 October 1731.
The Russian statutes of 1822-1824 abolished the khanate as an institution.

The Steppe Governorate-General, seated at Omsk, lasted from 1882 to 1918 and included the Ural and Turgay oblasts. The imperial census of 9 February 1897 covered the empire except Finland, but most local copies of its forms were later destroyed.
The Kirghiz ASSR was set up on 26 August 1920 and renamed the Kazakh ASSR in April 1925. The December 1926 census counted 6,503,006 people in the Kazakh ASSR.
The republic became a union republic on 5 December 1936.
The republic was renamed the Republic of Kazakhstan on 10 December 1991, declared independence on 16 December and was internationally recognised after the Soviet Union dissolved on 26 December.

regions.label: Northern Kazakhstan: Kostanay, Kokshetau and Astana
regions.sub: Kostanay, Rudnyy, Kokshetau, Astana, Atbasar

eras.polity: Kazakh Khanate: Middle Zhuz and Junior Zhuz lands
eras.note: Before registers. After Tauke Khan's death (1715 or 1718) the three zhuzes became in effect independent khanates.
Khan Semeke of the Middle Zhuz accepted Russian suzerainty shortly after 1731 (the year is not given). After the deaths of Vali (1817) and Bukei (1818) Russia abolished the Middle Zhuz khanate.

eras.polity: Russian Empire: steppe statutes and the Kenesary revolt
eras.note: The statutes of 1822-1824 abolished khan power. Kenesary's rebellion began in 1837; he surrendered in 1846 and died in 1847.
Akmolinsk and Turgay were two of the oblasts of the Steppe Governorate-General (1882-1918), which was governed from Omsk.
The Kirghiz ASSR was founded on 26 August 1920 and took the name Kazakh ASSR in April 1925. The famine of 1930/31-1933 killed between 1 and 2 million people (1.7 million in one historian's estimate).
The Virgin Lands campaign began in 1953 under Khrushchev and was abandoned in the 1960s.
Genealogy records in Kazakhstan are kept at the local level.

regions.label: Central Kazakhstan: Karaganda, Ulytau and Balkhash
regions.sub: Karagandy, Temirtau, Zhezqazghan, Balqash

eras.note: Before registers. The Oirat-Kazakh wars of the 1640s-1650s ended in an Oirat victory. The Dzungar Khanate fractured after Galdan Tseren's death in 1745.
Russian suzerainty began with the Junior Zhuz's oath of 10 October 1731, and the Middle Zhuz followed. The statutes of 1822-1824 ended the power of the khans.
The governorate-general sat at Omsk, in Siberia, from 1882 until 1918.
The name Kazakh ASSR dates from April 1925; the Kirghiz ASSR had been founded on 26 August 1920.
Alma-Ata (now Almaty) was the republic's capital; union-republic status dates from 5 December 1936.
The republic declared independence on 16 December 1991.

regions.label: Eastern Kazakhstan: the Irtysh and Altai
regions.sub: Pavlodar, Semey, Ust-Kamenogorsk, Ekibastuz, Altay

eras.polity: Kazakh Khanate and the Dzungar frontier
eras.note: Before registers. In the 1650s eastern Semirechye and the land between the upper Irtysh and Lake Balkhash depended on the Dzungar Khanate.

eras.polity: Kazakh Middle Zhuz under Russian suzerainty
eras.note: After the Dzungar Khanate fractured in 1745, Ablai Khan seized herds and territory. The statutes of 1822-1824 abolished khan power.
Semipalatinsk was one of the oblasts of the Steppe Governorate-General, whose capital was Omsk.
The Kirghiz ASSR was founded on 26 August 1920 and renamed the Kazakh ASSR in April 1925.
Independence was declared on 16 December 1991.

regions.label: Southern Kazakhstan: the Syr Darya and Talas
regions.sub: Shymkent, Turkistan, Taraz, Kyzylorda, Baikonur

eras.polity: Kazakh zhuzes and the Central Asian khanates
eras.note: Before registers. The Kazakh Khanate is dated to 1465 in Kazakh historiography.
General Chernyayev took Tashkent on 29 June 1865. The Turkestan Governorate-General was established on 23 July 1867 with Syr-Darya and Semirechye as its first two oblasts.

eras.polity: Turkestan ASSR, then the Kazakh ASSR
eras.note: The Turkestan ASSR was created in April 1918 within the Russian SFSR; its partition followed the national delimitation announced on 25 February 1924. The Kazakh ASSR was renamed in April 1925.

regions.label: Semirechye: Almaty, Bishkek and Issyk-Kul
regions.sub: Almaty, Taldykorgan, Bishkek, Karakol, Naryn

eras.polity: Kazakh Khanate and the Dzungar Khanate
eras.note: Before registers. Erdeni Batur's Dzungar attack of 1643 took much of Jetisu (Semirechye) and about 10,000 captives. The Qing destroyed the Dzungar state in 1756-57.

eras.polity: Kokand Khanate and the Kyrgyz and Kazakh tribes
eras.note: Kokand ruled the Kyrgyz from the early 19th century; Kyrgyz forces drove out its fortresses between 1842 and 1844. The Kyrgyz leader Umotaaly surrendered in 1867.
The capital was Verniy (now Almaty). The oblast was part of the Turkestan Governor-Generalship in 1867-1882.

eras.polity: Semirechye Oblast in the Steppe Governorate-General
eras.note: Semirechye belonged to the Steppe Governorate-General, seated at Omsk, from 1882 to 1899.
The oblast returned to Turkestan in 1899. In 1897 it had six uyezds: Verniy, Dzharkent, Kopal, Lepsinsk, Pishpek and Przhevalsk.

eras.polity: Turkestan ASSR, then split between Kazakh and Kyrgyz units
eras.note: The oblast joined the Turkestan ASSR on 30 April 1918 and was dissolved on 27 October 1924: its northern part went to the Kirgiz (Kazakh) ASSR and its southern part became the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast.
Both republics became union republics on 5 December 1936.
Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991 and Kyrgyzstan on 31 August 1991.

regions.label: Tashkent and the Chirchiq valley
regions.sub: Tashkent, Chirchiq, Angren, Almalyk, Guliston

eras.note: Alim Khan (reigned 1799-1811) conquered the western Fergana Valley, including Khujand and Tashkent. Irdana Biy had briefly taken Tashkent in 1765 before Ablay Khan retook it.
Chernyayev's troops took Tashkent on 29 June 1865. The Turkestan Governorate-General was established on 23 July 1867 with Tashkent as its capital, under Konstantin von Kaufman.
The Turkestan ASSR was created in April 1918 within the Russian SFSR.
The Uzbek SSR was formed in 1924 when the Turkestan ASSR was partitioned. The December 1926 census counted 5,272,801 people in it.
Uzbekistan has 12 provinces, one autonomous republic (Karakalpakstan) and the independent city of Tashkent. Genealogy records are kept at province level.

regions.label: The Fergana Valley and Khujand
regions.sub: Andijan, Namangan, Fergana, Kokand, Osh, Khujand

eras.note: The khanate was founded in 1709 and Kokand was its capital from 1740. Its principal provinces were Kokand, Marghilan, Andijan and Namangan. Khujand was lost to Russia in 1867, and in 1876 the khanate was abolished.

Fergana Oblast was formed in 1876 from the remnants of the Kokand Khanate, and the Kyrgyz lands were formally annexed the same year. In July 1916 anti-conscription violence at Khujand is cited as the root of the Basmachi movement.
The Turkestan ASSR was created in April 1918 within the Russian SFSR.

eras.polity: Uzbek, Tajik and Kyrgyz Soviet units
eras.note: After the 1924 delimitation the ground fell under the Uzbek SSR, the Tajik ASSR (within the Uzbek SSR until it became a union republic in 1929) and the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast (1924; Kirghiz ASSR 1926; Kirghiz SSR 5 December 1936).
Kyrgyzstan declared independence on 31 August 1991 and Tajikistan on 9 September 1991. Tajikistan's civil war began in 1992 and a peace agreement was reached in 1997.

regions.label: Samarkand, Bukhara and the Zeravshan
regions.sub: Samarkand, Bukhara, Jizzakh, Navoiy, Qarshi, Panjakent

eras.note: The Manghit emir Shah Murad assumed rule in 1785. Samarkand belonged to the emirate until the Russian annexation of 1868.

eras.polity: Zeravshan Okrug; Bukhara a Russian vassal
eras.note: The treaty of 18 June 1868 gave Russia Samarkand and the upper Zeravshan valley and made the emirate a vassal. The Zeravshan Okrug was formed in 1868 and in 1887 was reorganised as Samarkand Oblast. The remainder of the emirate became a protectorate in 1873. In 1870 the emir consolidated control of Shahr-e Sabz (Shahrisabz) with Russian help.

eras.polity: Samarkand Oblast and the Emirate of Bukhara
eras.note: The emirate survived as a protectorate until the Red Army took Bukhara on 2 September 1920.

eras.polity: Bukharan People's Soviet Republic and Turkestan ASSR
eras.note: The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed on 6 October 1920; the partition of the Khorezm and Bukhara people's republics was decided in April 1924.
National delimitation, with borders drawn in 1928, left Bukhara and Samarkand outside Tajikistan.

regions.label: Khorezm and Karakalpakstan
regions.sub: Nukus, Urganch, Khiva, Daşoguz

eras.note: Khiva was founded in 1511 with its capital at Konye-Urgench; the capital moved to Khiva around 1600. The Qungrat dynasty was formalised in 1804.

eras.polity: Khiva under Russian protectorate; Amu Darya Division
eras.note: Khiva fell on 10 June 1873 and a treaty of 12 August 1873 made it a Russian protectorate. The Amu Darya Division, annexed from Khiva in 1873, was added to the Turkestan Governorate-General. In 1894 part of Konye-Urgench was still in the Khanate of Khiva.
The last Qungrat khan, Sayid Abdullah, abdicated on 2 February 1920 and the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic was created; its partition was decided in April 1924.

eras.polity: Uzbek SSR, Karakalpak ASSR and Turkmen SSR
eras.note: The Karakalpak Autonomous Oblast was created in 1925 and became an ASSR in 1932; the republic joined the Uzbek SSR in 1936 (1932 in some accounts). The Turkmen SSR was formed in 1924.

Karakalpakstan declared sovereignty on 14 December 1990 and became the Republic of Karakalpakstan on 21 December 1991. Protests in July 2022 over a constitutional change that would have removed its autonomy ended with the change being dropped.

regions.label: Turkmen Caspian coast and Kopet Dag
regions.sub: Türkmenbaşy, Balkanabat, Gyzylarbat, Bakherden

eras.polity: Turkmen tribes between Persia and Khiva
eras.note: Khiva's invasion of 1645-1663 displaced many Turkmens toward Ahal, Etrek, Murgap and Tejen. Nader Shah conquered Turkmen territory in 1740.

Russia began with Krasnovodsk (now Türkmenbaşy) in 1869. The Battle of Geok Tepe was in 1881 and the Treaty of Akhal that year recognised Russian control. Transcaspian Oblast, seated at Askhabad, was administered from Tiflis until 1898.
In 1898 the oblast became part of Russian Turkestan and was governed from Tashkent.

In July 1918 anti-Bolshevik railway workers set up a provisional government at Ashkhabad; British forces supported it until the last British troops left on 14 April 1919. The Bolsheviks captured Krasnovodsk in February 1920.
The Turkmen SSR was formed on 27 October 1924, when the Turkestan ASSR was dissolved.
Turkmenistan became independent on 27 October 1991.

regions.label: Merv, Tejen and the Amu Darya
regions.sub: Mary, Tejen, Turkmenabat, Kerki, Bayramaly

eras.note: After Nader Shah's assassination in 1747 the khanates of Khiva and Bukhara recaptured Turkmen lands. Charjuy (Chardzhou) and Kerki were among the Emirate of Bukhara's regions.

eras.polity: Transcaspian Oblast; Chardzhou and Kerki under Bukhara
eras.note: Russia annexed the Panjdeh (Serhetabat) oasis in 1885, which nearly led to war with Britain. By 1894 Russia controlled nearly all Turkmen territory, but part of Chardzhou remained in the Emirate of Bukhara.

eras.polity: Transcaspian Oblast and the Emirate of Bukhara
eras.note: The Bolsheviks captured Merv in May 1919.

eras.polity: Bukharan People's Soviet Republic and Turkestan ASSR
eras.note: The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic, which had held Chardzhou and Kerki as emirate regions, was proclaimed on 6 October 1920.
The Karakum Canal, 1,375 km long and drawing water from the Amu Darya, was built in the 1950s.

regions.label: Surkhandarya and southern Tajikistan
regions.sub: Termez, Dushanbe, Kulob, Bokhtar, Hisor, Khorugh

eras.note: Kulob (Kulyab), Hisar (Hisor) and Karategin (now Rasht) are listed among the emirate's regions.

eras.polity: Emirate of Bukhara, a Russian protectorate
eras.note: In 1895 the principalities of the western Pamirs came under the emir with Russian help. The last emir was overthrown by Soviet troops in late August 1920.

eras.polity: Bukharan People's Soviet Republic, then the Tajik ASSR
