eras.note: The Bukharan People's Soviet Republic was proclaimed on 6 October 1920. The Tajik ASSR was created in 1924 within the Uzbek SSR, and the December 1926 census counted 827,200 people in it.
Tajikistan became a union republic in 1929; the source also gives 5 December 1929.
Tajikistan declared independence on 9 September 1991. A civil war began in 1992 and a peace agreement was reached in 1997.

regions.label: Baku, Shirvan, Quba and Lankaran
regions.sub: Baku, Sumgayit, Shamakhi, Quba, Salyan, Lankaran

eras.polity: Khanates of Baku, Quba, Shirvan and Talysh
eras.note: The Baku and Quba khanates lasted 1747-1806, Shirvan 1748-1820 and Talysh 1747-1828.

eras.polity: Russian Empire after the Treaty of Gulistan
eras.note: The Treaty of Gulistan (1813) and the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828) defined the border between Russia and Qajar Iran.
Baku Governorate existed from 1846 to 1920.
The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was established in 1918 and ended with the Soviet invasion of 1920.
The Azerbaijan SSR (1920-1922) joined the Transcaucasian SFSR (1922-1936) and was a separate union republic from 1936 to 1991. The December 1926 census counted 2,314,571 people in the Azerbaijan SSR.
Azerbaijan has 59 districts, 11 cities and one autonomous republic; genealogy records are kept at the local level.

regions.label: Ganja, Sheki, Zaqatala and Karabakh
regions.sub: Ganja, Mingachevir, Sheki, Zaqatala, Barda, Aghdam

eras.polity: Khanates of Shaki, Ganja and Karabakh
eras.note: The Shaki (Sheki) khanate lasted 1743-1819, Ganja 1747-1805 and Karabakh 1748-1822.

eras.polity: Russian Empire after the Treaty of Gulistan
eras.note: The treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828) defined the Russia-Qajar border; the Karabakh khanate lasted until 1822.
Elizavetpol Governorate (the Elisabethpol of older spellings) existed from 1867 to 1920.
The republic lasted from 1918 to 1920.
The Nagorno-Karabakh conflict dates from 1988.
The first Nagorno-Karabakh war ran from 1988 to 1994; a second war was fought in 2020 and an Azerbaijani offensive and ceasefire agreement followed in 2023.

regions.label: Nakhchivan
regions.sub: Nakhchivan, Ordubad, Sharur

eras.note: The khanate emerged in 1747 after the death of Nader Shah Afshar.

eras.polity: Nakhichevan uyezd, Armenian Oblast and Erivan Governorate
eras.note: After the Treaty of Turkmenchay the khanate passed from Iran to Russia and was dissolved in 1828. It became the Nakhichevan uyezd of the Armenian oblast, which became the Erivan Governorate in 1849.

eras.polity: Soviet occupation and the treaties of Moscow and Kars
eras.note: The Red Army occupied the region in July 1920. The Treaty of Moscow (16 March 1921) placed the region under Azerbaijan's orbit, and the Treaty of Kars (13 October 1921) described it as an autonomous territory under the protection of Azerbaijan.

eras.polity: Nakhchivan ASSR in the Azerbaijan SSR
eras.note: The Nakhchivan ASSR was established on 9 February 1924, and its constitution was adopted on 18 April 1926.

The Supreme Soviet declared its intention to secede from the USSR on 20 January 1990, and autonomous-republic status dates from 17 November 1990. The current constitution has been in force since 8 January 1999.

regions.label: Western Mongolia: Khovd, Uliastai and Uvs
regions.sub: Khovd, Olgii, Ulaangom, Uliastay, Altai

eras.polity: Qing: Uliastai and the Kobdo (Khovd) territory
eras.note: The Qing destroyed the Dzungars in 1756-57 (the source also gives 1759 for the conquest of Dzungaria). The military governor of Uliastai held jurisdiction over Outer Mongolia, and the Kobdo region later became a separate post; Kobdo Territory had 32 khoshuu.
Outer Mongolia declared independence from the Qing on 29 December 1911; the Bogd Khaganate is dated 1911-1919.
The Beiyang occupation lasted from 1919 to 1921.
The Mongolian Revolution of 1921 began on 1 March 1921, and the Mongolian People's Republic was proclaimed on 26 November 1924.
Protests began on 10 December 1989 and the first multiparty elections were held on 29 June 1990. Genealogy records are kept at the local level, and Mongolia has 21 provinces (aimags) and one city.

regions.label: Khalkha Mongolia: Ulaanbaatar and the eastern steppe
regions.sub: Ulaanbaatar, Erdenet, Darkhan, Choibalsan, Dalandzadgad

eras.note: The Khalkha khans swore allegiance to the Kangxi Emperor at Duolun in 1691. The four aimags were Tusheet Khan (20 khoshuu), Secen Khan (23), Sain Noyon (24) and Zasagtu Khan (19); by the early 19th century the Amban at Urga supervised the eastern part.
Independence from the Qing was declared in December 1911.

A referendum on 20 October 1945 preceded China's recognition of Mongolian independence on 5 January 1946. Between September 1937 and April 1939 an estimated 20,000 to 35,000 Mongols were executed in Mongolia and the USSR, and an estimated 17,000 monks were killed under communist repression.
A new constitution was adopted in January 1992 and took effect on 12 February 1992; the state was then officially the State of Mongolia.

regions.label: Northwest Korea: Pyongan, Hwanghae and Kaesong
regions.sub: Pyongyang, Nampo, Sinuiju, Sariwon, Haeju, Kaesong

eras.note: Joseon divided Korea into eight provinces in 1413, among them P'yongan and Hwanghae. The Gabo reform of 1895 briefly created 23 districts, and in 1896 thirteen provinces were restored: P'yongan was divided into north and south, and Hwanghae was not split.
The Korean Empire was proclaimed in October 1897.
Japan annexed Korea in 1910 (treaty signed 22 August, announced 29 August). The thirteen provinces stayed essentially unchanged, with Japanese readings of their names.

eras.polity: Soviet Civil Administration north of the 38th parallel
eras.note: Soviet forces reached Pyongyang on 24 August 1945 and the Soviet Civil Administration operated from 1945 to 1948. Pyongyang became a special city in 1946.

eras.polity: Democratic People's Republic of Korea: the Korean War
eras.note: The People's Assembly voted on 10 July 1948 to implement the constitution establishing the DPRK. Chagang Province was formed in 1949 from parts of North P'yongan. The Korean War began on 25 June 1950.
The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953. Hwanghae was divided into North and South in 1954. Kaesong is listed as a city in North Korea.

regions.label: Northeast Korea: Hamgyong and Wonsan
regions.sub: Hamhung, Wonsan, Chongjin, Hyesan

eras.note: Hamgyong and Gangwon were two of the eight provinces made in 1413. In 1896 Hamgyong was divided into north and south; Gangwon was not split.
The Korean Empire was proclaimed in October 1897.
The thirteen provinces stayed essentially unchanged under Japanese rule, with Japanese readings of their names; annexation was announced on 29 August 1910.

eras.polity: Soviet Civil Administration north of the 38th parallel
eras.note: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945 and Gangwon was split. Kangwon in the north was expanded in 1946 to include an area around Wonsan.

eras.polity: Democratic People's Republic of Korea: the Korean War
eras.note: The Korean War began on 25 June 1950.
Ryanggang Province was split from South Hamgyong in 1954. Flooding in 1995 led to a famine that lasted until 1998.

regions.label: Northern Taiwan: Taipei, Keelung, Taoyuan and Hsinchu
regions.sub: Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, Taoyuan, Hsinchu, Yilan

eras.note: Spain built Santisima Trinidad (Fort San Salvador) at Keelung and Fort Santo Domingo at Tamsui (1629, abandoned by 1638). The Dutch captured the Keelung fortresses in August 1642.
The Dutch held Keelung until 1668.
The Zheng family ruled Taiwan from 1662 to 1683; the Qing captured Penghu on 18 July 1683 and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan that October.
The Qing established Taiwan Prefecture under Fujian on 6 March 1684, with three counties: Taiwan, Zhuluo and Fengshan.

After the Mudan incident the Qing lifted the ban on settlement in 1875 and created a Taipei prefecture and Yilan county. Taiwan became its own province in 1887 (an 1885 reorganisation is also cited), and Taipei became the permanent capital in 1893. The French occupied Keelung in 1884 and withdrew in 1885.

The Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed on 17 April 1895 and the formal transfer was on 2 June 1895; the Republic of Formosa declared on 23 May was conquered on 21 October 1895. The colonial government took a detailed census every five years from 1905.
The ROC took over on 25 October 1945. The February 28 Incident began in 1947 and Chen Yi was recalled in May 1947. The ROC government moved to Taipei in 1949.

eras.polity: Republic of China: New Taipei and Taoyuan
eras.note: On 25 December 2010 Taipei County became New Taipei City; Taoyuan became a special municipality on 25 December 2014.

regions.label: Central Taiwan: Taichung, Changhua and Yunlin
regions.sub: Taichung, Changhua, Nantou, Douliu, Puli

eras.note: Zheng Chenggong died on 23 June 1662 and his son Zheng Jing succeeded him.
Taiwan Prefecture was set up under Fujian on 6 March 1684 with the counties of Taiwan, Zhuluo and Fengshan.

eras.polity: Taiwan Province: the capital at Toatun (Taichung)
eras.note: Under Liu Mingchuan Taiwan was reorganised in 1885 into Taiwan, Taipei, Tainan and Taidong regions, and it became a province in 1887. The capital moved from Tainan to Toatun (Taichung) in 1885-87.

Indigenous peoples were classed as acculturated (shufan), semi-acculturated (huafan) or non-acculturated (shengfan); acculturated indigenous people were treated as Chinese. The 1905 census put the island's population at roughly 3 million.
The ROC took over on 25 October 1945, and the Taiwan Province was re-established the same day.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Taichung special municipality
eras.note: On 25 December 2010 Taichung was elevated to a special municipality.

regions.label: Southern Taiwan: Tainan, Kaohsiung and Pingtung
regions.sub: Tainan, Kaohsiung, Chiayi, Pingtung, Hengchun

eras.note: The Dutch East India Company governed from Fort Zeelandia (present-day Anping, Tainan). Zheng Chenggong took the fort after a nine-month siege.
The Qing captured Penghu on 18 July 1683 and Zheng Keshuang surrendered Taiwan in October.
Taiwan Prefecture was created on 6 March 1684 with the counties of Taiwan, Zhuluo and Fengshan. Japan invaded southern Taiwan in 1874 and a new Hengchun county was created after the Mudan incident.
In 1885 the former Taiwan Prefecture was renamed Tainan, and Taiwan became its own province in 1887.
Japan conquered the Republic of Formosa on 21 October 1895. Taiwan was returned to Chinese control on 25 October 1945 under General Order No. 1.
Almost 350,000 Japanese civilians lived in Taiwan at the war's end; the Republic of China repatriated 90 percent of them by 25 April 1946.

eras.polity: Republic of China: Tainan and Kaohsiung special municipalities
eras.note: On 25 December 2010 Kaohsiung County merged into Kaohsiung City and Tainan became a special municipality.

regions.label: Eastern Taiwan: Hualien and Taitung
regions.sub: Hualien, Taitung, Chishang, Green Island

eras.polity: Qing Taiwan: the opening of the east
eras.note: The Qing lifted the ban on settlement in 1875 after the Mudan incident.

In 1885 Taiwan was reorganised into Taiwan, Taipei, Tainan and Taidong (Taitung) zhili regions, and Beinan subprefecture was governed by a new Taitung department. Liu Mingchuan launched more than 40 campaigns against Indigenous groups between 1884 and 1891; the eastward expansion ended after the defeat of the Mkgogan and Msbtunux.
Semi- and non-acculturated Indigenous groups lived outside the normal administrative units, and government laws did not apply to them.
The Taiwan Province was re-established on 25 October 1945.

eras.polity: Republic of China: counties of Taiwan Province
eras.note: On 21 December 1998 the province's administrative functions were streamlined and it ceased to be a self-governing body.

regions.label: Penghu (the Pescadores)
regions.sub: Magong, Huxi

eras.note: After losing the Battle of Macau in 1622 the Dutch seized Penghu and built a fort; a Fujian fleet expelled them in 1624 and they moved to Fort Zeelandia on Taiwan.
The Qing defeated Tungning at the Battle of Penghu in 1683.

eras.polity: Penghu sub-prefecture of Taiwan Prefecture, Fujian
eras.note: French forces captured the archipelago in March 1885 and evacuated four months later; Admiral Courbet died at Makung on 11 June 1885.
Japan occupied Makung in March 1895 and Penghu was ceded in April 1895. Japan called the county Hoko Prefecture.

On 25 October 1945 Governor-General Rikichi Ando handed administration of Taiwan and Penghu to Chen Yi. The Ministry of the Interior's household registration office publishes the population: 73,343 in 1946 and 106,716 in 2025.

regions.label: Heilongjiang north and east: the Amur, Sanjiang and Ussuri
regions.sub: Heihe, Jixi, Qitaihe, Shuangyashan, Suifenhe, Hunchun

eras.note: Heilongjiang was created in 1683 from the north-western part of Jilin. The seat moved to Nenjiang in 1690 and to Qiqihar in 1699.

eras.polity: Qing: Heilongjiang after the Treaty of Aigun
eras.note: In 1858 and 1860 the Qing gave up the land north of the Amur and Ussuri rivers to Russia, which gave the province its present northern and eastern borders.
Japan invaded Heilongjiang in 1931 and conquered it in 1932; it became part of the puppet state of Manchukuo.

eras.polity: Soviet occupation, civil war and the People's Republic
eras.note: Soviet forces defeated the Japanese in Manchuria in 1945. Heilongjiang became the first province fully controlled by the communists.

Heilongjiang and Songjiang provinces were merged in 1954. During the Cultural Revolution Heilongjiang expanded to include Hulunbuir League and other areas formerly in Inner Mongolia; this has since been mostly reversed.

regions.label: Hulunbuir and eastern Inner Mongolia
regions.sub: Hailar, Manzhouli, Yakeshi, Genhe, Xilinhot

eras.note: Hulunbuir was part of Heilongjiang province during the Qing. The Treaty of Aigun (1858) established roughly today's Sino-Russian border, and in 1901 the Chinese Eastern Railway linked Hulunbuir to northeast China and the Russian Far East.
In the winter of 1912 the Barga Mongols expelled Chinese troops, proclaimed the independence of Barga (Hulunbuir) and declared allegiance to the Bogdo Khan of Mongolia.

A Russia-Republic of China agreement of 1915 made Hulunbuir a special region under the central government, with Russia holding partial control of day-to-day administration and the economy. The Soviet Union broke that agreement and invaded Hulunbuir in 1929. During the Republic Hulunbuir was part of Xing'an and Heilongjiang provinces.
Hulunbuir became part of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo; Heilongjiang was conquered by Japan in 1932.

eras.polity: Chinese Civil War and the People's Republic
eras.note: The Communist Party gained Inner Mongol support, including from Ulanhu, and Hulunbuir was later annexed into Inner Mongolia (the year is not given).
Hulunbuir was returned to Heilongjiang from 1969 to 1979, during and after the Cultural Revolution.
On 10 October 2001 Hulunbuir ceased to be a league and became a prefecture-level city, with its seat at Hailar and Manzhouli as one of its county-level cities.

regions.label: Beihai and the Beibu Gulf coast
regions.sub: Beihai, Fangchenggang, Hepu, Pingxiang, Basuo

eras.note: Lianzhou town was Hepu County's capital in earlier times.
After the Sino-British treaty of Yantai (1876) eight Western nations set up consulates, hospitals, churches, schools and maritime customs at Beihai (Pakhoi).

eras.polity: People's Republic: Beihai between Guangdong and Guangxi
eras.note: Beihai became a town of Hepu County on 4 December 1949. It was a province-administered city of Guangdong from January 1951, was entrusted to Guangxi in May 1951, went back to Guangdong in May 1955 and passed to Guangxi again in June 1965.
Beihai was restored to prefecture-level city in October 1983.

regions.label: Taizhou and the Zhejiang coast
regions.sub: Taizhou, Jiaojiang, Linhai, Wenling

eras.note: The prefecture was renamed Taizhou in 622, with Linhai as the county under it. Under the Song the Linhai walls were repaired in 1045 and moved inward toward East Lake in 1071.
Qi Jiguang and Governor Tan Lun fortified and raised the walls of Linhai against Japanese pirates, with the source giving no exact years.
The barbican of the Linhai city wall was built in 1712. Taizhou Fu served as the prefectural seat from 591 until 1993.

eras.polity: People's Republic: Taizhou Prefecture at Linhai
eras.note: The eastern section of the Linhai wall was demolished in 1956.

The seat moved from Linhai to Jiaojiang in 1993, and on 22 August 1994 the State Council approved Taizhou Municipality, which replaced Taizhou Prefecture. Wenling and Linhai are county-level cities of the municipality.

regions.label: Shanwei: Haifeng and Lufeng
regions.sub: Shanwei, Haifeng, Lufeng, Jieshi, Jiazi

eras.note: Under the Ming the Shanwei area was administered as part of Huizhou Prefecture (Huizhoufu).
Under the Qing the area was still part of Huizhou Prefecture.
Shanwei gained prefectural and administrative independence from Huizhou during the Nationalist period (no year is given).

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Haifeng and Lufeng
eras.note: Haifeng is a county and Lufeng a county-level city; the combined name Hailufeng is sometimes used for Shanwei.
Shanwei City was established in 1988.

regions.label: Kosovo and Raška — Pristina, Prizren, Novi Pazar
regions.sub: Pristina, Prizren, Peja, Gjakova, Mitrovica, Novi Pazar

eras.polity: Kingdom and Empire of Serbia, then the Serbian Despotate
eras.note: Before registers. The Kingdom of Serbia dates from 1217 and the Empire from 1346; the Battle of Kosovo was fought on 28 June 1389. Novo Brdo fell to the Ottomans in 1455 and the Despotate in 1459.
Ottoman rule followed the fall of the Despotate in 1459.
The Ottomans formed the Vilayet of Kosovo in 1877. After Niš passed to Serbia in January 1878, Muslim Albanians from Niš were forced out and many settled in Pristina in the vilayet.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbia and Kingdom of Montenegro
eras.note: In the First Balkan War of 1912 most of Kosovo was taken by Serbia and Metohija (the west) by Montenegro. The Treaty of London of 1913 confirmed the incorporation of the vilayet into Serbia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia)
eras.note: The kingdom was formed in 1918. In 1929 Kosovo was divided among the Zeta, Vardar and Morava banovinas, so neighbouring places fell under different banovinas.

eras.polity: Axis occupation: Italian-controlled Albania, with German and Bulgarian zones
eras.note: After the Axis invasion of 1941 most of Kosovo was assigned to Italian-controlled Albania, and the rest to German and Bulgarian zones.

eras.polity: Yugoslavia: Autonomous Region (later Province) of Kosovo within Serbia
eras.note: The Autonomous Region of Kosovo was established in August 1945 within Serbia. The 1974 constitution extended autonomy, 1989 changes reduced it, and the Kosovo War began in 1998 and ended with NATO intervention in 1999.
United Nations administration followed the NATO intervention of 1999.
Independence was declared on 17 February 2008 and the constitution took effect on 15 June 2008.

regions.label: South-east Serbia — Niš, Leskovac, Zaječar
regions.sub: Niš, Leskovac, Vranje, Zaječar, Bor, Ćuprija

eras.note: Niš fell to the Ottomans in 1385 after a 25-day siege; Serbian rule returned briefly in 1443 and the Ottomans retook it in 1448. Austrian forces held Niš in 1689-90 and again in 1737.

eras.polity: Ottoman Niš beside the autonomous Principality of Serbia
eras.note: The Ottoman hatt-i sharif of 1830 recognised the Principality of Serbia, which expanded east, south and west in 1831-1833. Which side of the 1833 border and of the 1878 border a village lay on decides whether its papers are Serbian or Ottoman.

The Serbian army entered Niš on 11 January 1878 and the Treaty of Berlin extended Serbia to the south-east that year. Most Muslim Albanians of Niš left for the Vilayet of Kosovo; by 1884 Serbs were about 80 percent of the town.
The Central Powers conquered Serbia in November 1915 and Niš was ceded to Bulgaria; the First Serbian Army liberated it on 12 October 1918.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes (Yugoslavia)
eras.note: Niš became the centre of an oblast in 1921 and was capital of the Morava Banovina from 1929 to 1941.
Niš hosted the Crveni Krst concentration camp and about 10,000 people were shot on Bubanj hill. The city was liberated on 14 October 1944.

regions.label: Malta and Gozo
regions.sub: Valletta, Sliema, Birkirkara, Mosta, Victoria (Gozo)

eras.polity: Aghlabid and Muslim rule, then Norman and Angevin Sicily
eras.note: Before registers. Aghlabid Muslims took Melite in 870, the Normans under Roger I invaded in 1091, and the islands were granted to Charles of Anjou in 1266.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon, then Spanish crown
eras.note: Aragonese and Spanish rule began in 1283; in 1469 the Crown of Aragon joined Castile and Malta became part of the Spanish Empire.
The Order received the islands in 1530 and withstood the Great Siege of 1565. Valletta was founded after the siege.
The French occupied Malta from 1798 and were expelled in 1800.
Britain's protectorate began in 1800; the Bathurst Constitution of 1813 made Malta a de facto colony and the Treaty of Paris of 1814 reaffirmed British rule. Self-government was granted in 1921.
Malta became independent as a Commonwealth realm in 1964, a republic in 1974, and joined the European Union in 2004.

regions.label: Copenhagen — the capital and its coast
regions.sub: Copenhagen, Christianshavn, Tårnby, Charlottenlund, Hørsholm

eras.note: Before registers. Valdemar I gave control of the town to Bishop Absalon about 1160, and the town received its charter in 1254.

eras.polity: Crown town of the Danish kings
eras.note: Eric of Pomerania took control in 1416 and the town came under crown rule. The university was founded in 1479 and Christian IV's coronation in 1596 began a major expansion including Nyboder and Christianshavn.
The city withstood a Swedish siege in 1658-59. Fires destroyed about a third of it in 1728 and a quarter in 1795, and British attacks fell on it in 1801 and 1807.

Denmark became a constitutional monarchy on 5 June 1849; the ramparts were opened and removed from the 1850s to the 1870s. In 1901 surrounding communities were incorporated, leaving Frederiksberg as an enclave.
Occupation began on 9 April 1940 and ended with liberation by British troops in May 1945.

regions.label: Tournai and the Franco-Belgian border (Hainaut and West Flanders)
regions.sub: Tournai, Mouscron, Ieper, Péruwelz, Halluin, Chimay

eras.polity: Tournai: French crown enclave in Flanders
eras.note: Tournai came under the French crown as a seigneurie in 1187 and its bishopric was the religious capital of Flanders. Henry VIII held it from 1513 until it returned to France in 1519, the only Belgian city England ever ruled. The dates given for this ring are those of Tournai.
Charles V added Tournai to his Low Countries holdings in 1521 and the Duke of Parma took it after a long siege in 1581. Louis XIV besieged it in 1667.
The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle gave Tournai to France in 1668. Marlborough besieged it in 1709 and the Treaty of Utrecht passed it to the Austrian Habsburgs in 1713.
France besieged and retook the city in 1745; the Austrian Netherlands were annexed by France in 1794.
Tournai became part of the department of Jemmapes.
Tournai was part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands from 1815.
Tournai became part of independent Belgium in 1830 and was badly damaged in 1940.

regions.label: Twente and the Dutch–German border — Enschede, Hengelo, Winterswijk
regions.sub: Enschede, Hengelo, Oldenzaal, Winterswijk, Gronau, Bocholt

eras.note: Overijssel was made part of Guelders in 1336 and ceded to the Bishopric of Utrecht in 1347. Twente belonged to the Oversticht, a medieval unit that also included Drenthe.

eras.polity: Overijssel under Charles V and his heirs
eras.note: The bishops ceded the Oversticht to Charles V in 1528. Forces of the Bishop of Münster occupied Overijssel briefly in 1672-1674. The Achterhoek (Winterswijk, Aalten) lies in Gelderland, south of Twente.
The Batavian Republic was formed in 1795 and introduced French-style départements. Overijssel was merged with Drenthe as Ouden IJssel in 1798 and renamed Overijssel again in 1801.
France annexed the Batavian Republic in 1810 and Overijssel became the department of Bouches-de-l'Yssel.

Overijssel was recreated in 1814. In the 19th century Twente became a major Dutch textile centre, with Enschede, Hengelo and Oldenzaal among the main towns. Gronau, Bocholt and Vreden lie across the border in Germany.
German occupation of Overijssel lasted from May 1940 to April 1945.

regions.label: West Münsterland and Bottrop — Borken, Rhede, Stadtlohn
regions.sub: Bottrop, Borken, Rhede, Stadtlohn, Raesfeld

eras.polity: Münsterland under its bishop; Holy Roman Empire
eras.note: Borken received city rights from Bishop Dietrich II in 1226 and had walls and towers by 1391. The Prince-Bishopric of Münster was secularised in 1802-03; Prussia took possession in March 1803, other parts went to Oldenburg, Arenberg, Looz-Corswarem, Salm and Croÿ, and all parts became French within the following years.
Borken was part of the French Empire from 1810 to 1814.

Borken came under the Province of Westphalia in 1815 and became seat of the new Kreis Borken. Bottrop grew as a mining centre from the 1860s and was chartered as a city in 1921; Kirchhellen was its own town from 1919.

About 90 percent of Borken's old town was destroyed by air raids late in the war, and Bottrop was bombed in the oil campaign. A reform of 1975 united Bottrop with Gladbeck and Kirchhellen; Gladbeck left in 1976.

regions.label: Nassau — Wiesbaden, the Lahn and the Siegerland
regions.sub: Wiesbaden, Siegen, Limburg an der Lahn, Dillenburg, Idstein

eras.polity: Counties and principalities of Nassau, and the Electorate of Trier
eras.note: The Duchy of Nassau of 1806 was formed from the territories of Nassau-Usingen and Nassau-Weilburg; Limburg an der Lahn came to Nassau-Weilburg from Trier. In Siegen the town passed fully to Nassau in 1381, Nassau became Reformed in 1550, and the Reformed Nassau line died out in 1734.

eras.polity: Duchy of Nassau; the Siegerland under the Grand Duchy of Berg
eras.note: The duchy was created on 30 August 1806 as a member of the Confederation of the Rhine, with Weilburg as capital until 1816. In the Napoleonic era the Siegerland passed to the Grand Duchy of Berg.

eras.polity: Duchy of Nassau; Siegen in Prussia
eras.note: Wiesbaden was the duchy's capital from 1816 and the duchy gained part of the principality of Orange-Nassau in 1815. Siegen was ceded to Prussia in 1815, first assigned to the Koblenz region and from 1817 to Arnsberg within the Province of Westphalia, so Siegerland papers are Prussian rather than Nassau from that date.

eras.polity: Prussia: Province of Hesse-Nassau (Westphalia for Siegen)
eras.note: Prussia annexed Nassau on 23 August 1866 and incorporated it into the Province of Hesse-Nassau in 1868, capital Kassel.

eras.polity: Hesse (American zone); Siegen under British military government
eras.note: In 1945 most of the former duchy fell in the American zone and became part of Hesse; a small part in the French zone became the Montabaur region of Rhineland-Palatinate. Siegen was about 80 percent destroyed in the war, and British military government installed a new mayor and charter there in 1946.

regions.label: Mannheim and the Rhine plain of the Electoral Palatinate
regions.sub: Mannheim, Lampertheim, Waghäusel, Hemsbach

eras.note: Frederick IV, Elector Palatine, granted Mannheim city status on 24 January 1607. The town was largely levelled in the Thirty Years' War and badly damaged by the French army in 1689.

eras.polity: Electoral Palatinate: the capital moved to Mannheim
eras.note: The Electoral Palatinate's capital moved from Heidelberg to Mannheim in 1720.

eras.polity: Electoral Palatinate after the court left
eras.note: The court left Mannheim in 1778 when the elector became Elector of Bavaria and moved to Munich.

Mannheim was removed from the Palatinate and given to Baden in 1802, so earlier records are Palatine and later ones Baden. It was a centre of the revolutionary activity of 1848. Air raids destroyed the city centre, the first deliberate strategic bombing raid being on 16 December 1940.
United States forces entered Mannheim unopposed on 29 March 1945.

regions.label: The Lower Main — Hanau, Aschaffenburg and the Kinzig
regions.sub: Hanau, Aschaffenburg, Büdingen, Gelnhausen, Seligenstadt

eras.polity: County of Hanau, and the Archbishopric (Electorate) of Mainz
eras.note: Aschaffenburg belonged to the Archbishopric of Mainz from 982 for over 800 years. Hanau became a town in 1303 and Count Philipp Ludwig II founded Neustadt Hanau for Huguenot refugees in 1597.
The last Count of Hanau died in 1736 and the lands of Hanau-Münzenberg passed to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel; the separate state of Hesse-Hanau ended in 1786.

eras.polity: Principality of Aschaffenburg; Grand Duchy of Frankfurt
eras.note: Aschaffenburg went to Karl Theodor von Dalberg as a principality in 1803 and was merged into the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt in 1810. The Battle of Hanau in 1813 was won by the French.

Aschaffenburg was transferred to Bavaria in 1814 and included in Bavarian Lower Franconia in 1817. The old and new towns of Hanau merged their administrations in the 1820s, and Prussia annexed Hesse-Kassel in 1866.
Hanau was Prussian from 1866 to 1945 while Aschaffenburg stayed in Bavaria, so the Main towns follow different state archives in this period.
British air raids in March 1945 destroyed most of Hanau's inner city, and the Battle of Aschaffenburg was fought from 28 March to 3 April 1945.

regions.label: Lake Constance and the upper Rhine — Konstanz, Friedrichshafen, Feldkirch
regions.sub: Konstanz, Friedrichshafen, Radolfzell, Lindau, Feldkirch

eras.polity: Bishop's seat and free imperial city of Konstanz
eras.note: Before registers. The dates here are those of Konstanz; the ring also takes in towns now in Bavaria, Austria and Switzerland. The first bishop took residence about 585, Konstanz gained imperial-city status in 1192, and the Council of Constance sat from 1414 to 1418.
The Reformation took hold in the 1520s and in 1548 Charles V imposed the Imperial Ban; the city surrendered to Habsburg Austria and lost imperial status.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy and Republic of Baden
eras.note: Konstanz became part of the Grand Duchy of Baden in 1806 and the bishopric of Constance was dissolved into the Archdiocese of Freiburg in 1821. Konstanz and the Swiss town of Kreuzlingen (Thurgau) are separated only by the border.
Konstanz was not bombed in the war because it almost lies within Switzerland.

regions.label: Gera, Greiz and the Vogtland — the Reuss lands
regions.sub: Gera, Plauen, Greiz, Oelsnitz, Markneukirchen

eras.note: Before registers. Gera is first mentioned in 995 and the province was assigned to Quedlinburg Abbey by Otto III in 999.
The abbey gave protectorship to the Vögte of Weida in 1209, ancestors of the Reuss family. The Wettins introduced the Reformation in 1533, and in 1546 they lost Gera to the Bohemian Crown.
The Reuss became Imperial Counts in 1673 and Gera their residence. The Gera line died out in 1802 and there was no resident ruler until 1848; Napoleon set up headquarters in Gera in 1806.
Gera became capital of the Principality of Reuss-Gera in 1848. These dates are Gera's; Plauen, also a historical capital of the Vogtland, lies inside the ring.

eras.polity: People's State of Reuss, then Thuringia
eras.note: The prince abdicated in 1918 and the People's State of Reuss was formed from Reuss-Gera and Reuss-Greiz; in 1920 it became part of the new state of Thuringia.
Gera became part of the GDR in 1949 and capital of the Gera District in 1952.

regions.label: Wittenberg and the Elbe-Elster country — Saxon land ceded to Prussia
regions.sub: Wittenberg, Bitterfeld-Wolfen, Finsterwalde, Bad Düben

eras.polity: Saxe-Wittenberg and the Electorate of Saxony
eras.note: Wittenberg became the residence of the dukes of Saxe-Wittenberg in 1260. Luther posted the Ninety-five Theses there on 31 October 1517.
The Capitulation of Wittenberg in 1547 forced John Frederick to give up the electoral title and most of his territory to the Albertine Wettins.
Saxony became a kingdom in 1806; Prussian forces stormed Wittenberg in 1814.

Wittenberg was transferred to Prussia after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and administered in the Province of Saxony. The dates here are those of Wittenberg; the ring also takes in Bitterfeld-Wolfen and Finsterwalde.
Wittenberg was in the Soviet occupation zone from 1945 and in the GDR's Halle District from 1949.
Democratic local government began in 1990.

regions.label: Forez — Saint-Étienne, Roanne and Montbrison
regions.sub: Saint-Étienne, Roanne, Montbrison, Saint-Chamond, Firminy

eras.polity: Counts of Forez, also counts of Lyon
eras.note: Before registers. William I is recorded as count in 925; the counts of Forez were also counts of Lyon in the Empire until 1173, when the Archbishop of Lyon received the countship.
Before registers. Anne of the House of Albon ruled from 1372 to 1417.
John I of Bourbon ruled Forez from 1417. Montbrison is considered the historical capital of Forez.

eras.polity: Forez united to the French crown
eras.note: Forez was united to the French crown in 1531, after Louise of Savoy ruled it from 1521. Henry, later Henry III, held it as an appanage from 1566 to 1574.
Forez was united permanently to the French crown in 1574. It lay in the Ancien Régime gouvernement général of Lyon, together with Lyonnais and Beaujolais.

regions.label: Clermont and the Limagne — Auvergne
regions.sub: Clermont-Ferrand, Riom, Issoire, Thiers, Cournon-d'Auvergne

eras.polity: County of Auvergne within the Duchy of Aquitaine
eras.note: Before registers. Clermont was renamed Clairmont in 848, Pope Urban II called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont in 1095, and in 1120 the Counts of Auvergne founded the rival city of Montferrand.
Louis VIII granted Poitou and Auvergne to his third son Alfonso in 1225; they reverted to the royal domain on his death in 1271.
Clermont became a royal town in 1551 and was declared an inseparable property of the Crown in 1610.
The Edict of Troyes joined Clermont and Montferrand in 1630 and Louis XV confirmed the union in 1731, so records before 1630 are kept separately for the two towns.
In 1790 the province was divided into the départements of Puy-de-Dôme, Cantal, Haute-Loire and Allier; Haute-Loire and Allier include land from Velay, Bourbonnais and Lyonnais.

regions.label: Bourbonnais — Montluçon, Vichy and Moulins
regions.sub: Montluçon, Vichy, Moulins, Cusset, Yzeure

eras.polity: Sires de Bourbon: first House of Bourbon
eras.note: Before registers. Charles the Simple gave Aymar fiefs on the Allier in 913 that became the Bourbonnais; the first House of Bourbon ended in 1196.
Before registers. The second House of Bourbon began in 1218, and in 1272 Beatrice of Burgundy married Robert de France, Count of Clermont, beginning the line that later ruled France.
Charles IV raised the Bourbonnais to a duchy in 1327, with Moulins as capital and seat. Montluçon came into the lords' possessions through Guy II of Dampierre.
Bourbon kings ruled France from 1589 to 1848. The old Bourbonnais corresponds to the modern Allier département plus part of Cher.

regions.label: Barrois and the Meuse — Bar-le-Duc, Verdun and Commercy
regions.sub: Bar-le-Duc, Verdun, Commercy, Saint-Mihiel, Neufchâteau

eras.note: Before registers. Frederick I of Upper Lorraine built the frontier fortress of Bar on the Ornain about 960 and Sophia was the first to style herself Countess of Bar in 1033.

eras.polity: County, then Duchy of Bar: the Barrois mouvant
eras.note: The Treaty of Bruges in 1301 made the county's territory west of the Meuse a French fief, the Barrois mouvant, while the east stayed in the Empire. The count took the ducal title and became a Peer of France in 1354.

eras.polity: Duchy of Bar united with Lorraine; the Three Bishoprics
eras.note: Bar was united with Lorraine in 1480 under René II, and Stanisław Leszczyński received it in 1735-1738. Verdun belonged to the Three Bishoprics with Metz and Toul, listed as a separate entity from 1552 to 1790.
On Stanisław's death on 23 February 1766 the duchies passed to the French royal domain.

regions.label: Huelva and the Condado — Niebla's country
regions.sub: Huelva, Lepe, Almonte, Moguer, Isla Cristina, Aracena

eras.polity: Taifas of Saltés and Huelva, Seville and Niebla; Almoravids
eras.note: Before registers. A short-lived taifa of Saltés and Huelva existed about 1012-1051, Seville annexed it in 1051 and the Almoravids occupied it in 1091. By 1262 it belonged to the Taifa of Niebla.
Alfonso X of Castile took the Niebla country by 1262. Sancho IV granted the lordship of Huelva to Admiral Juan Mathé de la Luna in 1293 and the tenencia passed to Alonso Meléndez de Guzmán in 1338.
The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 heavily damaged Huelva.

Huelva became a provincial capital in 1833. The Rio Tinto mines were taken over by a British company about 1873, Huelva was granted city status on 17 September 1876, and a shooting at Rio Tinto on 4 February 1888 killed an estimated 100 to 200 people.
The coup of July 1936 failed in the city, and a rebel column from Seville took control on 29 July 1936; repression followed.

regions.label: Campo de Gibraltar — Algeciras, La Línea, San Roque
regions.sub: Algeciras, La Línea de la Concepción, San Roque, Tarifa, Estepona

eras.polity: Umayyad Córdoba, the Algeciras taifa, Marinids and Granada
eras.note: Before registers. Abd al-Rahman III took Algeciras in 914, it was an independent taifa from 1035 to 1058, Granada ceded it to the Marinids in 1274-75 and regained it in 1295.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile: territory of Gibraltar
eras.note: Alfonso XI took Algeciras in March 1344, but the Nasrids seized it in 1369 and the town was razed. Jurisdiction passed to Gibraltar in 1462, and until 1704 the Campo de Gibraltar was the municipal territory of Gibraltar, about 500 square kilometres.
Gibraltar was captured in 1704; the former inhabitants settled nearby and created Algeciras, San Roque and Los Barrios. By the Peace of Utrecht in 1713 the refugees abandoned plans to return.

Algeciras, San Roque and Los Barrios were each established as separate municipalities in 1759, and Charles III rebuilt Algeciras on a rectangular plan in 1760. The Algeciras Conference on Morocco met in the town hall in 1906, and the Gibraltar border was sealed from 1969 to 1982.

eras.polity: Comarca of the Campo de Gibraltar (province of Cádiz)
eras.note: The Junta de Andalucía established the comarca in 2003.

regions.label: Toledo and La Mancha — Talavera, Aranjuez
regions.sub: Toledo, Talavera de la Reina, Aranjuez, Cuenca, Ocaña

eras.note: Before registers. Toledo was the Visigothic capital from 546, possibly earlier, and a council confirmed the archbishop of Toledo's primacy in 681.

eras.polity: Umayyad rule and the Taifa of Toledo
eras.note: Tariq bin Ziyad captured Toledo in 711 or 712 and Abd-ar-Rahman III took it in 932. The Taifa of Toledo formed in the early 11th century.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Toledo, Crown of Castile
eras.note: Alfonso VI of León took Toledo on 25 May 1085. The city rose against taxes in 1449, and its population grew from 31,930 in 1528 to 56,270 in 1561.
Philip II moved the royal court to Madrid in 1561. The Madrid-Aranjuez railway was opened by Isabella II on 12 June 1858.
In the 1980s Toledo became the de facto capital of Castilla-La Mancha.

regions.label: Vega Baja del Segura — Orihuela and Torrevieja
regions.sub: Orihuela, Torrevieja, San Javier, Pilar de la Horadada

eras.polity: Kingdom of Tudmir, Emirate of Córdoba, taifas
eras.note: Before registers. Count Teodomiro proclaimed the Kingdom of Tudmir on 5 April 713, the capital moved to Murcia in 825, and the Principality of Murcia within the Kingdom of Denia (1053) became independent in 1086.
The area passed to the Kingdom of Murcia in 1212, and in 1304 Orihuela lay on the border between Castile and Aragon.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Valencia: the province of Orihuela
eras.note: Orihuela passed to the Kingdom of Valencia in 1366, was declared a city on 11 September 1437, and in 1507 Charles V made it capital of the province of Orihuela. The Jewish community was expelled in 1492.

Alicante and Elche separated from the province of Orihuela in 1737 to form the province of Alicante. Napoleon placed Orihuela in the Department of Segura, capital Murcia, in 1810, and in 1822 it passed to the province of Murcia.

Orihuela became part of the province of Alicante in 1833. It was an independent canton in the Cantonal Rebellion of 1873. The ring also reaches across into the Region of Murcia (San Javier, San Pedro del Pinatar).

regions.label: Lleida and the Segre plain
regions.sub: Lleida

eras.note: Before registers. Muslim rule began in the 8th century.
Count Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona took Lleida in 1149. Its university, founded in 1297, was the oldest in the Crown of Aragon until 1717.
Spanish forces under Felipe da Silva retook the city in 1644 during the Reapers' War; Philip V moved the university to Cervera in 1717.
The Seu Vella cathedral was turned into a military fortress in the 18th century.
The Condor Legion bombed Lleida on 2 November 1937, killing about 300 people across that day's raids.
Lleida was bombed and besieged again in 1938 and then taken by Franco's forces.

regions.label: Tortosa, the Ebro delta and the Maestrat coast
regions.sub: Tortosa, Amposta, Vinaròs, Benicarló, Peníscola

eras.note: Before registers. Tortosa was occupied around 714 and Muslim rule lasted more than 400 years; Louis the Pious besieged it in 808-809.

Ramon Berenguer IV of Barcelona conquered Tortosa in 1148 during the Second Crusade, and the land was granted to foreign crusaders and to military and religious orders. The castle became a residence of the Montcada family and the Templars, and from the 13th century a royal mansion.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon: the cathedral city
eras.note: The cathedral was begun in 1347 and consecrated in 1597. The Disputation of Tortosa was held in it in 1413-1414, and the town had a sizable Jewish community in the 14th and 15th centuries.
The ring runs from the Ebro delta north of Tortosa to the Castellón coast at Vinaròs, Benicarló and Peníscola.

regions.label: Southern Lazio — the Pontine coast and the old Neapolitan border
regions.sub: Terracina, Anzio, Nettuno, Fondi, Formia, Gaeta, Sora

eras.polity: Papal States, on the border with Naples
eras.note: Pope John VIII brought Terracina under the Holy See in 872 and the first papal conclave outside Rome met there in 1088. Neapolitan influence grew after 1357, and Gaeta and Formia were traditionally part of the Kingdom of Naples.
A revolt in 1798 against annexation to the Circeo département was suppressed.

eras.polity: Border between the Papal States and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
eras.note: The Concordat of 1818 between Pius VII and Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies officially set the border between the Papal States and the Kingdom of Naples at Terracina. Gaeta and Formia belonged to the region of Campania until 1934.

The Province of Latina was founded on 18 December 1934, mainly from drained Agro Pontino land previously in the province of Rome. The Pontine Marshes were drained under the Fascist government, and Sabaudia and Latina were built for workers from north-eastern Italy.

regions.label: Brăila and the lower Danube in Wallachia
regions.sub: Brăila, Oltenița, Călărași, Tutrakan

eras.polity: Wallachia: the fishing village of Brăila
eras.note: Before registers. The Mongols took the village in 1241; in the mid-14th century it was under rulers of Argeș, and it is first mentioned about 1368.

eras.polity: Principality of Wallachia: the Danube harbour
eras.note: Brăila had town status about 1400 and was Wallachia's main harbour. Mehmed the Conqueror's fleet burned it in 1462 and Bogdan III of Moldavia burned it in 1512.

The Ottomans made Brăila a kaza about 1538-1540 and built a stone stronghold; they called it Ibrail or Ibraila. Michael the Brave held it briefly in 1595-1596, a Wallachian-Russian army took it in 1711, and the Treaty of Adrianople returned it to Wallachia in 1829.

eras.polity: Wallachia, later Romania: a main Danube port
eras.note: Brăila was one of Wallachia's three main Danube ports with Turnu and Giurgiu; its population was 15,767 in 1859 and 58,392 in 1900. Between the wars it had about 68,000 people, among them about 11,000 Jews and 5,000 Greeks.
Soviet 3rd Ukrainian Front troops captured Brăila on 28 August 1944. The population peaked at 234,110 in 1992.

regions.label: Suceava and northern Moldavia — Bukovina's edge
regions.sub: Suceava, Dorohoi, Târgu Neamț, Darabani

eras.polity: Principality of Moldavia: the capital at Suceava
eras.note: Before registers. Suceava was the capital of Moldavia from 1388 to 1564, and Stephen the Great died there in 1504.

eras.polity: Principality of Moldavia: after the capital moved
eras.note: The seat moved to Iași in 1565. Michael the Brave captured Suceava in 1600 and was defeated the same year, and the town was besieged in 1653.

eras.polity: Habsburg Monarchy: Galicia, then the Duchy of Bukovina
eras.note: Suceava was under Habsburg rule from 1775, first in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria and later in the Duchy of Bukovina. The dates are Suceava's; Dorohoi and other towns of the ring should be checked against them.
Suceava became part of Romania in 1918 after a vote of the General Congress of Bukovina, was part of Ținutul Suceava in 1938-1940 and became a municipality in 1968.

regions.label: Zürich — the city and its outer districts
regions.sub: Zürich (Kreise 2-11), Adliswil, Rümlang

eras.note: Zürich joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1351.
Huldrych Zwingli became pastor of the Grossmünster in 1519 and Zürich soon became Reformed.
Under the Helvetic Republic the canton was a purely administrative division.

The western possessions went to the canton of Aargau in 1803. Zürich drew up a constitution in 1814, replaced it with a radical-liberal one in 1831, and the conservative Züriputsch of 1839 led to the 'Septemberregime' until 1844.

eras.polity: Swiss federal state: Canton of Zürich
eras.note: The first National Council under the 1848 federal constitution included Alfred Escher of Zürich; the canton adopted a new constitution in 1869. The Staatsarchiv Zürich holds the state archives.

regions.label: Hrodna (Grodno) on the Neman
regions.sub: Hrodna

eras.note: Before registers. The town was founded in 1127 or 1128.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
eras.note: A charter on Magdeburg Law was granted in 1441. In the 1580s Hrodna was the de facto capital of the Commonwealth under Stephen Báthory, and in 1793 it became capital of Grodno Voivodeship and hosted the last Sejm of the Commonwealth.
Russia annexed Hrodna in the Third Partition of 1795 and Poniatowski abdicated in the New Castle on 25 November 1795. It was the seat of Grodno Governorate from 1801.

German forces occupied the city on 3 September 1915. Russia ceded the area under the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918 and the Germans transferred authority to Poland under the Treaty of Białystok; the Polish Army took the city on 28 April 1919.
The Red Army took the city on 20 July 1920 and Poland recaptured it on 23 September 1920. Grodno remained a powiat capital, but the voivodeship seat moved to Białystok.
The Soviet Union invaded on 17 September 1939 and the Battle of Grodno was fought on 20-22 September; the city was annexed to the Byelorussian SSR.
German occupation lasted from 23 June 1941 to 16 July 1944. Jews were confined to two ghettos from 1 November 1942, and deportations to Auschwitz and Treblinka followed in February 1943.

regions.label: Uzhhorod (Ungvár) and Ung county
regions.sub: Uzhhorod, Velykyi Bereznyi

eras.note: Mongols burned the settlement in 1241-1242 and Béla IV granted town privileges in 1248. Uzhhorod became a free royal town in 1430.
The Union of Ungvár in 1646 established the Greek-Catholic church there, and Ferenc II Rákóczi resided in the town in 1707 during the anti-Habsburg war.

Ungvár became the capital of the Greek Catholic Eparchy in 1780; the first railway line opened in 1872. The town is Ungvár in Hungarian and Užhorod in Slovak; Uzhhorod became its official name some time after 1920.
Subcarpathia was allocated to Czechoslovakia on 10 September 1919 and Uzhhorod became its administrative centre.

eras.polity: Hungary after the First Vienna Award
eras.note: The First Vienna Award returned the city to Hungary in 1938 and Hungary took over the region in 1939. German troops entered on 19 March 1944 and the Jewish population was deported in May 1944.

eras.polity: Soviet Union: Ukrainian SSR, Zakarpatska oblast
eras.note: The Red Army captured Uzhhorod on 27 October 1944 and the Soviet Union annexed Subcarpathian Ukraine on 29 June 1945. The city became centre of the Zakarpatska oblast in January 1946.

regions.label: Pskov and Ostrov
regions.sub: Pskov, Ostrov

eras.note: Before registers. Novgorod formally recognised Pskov's independence in 1348 and the city became capital of the Pskov Republic.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Moscow, then Russia
eras.note: Moscow annexed Pskov in 1510 and deported about 300 families. The city withstood a Polish-Lithuanian siege in 1581-1582 and a Swedish siege in 1615, which led to the Treaty of Stolbovo.
Pskov became the seat of Pskov Governorate in 1777. Nicholas II abdicated at Pskov on 15 March 1917.
The German army invaded in 1918, and the Estonian army occupied Pskov from 25 May to 28 August 1919.
German occupation lasted from 9 July 1941 to 23 July 1944, with a forced-labour camp for Jews; Soviet bombing in February 1944 killed thousands.

regions.label: Syktyvkar and the Komi Sysola valley
regions.sub: Syktyvkar, Ezhva, Ust-Kulom

eras.note: The settlement of Ust-Sysola is believed to have been founded in 1586.

eras.polity: Russian Empire: the town of Ust-Sysolsk
eras.note: Catherine the Great granted city status in 1780. Early in the 20th century the town had about 6,000 people, and the tsarist authorities used the Komi region for political exile.
Ust-Sysolsk became the administrative centre of the Komi-Zyryan Autonomous Oblast in 1921 and was renamed Syktyvkar in 1930.
Syktyvkar became capital of the Komi ASSR in 1936. Executions took place outside the city in the 1930s.
Syktyvkar became capital of the Komi Republic in 1992.

regions.label: Suwałki, Augustów and Sejny — the Suwałki Region
regions.sub: Suwałki, Augustów, Sejny, Dąbrowa Białostocka

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Lithuania: the Wigry Camaldolese estate
eras.note: The Camaldolese monks were granted the land in 1667 and built a monastery at Wigry. Suwałki received town rights in 1715, confirmed on 2 May 1720.
Prussia annexed the area in the Third Partition of 1795 and dissolved the Wigry monastery in 1796.
In 1807 Suwałki became a salient of the Duchy of Warsaw and a centre of the Łomża Department.

eras.polity: Congress Poland: Augustów, later Suwałki Governorate
eras.note: The Augustów Voivodeship was created on 16 January 1816, with its capital moving to Augustów, and the governorate was renamed Suwałki Governorate in 1866.
Germany occupied the area in 1915; in 1919 the Germans handed the territory to Lithuanian authority, and the Paris Peace Conference granted the town to Poland that July.

The Sejny Uprising began on 23 August 1919 and a Polish-Lithuanian war followed, ending under Entente pressure in mid-September. In 1920 Suwałki was held in turn by the Bolsheviks, the Lithuanians and then Poland again.

eras.polity: Soviet then German occupation: Sudauen in East Prussia
eras.note: The Red Army took Suwałki in late September 1939 and handed it to Germany on 12 October 1939; the town was renamed Sudauen and annexed to East Prussia. The 3rd Belarusian Front captured it on 23 October 1944.
The Suwałki Voivodeship was created in 1975, and after 1989 a Special Economic Zone fostered border trade.

regions.label: Cascais and the Estoril coast
regions.sub: Cascais, Estoril, Alcabideche, Colares

eras.note: Before registers. Cascais was administratively subordinate to Sintra, and development began in earnest in the 12th century.
King Peter I raised the village to town status on 7 June 1364, ending its dependence on Sintra.
French forces occupied the citadel in 1807 during the Napoleonic invasion.
The royal family spent its summers in Cascais from 1870 to 1908, beginning under King Luís I.

A casino and other infrastructure were built in Estoril in the first half of the 20th century. In the Second World War Portugal's neutrality and Cascais's royal past drew exiled royal families from Spain, Italy, Hungary and Bulgaria.

regions.label: Vaasa and the Ostrobothnian coast
regions.sub: Vaasa, Korsholm, Närpes, Kristinestad

eras.note: Charles IX founded Mustasaari (Mussor) near Korsholm on 2 October 1606, and in 1611 it was chartered and renamed Vaasa after the House of Vasa. Finland's first library was founded there in 1794.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Finland under Russia
eras.note: Russian forces occupied Vaasa in 1808 and by the Treaty of Fredrikshamn on 17 September 1809 it became part of the Grand Duchy of Finland.
A fire on 3 August 1852 destroyed most of the old town. It was renamed Nikolaistad in 1855 and the new town rose in 1862 about 7 km north-west of the old one.

The city council reverted to the name Vaasa on 19 March 1917. Vaasa was the de facto capital of the Whites in the civil war from 29 January to 3 May 1918, and the majority became Finnish-speaking in the 1930s.

regions.label: Andorra — the co-principality
regions.sub: Andorra la Vella, Escaldes-Engordany, Encamp, Sant Julià de Lòria

eras.polity: Counts of Urgell and the Bishop of Urgell
eras.note: Before registers. Charles the Bald named the Count of Urgell overlord and a later descendant gave the lands to the Diocese of Urgell; in 1208 the Count of Foix became heir to the Lord of Caboet.

eras.polity: Paréage: Count of Foix and Bishop of Urgell
eras.note: A paréage signed under Peter III of Aragon in 1278 shared the lordship between the Count of Foix and the Bishop of La Seu d'Urgell; Andorra's borders have been unchanged since.

eras.polity: Co-principality: French head of state and Bishop of Urgell
eras.note: An edict of Henry IV in 1607 made the French head of state and the Bishop of Urgell co-lords. In 1716 Bishop Simeón de Guinda secured Andorra's separation from Catalonia after the Nueva Planta decrees.
Andorra was annexed to France in 1812-1813 and its independence was restored by decree in 1814.
France occupied Andorra in 1933 amid unrest, and a French detachment was garrisoned there from 1936 to 1940.
A new constitution took effect after a referendum in 1993, and Andorra joined the United Nations on 28 July 1993.

regions.label: Monaco — the Rock and Monte Carlo
regions.sub: Monaco, Monte-Carlo, La Condamine

eras.note: Before registers. Francesco Grimaldi seized the Rock of Monaco in 1297.
The Treaty of Burgos in 1524 placed Monaco under Spanish authority for about a century, with a Spanish garrison; Honoré II secured Spanish recognition of independent sovereignty in 1633.
The Treaty of Péronne in 1641 brought French recognition of Monaco's sovereignty.
France ruled Monaco from 1793 until 17 May 1814.
The Congress of Vienna in 1815 made Monaco a protectorate of the Kingdom of Sardinia, confirmed by the Treaty of Stupinigi in 1817. Menton and Roquebrune seceded in 1848.

The Franco-Monegasque Treaty of 1861 recognised Monaco's sovereignty and passed Menton and Roquebrune to France for four million francs. The Monte Carlo Casino opened in 1863 and a constitution was proclaimed in 1911 after the revolution of 1910.
A treaty of 1918 gave limited French protection, and a revised constitution followed in 1962.

regions.label: Norilsk and the Taymyr mining towns
regions.sub: Norilsk, Talnakh, Kayerkan, Dudinka

eras.note: The first log cabin was built in 1921 during Urvantsev's expedition and is later considered the city's first building.

Norilsk was officially founded in 1935 with the Norillag labour camp and the building of the mining and metallurgical plant, which operated until 1956; archives record 16,806 prisoner deaths. A narrow-gauge railway to Dudinka on the Yenisei was built in 1935-36.

eras.polity: Soviet Union, then Russia: Krasnoyarsk Krai
eras.note: Norillag was closed on 22 August 1956. Norilsk received city status in 1953, Talnakh was founded in 1966, and Talnakh and Kayerkan became districts of Norilsk in 2004. Norilsk remains a closed city.

regions.label: Blagoveshchensk and the Amur frontier
regions.sub: Blagoveshchensk, Poyarkovo, Konstantinovka

eras.polity: Russian Empire: the Ust-Zeysky military outpost
eras.note: The city began in 1856 as the military outpost of Ust-Zeysky at the mouth of the Zeya River.

eras.polity: Russian Empire: the Amur region's seat
eras.note: In 1858 Alexander II approved founding the city as the seat of the Amur region, to be named Blagoveshchensk. The Treaty of Aigun in 1858 and the Convention of Peking in 1860 made the Amur the border with China.
In July 1900 Qing and Boxer forces shelled the city, local authorities expelled the Chinese community, and many people died in the Amur on 4-8 July.
The city was part of the Far Eastern Republic, nominally independent but in practice a buffer state under the Russian SFSR.

eras.polity: Soviet Union, then Russia: Amur Oblast
eras.note: Blagoveshchensk became the administrative centre of Amur Oblast in 1932. It lies opposite the Chinese city of Heihe.

regions.label: Kinshasa and Kongo Central
regions.sub: Kinshasa, Matadi, Boma, Mbanza-Ngungu, Moanda

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kongo (founded about 1390) and the Tio kingdom
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kongo under Portuguese influence; Nshasa trading centres of the Tio kingdom
eras.note: Diogo Cão reached the coast in 1483 (some sources give 1484) and King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised in 1491. The site of Kinshasa was known as Nshasa, and Stanley made it a trading post named Léopoldville in 1881.

eras.polity: Congo Free State, Leopold II's personal possession
eras.note: Vivi was the first capital and Boma the capital from 1886. The Matadi–Léopoldville railway was built from 1890, and its completion is dated 1898 or 1911 depending on the source.

A royal decree of 1 July 1923 made Léopoldville the capital in place of Boma, with the transfer of services finalised on 31 October 1929; it received city status in 1941. The FamilySearch catalogue lists digitized birth and marriage record images for several Kinshasa communes.
Independence was on 30 June 1960. On 2 May 1966 the government announced that Léopoldville would be renamed Kinshasa from 30 June 1966.
The country was renamed Zaire in 1971, and Mobutu was overthrown in May 1997.

regions.label: Kwango, Kwilu and Mai-Ndombe
regions.sub: Kikwit, Idiofa, Bulungu, Inongo, Nioki

eras.polity: Chiefdoms and kingdoms of the Kwango, Kwilu and Lake Mai-Ndombe country
eras.note: Before registers.
Decrees of 1891 and 1892 turned vacant land into state property and gave the state a monopoly on ivory and rubber, and concessions went to private companies in October 1892.

FamilySearch estimates that civil registration covered about 50 percent of Belgians and 20 percent of Congolese from 1900 to 1930, rising to 75 and 50 percent after 1930, and stresses that these are estimates. The four original provinces were increased to six by an administrative reform dated 1932 or 1933 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, called Zaire from 1971

regions.label: Kasai
regions.sub: Mbuji-Mayi, Kananga, Tshikapa, Kabinda, Ilebo

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Lunda and Luba influence; Kanyok, Kalundwe and Lulua polities
eras.note: Lunda expansion west past the Kasai River in the 1720s met resistance from the Lulua, and Luba attempts in the 19th century to subdue the Kanyok and Kalundwe buffer states failed.
The state was divided into 14 districts, each split into zones, sectors and posts, with a European at the head of every level from district commissioner down.
Congo-Kasaï was one of the four provinces the colony started with.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, called Zaire from 1971
eras.note: The National Archives of the DR Congo (INACO) in Kinshasa hold civil registration from after 1960.

regions.label: Katanga
regions.sub: Lubumbashi, Kolwezi, Likasi, Kamina, Kalemie

eras.polity: Luba heartland in the Upemba Depression
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Luba Empire and the Lunda confederation of the Mwata Yamvo
eras.note: The Luba capital was Mwibele near Lake Boya, and Congolese historians date the founding to the 8th, 12th, 14th or 15th century, while some Western scholars place it in the 18th. The Lunda paramount ruler is dated c. 1665 in one account and from about 1695 in another.

eras.polity: Yeke Kingdom of Msiri, capital Bunkeya
eras.note: Msiri rose to power in 1856. In 1889 a succession dispute split the Luba realm in two, and a Congo Free State expedition under Captain Stairs killed Msiri on 20 December 1891.
Stairs placed Msiri's adopted son Mukanda-Bantu over a small area of about 20 km around Bunkeya, and the territory was taken for the Congo Free State with its own administration.
The Belgian State Archives in Brussels hold some records from 1908 to 1960.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, and the secessionist State of Katanga
eras.note: Katanga declared independence on 11 July 1960 under Moïse Tshombe, with Élisabethville as its capital. UN forces launched Operation Grandslam on 28 December 1962, and the secession ended on 15 January 1963 or 21 January 1963 depending on the source.

regions.label: Équateur and the Ubangi border
regions.sub: Mbandaka, Gemena, Bumba, Lisala, Gbadolite

eras.polity: Riverine chiefdoms of the Congo basin
eras.note: Before registers.
Stanley founded Équateurville in 1883, and it was renamed Coquilhatville in 1886. Plans to make it the state's capital were never carried out.
One copy of each civil registration act goes to the Central Records Office in Kinshasa, with further copies at the High Court registry and the issuing registry office.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, called Zaire from 1971
eras.note: Coquilhatville was renamed Mbandaka in 1966.

regions.label: Kivu and Maniema
regions.sub: Bukavu, Uvira, Butembo, Kindu, Beni

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Swahili-Arab state of Tippu Tip, centred on Kasongo
eras.note: Tippu Tip claimed the eastern Congo between 1884 and 1887 for himself and Sultan Barghash of Zanzibar.

eras.polity: Congo Free State after the Congo Arab War
eras.note: Sefu bin Hamid attacked Belgian ivory traders in 1892, and the Free State force under Francis Dhanis defeated its opponents in several engagements after Sefu died on 20 October 1893. Rumaliza fled into German territory in 1895, and local Arab or Swahili strongmen kept much of the power in the east.
FamilySearch's coverage estimates for civil registration in the Congo begin in 1900.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, called Zaire from 1971

regions.label: Orientale — Stanley Falls, Uele and Ituri
regions.sub: Kisangani, Bunia, Isiro, Buta, Basoko

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the upper Congo and Uele
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Congo Free State — Stanley Falls District
eras.note: Fighting between Swahili forces and Leopold II's representatives broke out at Stanley Falls in August 1886, and on 24 February 1887 Tippu Tip accepted appointment as governor of the Stanley Falls District.
Orientale was among the four provinces created at the start of the colony.

eras.polity: Republic of the Congo, called Zaire from 1971
eras.note: Mobutu seized power in November 1965.
Mobutu was overthrown in May 1997 by Laurent-Désiré Kabila.

regions.label: Zaire and Uíge — the old Kingdom of Kongo
regions.sub: Uíge, Soyo, Mbanza Kongo, Negage

eras.note: Before registers.

Afonso I became king in 1509 and Catholicism became the state cult; the capital São Salvador is today M'banza-Kongo. Soyo, a coastal province ruled by a count, was one of the kingdom's most important offices.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kongo, a civil-war kingdom and intermittent Portuguese vassal
eras.note: Portugal defeated Kongo at Mbwila on 29 October 1665, and the Kongo civil war ran from 1665 to 1709. Soyo beat the Portuguese at Kitombo on 18 October 1670, and its counts later styled themselves Grand Princes.
The kingdom functioned intermittently as a Portuguese vassal from 1862 to 1914, with the start dated 1857 or 1862 depending on the source.
Portugal suppressed a Kongo revolt in 1914 and abolished the titular monarchy, which was restored from 1915 to 1975 as an honorary title.
On 15 March 1961 Holden Roberto launched an incursion into northern Angola, and guerrilla warfare began that year.

eras.polity: People's Republic of Angola, the Republic of Angola from the 1992 constitution

regions.label: Cabinda
regions.sub: Cabinda, Cacongo, Buco Zau, Belize

eras.polity: Coastal chiefdoms north of the Congo estuary
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Portuguese protectorate of Cabinda, then part of Angola
eras.note: The Treaty of Simulambuco in 1885 made Cabinda a Portuguese protectorate, and it was incorporated into Portuguese Angola in the 1920s.
After the Alvor Agreement the Republic of Cabinda declared independence in 1975 but was soon re-annexed.

regions.label: Luanda, Kwanza and Malanje
regions.sub: Luanda, Viana, Malanje, N'dalatando, Porto Amboim

eras.polity: Kingdom of Ndongo and neighbouring chiefdoms
eras.note: Before registers.
Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda as São Paulo da Assumpção de Loanda, dated 1575 or 25 January 1576 depending on the source.
The Dutch held the city as Fort Aardenburgh, with the start dated 1640 or 1641 depending on the source.
Luanda was the centre of the slave trade to Brazil from about 1550 to 1836. Portugal annexed what remained of Ndongo after the Battle of Pungo Andongo.
FamilySearch lists civil registration marriage indexes and registers for Angola from 1901 to 1928, and names the National Institute of Statistics in Luanda as an office to contact.
Luanda's population was 475,328 in 1970.
Most white Portuguese residents left as refugees, and migration from the war-affected provinces swelled the city, with slums called musseques spreading far beyond the old limits.
The census counted 6,760,439 people in Luanda in 2014 and 8,816,297 in 2024.

regions.label: The Central Plateau — Benguela, Huambo and Bié
regions.sub: Benguela, Lobito, Huambo, Cuíto, Caála

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Ovimbundu kingdoms of the plateau and the Portuguese coast at Benguela
eras.note: Benguela was settled in the 17th century, and the Kingdom of Viye was annexed in 1890.
FamilySearch holds a collection, Civil registration (Marriages), Angola, 1908–1928, covering marriages only.
Angola became an overseas province in 1951.
The civil war ran from 1975 to 2002.

regions.label: Huíla, Namibe and Cunene
regions.sub: Lubango, Moçâmedes, Ondjiva, Matala, Tômbua

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the southwestern highlands and coast
eras.note: Before registers.
Portuguese campaigns into the interior began in 1838.
The colonial war of independence ran from 1961 to 1974.
Angola became a sovereign state on 11 November 1975 under the Alvor Agreement.

regions.label: Lunda and Moxico
regions.sub: Saurimo, Luena, Dundo, Lucapa, Cafunfo

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Lunda Empire of the Mwata Yamvo
eras.note: The Lunda domain covered about 150,000 km² by 1680 and roughly doubled at its height in the 19th century, until the gun-armed Chokwe invaded and founded their own kingdom. The end of the empire is dated 1887 or 1893 depending on the source.

At the start of the colonial era in 1884 the Lunda heartland was divided among Portuguese Angola, the Congo Free State and British North-Western Rhodesia. Full administrative control of Angola was reached in the early 20th century, with no exact year given.

regions.label: Cuando Cubango
regions.sub: Menongue, Lumbala, Cuchi, Mavinga

eras.note: Before registers.
The Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1891 set the southeast frontier, and an arbitration award by Victor Emmanuel III of Italy in 1905 settled part of it.
The country was renamed the Republic of Angola under the 1992 constitution.

regions.label: Buganda and Kampala
regions.sub: Kampala, Mukono, Nansana, Kira, Entebbe area

eras.polity: Early Buganda, traditionally founded by Kato Kintu
eras.note: Before registers.

Tradition credits Kato Kintu as founder, with a likely founding between the 12th and 14th centuries and a wave of immigration assisted by Kimera around 1370. Speke and Burton were the first Europeans to enter in 1862, and Stanley visited in 1875.

eras.polity: Imperial British East Africa Company, then the British government
eras.note: A July 1890 agreement gave Britain the Buganda region, the Company ended its involvement on 31 March 1893 and its administration rights passed to the British government.

eras.polity: Uganda Protectorate, with Buganda as a kingdom under the 1900 agreement
eras.note: Britain declared the protectorate on 18 June 1894, with Entebbe as capital. The Uganda Agreement of 1900 strengthened the Protestant chiefs, imposed a tax on huts and guns and made the chiefs tax collectors.

eras.polity: Independent Uganda with the Kingdom of Buganda
eras.note: Uganda became independent on 9 October 1962, and the 1962 constitution gave Buganda a high degree of autonomy.
On 17 September 1967 Milton Obote overthrew the monarchy, and the Kabakaship and the Lukiiko were disestablished.

eras.polity: Republic of Uganda with the restored Kingdom of Buganda
eras.note: The monarchy was restored in 1993, dated 24 or 31 July depending on the source. FamilySearch lists the National Identification and Registration Authority in Kampala as the office for births and deaths.

regions.label: Busoga, Teso and Bugisu
regions.sub: Jinja, Mbale, Soroti, Iganga, Kapchorwa

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of Busoga, Teso and Bugisu
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Imperial British East Africa Company, then the British government
eras.note: The Company's administration rights passed to the British government after 31 March 1893.

Busoga, Mbale and Teso are among the regions named in the protectorate's history, and in 1902 the British decided to transfer the eastern section of the protectorate to the East Africa Protectorate. Findmypast lists overseas births and baptisms, banns and marriages, and deaths and burials sets for Uganda.
Self-government came in 1961.

regions.label: Acholi, Lango and West Nile
regions.sub: Gulu, Lira, Arua, Kitgum, Koboko

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of Acholi, Lango and West Nile
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Uganda Protectorate; West Nile within the Lado Enclave leased to Leopold II
eras.note: The British-Congolese Treaty of 12 May 1894 leased the Nile basin south of 10° N to Leopold II for his lifetime, and Congo Free State troops under Chaltin reached the Nile in February 1897.

eras.polity: Uganda Protectorate; the Lado district in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
eras.note: After Leopold's death in December 1909 the district became a province of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan on 10 June 1910, and one account says the southern half was ceded to Uganda in 1912.

eras.polity: Uganda Protectorate with the West Nile sub-region
eras.note: On 1 January 1914 Sudan formally exchanged part of the enclave for a stretch of the Upper Nile, and the Ugandan part became the West Nile sub-region. Ancestry offers an index titled UK, Foreign and Overseas Registers of British Subjects, 1628–1969 for Uganda.

regions.label: Bunyoro, Toro, Ankole and Kigezi
regions.sub: Mbarara, Hoima, Masindi, Kasese, Ibanda

eras.polity: Empire of Kitara and the Bachwezi
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Bunyoro-Kitara under the Babiito
eras.note: Rukidi-Mpuga founded the kingdom in the 16th century after the Empire of Kitara dissolved. Internal divisions began its decline in the late 18th century, when Buganda seized Kooki and Buddu.
Tooro separated from Bunyoro in the 1830s and took much of its salt works, and Ankole grew rapidly in the 19th century. In the mid-19th century the Bunyoro capital moved from Masindi to Mparo.
Kabalega resisted British efforts to take control until his capture.

eras.polity: Uganda Protectorate with the kingdoms of Bunyoro, Toro and Ankole
eras.note: Kabalega was captured in 1899 and exiled to the Seychelles, and Bunyoro was annexed with part of its territory going to Buganda and Tooro. The Banyoro revolt of 1907 was put down, and a new agreement in 1933 gave the region more autonomy.
A referendum in 1964 returned the lost counties of Buyaga and Bugangaizi to Bunyoro.
Obote's government forcibly disbanded the kingdom in 1967, and kingdoms stayed banned under Amin (1971–1979) and Obote's second government (1980–1985).

eras.polity: Republic of Uganda with restored kingdoms
eras.note: The Bunyoro kingdom was re-established in 1993 and the 1995 constitution recognized the kingdoms. FamilySearch lists the Uganda Registration Service Bureau in Kampala as the office for marriages.

regions.label: Rwanda and Burundi — Ruanda-Urundi
regions.sub: Kigali, Bujumbura, Gisenyi, Musanze, Gitarama

eras.polity: Separate kingdoms of Ruanda and Urundi
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: German East Africa — the districts of Ruanda and Urundi
eras.note: Germany established a presence in Rwanda in 1897 through an alliance with the king, and both kingdoms were administered as districts of German East Africa. The Tanzania National Archives hold the administrative records for 1884 to 1917.
Ruanda was occupied in April–May 1916 and Urundi in June 1916, and a Royal Commissioner's administration was set up in February 1917.

eras.polity: Ruanda-Urundi, a League of Nations mandate under Belgium
eras.note: The mandate was awarded on 20 July 1922 and Belgium's parliament did not approve it until 1924. The infobox gives 1 March 1926 for the administrative union with the Belgian Congo, and the governor in Usumbura also served as Vice-Governor-General of the Congo.

eras.polity: Ruanda-Urundi, a UN trust territory under Belgium
eras.note: The UN trust territory replaced the mandate in December 1946. Rwanda gained autonomy on 18 October 1960 and its monarchy was abolished in September 1961, while Burundi gained autonomy on 21 December 1961.
Both became independent on 1 July 1962, as Rwanda and the Kingdom of Burundi.

regions.label: Lake Victoria zone — Mwanza, Musoma and Bukoba
regions.sub: Mwanza, Musoma, Bukoba, Geita, Bunda

eras.polity: Chiefdoms and kingdoms around Lake Victoria
eras.note: Before registers.

Germany and Britain agreed their spheres of influence in November 1886, and the Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty of 1 July 1890 set the border with the British East Africa Protectorate, though the exact boundaries were not surveyed until 1910.
Anglo-Belgian forces invaded in 1916, and German resistance continued until 1918.

eras.polity: Tanganyika, a UN trust territory under Britain

regions.label: Western Tanzania — Tabora, Kigoma and Rukwa
regions.sub: Tabora, Kigoma, Sumbawanga, Kasulu, Mpanda

eras.polity: Nyamwezi chiefdoms and the Tanganyika shore
eras.note: Before registers.
Tippu Tip campaigned at Unyanyembe, in today's Tabora Region, against Nyamwezi forces in 1859 and 1860.
Tabora was briefly the capital in 1916, and the Battle of Tabora was among the engagements of the East African campaign.
Belgium ceded the Kigoma District to Tanganyika on 21 or 22 March 1921 depending on the source.

eras.polity: Tanganyika, a UN trust territory under Britain

regions.label: Central Tanzania — Dodoma and Singida
regions.sub: Dodoma, Singida, Kondoa, Manyoni

eras.note: Before registers.

Hermann Wissmann was Reichskommissar from 1888 to 1891, and imperial governors ruled from 1891, beginning with Julius von Soden. Bernhard Dernburg was appointed in 1907 to reform the colonial administration.
The territory became a League of Nations Class B mandate under British administration on 20 July 1922.

eras.polity: Tanganyika, a UN trust territory under Britain
eras.note: The first elections were held in 1958 and 1959, and TANU won the 1958 contest. Internal self-government was granted in 1960.
Independence came on 9 December 1961, and Tanganyika became a republic in 1962.
The union with Zanzibar took place on 26 April 1964.

regions.label: Northern Tanzania — Arusha and Kilimanjaro
regions.sub: Arusha, Moshi, Babati, Mbulu

eras.note: Before registers.
The East African campaign of World War I began on 3 August 1914 under General Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck.
Britain was given control of the territory under the Treaty of Versailles, which took effect on 10 January 1920, and the name Tanganyika dates from 1920.

eras.polity: Tanganyika, a UN trust territory under Britain

regions.label: Southern Highlands — Mbeya, Iringa and Njombe
regions.sub: Mbeya, Iringa, Njombe, Tunduma, Mafinga

eras.note: Before registers.
Lettow-Vorbeck withdrew into Portuguese Mozambique and Northern Rhodesia, and the infobox gives the German surrender as 25 November 1918.
Ruanda and Urundi went to Belgium under the Anglo-Belgian agreement of 30 May 1919.

eras.polity: Tanganyika, a UN trust territory under Britain

regions.label: The Tanzanian coast — Dar es Salaam, Tanga and Morogoro
regions.sub: Dar es Salaam, Tanga, Morogoro, Kibaha, Kilosa

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Omani holdings and the Sultanate of Zanzibar
eras.note: Zanzibar became part of the Omani overseas holdings after Saif bin Sultan defeated the Portuguese at Mombasa in 1698, and in 1856 Majid became the first Sultan of Zanzibar. German warships arrived off Zanzibar on 7 August 1885.

An imperial charter signed by Bismarck on 27 February 1885 was granted to Carl Peters's company, and the Abushiri revolt of 1888–1889 was put down with British help. Bagamoyo was the capital from 1885 to 1890, then Dar es Salaam from 1890 to 1916.

The Tanzania National Archives hold the German administrative records for 1884 to 1917, which UNESCO inscribed in its Memory of the World Register in 1997. FamilySearch lists the Registration Insolvency and Trusteeship Agency (RITA) in Dar es Salaam as an office to contact.

regions.label: Southern Tanzania — Lindi, Mtwara and Ruvuma
regions.sub: Songea, Mtwara, Lindi, Masasi, Tunduru

eras.note: Before registers.
The Maji Maji rebellion began in 1905, and Governor Gustav Adolf von Götzen suppressed it with famine tactics; estimates of deaths reach 300,000.
The Kionga Triangle on the Rovuma went to Portugal in the 1919 settlement and later became part of Mozambique.

regions.label: Zanzibar and Pemba
regions.sub: Zanzibar Town, Chake Chake, Wete, Mkoani, Nungwi

eras.note: Before registers.
Said bin Sultan moved his court from Muscat to Stone Town on Unguja in 1832 or 1840 depending on the source.
