After Said's death his sons Majid and Thuwaini divided the realms, and Majid paid tribute to the Omani court in Muscat. A blockade of Zanzibar in 1888 and 1889, led by Germany with British, Portuguese and Italian support, aimed to end the slave and arms trade.

eras.polity: British protectorate under the Sultan of Zanzibar
eras.note: The Heligoland–Zanzibar Treaty of 1 July 1890 made Zanzibar a British protectorate.
The UK ended the protectorate on 10 December 1963 under the Zanzibar Act 1963, and the Zanzibar Revolution of 12 January 1964 deposed the Sultan.

eras.polity: People's Republic of Zanzibar, united with Tanganyika
eras.note: Zanzibar united with Tanganyika in April 1964, 26 April 1964 in the Tanganyika account, and the union became Tanzania six months later.

regions.label: The Kenyan coast — Mombasa, Malindi and Lamu
regions.sub: Mombasa, Malindi, Kilifi, Ukunda, Mtwapa

eras.note: Before registers.
Fort Jesus was built in 1593–1596 on the orders of Philip II of Spain, who was also Philip I of Portugal. The Portuguese lost it in 1631 to the Sultan of Mombasa and retook it in 1632.

Omani forces under Saif bin Sultan besieged the fort in 1696–1698 and ended the Portuguese presence on the coast. The Portuguese briefly reoccupied it in 1728–1729, and it fell under local rule from 1741 to 1837.
The Omanis recaptured Fort Jesus in 1837 and used it as a barracks.
The Company took over the administration of Mombasa in 1888.
Britain proclaimed the protectorate on 1 July 1895 and occupied Fort Jesus that year, while a 14 December 1895 agreement governed the coastal strip, treated as part of Zanzibar.

eras.polity: Colony of Kenya, and the Protectorate of Kenya on the coastal strip
eras.note: The coastal strip, about 16 km wide, became the Protectorate of Kenya on 29 November 1920 under the Sultan of Zanzibar's sovereignty. British government records for Africa and Asia from 1895 to 1965 are in class RG36 at the National Archives at Kew.
Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963, and the coastal strip ceased to be under the Sultan's sovereignty that day.

regions.label: Nairobi, Central Kenya and Ukambani
regions.sub: Nairobi, Thika, Ruiru, Kikuyu, Machakos area

eras.note: Before registers.

Nairobi was founded in 1898 as a rail depot on the Uganda Railway, dated 1899 in the infobox, and the railway reached the site on 30 May 1899. Registration of births and deaths began in 1904 and applied only to Europeans and Americans.
Nairobi replaced Mombasa as capital in 1907 and was declared a municipality in 1919.
The Colony of Kenya was established on 23 July 1920, and the reservation of the White Highlands for Europeans drew objections in the 1920s.

eras.polity: Colony of Kenya during the Mau Mau rebellion
eras.note: The Mau Mau rebellion lasted from 1952 to 1960, and files on the detention camps are reported to have been burned or dumped at sea.
Kenya became a republic on 12 December 1964.

regions.label: The Rift Valley Highlands
regions.sub: Nakuru, Eldoret, Naivasha, Kitale, Narok

eras.polity: Chiefdoms and pastoral peoples of the Rift Valley
eras.note: Before registers.
Britain proclaimed the East Africa Protectorate on 1 July 1895.
In 1902 the British decided to transfer the eastern section of the Uganda Protectorate to the East Africa Protectorate, so that the railway would fall under one administration.
Compulsory registration of African deaths came with the 1928 Act (CAP 149), but births were not included.
The Kenya Independence Act 1963 gave independence on 12 December 1963 with the Queen as head of state.

regions.label: Nyanza and Western Kenya
regions.sub: Kisumu, Kakamega, Kisii, Bungoma, Migori

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the Lake Victoria basin
eras.note: Before registers.
The colony covered 639,200 km² in 1924 with about 2,807,000 people, and the 1921 population estimate of 2,376,000 included 9,651 Europeans, 22,822 Indians and 10,102 Arabs.
Self-rule began on 1 June 1963.
Compulsory registration of all births and deaths was phased in after 1963 and became nationwide on 1 September 1971.

regions.label: The Northern Frontier — Garissa, Wajir, Mandera and Isiolo
regions.sub: Garissa, Wajir, Mandera, Lodwar, Isiolo

eras.polity: Somali, Boran, Gabbra, Rendille and Turkana country
eras.note: Before registers.

Administration began unofficially in 1909 with stations at Marsabit and Moyale, and the district was officially recognised in 1910 with its headquarters at Moyale. The headquarters moved to Meru in 1919 and to Isiolo around 1929, and provincial status was withdrawn in 1934.
The province was formed in 1947 and administered from Marsabit. On 8 March 1963 Britain created the North Eastern Region from the district despite a plebiscite favouring union with Somalia.
Somali-backed insurgents fought Kenyan forces from 1963 to 1967, when a ceasefire ended the main conflict.
The Department of Civil Registration Services in Nairobi holds Kenyan civil registration.

regions.label: Northern Malawi — Karonga, Mzuzu and Mzimba
regions.sub: Mzuzu, Karonga, Mzimba, Rumphi, Chitipa

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the Lake Malawi northwest
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Northern Ngoni kingdom and the lakeshore trading settlements
eras.note: The African Lakes Company was founded in Glasgow in 1878 by businessmen linked to the Presbyterian missions. The Ngoni formed expansionist kingdoms, and the Livingstonia mission was influential in the Northern Ngoni kingdom.

The Nyasaland Districts Protectorate was endorsed in May 1891, and Mlozi was hanged at Karonga on 5 December 1895. The Northern Ngoni kingdom accepted British rule in 1904 on condition that it kept its traditions.
The protectorate took the name Nyasaland on 6 July 1907. FamilySearch gives civil registration as 1904 to present, with the National Registration Bureau in Lilongwe as the contact.
Nyasaland was part of the Federation from 1 August 1953 until it was dissolved on 31 December 1963.
Independence as Malawi came on 6 July 1964.

regions.label: Central Malawi — Lilongwe, Kasungu and the lakeshore
regions.sub: Lilongwe, Kasungu, Mangochi, Salima, Nkhotakota

eras.note: Before registers.
Gomani's forces were defeated on 23 October 1896 and Gomani was shot four days later. The only official census, in 1901, recorded a population of 736,724.
The 1911 census recorded 969,183 Africans, 766 Europeans and 481 Asians.
A State of Emergency was declared on 3 March 1959, and Nyasaland achieved internal self-government in February 1963.
Malawi became a republic on 6 July 1966, and Lilongwe is the capital of independent Malawi.

regions.label: Southern Malawi — the Shire Highlands and Blantyre
regions.sub: Blantyre, Zomba, Liwonde, Mulanje, Nsanje

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the Shire valley and highlands
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Mission and trading settlement at Blantyre; Yao chiefdoms
eras.note: Blantyre had a mission and trading settlement from 1876, and a British consul took up residence in 1883.

eras.polity: Shire Highlands Protectorate, then British Central Africa Protectorate
eras.note: John Buchanan declared a Shire Highlands Protectorate in September 1889, and Britain's ultimatum of 11 January 1890 forced Portugal to withdraw from the Shire valley by 12 March. The 1891 Anglo-Portuguese treaty fixed the southern borders and gave Britain a 99-year lease over Chinde; a hut tax was introduced in the Shire Highlands in 1895.
Zomba was the capital and Blantyre remained the commercial centre. John Chilembwe's uprising took place in January 1915.
The Malawi Congress Party won 22 of 28 Legislative Council seats in the August 1961 elections.
FamilySearch's coverage estimates for civil registration are 95 percent of the White population and 0 to 5 percent of the African population.

regions.label: Lake Mweru and the Luapula border
regions.sub: Nchelenge, Kaputa, Mwansabombwe, Chiengi

eras.polity: Chiefdoms of the Luapula and Lake Mweru country
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Luba vassal chiefdoms and Kazembe's neighbours
eras.note: Katondo's chiefdom was established in the mid-19th century around the Zela lands northwest of Lake Mweru, after a war with Kazembe.

The Company was given power in 1889 to set up a police force and administer justice, and an Order-in-Council of 1900 recognised North-Eastern Rhodesia as a protectorate under its administration. Hut tax was first collected there in 1901.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company
eras.note: The Company merged the two territories as Northern Rhodesia in 1911.
The Colonial Office took over on 1 April 1924, and the capital moved from Livingstone to Lusaka in 1935. The territory was part of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963.
Independence as Zambia came on 24 October 1964.

regions.label: Western Niassa — Mandimba and the Lake Niassa border
regions.sub: Mandimba, Metangula, Lichinga area

eras.note: Before registers.

The concession ran for 35 years over more than 160,000 km² between the Rovuma and Lúrio rivers, and a French and British consortium bought it in 1892–1893 and moved the headquarters to London. The company occupied inland areas, including Metangula on Lake Niassa, in 1900–1902, and the Portuguese government refused to extend the concession on 27 October 1929.
FRELIMO's guerrilla campaign against Portuguese rule began in September 1964.
RENAMO, formed in 1975, launched attacks and the country descended into civil war. The Rome General Peace Accords were signed on 4 October 1992 and took effect on 15 October 1992.

regions.label: Tigray - Mekele, Aksum and Adwa
regions.sub: Mek'ele, Adwa, Aksum, Adigrat, Inda Silase, Humera

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Era of the Princes (Zemene Mesafint)
eras.note: Before registers. The Era of the Princes is dated from the deposition of Emperor Iyoas on 7 May 1769 to 1855.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Tewodros II, Tekle Giyorgis II and Yohannes IV
eras.note: Tewodros II is dated 1855 to 1868 in one history and the 1855-1872 period is headed Tewodros II and Tekle Giyorgis II in another; Yohannes IV ruled 1872-1889. Egypt received Massawa from the Ottomans in 1865 and was defeated in the Egyptian-Ethiopian War of 1876.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Menelik II to Haile Selassie
eras.note: Menelik II proclaimed himself emperor on 25 March 1889, signed the Treaty of Wuchale with Italy on 2 May 1889 and defeated the Italians at Adwa on 1 March 1896. Italy's colony of Eritrea lay immediately north of Tigray from 1890.
Italian forces took Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936 and annexed Ethiopia on 9 May; on 1 June 1936 Ethiopia, Eritrea and Somalia were united as Italian East Africa under one Governor-General.
Haile Selassie was restored in May 1941. Eritrea, on Tigray's northern edge, was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and declared a province in 1962; Ethiopian provinces were then divided into awrajjas.

eras.polity: Derg military government and civil war
eras.note: The Derg coup of 12 September 1974 ended Haile Selassie's reign and the monarchy was formally abolished in March 1975; a civil war ran from 1974 to 1991.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Tigray Region
eras.note: Since the 1995 Constitution the old provinces and awrajjas have been replaced by regions and zones drawn on ethno-linguistic lines; Tigray is one of the regions. Proclamation 760/2012, published 22 August 2012, made registration of births, marriages and deaths compulsory.

regions.label: Amhara highlands - Gondar, Gojjam and Wollo
regions.sub: Gondar, Bahir Dar, Dessie, Debre Tabor, Debre Markos, Lalibela

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Era of the Princes (Zemene Mesafint)
eras.note: Before registers. The Era of the Princes is dated from the deposition of Emperor Iyoas on 7 May 1769 to 1855.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Tewodros II to Yohannes IV
eras.note: Menelik pacified Wollo in 1868-1871 as King of Shewa. A Mahdist army invaded Ethiopia as far as Gondar in 1887, and Yohannes IV was killed at the Battle of Gallabat (Metemma) on 10 March 1889.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Menelik II to Haile Selassie
eras.note: Menelik II was proclaimed emperor on 25 March 1889 and moved his capital to Addis Ababa in 1886; Haile Selassie was crowned on 2 November 1930 and the first written constitution followed on 16 July 1931.

eras.polity: Italian East Africa - Amhara Governorate, capital Gondar
eras.note: Italian East Africa was created on 1 June 1936 with six governorates; Amhara had its capital at Gondar, where the Italian garrison fought the Battle of Gondar in November 1941.
After the Italian defeat Haile Selassie was restored in May 1941. Before the 1995 Constitution the highest administrative level was the province, divided into awrajjas.

eras.polity: Derg military government and civil war
eras.note: The coup of 12 September 1974 ended Haile Selassie's reign; the monarchy was abolished in March 1975 and a civil war lasted until 1991.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Amhara Region
eras.note: The 1995 Constitution replaced provinces with ethnically based regions; Amhara is one of twelve. Church and civil dates are usually in the Ethiopian calendar, which runs 7 or 8 years behind the Gregorian one (new year on 11 or 12 September) and is valid for conversion from March 1900 to February 2100 only.

regions.label: Shewa and Arsi - Addis Ababa and the central highlands
regions.sub: Addis Ababa, Bishoftu, Adama, Debre Birhan, Asela, Ambo, Shashamane

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Era of the Princes (Zemene Mesafint)
eras.note: Before registers. The Era of the Princes is dated from the deposition of Emperor Iyoas on 7 May 1769 to 1855.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Shewa - Menelik as Negus
eras.note: Menelik escaped from Magdala on 1 July 1865 and proclaimed himself Negus of Shewa in August 1866. The Arsi were fully brought under Shoan control in 1886, Wollega was occupied in 1886, Menelik moved his capital to Addis Ababa that year, and the Gurage region was annexed in 1889.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Addis Ababa the capital
eras.note: Menelik was proclaimed emperor on 25 March 1889 and crowned on Mount Entoto on 3 November 1889. Haile Selassie was crowned on 2 November 1930 and a constitution was adopted on 16 July 1931.

eras.polity: Italian East Africa - Addis Abeba, then Scioa Governorate
eras.note: Addis Ababa was the capital of Italian East Africa from 1936. In November 1938 the Addis Abeba Governorate was enlarged into the Scioa Governorate with territory taken from Harar, Galla-Sidamo and Amhara, so Italian files for this ground are not under the older provincial names.
Haile Selassie was restored in May 1941. Before the 1995 Constitution provinces were divided into awrajjas, and boundaries were sometimes redrawn.

eras.polity: Derg military government and civil war
eras.note: The Derg took power on 12 September 1974; the monarchy was abolished in March 1975 and the civil war lasted to 1991.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Oromia and the Addis Ababa city administration
eras.note: Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa are chartered cities on the same level as the regions; most of the surrounding ground is Oromia. The Federal Vital Event Registration Agency is in Addis Ababa, and Proclamation 760/2012, published 22 August 2012, created the compulsory registration system.

regions.label: Western and southern Ethiopia - Wollega, Kaffa, Sidamo and Bale
regions.sub: Jimma, Nekemte, Gambela, Hawassa, Arba Minch, Sodo, Goba

eras.polity: Kingdom of Kaffa and the Oromo, Gibe and Sidama polities
eras.note: Before registers. Oral tradition dates the Kingdom of Kaffa, capital Bonga, to about 1390; in the 18th century Mecha Oromo invasions took all of its territory north of the Gojeb River.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Shoan conquest of the west and south
eras.note: Kaffa, Jimma, Limmu, Gera and Guma became tributary in 1881; Wollega was occupied in 1886, Illubabor in 1887, Bale, Sidamo and Welayta from 1891, Kambata in 1893 and Wollamo in 1894. Kaffa's king was captured on 11 September 1897 and Kaffa was held as a fief by Wolde Giyorgis until 1914.

eras.polity: Italian East Africa - Galla-Sidamo Governorate, capital Jimma
eras.note: Italian East Africa was created on 1 June 1936; the Galla-Sidamo Governorate had its capital at Jimma.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Haile Selassie restored; provinces reorganised in 1942
eras.note: In the 1942 reorganisation of provinces Kaffa was enlarged with the former Gibe kingdoms. Provinces were divided into awrajjas until the 1995 Constitution.

eras.polity: Derg military government and civil war
eras.note: The Derg took power on 12 September 1974 and the monarchy was abolished in March 1975; the civil war ran to 1991.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Oromia, Southern, Sidama, South West and Gambela regions
eras.note: The ground is now split between several regions: Sidama is one, and the South West Ethiopia Peoples' Region was created in 2021 by a special referendum that took several zones from the Southern Nations, Nationalities and Peoples' Region. Registration of births, marriages and deaths is compulsory under Proclamation 760/2012.

regions.label: Harar, Dire Dawa and the Afar lowlands
regions.sub: Harar, Dire Dawa, Jijiga, Asaita, Semera, Babile

eras.polity: Emirate of Harar (from 1647) and Sultanate of Aussa (from 1734)
eras.note: Before registers. The Harari broke away from the Imamate of Aussa in 1647 under 'Ali ibn Da'ud; the Mudaito Afar sultanate of Aussa, with its capital at Asaita, was founded in 1734 by Data Kadafo.

eras.polity: Egyptian occupation and the restored emirate of Harar
eras.note: Egyptian forces seized Harar on 11 October 1875; Egyptian control is dated as ending in 1882 or 1884, with a British occupation of 1882-1884, after which Emir 'Abdullah II ruled until 1887.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Harar annexed; Aussa a tributary
eras.note: Harar was annexed by Shewan forces on 6 January 1887 after the Battle of Chelenqo. Aussa signed an Italian protectorate treaty on 6 December 1889 but became an Ethiopian tributary after the defeat at Arraddo in January 1896.

eras.polity: Italian East Africa - Harar Governorate, capital Harar
eras.note: Italian forces occupied the Sultanate of Aussa on 1 April 1936, and the Harar Governorate of Italian East Africa had its capital at Harar.

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - Harerge province and the Afar sultanate
eras.note: After the Italian defeat the Ethiopian government installed a new Sultan of Aussa in 1943 (the succession list gives 1944). Provinces were divided into awrajjas until 1995.

eras.polity: Derg military government and civil war
eras.note: The Derg took power in 1974 and the civil war ran to 1991; the Sultan of Aussa was exiled in 1975 and returned in 1991.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Afar, Harari, Oromia and Somali regions
eras.note: The ground is now divided among the Afar, Harari and Somali regions, Oromia and the chartered city of Dire Dawa. The Federal Vital Event Registration Agency keeps the registration made compulsory by Proclamation 760/2012.

regions.label: Ogaden - the Somali Region of Ethiopia
regions.sub: Gode, Degeh Bur, Kebri Dahar, Warder, Dolo Ado

eras.polity: Ethiopian Empire - the Ogaden after Harar fell
eras.note: Menelik took Harar in 1887 and Ethiopian raids caused repeated devastation in the Ogaden between 1890 and 1900; Jijiga was under intermittent Ethiopian occupation until 1900. The Anglo-Ethiopian Treaty of 1897 ceded almost half of British Somaliland to Ethiopia, a boundary the Somali Republic rejected.

eras.polity: Italian East Africa - attached to the Somalia Governorate
eras.note: After Italy conquered Ethiopia in 1936 the Ogaden was attached to Italian Somaliland as part of the Somalia Governorate; the Wal Wal incident was in 1935.
After 1941 all the former Italian East African territories came under British military administration; Britain ceded the Ogaden to Ethiopia in 1948.
On 23 September 1948 the areas east of Jijiga came under Ethiopian governance for the first time; the last British-controlled parts of the Haud were handed over in 1955.

eras.polity: Derg military government - Ogaden War of 1977-78
eras.note: Ethiopia and Somalia fought over the region in 1977-78, and an estimated 800,000 people crossed into Somalia as refugees.

eras.polity: Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia - Somali Region
eras.note: A founding conference at Dire Dawa in 1992 named it the Somali Region; the state capital moved from Gode to Jigjiga in 1994. Registration of births, marriages and deaths has been compulsory since Proclamation 760/2012.

regions.label: Eritrea - Asmara, Massawa and the highlands
regions.sub: Asmara, Keren, Massawa, Mendefera, Barentu, Assab

eras.polity: Ottoman Habesh Eyalet - Massawa and the Dahlak Islands
eras.note: The Ottomans occupied the Dahlak Islands and then Massawa in the 16th century; the Habesh Eyalet is dated 1554-1872 by some accounts, and Egypt obtained Massawa from the Ottomans in 1865.
Egypt held Massawa from 1865 and was defeated in the Egyptian-Ethiopian War of 1876. The Sultan of Raheita sold land around the Bay of Assab to the Rubattino Shipping Company in 1869 or 1870.

eras.polity: Italian Massawa and Assab before the colony
eras.note: Italy took Massawa in 1885 (1882 in some accounts); the first Italian settlers at Assab arrived in 1880.
The colony was established on 1 January 1890 by royal decree with Massawa as its first capital; Asmara became the capital in 1897. The Treaty of Wuchale was signed with Menelik II in 1889.
Eritrea became a governorate of Italian East Africa on 1 June 1936; the 1939 Italian census counted 75,000 Italians in Eritrea, 53,000 of them in Asmara.

British military administration ran from 19 May 1941 to 1952. Italy gave up its claim under the Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1947, and UN Resolution 390A of 2 December 1950 provided for federation with Ethiopia.

eras.polity: Federation with Ethiopia, then annexation and war
eras.note: Eritrea became an autonomous part of Ethiopia on 15 September 1952; the Eritrean Assembly voted to dissolve the federation in November 1962. The Eritrean Liberation Front began military operations in 1961 and the EPLF was founded in 1972.
A provisional government was established in May 1991. A referendum on 23-25 April 1993 returned 99.83 percent for independence, declared on 27 April 1993.

regions.label: Djibouti - French Somaliland and the Afar coast
regions.sub: Djibouti, Ali Sabieh, Dikhil, Tadjoura, Obock

eras.polity: French protectorate on the Gulf of Tadjoura
eras.note: The French colony of French Somaliland is dated from 1884; protectorate treaties were signed with the Gadabuursi and Issa clans in 1885, and after French sailors were killed at Ambado in 1886 France claimed the whole southern territory.

The colony was formally established in 1896. The Imperial Ethiopian Railway made Djibouti a boomtown and let it overtake Zeila in trade. Civil registers of the Cote francaise des Somalis are among the colonial registers held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

French Somaliland became an overseas territory in 1946. The Cote francaise des Somalis fonds at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer, made up of documents repatriated from Djibouti at independence, was long inaccessible and is now open.

eras.polity: French Territory of the Afars and the Issas
eras.note: The territory was renamed in 1967.
Djibouti became independent in 1977 as the legal successor of the French territory.

regions.label: British Somaliland - Hargeisa, Berbera and Burao
regions.sub: Hargeysa, Berbera, Burao, Borama, Erigavo, Las Anod

eras.polity: British Somaliland protectorate, administered from British India and Aden
eras.note: The British protectorate is dated from 1884, with protection treaties with the local sultanates dated 1888. The Anglo-Ethiopian Treaty of 1897 ceded almost half of the protectorate to Ethiopia; the Somali Republic rejected it as invalid.

eras.polity: British Somaliland - Foreign Office, then Colonial Office from 1905
eras.note: The Foreign Office took over administration in 1898 and the Colonial Office in 1905; Berbera was the capital. The Dervish movement was defeated by British air power in 1920. The Colonial Office series CO 535 (Somaliland, 1905-1951) is at The National Archives, Kew.
Italian troops invaded on 3 August 1940 and took Berbera by 14 August. British forces retook the protectorate in March 1941 (8 April 1941 in some accounts).
Hargeisa was the capital from 1941. British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960 as the State of Somaliland.
The State of Somaliland united with the Trust Territory of Somaliland on 1 July 1960 to form the Somali Republic; Siad Barre seized power in 1969.
The Supreme Revolutionary Council collapsed in 1991 with the start of the Somali Civil War, and the Republic of Somaliland was proclaimed in May 1991.

regions.label: Majeerteen and Hobyo - north-eastern Somalia
regions.sub: Bosaso, Garoowe, Gaalkacyo, Eyl, Qandala, Cabudwaaq

eras.polity: Italian protectorates over the Sultanates of Hobyo and the Majeerteen
eras.note: Italy signed protectorate treaties with the Sultanate of Hobyo on 8 or 9 February 1889 and the Majeerteen Sultanate on 7 April 1889.
The Hobyo and Majeerteen sultanates were annexed in 1927 after the Campaign of the Sultanates.
Italian Somaliland became the Somalia Governorate of Italian East Africa on 1 June 1936, capital Mogadishu.
British forces occupied Italian Somaliland on 26 February 1941 and a British Military Administration followed.

eras.polity: Trust Territory of Somaliland under Italian Administration
eras.note: The Italian trust administration began on 1 April 1950, with independence due within ten years under the arrangement agreed in 1945.
The trust territory united with British Somaliland on 1 July 1960 to form the Somali Republic.
The Supreme Revolutionary Council collapsed in 1991 with the start of the Somali Civil War.

regions.label: Southern Somalia - Benadir, the Shabelle and Jubaland
regions.sub: Mogadishu, Merca, Afgooye, Baidoa, Kismayo, Beledweyne

eras.polity: Italian Benadir - ports run by a chartered company
eras.note: Italy occupied Adale in 1891, and Merca, Mogadishu, Barawa and Warsheekh in late 1893; a chartered company ran the Banaadir ports in the 1890s.
The Banaadir colony was officially established on 19 March 1905; Afgooye and Balad were added in 1907-1908 after campaigns against Bimaal resistance.
Britain ceded Oltre Giuba (Trans-Juba, present-day Jubaland) to Italy in 1925, the last land Italy acquired in Somalia, so Kismayo and the south-west were British before that year.
The colony became the Somalia Governorate of Italian East Africa on 1 June 1936.
British forces occupied the territory on 26 February 1941 and a British Military Administration followed.

eras.polity: Trust Territory of Somaliland under Italian Administration
eras.note: The Italian trust administration began on 1 April 1950.
The trust territory united with British Somaliland on 1 July 1960; Siad Barre seized power in 1969.
The central government collapsed in 1991 with the start of the Somali Civil War.

regions.label: Northern Sudan - Dongola, Shendi and Atbara
regions.sub: Dongola, Merowe, Atbara, Ad-Damir, Shendi, Wadi Halfa

eras.note: Before registers. The Funj Sultanate was founded in 1504 (a reference gives 1504/5) by Amara Dunqas, with its capital at Sennar on the Blue Nile. At its late 17th-century peak its northern limit was the Third Cataract.

eras.polity: Funj Sultanate under the Hamaj regency
eras.note: Muhammad Abu Likaylik entered Sennar on 27 March 1762 and the Funj monarchs became puppets of the Hamaj; Sultan Badi VII formally submitted to Egypt on 14 June 1821.
Ismail, son of Muhammad Ali, began the Egyptian campaign in 1820 and the Funj sultan submitted on 14 June 1821; Egypt kept its Sudanese territories after 1841.

Mahdist forces took Khartoum on 26 January 1885 and the Mahdi died on 22 June 1885; the capital was Omdurman. The Khalifa was defeated at Omdurman on 2 September 1898, and the state is dated to end on 18 January 1899 (the Sudan Convention) or at Umm Diwaykarat in November 1899.
The condominium agreement is dated 19 January 1899 in one account and 18 January 1899 (the Sudan Convention) in others. Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.
Genealogy records are kept at state level and tribal lineages are most often oral. A war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces began on 15 April 2023.

regions.label: Eastern Sudan - Kassala, Gedaref and the Red Sea coast
regions.sub: Port Sudan, Suakin, Kassala, Gedaref, New Halfa

eras.note: Before registers. The Funj Sultanate was founded in 1504 (a reference gives 1504/5) by Amara Dunqas, with its capital at Sennar on the Blue Nile. At its peak the sultanate reached east to the Red Sea.

eras.polity: Funj Sultanate under the Hamaj regency
eras.note: Muhammad Abu Likaylik entered Sennar on 27 March 1762 and the Funj monarchs became puppets of the Hamaj; Sultan Badi VII formally submitted to Egypt on 14 June 1821.

eras.polity: Turco-Egyptian Sudan - Eastern Sudan and the Red Sea coast
eras.note: Egypt conquered the Funj lands in 1820-1821. In 1872 Werner Munzinger Pasha governed the Province of Eastern Sudan and the Red Sea Coast.
Kassala and Sennar fell soon after Khartoum on 26 January 1885. The Italians repulsed a Mahdist attack at Akordat, in Eritrea, in 1893.
The condominium is dated to the January 1899 agreement. Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.
Genealogy records are kept at state level in Sudan.

regions.label: Central Sudan - Khartoum, the Gezira and Sennar
regions.sub: Khartoum, Omdurman, Wad Medani, Kosti, Sennar, Ad-Damazin

eras.note: Before registers. The Funj Sultanate was founded in 1504 (a reference gives 1504/5) by Amara Dunqas, with its capital at Sennar on the Blue Nile. Sennar remained the Funj capital until the Egyptian conquest.

eras.polity: Funj Sultanate under the Hamaj regency
eras.note: Muhammad Abu Likaylik entered Sennar on 27 March 1762 and the Funj monarchs became puppets of the Hamaj; Sultan Badi VII formally submitted to Egypt on 14 June 1821.
Egypt invaded in 1820-1821 and the Funj sultan submitted on 14 June 1821; Khartoum was the Sudanese capital under Egyptian rule, which lasted until the Mahdist capture of Khartoum in 1885.

Khartoum fell on 26 January 1885 and the Khalifa ruled from Omdurman, across the river from the ruined city; Kassala and Sennar fell soon after Khartoum. The Mahdist army was defeated at Omdurman on 2 September 1898.

eras.polity: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan - Khartoum restored as capital
eras.note: Khartoum was restored as the administrative capital after the reconquest and the condominium agreement of January 1899. Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.

Genealogy records are kept at state level in Sudan. Fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces began on 15 April 2023, and the RSF took most of Khartoum by late 2023; the army retook it by March 2025.

regions.label: Kordofan - El Obeid and the Nuba Mountains
regions.sub: El Obeid, An Nuhud, Dilling, Kadugli, Umm Ruwaba

eras.polity: Funj Sultanate and the exiled Darfuri Musabb'at
eras.note: Before registers. Kordofan was contested between the Funj Sultanate and an exiled faction of the Darfuri royal house, the Musabb'at.
The Fur Sultanate of Darfur conquered Kordofan in 1785 or 1786 and held it until the Egyptian invasion of 1821.
Turco-Egyptian forces took Kordofan in 1821, and Egypt kept its Sudanese territories after 1841.
In early 1882 the Ansar defeated a British-led Egyptian force near El Obeid (Al Ubayyid) and then a relief force at Sheikan. Mahdist authority is dated to 1885-1899.
The condominium is dated to the January 1899 agreement; Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.
Genealogy records are kept at state level in Sudan and tribal lineages are most often oral.

regions.label: Darfur - El Fasher, Nyala and Geneina
regions.sub: El Fasher, Nyala, El Geneina, El Daein, Kas, Gereida

eras.note: Before registers. The sultanate was established in the mid-16th century under the Keira dynasty; Sulayman Solong is credited with making Islam the state religion.
Sultan 'Abd al-Rahman moved the capital to al-Fashir (El Fasher) in 1792. Kordofan was lost to Turco-Egyptian forces in 1821.
Sultan Ibrahim died in 1874 at the Battle of al-Manawashi and al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur, allied with the Turco-Egyptians, conquered the sultanate, which was then administered as a province.
The Mahdists took Darfur in 1885; Mahdist rule later collapsed under rebellions.

eras.polity: Sultanate of Darfur restored under Ali Dinar
eras.note: Sultan Ali Dinar restored self-rule in 1898.
The British conquered Darfur in 1916 when Ali Dinar was killed; it was incorporated into the condominium in 1916 or 1917 depending on the source. Sudan became independent on 1 January 1956.
Genealogy records are kept at state level in Sudan. The Rapid Support Forces besieged El Fasher from April 2024 and the city fell on 26 October 2025.

regions.label: Equatoria - Juba, Yei and Yambio
regions.sub: Juba, Yei, Yambio, Torit, Kapoeta, Maridi

eras.polity: Turco-Egyptian Sudan - White Nile expeditions to Juba
eras.note: Egypt invaded Sudan in 1821; Salim Qabudan's expedition reached the present Juba area in 1839-1842.

Isma'il Pasha established Equatoria; Samuel Baker was hired to govern it in 1869, Charles Gordon became governor in 1874 and Emin Pasha replaced him in 1878. Equatoria ceased to exist as an Egyptian outpost in 1889.
The Mahdist War cut southern Sudan off from Egypt, and Belgian forces blocked Mahdist advances into Equatoria.
The Southern Policy was written in 1928 and legalised by a 1930 announcement; the British reversed it in 1946. The Torit mutiny of 18 August 1955 began the First Sudanese Civil War.

The First Sudanese Civil War ran 1955-1972 and the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 set up the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region. The second war ran 1983-2005 and ended with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005.
The independence referendum of 9-15 January 2011 returned about 98.83 percent for independence, and South Sudan became independent at midnight on 9 July 2011. Fighting began on 14 December 2013.

regions.label: Bahr el Ghazal and Upper Nile - Wau, Malakal and Bentiu
regions.sub: Wau, Malakal, Aweil, Rumbek, Bor, Bentiu, Gogrial

eras.polity: Funj Sultanate (northern Upper Nile at its peak)
eras.note: Before registers. At its late 17th-century peak the Funj Sultanate reached the Sobat River, which is the northern part of present Upper Nile.
Egypt invaded in 1821 when the Funj Sultanate collapsed; Equatoria, to the south, was established under Isma'il Pasha.
The Mahdist state's former territory lies within present Sudan, South Sudan and the Central African Republic; the Mahdist War cut southern Sudan off from Egypt.
From 1924 the British divided Sudan into a northern, Arabic-speaking Muslim area and a southern area; the Torit mutiny of 18 August 1955 began the First Sudanese Civil War.
The wars of 1955-1972 and 1983-2005 were separated by the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972; the Comprehensive Peace Agreement was signed in 2005.
South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after the January 2011 referendum.

regions.label: Mauritius and Rodrigues
regions.sub: Port Louis, Curepipe, Mahebourg, Vacoas, Port Mathurin

eras.note: Dutch colonisation is dated 1638-1710, with the island abandoned in 1710; the island then remained free of Europeans until 1721.

eras.polity: Isle de France - French East India Company
eras.note: Guillaume Dufresne d'Arsel took possession in September 1715 and named the island Isle de France; the French occupation began in 1721, and until 1735 it was administered from Ile Bourbon. FamilySearch indexes births, marriages and deaths of slaves and free people as 'Mauritius (Ile de France), ANOM, Civil Registration, 1700-1820'.
The island was transferred to the French Crown in 1767. Civil registration for 1728-1811 is held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer, with a free index and images through iREL.

The British took the island on 3 December 1810 after the French capitulated, and Rodrigues was taken in 1809 or 1810 depending on the account; Isle de France and its dependencies were ceded to Britain in 1814 (30 May 1814 in some accounts) and the name Mauritius returned. The Civil Status Division in Port Louis holds records from 1812; older records of genealogical interest are at the National Archives at Coromandel. Colonial Office correspondence is at The National Archives, Kew.

Slavery was abolished effective 1 February 1835, and most Indo-Mauritians arrived between 1835 and 1924 through the Coolie Ghat (Aapravasi Ghat). FamilySearch has filmed most pre-1930 civil registration, including 1861-1930 ten-year indexes.
Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968 and a republic on 12 March 1992.

regions.label: Seychelles - Mahe, Praslin and La Digue
regions.sub: Victoria, Cascade, Baie Sainte Anne

eras.note: France claimed the islands on 1 November 1756.
The first settlers landed on Ste Anne on 12 August 1770.

Captain Newcome's squadron took the colony on its surrender in 1794, and Captain Beaver took possession for Britain as a permanent colony in 1811. The Seychelles National Archives hold marriage registers for 1794-1840.

Slavery was abolished in 1835 and the town was named Victoria in 1841; about 2,400 liberated Africans were apprenticed to plantation owners from 1861. The Civil Status Act of 1883 made the Victoria office the central registry for Mahe and other islands.
Seychelles became a separate Crown Colony in 1903; in 1965 Aldabra, Farquhar and Des Roches were transferred to the British Indian Ocean Territory.
Seychelles became independent on 29 June 1976 and the three islands returned. The Seychelles National Archives are at Victoria on Mahe.

regions.label: Comoros - Grande Comore, Anjouan and Moheli
regions.sub: Moroni, Mutsamudu, Fomboni, Domoni, Ouani

eras.note: Before registers. Shirazi elites established ports and ruling houses in the 15th century; the sultanates are dated 1676-1912 in one source.

eras.polity: The Comorian sultanates beside French Mayotte
eras.note: France acquired Mayotte in 1841; the other islands stayed under their own rulers until 1886.

eras.polity: French protectorates over Ngazidja, Nzwani and Mwali
eras.note: France signed protectorate treaties with the rulers of the three islands in 1886; the four islands became part of France's colony of Madagascar in 1908.

The last sultan abdicated in 1912 and a colonial administration took over with its capital at Dzaoudzi on Mayotte; administrative ties to Madagascar were severed in 1947. The Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence hold Comoros civil registers and the fonds of the Delegation generale de la Republique aux Comores.

In the December 1974 referendum Mayotte voted against independence (63.8 percent); the Comorian parliament declared independence unilaterally on 6 July 1975. Mayotte stayed under French administration after a second referendum in February 1976.

regions.label: Mayotte
regions.sub: Mamoudzou, Dzaoudzi, Koungou, Sada, Bandrele

eras.note: The ruler of Mayotte ceded the island to France in 1841 (sources describe it as a negotiated cession or a purchase).

France took control of the whole archipelago in 1885 and the colony was named Mayotte and Dependencies. Civil registers of Mayotte are among the colonial registers held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

eras.polity: French Mayotte - Dzaoudzi the colonial capital
eras.note: The colonial administration of the Comoros had its capital at Dzaoudzi, on Petite-Terre, from 1912.

eras.polity: French Mayotte after the break with Madagascar
eras.note: Administrative ties with Madagascar were severed in 1947. Mayotte voted to remain French in December 1974 (63.8 percent) and February 1976 (99.4 percent).

Mayotte's capital moved from Dzaoudzi to Mamoudzou in 1977 and its status became a departmental collectivity in 2001. Mayotte has a special civil-status regime: traditional Islamic law is being gradually replaced by the French civil code.
Mayotte became France's 101st department on 31 March 2011 and an outermost region of the European Union on 1 January 2014.

regions.label: Lebanon: Mount Lebanon and the coast
regions.sub: Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon, Tyre, Zahlé, Baalbek

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Mount Lebanon within the provinces of Sidon and Tripoli
eras.note: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516. The Tripoli Eyalet dates from 1579 and the Eyalet of Safed (1660), later renamed Sidon and then Beirut, held the southern coast. Mount Lebanon had a special autonomous status inside the Sidon province, dated from 1667.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Muhammad Ali's forces took Tyre in December 1831 and he formally took overlordship of Lebanon in 1832; the Convention of Kütahya (1833) ceded the Syrian provinces to him. The Second Egyptian-Ottoman War ran 1839-1841.

Mount Lebanon was ruled as two districts under the Double Qaimaqamate, dated 1843-1861 (some accounts start in 1842). The system ended after the 1860 conflict, in which about 60 villages near Beirut were destroyed in three days in late May 1860.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate and the Beirut Vilayet
eras.note: The Protocol of 9 June 1861 created the Mutasarrifate and the Basic Law of 6 September 1864 made it permanent. The Protocol left Beirut, Akkar, Marjayoun and Jabal Amel outside it, and the Beirut Vilayet is dated 1888-1917. The first general Ottoman census took from 1881 to 1893.

eras.polity: Allied (French) administration after the Ottoman defeat
eras.note: The French invasion of 1918 followed the Ottoman defeat, and the Mutasarrifate is dated to end in September 1918. Allied administration is listed to 1920.

eras.polity: French Mandate: State of Greater Lebanon
eras.note: France received the mandate for Syria including Lebanon at San Remo on 25 April 1920. Arrêté 318 of 31 August 1920 created the State of Greater Lebanon, proclaimed on 1 September 1920, which became the Lebanese Republic on 23 May 1926. The mandate is dated 1923-1946 in one source and French rule 1920-1943 in another.

Lebanon declared independence during the Second World War and French troops left in 1946. Israel occupied the south of Lebanon from 1982 to 2000. Civil records are kept locally, at district and municipality level.

regions.label: Israel: Coastal Plain, Galilee and Haifa
regions.sub: Tel Aviv-Yafo, Haifa, Netanya, Nazareth, Tiberias, Acre

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: the coast and Galilee within Ottoman Syria
eras.note: Syria passed to the Ottomans after Selim I defeated the Mamluks in 1516-1517 and was reorganised in 1517 as one eyalet named Şam. The Eyalet of Safed was created in 1660 and later renamed Sidon, then Beirut.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule over the Syrian provinces is dated 1831-1841; the Convention of Kütahya (1833) ceded them to Muhammad Ali.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Beirut and Syria vilayets, Jerusalem Mutasarrifate
eras.note: The vilayet law of 1864 created the vilayets of Syria, Aleppo and Beirut, and the Beirut Vilayet is dated 1888-1917. Ottoman population (nüfus) registers, begun in 1837, survive for Haifa, Acre, Safed, Tiberias, Nazareth and Jaffa; they are held by the Israel State Archives, which microfilmed them in 1969, and the 1905 census is the most complete.
British forces drove the Ottomans out of the Levant in 1917-1918 and the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration governed until July 1920.

A civil administration under a High Commissioner replaced military rule in July 1920; the League of Nations granted the Mandate in 1922 and Britain officially assumed control on 29 September 1923. The 1922 census counted 757,182 people in all of Mandatory Palestine. The Israel State Archives, founded in 1949, hold the government records from the Ottoman era to the end of the Mandate.

The Mandate expired at midnight on 14-15 May 1948 and Israel was declared. Armistice agreements followed in 1949 (Lebanon 23 March, Jordan 3 April). Towns on the ring's eastern edge, such as Qalqilya, were taken by Transjordan, which annexed the West Bank in 1950, and not by Israel.

regions.label: Israel: the Negev and Eilat
regions.sub: Beersheba, Dimona, Eilat, Mitzpe Ramon, Ofakim

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: southern Palestine within Ottoman Syria
eras.note: Syria was reorganised in 1517 as one eyalet named Şam after Selim I's victory over the Mamluks.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule over the Syrian provinces is dated 1831-1841.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Jerusalem Mutasarrifate and the Syria vilayet
eras.note: The Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem was created in 1872. The Ottoman nüfus registers, begun in 1837, cover towns such as Jerusalem, Hebron and Gaza; the originals were collected by Britain after the First World War and by Israel after 1948.
The British occupation began in 1917-1918 and the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration lasted until July 1920.
Mandatory Palestine ran from the 1922 grant (Britain assumed control on 29 September 1923) to 14-15 May 1948. Its government records are in the Israel State Archives.
The Israel-Egypt armistice agreement was signed on 24 February 1949, on Rhodes.

regions.label: Jordan: Transjordan, Amman and Aqaba
regions.sub: Amman, Zarqa, Irbid, Aqaba, Karak, Ma'an

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Transjordan within Ottoman Syria
eras.note: Syria was reorganised in 1517 as one eyalet named Şam after the Ottoman victory over the Mamluks.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule over the Syrian provinces is dated 1831-1841.
Most of Transjordan belonged to the Vilayet of Syria, mainly the Hauran and Ma'an sanjaks, with the districts of Ajlun, al-Balqa, al-Karak and Ma'an. A Mutasarrifate of Karak was created in 1895.
Abdullah reached Ma'an on 21 November 1920 and Amman on 2 March 1921, and was appointed emir on 1 April 1921.

eras.polity: Emirate of Transjordan under the British Mandate
eras.note: The emirate dates from 11 April 1921, when Abdullah formed his first government. Britain recognised an independent government in 1923 (dated 15 or 25 May) and the Anglo-Transjordan treaty was signed on 20 February 1928. Ma'an was announced as annexed to Transjordan after the 1924-25 Saudi conquest of the Hejaz.
Independence is dated 25 May 1946, when Abdullah was re-designated king, or 17 June 1946, when the treaty ratifications were exchanged and the mandate ended.
In April 1950, after annexing the West Bank, the state was renamed the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

regions.label: Syria: Damascus, Hauran and the Golan
regions.sub: Damascus, Daraa, Suwayda, Quneitra, Zabadani

eras.note: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and in 1517 Syria was reorganised as one eyalet named Şam. Aleppo was given a separate administration in 1534 and the Tripoli Eyalet in 1579.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule is dated 1831-1841, from the First Egyptian-Ottoman War to the end of the second.
The 1864 vilayet law created the Vilayet of Syria. The Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem (1872) and of Karak (1895) were later carved from its south. The first general Ottoman census ran from 1881 to 1893.

eras.polity: Occupied Enemy Territory Administration, then Arab Syria
eras.note: The Occupied Enemy Territory Administration succeeded Ottoman Syria in 1918. The Franco-Syrian War ended at the Battle of Maysaloun in July 1920 and Damascus fell on 24 July 1920.

eras.polity: French Mandate: State of Damascus, State of Syria, Jabal Druze
eras.note: The mandate was assigned at San Remo on 25 April 1920 and formally on 29 September 1923. The State of Damascus existed 1920-1925, the State of Syria was formally established on 1 January 1925 and the name Syrian Republic dates from 1930. The Jabal Druze State (Suwayda) was created on 24 October 1922 and incorporated into Syria in 1936.

eras.polity: Syria: independence, the United Arab Republic and the Ba'ath
eras.note: Independence is dated 17 April 1946. Union with Egypt as the United Arab Republic was announced on 1 February 1958 (merger 21 February); Syria seceded on 28 September 1961. The Ba'ath took power on 8 March 1963. Civil records are kept locally in Syria.

eras.polity: Syria: the Golan under Israeli control, the civil war
eras.note: Israel captured the Golan Heights in the 1967 war and annexed it in 1981. Hafez al-Assad took power on 13 November 1970 and the civil war began in 2011.

regions.label: Syria: the Coast, Homs and Hama
regions.sub: Latakia, Tartus, Homs, Hama, Idlib, Palmyra

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: eyalets of Tripoli, Aleppo and Damascus
eras.note: Aleppo was given a separate administration in 1534 (the same source also dates the two-eyalet split to 1549) and the Tripoli Eyalet was established in 1579.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule over the Syrian provinces is dated 1831-1841.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: vilayets of Aleppo, Beirut and Syria
eras.note: The 1864 vilayet law created the vilayets of Syria, Aleppo and Beirut, and the Beirut Vilayet (the coast) is dated 1888-1917.

Arrêté 319 of 31 August 1920 delimited the Alawite State (Latakia). It was made independent in December 1924, renamed the Independent Government of Latakia on 22 September 1930 and joined the Syrian Republic on 5 December 1936.
The Sanjak of Alexandretta (Hatay), just to the north, became a Turkish province in 1939 after a referendum, so records of Hatay families are Turkish after that year. French troops left in 1946.
Independence is dated 17 April 1946. Syria was joined to Egypt in the United Arab Republic from 1958 until 28 September 1961. The civil war began in 2011.

regions.label: Syria: Aleppo, the Euphrates and the Jazira
regions.sub: Aleppo, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor, Hasakah, Qamishli

eras.note: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq, near Aleppo, in 1516. Aleppo was given a separate administration in 1534; the same source also dates the split to 1549.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's occupation of Syria
eras.note: Egyptian rule over the Syrian provinces is dated 1831-1841.
The 1864 vilayet law created the Vilayet of Aleppo.
The State of Aleppo was created on 1 September 1920 (Arrêté 330) and was active until 1925.

eras.polity: French Mandate: State of Syria and Syrian Republic
eras.note: The State of Syria was formally established on 1 January 1925 and the Syrian Republic name dates from 1930. French troops left in 1946.
Independence is dated 17 April 1946. The union with Egypt as the United Arab Republic lasted from 1958 to 28 September 1961, and the civil war began in 2011.

regions.label: Iraq: Baghdad and the Middle Euphrates
regions.sub: Baghdad, Karbala, Najaf, Hillah, Samarra, Ramadi

eras.note: Suleiman I captured Baghdad in 1534, which began Ottoman rule.
The Safavids captured Baghdad in 1623 and the Ottomans retook it in 1638. The Treaty of Zuhab (1639) confirmed Ottoman sovereignty over Baghdad, Basra and Mosul.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Baghdad under Mamluk governors
eras.note: Georgian-origin Mamluk governors ruled semi-autonomously until 1831; the start of their rule is dated 1749 in one account and earlier in others. Basra came under Baghdad's control in 1705.

Direct Ottoman rule was restored in 1831; Namık Pasha took military command in 1851 and Midhat Pasha began reforms in 1869. The 1831 census counted only taxable men over 15 and the first general census ran from 1881 to 1893.

eras.polity: British occupation and the Mandate of Mesopotamia
eras.note: British forces entered Baghdad on 11 March 1917. The mandate was assigned at San Remo on 25 April 1920, the Iraqi Revolt followed that year, and Faisal I was crowned king on 23 August 1921.
Iraq became independent on 3 October 1932, under the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 30 June 1930.
The monarchy fell in the 14 July 1958 revolution.

regions.label: Iraq: Mosul and Kurdistan
regions.sub: Mosul, Erbil, Kirkuk, Duhok, Sinjar

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Mosul under the Treaty of Zuhab
eras.note: The Treaty of Zuhab (1639) confirmed Ottoman sovereignty over Baghdad, Basra and Mosul.
Mehmed Said Pasha was appointed governor of Mosul in 1834, subordinating it to Baghdad. Ankara published a collection of Ottoman documents on Mosul and Kirkuk dated 1525-1919.

eras.polity: British occupation of the Mosul vilayet
eras.note: The Armistice of Mudros was signed on 30 October 1918 and British troops entered Mosul unopposed on 14 November 1918 (another account says 10 November). The Sykes-Picot agreement of 1916 had allotted the vilayet to France, which gave up its claim on 1 December 1918.

eras.polity: Mosul vilayet allotted to Iraq under the Mandate
eras.note: The League of Nations decided on 16 December 1925 to allot the Mosul vilayet to Iraq; the frontier treaty with Turkey is the Treaty of Ankara of 5 June 1926. Oil was found at Kirkuk in 1927.
Iraq became independent on 3 October 1932.

eras.polity: Republic of Iraq: Kurdish autonomy and the Anfal
eras.note: A peace plan of March 1970 promised broader Kurdish autonomy. The Anfal campaign ran from 29 March 1987 to 23 April 1989.

After the 1991 uprising a UN safe haven was set up and Iraqi government forces withdrew in October 1991; parliamentary elections followed in June 1992. The 2005 constitution recognised the Kurdistan Region (Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Duhok). Kurdish forces seized Kirkuk in 2014 and the Iraqi government retook it in October 2017; its status is disputed.

regions.label: Iraq: Basra and the Southern Marshes
regions.sub: Basra, Nasiriyah, Amarah, Umm Qasr, Az Zubayr

eras.note: The Treaty of Zuhab (1639) confirmed Ottoman sovereignty over Basra. Basra came under Baghdad's control in 1705. The Treaty of Erzurum (1847) made Muhammara (Khorramshahr), across the Shatt al-Arab, Persian territory.
The Basra Vilayet existed by 1875, when Kuwait was included in it.
Naval bombardment of Fao began on 6 November 1914 and the British occupied Basra on 22 November 1914. The Armistice of Mudros followed on 30 October 1918.
The mandate was assigned at San Remo on 25 April 1920 and Faisal I was crowned king on 23 August 1921.
Iraq became independent on 3 October 1932.
The monarchy fell in the 14 July 1958 revolution.

regions.label: Kuwait
regions.sub: Kuwait City, Al Ahmadi, Hawalli, Al Jahra, Al Farwaniyah

eras.polity: Sheikhdom of Kuwait: the Al Sabah
eras.note: Sabah I bin Jaber was chosen as ruler of Kuwait, usually dated about 1752. The Bani Utub had settled in Kuwait in the mid-1700s.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Kuwait in the Basra Vilayet
eras.note: Kuwait was under Ottoman administration from 1871 and was included in the Basra Vilayet in 1875. Mubarak was recognised as Ottoman qaimmaqam in 1897.

eras.polity: Anglo-Kuwaiti agreement and the Ottoman claim
eras.note: In January 1899 Mubarak agreed not to cede territory or receive foreign representatives without British consent. The Anglo-Ottoman Convention of 1913 defined Kuwait as an autonomous Ottoman kaza.

In 1914 Britain recognised Kuwait as an independent government under British protection. The Uqair Protocol of 1922 set Kuwait's boundaries and Kuwait lost about two-thirds of its territory to Najd; a Saudi trade blockade ran 1923-1937.
Kuwait became independent in June 1961.
Iraq invaded on 2 August 1990 and annexed Kuwait on 8 August. The coalition ground assault of 23 February 1991 removed Iraqi forces within four days.
Kuwait's independence of 1961 was restored when Iraqi forces were removed in February 1991.

regions.label: Bahrain
regions.sub: Manama, Muharraq, Riffa, Isa Town, Sitra

eras.note: The Portuguese conquered Bahrain in 1521 and held it until a 1602 uprising drove them out.
The Safavids took control after the Portuguese departure and held Bahrain until Oman invaded in 1717.
Nader Shah's forces retook the islands in 1736 and the Al Madhkur family later ruled on behalf of Persia.
Ahmed Al Fateh and the Bani Utbah took control in 1783 and are the origin of Al Khalifa rule. The General Maritime Treaty of 1820 recognised the Al Khalifa as rulers.
Agreements of 1861, 1868, 1880 and 1892 established British protection. Oil was discovered in 1932.
The British protectorate ended in 1971.

regions.label: Qatar
regions.sub: Doha, Al Rayyan, Al Wakrah, Al Khor, Dukhan

eras.note: The Al Khalifa claimed Qatar and Bahrain by 1783. Qatar had no centralised authority and Doha developed around the settlement of Al Bidda.
Colonel Lewis Pelly's settlement after the Qatari-Bahraini War recognised that Qatar was distinct from Bahrain.

The Ottomans expanded into Eastern Arabia in 1871 and incorporated Qatar by January 1872. Qatari forces defeated an Ottoman column at Al Wajbah in 1893; the Ottomans renounced sovereignty in 1913 and withdrew in 1915.
Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani signed a treaty with Britain in 1916 that placed Qatar under the trucial system.
Qatar declared independence on 3 September 1971.

regions.label: Saudi Arabia: Al-Hasa and the Eastern Province
regions.sub: Dammam, Hofuf, Jubail, Qatif, Khobar, Dhahran

eras.note: The Ottomans invaded in 1551 (the beglerbegilik is dated 1552 and the eyalet 1560) and held the region until 1670 or 1671. Qatif, one of its main cities, was raided by the Portuguese in 1552, 1559 and 1573.
The Al-Humaid section of the Banu Khalid defeated the Ottoman garrison at al-Ahsa in 1669-1670 and the Bani Khalid Emirate was set up in 1670.
The Ottomans expanded into Eastern Arabia in 1871, and the region was the Najd Sanjak of the Empire when Ibn Saud took it.
Ibn Saud took al-Hasa on 4-6 May 1913 and integrated Qatif; the territory became part of the Emirate of Nejd and Hasa.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia: Eastern Province
eras.note: The Kingdom was proclaimed on 23 September 1932. The Dawasir of Bahrain moved to the site of Khobar in 1923, and Dammam No. 7 was the first well to produce oil in commercial quantity.

regions.label: Saudi Arabia: the Hejaz
regions.sub: Jeddah, Mecca, Medina, Taif, Yanbu, Tabuk

eras.note: The Hejaz came under Ottoman rule after Selim I took Egypt in 1517, and the sultan took the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. The Sharif of Mecca was appointed by the sultans.

eras.polity: First Saudi State in the Hejaz
eras.note: The Wahhabis captured the holy cities in 1801 (another source dates the Saudi conquest of the Hejaz from 1803). Muhammad Ali's forces retook Medina in 1812 and Mecca in 1813.

eras.polity: Egypt: Muhammad Ali's administration of the Hejaz
eras.note: Egypt administered the region from 1818 (its forces held the holy cities from 1812-1813) until Muhammad Ali was forced to return the Hejaz to the sultan in 1845.
The Hejaz was reorganised as a vilayet in 1872 under the 1864 law; the Hejaz Railway to Medina was completed in 1908 and Medina became an independent sanjak in 1910.

Hussein bin Ali declared himself king on 10 June 1916 and abdicated on 3 October 1924, with Jeddah the capital in 1924-1925. The conquest by Nejd is dated 19 December 1925 or 23 December 1925, when Hussein's successor surrendered.
Ibn Saud was crowned King of Hejaz on 8 January 1926. From 1927 to 1932 Nejd and Hejaz were administered as separate units.
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was proclaimed on 23 September 1932.

regions.label: Saudi Arabia: Najd, Riyadh, Qassim and Ha'il
regions.sub: Riyadh, Buraydah, Unaizah, Ha'il, Al Kharj, Diriyah

eras.note: Muhammad bin Saud and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab made their pact in 1744; Muhammad bin Saud had led Diriyah since 1727. Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian forces took Diriyah in 1818.
Ottoman-aligned Egyptian forces took Diriyah in 1818; the Second Saudi State began in 1824 when Turki ibn Abdallah captured Riyadh.

eras.polity: Emirate of Nejd (Second Saudi State) and the Rashidi emirate of Ha'il
eras.note: Ibn Rashid became governor of Ha'il in 1836 as a vassal of the Second Saudi State. The Rashidis occupied Riyadh in 1865 and ended the Second Saudi State at the battle of Mulayda in 1891.
After Mulayda the Saudi territory was incorporated into Jabal Shammar, whose rulers were allied with the Ottoman Empire. The Saudi leader Abdul Rahman bin Faisal fled into exile in 1893.

eras.polity: Third Saudi State and the Rashidi emirate
eras.note: Ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh on 13 January 1902. Ha'il was conquered on 2 November 1921 (3 November in some accounts), ending the Rashidi emirate.

eras.polity: Sultanate of Nejd, then Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd
eras.note: Ha'il was incorporated into the Sultanate of Nejd after 1921. In 1926 Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of Hejaz and the realm was called the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd.
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was proclaimed on 23 September 1932.

regions.label: Saudi Arabia: Asir, Najran and Jizan
regions.sub: Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jizan, Najran, Bisha, Al Bahah

eras.note: Ottoman forces destroyed the First Saudi State in 1818, and the people of Asir continued to resist Ottoman Egypt's forces in the region.

eras.polity: Al-Ayedh rulers of the Asir highlands
eras.note: The Ottomans withdrew in 1840 and the Al-Ayedh dynasty took control of the Asir highlands.

eras.polity: Ottoman Empire: Abha sub-governorate in the Yemen Vilayet
eras.note: The Ottomans defeated and executed the Al-Ayedh leader in 1872 and set up a sub-governorate at Abha attached to the Yemen vilayet. Their control rarely extended beyond their forts.

Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi began establishing control about 1906; Hashemite forces under Hussein bin Ali defeated the Idrisis in 1911 and a secret alliance with Britain followed in 1915. He died in 1920, the year Ibn Saud's forces took Abha.
The Saudis incorporated the rest of Asir in 1923. In the Saudi-Yemeni War of 20 March to 14 June 1934 Saudi forces repelled a Yemeni claim, and the war ended Yemeni claims to Asir, Najran and Jazan.
Asir became a separate governorate in 1935.

regions.label: Saudi Arabia: the Jawf and the Northern Frontier
regions.sub: Arar, Sakaka, Qurayyat, Turaif, Dumat al-Jandal

eras.polity: Tribal territory before the Rashidi emirate
eras.note: The Rashidi emirate of Ha'il was founded in 1836; before that the northern frontier was tribal territory.

eras.polity: Rashidi Emirate of Ha'il and its dependencies
eras.note: The Rashidi emirate was founded at Ha'il in 1836 and its rulers allied with the Ottoman Empire. It lasted until its conquest on 2 November 1921.
Ha'il was incorporated into the Sultanate of Nejd after 1921. The conquest of al-Jawf and Wadi as-Sirhan followed, dated 1921 or 1922 depending on the account.
Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of Hejaz in 1926 and the realm was called the Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd.
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia was proclaimed on 23 September 1932.

regions.label: United Arab Emirates and the Trucial Coast
regions.sub: Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah, Al Ain, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah

eras.note: The General Maritime Treaty was signed on 8 January 1820 with the coastal sheikhdoms after British campaigns against the Qasimi ports.
The Perpetual Maritime Truce was signed on 4 May 1853.

eras.polity: Trucial States under the Exclusive Agreement
eras.note: On 6-8 March 1892 the rulers of Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Ras Al Khaimah and Umm Al Quwain signed the Exclusive Agreement, which placed them under British protection.
The Trucial States Council was established on 21 March 1952 and Fujairah was recognised as a Trucial State.

The treaties were revoked on 1 December 1971 and six emirates formed the UAE on 2 December 1971; Ras Al Khaimah joined on 10 February 1972. Khasab (Musandam) and Al Buraimi fall inside this ring but are in Oman today.

regions.label: Oman: Muscat, the Batinah and the Interior
regions.sub: Muscat, Seeb, Sohar, Nizwa, Sur, Salalah road

eras.note: Portugal took Muscat on 1 April 1515 and held it until 26 January 1650; a Portuguese presence on the north-eastern coast dates from 1508.
The Yarubid Imamate dates from 1624, and the Yarubids recaptured Muscat from the Portuguese in 1650.

Ahmad bin Said defeated Bal'arab in 1744 and was elected sultan of Muscat and imam of Oman. After Said bin Sultan died in 1856, Britain mediated a division in 1861 into the Sultanate of Zanzibar and Muscat and Oman.
The Treaty of Seeb gave the Ibadi imam rule of the interior; the Jebel Akhdar War ran from 1954 to 1959.
Said bin Taimur was ousted in a coup that brought Qaboos to power on 23 July 1970, and the name changed from Muscat and Oman to the Sultanate of Oman that year.

regions.label: Oman: Dhofar
regions.sub: Salalah, Thumrait, Mirbat, Taqah

eras.note: Local sheikhs held Dhofar until they expelled Sayyid Fadhl bin Alawi in January 1879.

Local sheikhs expelled Sayyid Fadhl bin Alawi, who had claimed to rule Dhofar, in January 1879. A 1943 account has the Sultan of Muscat administering Dhofar as a private estate with a separate treasury.
A separatist revolt began in 1964 (another dating of the Omani civil war is 1963-1976).

eras.polity: Sultanate of Oman: end of the Dhofar war
eras.note: The campaign was declared over in December 1975.
Salalah is the capital and largest city of Dhofar.

regions.label: Yemen: the Highlands and Tihama
regions.sub: Sana'a, Taiz, Hodeidah, Ibb, Dhamar, Sa'dah

eras.note: The Ottomans conquered Yemen in 1538. The Qasimid state rose in 1597 and expelled the Ottomans in 1635.
Zaydi imams ruled the highlands after the Ottoman withdrawal of 1635.
The Ottomans returned in 1872 and organised the Vilayet of Yemen.
Imam Yahya took power in 1918 as the Ottoman Empire collapsed. In the Saudi-Yemeni War of 1934 Yemen lost its claims to Asir, Najran and Jazan.
The Yemen Arab Republic replaced the imamate in 1962.
North and South Yemen were unified on 22 May 1990.

regions.label: Yemen: Aden, Lahej and the South
regions.sub: Aden, Mukalla, Seiyun, Lahej, Mukayras, Ataq

eras.note: The Abdali sultans of Lahej took Aden from the Zaydi imams, dated 1728 or 1731 depending on the account.
The British captured Aden on 19 January 1839.

eras.polity: British Crown Colony of Aden and the Federation of South Arabia
eras.note: Aden became a Crown Colony in 1937. The Federation of South Arabia was formed in 1962-1963.
Independence was declared on 30 November 1967.
South Yemen merged with the north on 22 May 1990.

regions.label: Cyprus
regions.sub: Nicosia, Limassol, Larnaca, Paphos, Famagusta, Kyrenia

eras.polity: Kingdom of Cyprus under the Lusignans
eras.note: Guy de Lusignan acquired the island in 1192 after Richard I sold it to the Knights Templar, who gave it up.
Venice took the island in 1489 after Catherine Cornaro ceded it.
The Ottoman-Venetian War of 1570-1573 brought the island under Ottoman rule. The Orthodox Church was recognised as the leader of the Greek Cypriot community under the millet system.
Britain took over administration under the Cyprus Convention of 1878.
Britain annexed the island in 1914 and it became a Crown Colony in 1925. The EOKA campaign ran from 1955 to 1959.
Cyprus became independent in 1960 and a UN peacekeeping force arrived in 1964.

eras.polity: Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish-held north
eras.note: A coup was followed by the Turkish invasion in 1974, and the island has been divided since. The Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus declared in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey. Cyprus joined the EU in 2004.

regions.label: Iran: Khorramshahr and Muhammara
regions.sub: Khorramshahr, Abadan, Shadegan

eras.polity: Sheikhdom of Muhammara, claimed by Persia and by the Ottomans
eras.note: Persian and Ottoman authorities each claimed the district around Muhammara.
The Treaty of Erzurum (Article II) of 1847 recognised the city as Persian territory.

eras.polity: Iran: Khorramshahr in the Iran-Iraq War
eras.note: The population was 146,706 in the 1976 census and 0 in the 1986 census, after the city was fought over in the Iran-Iraq War.
The 1991 census recorded 34,750 people.
The population was 123,866 in 2006 and 133,097 in 2016.

regions.label: Iran: Sistan and Zabol
regions.sub: Zabol, Zahedan, Zahak, Hamun lakes

eras.note: The Safavids deposed the Mihrabanid dynasty in 1537; Uzbek rule is dated 1524-1528 and 1578-1598.
Nader Shah reconquered Sistan in 1727.

eras.polity: Durrani Empire and Persia: contested Sistan
eras.note: Persia and Afghanistan contested Sistan from 1747 to 1872.

eras.polity: Persia: Sistan after the Goldsmid arbitration
eras.note: The Goldsmid arbitration of 1872 divided Sistan between Persia and Afghanistan.

eras.polity: Persia and Iran: Sistan and Baluchestan
eras.note: The McMahon arbitration of 1903-1905 fixed the border again. Persia's share became the province of Baluchistan, later Sistan and Baluchestan in 1986, with Zahedan as capital.

regions.label: Iran: Salmas, Maku and Khoy
regions.sub: Khoy, Salmas, Maku, Urmia, Piranshahr, Mahabad

eras.note: The siege of Dimdim lasted 1609-1610.
The Ottomans seized the region after the fall of Safavid power.
Maku, Khoy, Salmas, Arasbaran and Urmia lay in the northwestern province of Azerbaijan in the 19th century. The Kurdish rising of Ubeidullah was in 1880.
Russian troops occupied the area in 1909, 1912-1914 and 1915-1918; Ottoman forces held it in 1914-1915 and 1918-1919. Simko's insurrections ran from 1918 to 1922.

eras.polity: Iran: Shomal-e Gharb and the Mahabad period
eras.note: The province was renamed Shomal-e Gharb in 1937 and later split. Soviet forces entered in 1941, and the Republic of Mahabad existed from November 1945 to November 1946.
West Azerbaijan was formed in 1961; Kurdish fighting began in 1979.

regions.label: Iran: Parsabad, Moghan and Astara
regions.sub: Parsabad, Bilasuvar border, Astara, Ardabil

eras.note: Ismail I proclaimed Tabriz his capital in 1500.

eras.polity: Treaty of Gulistan: Talysh Khanate ceded to Russia
eras.note: Part of the Talysh Khanate and the Lenkoran fortress passed to Russia by the Treaty of Gulistan, dated 14 or 24 October 1813.

eras.polity: Persia and Iran: border along the Araxes
eras.note: The Treaty of Turkmenchay set the border along the Araxes.

eras.polity: Iran: Azerbaijan independent across the Aras
eras.note: Azerbaijan became independent across the Aras in 1991.
Ardabil Province was established in 1993.

regions.label: Lagos and Yorubaland (south-west Nigeria)
regions.sub: Lagos, Ibadan, Abeokuta, Ijebu Ode, Ogbomoso, Osogbo, Akure

eras.polity: Oyo Empire and the Yoruba kingdoms
eras.note: Before registers. Oyo is dated to about 1300, which is an estimate; the dynasty was in exile in Borgu after the Nupe sack of Oyo-Ile about 1535 and the empire was re-established about 1608. Afonja seceded Ilorin in 1817 and Ilorin destroyed Oyo-Ile in 1835.

eras.polity: Yoruba successor states: Ibadan, Ago d'Oyo and their neighbours
eras.note: The Oyo capital moved south to Ago d'Oyo after 1835. Ibadan had been settled in 1830 as a war camp by Oyo commanders.

Lagos was annexed on 6 August 1861 and declared a colony in March 1862. It was merged with Sierra Leone in 1866, transferred to the Gold Coast in 1874 and made a separate colony again in 1886. Protectorate agreements followed at Ilaro (1891), Oyo (1893) and Ibadan (1893). Birth registration was first attempted in the colony by Ordinance No. 21 of 1863; actual registration began in 1892.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Southern Nigeria: Western Province
eras.note: Lagos Colony was merged with the Southern Nigeria Protectorate on 28 February 1906; the former colony became the Western Province and Lagos the administrative centre.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria: Lagos and the Western Provinces
eras.note: Lagos became the capital of the amalgamated Protectorate of Nigeria in January 1914. The Western Region was created in 1954 with Ibadan as its capital. Colonial registration was uneven: a 1917 law widened it and the 1948 Births, Deaths and Burial Ordinance consolidated it, mainly for townships.

eras.polity: Nigeria: Western Region, then Western and Lagos states
eras.note: The Mid-Western Region was cut from the Western Region on 9 August 1963; on 27 May 1967 the remainder was split into Western State and Lagos State. The National Archives zonal office for the west is at the University of Ibadan (established 1958). A nationwide civil registration system began with a decree effective 1 September 1979, and a 1992 decree gave the National Population Commission sole authority. The federal capital moved from Lagos to Abuja on 12 December 1991.

regions.label: Benin, Warri and the Niger Delta
regions.sub: Benin City, Warri, Sapele, Asaba, Port Harcourt, Yenagoa

eras.note: Before registers. The Oba monarchy replaced the Ogiso monarchy about 1180; Oba Ewuare came to power in 1440 and expanded the kingdom's borders.

eras.polity: Benin, Warri and the Delta ports
eras.note: Portuguese explorers reached Benin in 1485. The Oba was said to rule Delta peoples including the Western Igbo, Ijaw, Itsekiri, Isoko and Urhobo. Portuguese missionaries brought Christianity to the Kingdom of Warri in the fifteenth century, and Delta ports such as Bonny took part in the transatlantic slave trade after 1480.

eras.polity: Oil Rivers (Niger Coast) Protectorate and the Royal Niger Company
eras.note: The Oil Rivers Protectorate was set up in 1884, confirmed at Berlin in 1885 and renamed the Niger Coast Protectorate on 12 May 1893, with Old Calabar as capital. The Royal Niger Company held its charter from July 1886 along the lower Niger. A British expedition captured Benin City in 1897 and the kingdom was absorbed into the Niger Coast Protectorate.

The Niger Coast Protectorate and the Royal Niger Company territory below Lokoja were joined on 1 January 1900 as the Southern Nigeria Protectorate. Warri was the capital of the Central Province. Birth registration was extended to Warri in 1903.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria: Benin and Warri provinces, and the Delta in the east
eras.note: The railway terminus opened at Port Harcourt in 1916. Benin and Warri lay in the Western Region from 1954; the Delta east of the Niger lay in the Eastern Region, created on 1 October 1954.

eras.polity: Nigeria: Mid-Western Region, then Edo, Delta and Rivers
eras.note: Benin and Warri provinces were separated from the Western Region on 9 August 1963 to form the Mid-Western Region, with its capital at Benin City. In 1967 the Eastern Region was divided into East-Central, Rivers and South-Eastern states.

regions.label: Igboland (south-east Nigeria)
regions.sub: Onitsha, Enugu, Owerri, Aba, Awka, Umuahia, Nnewi, Abakaliki

eras.polity: Igbo communities and the Atlantic coast trade
eras.note: Before registers. The Kingdom of Nri is named among Nigeria's early states; the coastal ports took part in the transatlantic slave trade after 1480.

eras.polity: Niger Coast Protectorate and the Royal Niger Company
eras.note: The Niger Coast Protectorate, capital Old Calabar, was set up to regulate the palm oil trade and extended in theory inland as far as Lokoja. The Royal Niger Company traded along the Niger under its 1886 charter.
Calabar was the capital of the Eastern Province. Birth registration reached Calabar in 1904.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria: Eastern Provinces
eras.note: The Eastern Region was created on 1 October 1954 with Enugu as its first capital. The National Archives zonal office for the east is at Enugu (established 1958).

Biafra was declared on 30 May 1967 (27 May in another account) over the former Eastern Region and ended on 15 January 1970. Its capital was Enugu in 1967, Umuahia from 1967 to 1969, Owerri in 1969-1970, and Awka in 1970.

eras.polity: Nigeria: East-Central State and its successors
eras.note: The Eastern Region had been divided in 1967 into East-Central, Rivers and South-Eastern states. Enugu, the East-Central capital, is now in Enugu State.

regions.label: Calabar and the Cross River
regions.sub: Calabar, Uyo, Ikot Ekpene, Oron, Ikom, Ugep

eras.polity: Efik of Duke Town and Old Calabar
eras.note: Before registers. Duke Town is believed to have been founded about 1650; by the early eighteenth century the Efik were a power on the Bight of Biafra coast.

eras.polity: Efik kingdoms of Duke Town and Creek Town
eras.note: Britain outlawed its slave trade in 1807 and Spanish traders kept buying at Calabar until 1841. The United Presbyterian Church founded a mission between Duke Town and Henshaw Town in 1846, with King Eyo's support.

eras.polity: Niger Coast Protectorate (Old Calabar its headquarters)
eras.note: The chiefs of Akwa Akpa placed themselves under British protection in 1884. Old Calabar was the headquarters of the Niger Coast Protectorate from 1884 to 1906.

eras.polity: Southern Nigeria Protectorate: Eastern Province (Calabar capital)
eras.note: Calabar was the capital of the Eastern Province. Birth registration was extended to Calabar in 1904.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria: Calabar and the Eastern Provinces
eras.note: The railway terminus opened at Port Harcourt in 1916 and Calabar's role as a major port declined. The Eastern Region was created on 1 October 1954.

eras.polity: Nigeria: Eastern Region, then South-Eastern State and its successors
eras.note: The Eastern Region was divided in 1967 into East-Central, Rivers and South-Eastern states.

regions.label: Ilorin, Nupe and the lower Niger
regions.sub: Ilorin, Bida, Minna, Kontagora, Okene, Lafiagi

eras.polity: Nupe, Borgu and the northern frontier of Oyo
eras.note: Before registers. Nupe forces sacked Oyo-Ile about 1535; Oyo's campaigns against Borgu in 1783 and against Nupe in 1789 failed. Afonja seceded Ilorin in 1817.

eras.polity: Emirates of Ilorin and Nupe (Sokoto Caliphate)
eras.note: Ilorin joined the Sokoto Caliphate in 1823 as an emirate under the authority of Gwandu; the sources date its first emir's rule from 1824. Nupe (Bida) was one of the caliphate's named emirates.

eras.polity: Royal Niger Company sphere along the Niger
eras.note: The Royal Niger Company held a charter from July 1886 and had about 30 trading posts along the lower Niger and at the Niger-Benue confluence in the mid-1880s; its precise boundaries are not given. Its charter was revoked in 1899 and its territories passed to the Crown on 1 January 1900.

Northern Nigeria was proclaimed on 1 January 1900 with its capital at Lokoja; headquarters moved to Zungeru in 1902. Ilorin was brought under the protectorate by diplomacy and minimal force; the date is uncertain.

eras.polity: Northern Province of the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria
eras.note: On 1 January 1914 the protectorate became the Northern Province of Nigeria. The National Archives zonal office for the north is at Kaduna.

regions.label: Abuja, the Jos Plateau and the Benue valley
regions.sub: Abuja, Jos, Makurdi, Lafia, Keffi, Gboko, Otukpo

eras.polity: Southern frontier of the Sokoto Caliphate
eras.note: Zazzau (Zaria), Bauchi and Nupe (Bida) are among the named emirates of the caliphate; which of the plateau and Benue peoples lay inside it is not set out in the sources.
The protectorate was proclaimed on 1 January 1900; its headquarters were at Lokoja, and from 1902 at Zungeru.

eras.polity: Northern Province of the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria
