eras.note: In the early twentieth century the name Abuja belonged to the town now called Suleja. The National Archives zonal office for the north is at Kaduna.

eras.polity: Nigeria; the federal capital planned at Abuja
eras.note: Decree No. 6 of 4 February 1976 began the move of the federal capital from Lagos to Abuja. Construction began in 1979 and Abuja was incorporated on 1 October 1984.

eras.polity: Nigeria: Federal Capital Territory and the Middle Belt states
eras.note: Abuja was declared the capital on 12 December 1991, replacing Lagos.

regions.label: Bauchi, Gombe and Adamawa
regions.sub: Bauchi, Gombe, Yola, Jalingo, Mubi, Wukari

eras.polity: Adamawa (Fombina), Bauchi and Gombe emirates of the Sokoto Caliphate
eras.note: Usman dan Fodio appointed Modibbo Adama leader in Fombina in March 1809 (another dating gives 1807). The emirate was a vassal of Sokoto, with capitals at Gurin, Ribadu and Njoboliyo and from 1841 at Yola. Bauchi and Gombe were named flag-bearer emirates of the caliphate.
Treaties of 1893 and 1894 divided the emirate among Chad, the Central African Republic, Nigeria and Cameroon. Germany invaded southern Adamawa in January 1898.
British forces under Colonel Morland captured Yola on 2 September 1901; Bobbo Ahmadu was installed on 10 September under British protection, and in 1903 the emirate became a British native authority.

eras.polity: Northern Province of Nigeria; the Northern Cameroons on the eastern border
eras.note: Along the eastern border Britain also administered Northern Cameroons, under a League of Nations mandate from 1922 and a UN trusteeship approved on 6 December 1946. After the plebiscite of 11 February 1961 it joined Nigeria on 1 June 1961 as Sardauna Province.

regions.label: Sokoto, Kano, Katsina and Zaria
regions.sub: Sokoto, Kano, Kaduna, Katsina, Zaria, Gusau, Birnin Kebbi

eras.note: Before registers. Islam reached the north through Bornu and the Hausa kingdoms in the eleventh century.

Sultan Yunfa of Gobir declared war on Usman dan Fodio on 21 February 1804. Alkalawa fell on 3 October 1808 and Muhammed Bello founded Sokoto in 1809. Named emirates include Gwandu, Katsina, Kano, Daura and Zazzau (Zaria).

The caliphate was defeated at the Battle of Kano in 1903 and the British conquest was complete that year; accounts date the end at Burmi to June or 27 July 1903. Lugard abolished the caliphate but kept the title of sultan. The last major armed resistance was the Satiru rising of 1906.

eras.polity: Northern Province of the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria
eras.note: The Northern Nigeria Protectorate ended on 1 January 1914 and became the Northern Province of Nigeria. The National Archives zonal office for the north is at Kaduna.

regions.label: Borno and the Lake Chad basin
regions.sub: Maiduguri, Bama, Gashua, Potiskum, Biu, Gamboru

eras.note: Before registers. The Bilala ousted the Sayfawa from Kanem about 1380 and the centre moved to Bornu; Mai Ali I Gaji founded Ngazargamu about 1472. Fulani forces took it in 1808-1809.

eras.polity: Bornu under the Shehus of the al-Kanemi dynasty
eras.note: Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi took the title shehu in 1814. Kukawa became the formal capital in 1846, when the office of mai ended.
Rabih conquered Bornu in 1893. Sanda Kura was installed as shehu on 14 January 1900 and Rabih was killed at Kousséri on 22 April 1900.

eras.polity: Northern Nigeria Protectorate; Dikwa in German Kamerun
eras.note: British forces occupied much of Bornu in March 1902. French forces occupied Dikwa in April 1902; later that year it passed to German control as part of Kamerun, and the empire was divided among French, British and German colonies.

eras.polity: Northern Province of the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria
eras.note: Northern Cameroons, the northern part of the British mandate and trust territory, joined Nigeria on 1 June 1961 as Sardauna Province.

regions.label: South-West and North-West Cameroon (Southern Cameroons)
regions.sub: Buea, Limbe, Kumba, Tiko, Bamenda, Kumbo, Wum

eras.note: Before registers.
Gustav Nachtigal signed agreements with Duala leaders from 5 July 1884; the German protectorate is dated officially from 17 August 1884. The last German fort surrendered in February 1916.
British and French troops invaded in 1914. The partition is dated 20 July 1916 in one account; the mandates were formalised on 28 June 1919.

eras.polity: British Cameroons: Southern Cameroons (League of Nations mandate)
eras.note: The League of Nations granted Britain its mandate in 1922. The British territory was administered as two areas, Northern and Southern Cameroons.

eras.polity: British Cameroons: Southern Cameroons (UN trust territory)
eras.note: The United Nations approved the trusteeship on 6 December 1946. The plebiscite of 11 February 1961 offered no choice of independence; the Southern area voted to join Cameroon.

eras.polity: West Cameroon, a state of the Federal Republic of Cameroon
eras.note: The Foumban Conference of 16-21 July 1961 negotiated the union and the federal constitution was adopted on 14 August 1961; Southern Cameroons became West Cameroon on 1 October 1961. A referendum was held in 1972. Anglophone protests began in November 2016 and became armed conflict from September 2017.

regions.label: Douala, Yaoundé and southern Cameroon
regions.sub: Douala, Yaoundé, Édéa, Kribi, Ebolowa, Nkongsamba, Mbalmayo

eras.note: Before registers.
Nachtigal began signing agreements with Duala leaders on 5 July 1884 and the protectorate is dated officially from 17 August 1884. Jaunde (Yaoundé) is given as the colony's capital.
The last German fort surrendered in February 1916. Britain and France partitioned the colony, a partition dated 20 July 1916 in one account, and the mandates were formalised on 28 June 1919.

The League of Nations mandate dates from 1922. After the First World War French Cameroon was not joined to French Equatorial Africa but made an autonomous commissariat. In 1940 it rallied to Free France; Leclerc's troops captured Douala on 27 August.
The territory was a UN trust territory under French administration from 1946 to 1960, with internal autonomy from 1956.
French Cameroon became independent as the Republic of Cameroon on 1 January 1960.

regions.label: West Grassfields: Bamum and Bamileke country
regions.sub: Bafoussam, Foumban, Dschang, Bafang, Mbouda, Bangangté

eras.note: Before registers. The kingdom is dated to 1394, with Nchare Yen as its first ruler (1394-1418).

eras.polity: German Kamerun: the Bamum kingdom under Njoya
eras.note: Bamum became part of German Kamerun in 1884, and Njoya later placed his kingdom under German protection. Njoya reigned about 1883-1931 (1886-1933 in other dating). A school for teaching the Bamum script, which he invented, was built in 1910.
After Germany's colonies were divided in 1918, Bamum fell under French rule.
The French deposed Njoya in 1923 and banned his script; the Bamum monarchy is dated as ending in 1923.

regions.label: East Cameroon (Neukamerun)
regions.sub: Bertoua, Batouri, Yokadouma, Garoua Boulaï

eras.note: Before registers. Neukamerun was added to German Kamerun in 1911 under the settlement of the Agadir Crisis, the Treaty of Fez.
The colony covered about 495,000 square kilometres in 1910 and 790,000 in 1912; the 1912 figure includes Neukamerun.
French and British forces fully occupied Kamerun by February 1916.
French Cameroon was formed from the eastern part of German Kamerun and was not joined to French Equatorial Africa.

regions.label: Adamawa plateau (Fombina to Ngaoundéré)
regions.sub: Ngaoundéré, Meiganga, Tibati, Banyo, Ngaoundal

eras.note: Modibbo Adama's jihad in Fombina dates from 1809. Tibati was founded in 1818; Njobdi established Fulani rule in Ngaoundéré in 1835-1837. The emirate had over 42 sub-emirates.
Treaties of 1893 and 1894 divided the emirate between several colonies. Germany invaded southern Adamawa in January 1898 and held Tibati by 1901.
The partition of Kamerun between Britain and France is dated 1916 in one account and formalised on 28 June 1919.

regions.label: North and Far North Cameroon
regions.sub: Garoua, Maroua, Kousséri, Mokolo, Yagoua, Guider

eras.polity: Bornu, Baguirmi and the northern edge of the Adamawa emirate
eras.note: Before registers. Baguirmi surrendered to France in 1893, and the Adamawa emirate reached into northern Cameroon.
Rabih conquered Bornu in 1893. The decisive Battle of Kousséri was fought on 22 April 1900 and both Rabih and the French commander Lamy were killed.

eras.polity: German Kamerun: Dikwa and the northern districts
eras.note: Dikwa passed to German control as part of Kamerun in 1902 after French forces had occupied it in April.
The mandates were formalised on 28 June 1919.

regions.label: Southern Chad: Logone, Mayo-Kebbi and Chari
regions.sub: Moundou, Sarh, Doba, Bongor, Kélo, Pala

eras.polity: Baguirmi and the peoples of the southern savanna
eras.note: Before registers. Baguirmi adopted Islam under Abdullah IV (1568-1598) and surrendered to France in 1893.

The French first invaded in 1891. Chad fell under a governor-general at Brazzaville in 1905, and Ubangi-Shari-Chad was a combined territory from 11 February 1906. Federation in French Equatorial Africa dates from 15 January 1910.

eras.polity: Chad colony in French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: Chad became a separate colony under a lieutenant-governor at Fort-Lamy in 1920. The federation became a unitary entity in 1934. Chad was the first French colony to rejoin the Allies, on 26 August 1940. French Equatorial Africa papers are described in published inventories at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

eras.polity: Chad, overseas territory then autonomous republic
eras.note: After the September 1958 referendum the territories became autonomous within the French Community and the federation was dissolved.
Chad became independent on 11 August 1960. A tax revolt in Guéra on 2 September 1965 marked the start of the civil war. Oil exploitation at Doba began in June 2000.

regions.label: N'Djamena, Baguirmi and Kanem
regions.sub: N'Djamena, Bol, Mao, Massakory, Bokoro, Moussoro

eras.note: Before registers. Bulala invaders forced the Kanembu to move to Bornu about 1396. Baguirmi adopted Islam under Abdullah IV (1568-1598) and surrendered to France in 1893.

eras.polity: Rabih az-Zubayr's state and the French advance
eras.note: The French first invaded in 1891. Rabih conquered Bornu in 1893 and was killed at the Battle of Kousséri on 22 April 1900.
Chad fell under a governor-general at Brazzaville in 1905 and joined French Equatorial Africa on its creation on 15 January 1910.

Chad became a separate colony in 1920 with its governor at Fort-Lamy. Records of French Equatorial Africa are covered by inventories at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer, which opened in Aix as the Dépôt des Archives d'Outre-Mer in 1966.

eras.polity: Chad, overseas territory then autonomous republic
eras.note: Political parties were founded in 1947: the Chadian Progressive Party in February and the Chadian Democratic Union in November.
N'Djamena was taken in June 1982 and again in December 1990, and the Battle of N'Djamena was fought on 13 April 2006.

regions.label: Ouaddai, Guéra, Salamat and the north
regions.sub: Abéché, Am Timan, Goz Beida, Mongo, Faya-Largeau, Iriba

eras.note: Before registers. Wadai was established in the early sixteenth century and Abd al Karim founded an Islamic sultanate there in the 1630s.
Ouaddai lost its independence to France after a war from 1909 to 1912.

eras.polity: Chad colony in French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: Chad became a separate colony in 1920 and the federation a unitary entity in 1934.

eras.polity: Chad, overseas territory then autonomous republic

eras.note: FROLINAT was formed in Sudan in 1966. The International Court of Justice ruled on the Aouzou Strip in 1994.

regions.label: Bangui and western Central African Republic
regions.sub: Bangui, Bimbo, Berbérati, Bouar, Bossangoa, Paoua, Mbaïki

eras.polity: Peoples of the Ubangi and Sangha basins
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: French Congo: Bangi outpost and the Upper Ubangi
eras.note: French activity began in 1889 with the outpost of Bangi, later Bangui. The Upper Ubangi was folded back into French Congo on 10 December 1899.

Ubangi-Shari was established on 29 December 1903, merged with the Lake Chad territories as Ubangi-Shari-Chad on 11 February 1906 and joined French Equatorial Africa on 15 January 1910. It became a separate colony again on 12 April 1916. Bangui was the capital from 1906 to 1958.

eras.polity: Ubangi-Shari in unitary French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: The colony was folded back into French Equatorial Africa on 30 June 1934, became an overseas territory on 31 December 1937 and gained autonomy as the Central African Republic on 1 December 1958. Published inventories of French Equatorial Africa papers are at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer.
Independence came on 13 August 1960. The Central African Empire existed from 1976 to 1979.

regions.label: Eastern Central African Republic
regions.sub: Bambari, Bria, Bangassou, Alindao, Ndélé, Kouango

eras.polity: Peoples and sultanates of the upper Ubangi
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: French Congo: concession of the Upper Ubangi Sultanates
eras.note: In 1900 the Company of the Upper Ubangi Sultanates took over about 140,000 square kilometres as a concession.
The Kongo-Wara rebellion ran from 1928 to 1931.

eras.polity: Ubangi-Shari in unitary French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: The territory had autonomy as the Central African Republic from 1 December 1958.
Independence came on 13 August 1960.

regions.label: Pointe-Noire, Niari and the Loango coast
regions.sub: Pointe-Noire, Dolisie, Nkayi, Sibiti, Mossendjo

eras.note: Before registers. The Kingdoms of Loango and Kongo are listed as the predecessors of the French Congo.
The French Congo was formally established on 30 November 1882 and confirmed at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85. Concessions to some thirty French companies were planned for ivory, rubber and timber.
The colony was officially renamed Middle Congo in 1903.

eras.polity: Middle Congo in French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: The federation, created on 15 January 1910, was administered from Brazzaville. Published inventories for French Equatorial Africa are at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

regions.label: Brazzaville, the Cuvette and the Sangha
regions.sub: Brazzaville, Kinkala, Ouesso, Impfondo, Owando, Djambala

eras.note: Before registers.
The French Congo began at Brazzaville on 10 September 1880 as a protectorate over the Bateke, by a treaty with King Iloo I, and was formally established on 30 November 1882.
The colony was officially renamed Middle Congo in 1903.

eras.polity: Middle Congo; Brazzaville, capital of French Equatorial Africa
eras.note: The federation was created on 15 January 1910 and administered from Brazzaville. Most of it joined the Free French in August 1940. The territories voted in September 1958 to become autonomous within the French Community.
The federation's republics became fully independent in August 1960.

regions.label: Libreville, Estuaire and Woleu-Ntem
regions.sub: Libreville, Oyem, Bitam, Ntoum, Kango, Makokou

eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese navigators reached the Gabon estuary in 1472.
France established a protectorate over the coast through treaties with coastal chiefs in 1838 and 1841. Libreville was founded in 1849 near a mission station by people freed from a seized slave ship.
France occupied Gabon in 1885 but did not administer it until 1903. Gabon was formally added to the French Congo in 1891.
Gabon became one of the four territories of the federation in 1910. Most of the federation joined the Free French in August 1940, but Gabon stayed loyal to Vichy until November 1940.
Gabon became independent on 17 August 1960.

regions.label: Ogooué, Ngounié and southern Gabon
regions.sub: Port-Gentil, Lambaréné, Franceville, Mouila, Tchibanga, Koulamoutou

eras.polity: Orungu kingdom and the Ogooué peoples
eras.note: Before registers. Orungu rulers concentrated power at Sangatanga from the late eighteenth to the mid-nineteenth century.

eras.polity: French protectorate and the Fang migrations
eras.note: Fang groups arrived on the coast in the later nineteenth century and disrupted the coastal balance.
France occupied Gabon in 1885 but did not administer it until 1903.
The federation was created on 15 January 1910 and administered from Brazzaville.
Independence came on 17 August 1960.

regions.label: Río Muni (mainland Equatorial Guinea)
regions.sub: Bata, Ebebiyin, Evinayong, Mongomo, Añisoc

eras.note: Before registers.
A protectorate was established over Río Muni in 1885.
The Treaty of Paris in 1900 set the final boundaries and left Spain with Río Muni.
The territories on the Gulf of Guinea were administratively united as a single colony in 1926.
In 1959 the territory was reclassified and split into two provinces, Fernando Poo and Río Muni. A regime of autonomy followed a referendum in 1963.
Spain handed power to the new Republic on 12 October 1968.

regions.label: Bioko (Fernando Po)
regions.sub: Malabo, Luba, Rebola

eras.note: Before registers. The colony dates from the Treaty of El Pardo between Spain and Portugal in 1778.
The United Kingdom had a base on Bioko from 1827 to 1843 to combat the slave trade, and moved it to Sierra Leone after an agreement with Spain in 1843.

eras.polity: Spanish Territories on the Gulf of Guinea
eras.note: Spanish rule was restored in 1844. Captain Carlos Chacón was the first governor, in 1858.

eras.polity: Spanish Guinea; Province of Fernando Poo
eras.note: The territories were united as one colony in 1926 and split into two provinces in 1959. A regime of autonomy followed a referendum in 1963.
Spain handed power to the new Republic on 12 October 1968.

regions.label: São Tomé and Príncipe
regions.sub: São Tomé, Neves, Água Izé, Santo António

eras.polity: Uninhabited islands reached by the Portuguese
eras.note: Portuguese navigators arrived about 1469-1471 on the uninhabited islands; João de Santarém and Pero Escobar are credited with the discovery.

Álvaro Caminha founded the first successful settlement on São Tomé in 1493 as a crown grant, and Príncipe followed in 1500. The crown took direct control of São Tomé in 1522 and of Príncipe in 1573. Sugar worked by enslaved Africans made the islands Africa's leading sugar exporter in the mid-sixteenth century.
The Dutch occupied São Tomé for seven years from 1641 and destroyed over 70 sugar mills.
Coffee and cocoa became the main crops, grown on plantations called roças. Portugal officially abolished slavery in 1876.

Forced labour continued after abolition, and by 1908 the islands were the world's largest cocoa producer. The Batepá massacre of 1953 killed several hundred African labourers. São Tomé was the main base for the Biafran airlift of 1967-1970.

eras.polity: Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe
eras.note: Independence came on 12 July 1975. Democratic reforms in 1990-1991 legalised opposition parties.

regions.label: Cairo, the Nile Delta and Alexandria
regions.sub: Cairo, Alexandria, Giza, Tanta, Mansoura, Damietta

eras.polity: Ottoman Egypt - eyalet governed from Cairo
eras.note: Egypt became an Ottoman province in 1517 when the Mamluk sultanate fell; Mamluk beys held real power from 1631 and deposed at least 34 governors between 1688 and 1755. Catholic registers start with the Church of the Assumption in Cairo (1611), then Armenian Catholic (Cairo, 1736) and Greek Catholic (Cairo, 1774); Coptic Orthodox registers are requested from the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate in Cairo. The Cairo sharia-court registers of the period are reported to be preserved in the National Archives.
French forces under Napoleon invaded in 1798 (Battle of the Pyramids) and were expelled by Anglo-Ottoman forces in 1801.

eras.polity: Egypt under Muhammad Ali and his line (Ottoman wali, hereditary from the 1840-42 settlement)
eras.note: Muhammad Ali was named wali on 17 May 1805, and the Mamluk leaders were killed at the Cairo Citadel on 1 March 1811; hereditary rule for his descendants came with the settlement of 1840-42. Civil registration of births and deaths dates from 1839 but is sparse before 1907. Coptic Catholic registers (Cairo Patriarchate) start in 1821, Greek Catholic at Alexandria in 1837 and Armenian Catholic at Alexandria in 1845.
The ruler's title changed from pasha to khedive in 1867. Greek Catholic registers at Tanta start in 1877.

eras.polity: British occupation of Egypt - protectorate from 1914
eras.note: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 (Tel el-Kebir, September); in 1914 Egypt was declared a protectorate and the ruler became sultan, and Britain unilaterally declared Egyptian independence on 22 February 1922. Census returns exist for 1882, 1897, 1907 and 1917, and Chaldean Catholic registers at Alexandria start in 1885.
Kingdom from 1922 until the republic was proclaimed on 18 June 1953. Censuses fall in 1927, 1937 and 1947.

eras.polity: Republic of Egypt (United Arab Republic with Syria, 1958-61)
eras.note: Egypt formed the United Arab Republic with Syria in 1958; Syria seceded in 1961. Births and deaths are registered at local health units and marriages and divorces at Family Affairs Courts, with the central Department of Civil Status in the Ministry of Interior, Cairo.

regions.label: Suez Canal Zone and Sinai
regions.sub: Port Said, Ismailia, Suez, Arish

eras.polity: Ottoman Egypt - Sinai and the isthmus
eras.note: Sinai was incorporated into the Ottoman Empire with Egypt in 1517.
Ferdinand de Lesseps received concessions to build a canal from Sa'id Pasha in 1854 and 1856.

eras.polity: Khedivate of Egypt - Suez Canal Company works
eras.note: The Suez Canal Company was formed on 15 December 1858 and digging began at the future Port Said on 25 April 1859. Ismailia was founded in 1862 and the canal opened on 17 November 1869.

eras.polity: British-occupied Egypt - Sinai administered by Egypt from 1906
eras.note: Britain occupied Egypt in 1882. In 1906 the Ottoman government transferred the administration of Sinai to Egypt, and the British-imposed border from Rafah to Taba became Egypt's eastern border.

eras.polity: Kingdom and Republic of Egypt - British Canal Zone to 1956
eras.note: The 1936 Anglo-Egyptian Treaty kept British control of the canal; Egypt repudiated it in 1951, Britain agreed in October 1954 to remove its troops, and Nasser nationalised the canal on 26 July 1956. Israel occupied much of Sinai in the Suez crisis of 1956-57 and withdrew in March 1957.

Israel occupied the whole peninsula after the Six-Day War; the canal was closed from 5 June 1967 to 5 June 1975. Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in 1979 and the Israeli withdrawal ended in 1982.

eras.polity: Egypt - governorates of the canal and Sinai
eras.note: Taba was returned to Egypt in 1989 after an arbitration ruling.

regions.label: Middle and Upper Egypt, Nubia and the Red Sea coast
regions.sub: Fayyum, Minya, Asyut, Sohag, Luxor, Aswan, Hurghada

eras.note: The south formed part of the Ottoman province of Egypt from 1517, governed from Cairo.

eras.polity: Egypt under Muhammad Ali's line (khedivate from 1867)
eras.note: Muhammad Ali, wali from 1805, sent an army south in 1820-21 and conquered Sudan (1820-24). Civil registration of births and deaths dates from 1839 and is sparse before 1907.
Britain occupied Egypt in 1882 and declared a protectorate in 1914; independence was declared unilaterally on 22 February 1922.
The kingdom lasted from 1922 to the proclamation of the republic on 18 June 1953.
Parish and diocesan Christian registers are held locally; the Catholic Directory: Egypt lists addresses. Vital events are registered at local health units and Family Affairs Courts.

regions.label: Tripolitania
regions.sub: Tripoli, Misrata, Zliten, Al Khums, Zawiya, Gharyan

eras.note: The Ottomans took Tripoli in 1551; janissaries and deys later gained power in the province.

eras.polity: Karamanli dynasty of Tripoli (nominal Ottoman suzerainty)
eras.note: The Karamanli dynasty ruled largely independently from 1711 to 1835, including during the Barbary Wars with the United States.
The Ottomans reasserted control in 1835. Consular marriage documents, wills and death certificates from Tripoli, 1860-1940, created by the British consulate, are catalogued at FamilySearch.

Italy invaded in 1911 and the Ottomans gave up control in 1912; a short-lived Tripolitanian Republic formed in 1918. Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and Fezzan were unified as Italian Libya on 1 January 1934, divided into four provinces in 1937, and 20,000 Italian farmers were settled in 1938; the coastal regions were incorporated into metropolitan Italy on 9 January 1939.

Italian forces were pushed out in early 1943 (the end of Italian rule is also dated 13 May 1943), and Italy relinquished its claims in the Paris peace treaty, in force 10 February 1947. Libya became independent on 24 December 1951.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Libya under Idris I
eras.note: Libya became a monarchy under King Idris I on independence on 24 December 1951.

eras.polity: Libya - Gaddafi era, civil wars and rival governments
eras.note: Gaddafi seized power on 1 September 1969; protests began on 17 February 2011 and led to civil war. Rival governments and militias have fought since 2014. The Civil Registry Authority is in Tripoli and each municipality keeps a civil registration office; religious law courts also keep marriage and divorce records.

regions.label: Cyrenaica
regions.sub: Benghazi, Derna, Tobruk, Al Bayda, Ajdabiya, Kufra

eras.polity: Ottoman Libya - Senussi zawiyas in Cyrenaica
eras.note: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi founded the Senussi order in Mecca in 1837 and built the Zawiya Bayda in Cyrenaica in 1843. He moved the order to Jaghbub in 1855.
Cyrenaica became an Ottoman wilayah in 1879. The Senussi headquarters moved to Jof in the Kufra oases in 1894.

Italy invaded in 1911; Egypt ceded the Kufra and Jarabub districts on 6 December 1925 and Kufra was conquered in 1931. Omar Mukhtar was executed in 1931, resistance was put down in 1932, and the camps closed in September 1933; Cyrenaica was merged into Italian Libya on 1 January 1934.
British administration followed the Italian withdrawal in 1943.
Sayyid Idris declared Cyrenaica a Senussi emirate in 1949, with Benghazi as capital; Libya's independence was declared on 24 December 1951.
Cyrenaica was organised into provinces within the kingdom until 1963.

The 2011 civil war began in Cyrenaica, and the Cyrenaica Transitional Council declared the region autonomous in 2012. The Libyan National Army has controlled the east since 2017, and floods at Derna in September 2023 killed nearly 7,000 people.

regions.label: Fezzan
regions.sub: Sabha, Murzuk, Ubari, Ghat

eras.note: Before registers. The Awlad Muhammad dynasty was founded in the early 16th century with Murzuk as its capital.
Ottoman Tripolitania invaded and occupied Fezzan in 1574, and its rulers gave allegiance to the Ottoman sultan in the 1580s. Between 1876 and 1909 Fezzan was a place of exile for Young Turks.
Italy began occupying Fezzan in 1911, and its control stayed precarious until at least 1923. Fezzan became one of Libya's three provinces on 1 January 1934.
Free French troops occupied Murzuk on 16 January 1943; French military control ended in 1951.
Fezzan became part of the Kingdom of Libya in 1951.
Anti-Gaddafi forces took Sabha in mid-to-late September 2011.

regions.label: Tunisia
regions.sub: Tunis, Sfax, Sousse, Kairouan, Bizerte, Gabes, Djerba

eras.note: Before registers. The Hafsid dynasty ruled Tunis from 1229 to 1574.
The Ottomans conquered Tunis in 1574, ending Hafsid rule.

eras.polity: Husainid Beylik of Tunis (autonomous Ottoman province)
eras.note: The Husainid dynasty ruled from 1705 to 1881. About 15,000 Europeans, mostly Italians and Maltese, lived in Tunisia in 1870.

The Treaty of Bardo of 12 May 1881 began the protectorate, formalised by the Conventions of La Marsa in 1883, and the bey stayed nominal head of state. Civil registration is dated from 1881, and a beylical decree of 28 December 1908 regulated civil status for Tunisians but is said not to have been applied across the board; records are at the National Archives in Tunis and the Archives nationales d'outre-mer. Germany occupied Tunisia in 1942, the Axis was forced out in 1943, and Moncef Bey was deposed on 13 May 1943.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Tunisia under the last bey
eras.note: The protectorate was abolished and independence recognised on 20 March 1956.
The republic was established on 25 July 1957. A law dated 1 August 1957 reorganised Tunisian civil status and made declaration of births and deaths compulsory.

regions.label: Algiers, Kabylie and the central Tell
regions.sub: Algiers, Blida, Tizi Ouzou, Medea, Bouira, Djelfa

eras.polity: Regency of Algiers (Ottoman province, de facto independent)
eras.note: Aruj and Hayreddin Barbarossa captured Algiers in 1516, Hayreddin pledged allegiance to the Ottoman government in 1519, and Algiers became an eyalet in 1521. After a janissary revolt in 1659 the Regency became a military republic ruled by an elected diwan. Algiers registers from 1807 are catalogued at FamilySearch.

eras.polity: French conquest - occupied Algiers annexed as a colony (1834)
eras.note: French forces landed at Sidi Ferruch on 14 June 1830 and Algiers surrendered on 5 July; the occupied areas were annexed as a colony in 1834. European civil status registers were kept in two copies from 1830 to 1962.

The 1848 constitution made Algeria departments of France. The law of 23 March 1882 set up a civil status for Muslims by requiring a family name for every Algerian, but it is described as widely applied in northern Algeria only from 1894. Famine and cholera in 1866-68 killed an estimated 300,000 to 500,000 people.

The Algerian War ran from 1954 to 1962 and the Evian Accords were signed in March 1962. The European registers for 1830-1962 are held by ANOM (index 1830-1904); acts concerning Algerians were concealed when the registers were microfilmed in 1967-72, and registers under 100 years old are kept in Nantes.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962; the European registers stayed in Algeria and the National Archives at Birkhadem is the contact for them.

regions.label: Oranie - Oran, Tlemcen and Sidi Bel Abbes
regions.sub: Oran, Tlemcen, Sidi Bel Abbes, Mostaganem, Mascara, Saida

eras.note: Spain captured the city of Oran on 17 May 1509; the Regency of Algiers, founded in 1516, governed the region through its western beylik.
The Bey of Mascara, Mustapha Ben Youssef, drove the Spanish out of Oran in 1708.
Spain returned in 1732. A severe earthquake in October 1790 killed more than 3,000 people and weakened its hold.
After a siege Spain agreed to withdraw in 1792 and the forces of Mohammed el Kebir took control of Oran.
The French occupied Oran on 4 January 1831; in 1832 Emir Abd al-Qadir attacked the city but the defenders held.
Oran became the capital of the Département of Oran under French rule; the 1848 constitution made Algeria departments of France.
The Algerian War ran from 1954 to 1962; the Evian Accords were signed in March 1962.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

regions.label: Constantine, Annaba and the Aures
regions.sub: Constantine, Annaba, Setif, Batna, Biskra, Tebessa, Bejaia

eras.polity: Regency of Algiers - Beylik of Constantine (the Beylik of the East)
eras.note: The Beylik of Constantine, the most populous and wealthiest of the Regency's three beyliks, is dated to 1528 with Constantine as its capital; Salah Bey governed it from 1771 to 1792. After the French took Algiers in 1830 Ahmed Bey organised resistance, and the beylik collapsed in the siege of Constantine, which the French captured on 13 October 1837.
Ahmed Bey fought on from the Aures Mountains until he surrendered in 1848.

The Département of Constantine was formed in 1848 on the bases of the former beylik; a register for Guelma, 1847-1882, is catalogued at FamilySearch. The Sétif and Guelma massacre took place from 8 May to 26 June 1945.
The Algerian War ran from 1954 to 1962, and the Evian Accords were signed in March 1962.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

regions.label: Sahara West - Ain Sefra, Bechar, Saoura and Touat
regions.sub: Bechar, Ain Sefra, Adrar, Timimoun, Tindouf

eras.note: Before registers. French rule reached the oases of the Saoura, Gourara, Touat and Tidikelt around 1900-1902; the status of the Saoura before 1902 is disputed between Moroccan and Algerian accounts.

eras.polity: Territoires du Sud - military territories (Ain-Sefra and Oasis)
eras.note: The Southern Territories were created as military territories under the governor-general of Algeria by the law of 24 December 1902; a decree of 14 August 1905 divided them into four territories (Ain-Sefra, Ghardaia, Oasis and Touggourt). Boundaries were fixed on 12 December 1905 and redrawn in 1907, 1920 and 1938.

eras.polity: Territoires du Sud under the 1947 statute
eras.note: Under the Statute of 24 September 1947 the territories were treated as departments, with full departmentalisation planned.
Decree 57-903 of 7 August 1957 abolished the territories and created the Saoura department in the west and the Oasis department in the east.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

regions.label: Sahara East - Ghardaia, Laghouat, Ouargla, Touggourt, El Oued and the Hoggar
regions.sub: Laghouat, Ghardaia, Ouargla, Touggourt, El Oued, Tamanrasset

eras.polity: Oasis towns, the M'zab and nomadic peoples
eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Territoires du Sud - military territories (Ghardaia, Touggourt and Oasis)
eras.note: Created by the law of 24 December 1902 and split by decree of 14 August 1905 into Ain-Sefra, Ghardaia, Oasis and Touggourt territories; the Ghardaia, Touggourt and Oasis territories cover this ring.

eras.polity: Territoires du Sud under the 1947 statute
eras.note: The Statute of 24 September 1947 treated the territories as departments.
The Oasis department was created in the east by decree 57-903 of 7 August 1957. In 1958 northern fractions were attached to the departments of Medea and Saida.
Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.

regions.label: Tangier and its International Zone
regions.sub: Tangier, Cap Spartel, Cape Malabata

eras.note: Portugal occupied Tangier on 28 August 1471 after its garrison fled; from 1580 to 1661 it was under Iberian rule with a Portuguese garrison and administration.

Tangier was given to England in 1661 as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry and fully occupied in January 1662. English forces destroyed the town and port before Morocco retook it on 7 February 1684.

eras.polity: Alaouite sultanate - diplomatic and consular hub
eras.note: Consulates arrived from the 1770s, several European states and the United States had them by 1830, and they were upgraded to legations in 1856.

eras.polity: Tangier International Zone (France, Spain, United Kingdom)
eras.note: The Paris Convention of 18 December 1923 created the zone, which began on 1 June 1925 under a dahir of 15 May 1925; a protocol of 25 July 1928 admitted Italy as an equal participant. It was a tax haven, and its banks rose from 15 in 1939 to 85 in 1950.
Spanish troops occupied the zone from 14 June 1940 to 11 October 1945, and Tangier was annexed to the Spanish protectorate on 23 November 1940.
The pre-war status returned in 1945 and a reformed International Jurisdiction took effect on 10 June 1953. Around 1956 the population was roughly 40,000 Muslims, 31,000 Christians and 15,000 Jews.
A protocol of 29 October 1956 returned Tangier to full Moroccan sovereignty; its special economic privileges lasted until April 1960.

regions.label: Spanish Morocco - Tetouan, the Rif and Larache
regions.sub: Tetouan, Larache, Ksar el-Kebir, Chefchaouen, Al Hoceima, Nador

eras.note: The Saadi dynasty ruled from 1549 to 1659; the Alawi dynasty began in the mid-1660s, a start date that varies by source.
A Franco-Spanish treaty of 27 November 1912 turned Spain's sphere of influence in the north into a formal protectorate; Tangier was excluded and given international status.

eras.polity: Rif War - the Republic of the Rif
eras.note: The Republic of the Rif under Abd el-Krim fought Spanish forces, which suffered heavy losses at Annual in 1921. France and Spain jointly defeated the Rif in 1925.

The 1936 uprising against the Republican government began in Spanish Morocco, where Franco's forces, including Moroccan troops, were based. Spain returned the northern zone to Morocco on 7 April 1956.
The northern zone rejoined Morocco on 7 April 1956; Ceuta and Melilla remain Spanish, though Morocco claims them.

regions.label: French Morocco - Rabat, Casablanca, Fes and the Oriental
regions.sub: Rabat, Casablanca, Fes, Meknes, Kenitra, Oujda, Taza

eras.note: The Saadi dynasty ruled from 1549 to 1659; the Alawi dynasty began in the mid-1660s, a start date that varies by source.
The Alawi dynasty began in the mid-1660s and still reigns.

The Treaty of Fez of 30 March 1912 established the protectorate, and Hubert Lyautey was Resident-General until 1925. A local civil status was instituted by the dahir of 4 September 1915, though accounts differ on whether Moroccans could use it; the French diplomatic archives hold consular registers for 1881-1924 for Casablanca, Fes, Rabat and other posts.

France and Spain defeated the Rif rebels in 1925, and the court moved from Fez to Rabat, which has been the capital since. The Berber Dahir was issued on 16 May 1930, and Sultan Mohammed V and his family were sent to Madagascar in January 1954. Registration of Moroccan births and deaths became optional by a dahir of 1931, and a separate Moroccan civil status is attributed to a dahir of 8 March 1950.
A Franco-Moroccan agreement signed in Paris on 2 March 1956 dissolved the Treaty of Fez; independence is also dated 7 April 1956, the date of the joint declaration with Spain.

regions.label: Southern Morocco - Marrakech, the Souss, Draa and Tarfaya
regions.sub: Marrakech, Agadir, Essaouira, Ouarzazate, Tiznit, Guelmim, Tan-Tan

eras.note: The Saadi dynasty ruled from 1549 to 1659; the Alawi dynasty began in the mid-1660s, a start date that varies by source.

eras.polity: French protectorate - with the Spanish southern zone around Cape Juby
eras.note: The Treaty of Fez of 30 March 1912 established the French protectorate. The Spanish protectorate had a southern zone around Cape Juby, separate from the northern one.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Morocco - Cape Juby and Ifni still Spanish
eras.note: France ended its protectorate in 1956, but the Spanish southern zone remained.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Morocco - Ifni still Spanish
eras.note: After the Ifni War the Treaty of Angra de Cintra of 1 April 1958 transferred the Spanish southern zone to Morocco.
Spain ceded Ifni to Morocco in 1969.

regions.label: The Punjab plains: Lahore, Rawalpindi and Faisalabad
regions.sub: Lahore, Faisalabad, Rawalpindi, Islamabad, Sargodha, Wah Cantt

eras.note: Before registers.
Ranjit Singh captured Lahore on 7 July 1799 and was crowned on 12 April 1801. The empire was dissolved by proclamation on 30 March 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Punjab annexed
eras.note: The Punjab was annexed on 29 March 1849 (the formal annexation is dated 2 April in one account). A Board of Administration ran it until 1853 and a Chief Commissioner until 1858.

The Punjab became a Lieutenant-Governor's province in 1859 (some accounts say 1858) and a Governor's province in 1921. The Delhi Territory was added in 1858 and the North-West Frontier Province cut out of it in 1901, so frontier-district records before 1901 sit in the Punjab series. Baptisms, marriages and burials of Christians were returned to London and survive as the India Office ecclesiastical returns (1698-1968) in the British Library.
Pakistan and India came into being at midnight on 14-15 August 1947 and the Punjab was partitioned on 17 August 1947. The Radcliffe award, published on 17 August 1947, gave Lahore to Pakistan.
The One Unit scheme merged the provinces of the west into West Pakistan in 1955. Balochistan was re-created as a province on 1 July 1970.

regions.label: Multan and Bahawalpur: the south-west Punjab
regions.sub: Multan, Bahawalpur, Dera Ghazi Khan, Rahim Yar Khan, Muzaffargarh, Sahiwal

eras.note: Before registers.
Bahawal Khan of the Daudpotra tribe, who came from Shikarpur in Sindh, founded Bahawalpur state in 1748.

eras.polity: Sikh Empire - Multan; Bahawalpur under its Nawabs
eras.note: The Sikh Empire conquered Multan in 1818. Bahawalpur kept its own rulers and made its first treaty with the British in 1833 (22 February), followed by the Treaty of Ahmudpore on 5 October 1838.

eras.polity: East India Company: Multan in the annexed Punjab
eras.note: The Punjab was annexed in 1849 and run by a Board of Administration to 1853, then a Chief Commissioner to 1858. Bahawalpur remained a state in subsidiary alliance with the British.

eras.polity: British Raj: Multan in the Punjab; Bahawalpur a princely state
eras.note: Multan was in the Punjab Province. Bahawalpur kept its own administration, so its census and registers are separate from the provincial series; its 1941 population was 1,341,209 and censuses were counted each decade from 1871.
Bahawalpur signed its accession to Pakistan on 5 October 1947 and Pakistan accepted it on 9 October 1947, the first state to accede.
Bahawalpur merged into West Pakistan on 14 October 1955, with the Nawab keeping his titles and a privy purse. Balochistan was re-created as a province in 1970.

regions.label: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Peshawar, Mardan, Bannu and Swat
regions.sub: Peshawar, Mardan, Mingora, Bannu, Dera Ismail Khan, Battagram

eras.note: Before registers.
Ahmad Shah Durrani invaded Peshawar in 1748. Maratha control in 1758-1759 interrupted Durrani rule, which was re-established in early 1759.
Ranjit Singh took Peshawar in 1818 according to one account; another dates it as a tribute-paying province in 1823 and annexed in 1834 by Hari Singh Nalwa. The dates differ by source.

eras.polity: East India Company: the frontier districts of the Punjab
eras.note: After the Second Anglo-Sikh War the British incorporated the western parts of the region into British India. The districts were run as part of the Punjab.

eras.polity: British Raj: the Punjab frontier districts
eras.note: The frontier districts stayed in the Punjab Province. The Durand Line agreement of 12 November 1893 set the limit of British and Afghan influence to the west.

eras.polity: British Raj: the North-West Frontier Province
eras.note: The North-West Frontier Province was formed in 1901 (9 November) by separating five districts from the Punjab, so earlier records of its districts are in the Punjab series.
The province acceded to Pakistan on 14 August 1947, after a referendum in July.

eras.polity: Pakistan - NWFP within West Pakistan, then a province again
eras.note: The province was merged into West Pakistan under One Unit in 1955.
The name Khyber Pakhtunkhwa took effect on 15 April 2010 through the 18th Amendment. The former tribal areas (FATA) were merged into the province by a law signed on 31 May 2018.

regions.label: Sindh: Karachi, Hyderabad, Sukkur and Larkana
regions.sub: Karachi, Hyderabad, Sukkur, Larkana, Nawabshah, Mirpur Khas

eras.note: Before registers.
Akbar's army conquered Sindh from the Tarkhan dynasty in 1591 (one date given is 1593). Thatta was the provincial capital.
The Kalhora dynasty ruled Sindh from 1701 to 1783.
The Talpur dynasty ruled from 1783 to the British conquest of 1843.
The British conquered Sindh in 1843 after the battles of Miani and Dubba and the Battle of Hyderabad, and annexed it.

eras.polity: British Raj: Sind in the Bombay Presidency
eras.note: Sind formed part of the Bombay Presidency, and its separation as a province did not come until 1936.

eras.polity: British Raj: the Province of Sind
eras.note: Sind became a separate province on 1 April 1936.
Sindh became part of Pakistan in 1947.
Khairpur was fully amalgamated into West Pakistan in 1955; Balochistan was re-created as a province in 1970.

regions.label: Balochistan: Quetta, Khuzdar and the Makran coast
regions.sub: Quetta, Khuzdar, Jiwani, Gwadar, Turbat, Zhob

eras.note: Before registers.

The Brahui Qambrani dynasty established the Khanate of Kalat in the late 17th century. Nader Shah gave the Kach Gandava plains to Muhabat Khan in 1739 and Ahmad Shah Durrani gave Quetta to Nasir Khan I in 1751; the khanate declined after Nasir Khan died in 1795.

eras.polity: British Raj: Kalat under protection; British Baluchistan
eras.note: The Treaty of Kalat of 1876 put Kalat, Makran, Kharan and Las Bela under British protection. The Treaty of Gandamak (1879, dated 1880 in one account) gave Quetta, Pishin, Harnai and Sibi to the British, and small further areas were declared British territory in 1887.

eras.polity: Pakistan - Kalat and the Balochistan states
eras.note: Lasbela, Makran and Kharan acceded in March 1948 and the Khan of Kalat signed the Instrument of Accession on 27 March 1948. The Baluchistan States Union was set up in 1952.
Balochistan was dissolved into West Pakistan in 1955.
Balochistan was established as a province on 1 July 1970.

regions.label: Herat, Farah and Kandahar: the south-west of Afghanistan
regions.sub: Herat, Kandahar, Farah, Lashkar Gah, Zaranj, Gereshk

eras.note: Uzbeks occupied Herat in 1507; Shah Isma'il I took it in 1510 and Shah Tahmasp retook it from the Uzbeks in 1528. Herat stayed under Safavid Iran into the early 18th century.

eras.polity: Hotak, Sadozai Herat and Afsharid Iran
eras.note: The Hotak dynasty is dated 1709-1738. Abdali Afghans founded the Sadozai Sultanate of Herat in 1716, and Herat became part of Afsharid Iran in 1732.
The Durrani Empire was founded in 1747 under Ahmad Shah Durrani, who took Herat into it after Nader Shah's death. Timur Shah died in 1793.

Herat became independent in 1793 in a civil war among Timur Shah's sons. Iran besieged it in 1837 and held it briefly from 25 October 1856, ending with the Treaty of Paris in 1857; the Emirate is dated from 1823 and Dost Mohammad Khan conquered Herat on 26 May 1863.
Herat was incorporated into Afghanistan in 1863. Britain and Afghanistan fought the Second Anglo-Afghan War in 1878-1880, and the Durand Line was agreed on 12 November 1893.
The Third Anglo-Afghan War of 1919 ended with the Treaty of Rawalpindi on 8 August 1919, and the Kingdom of Afghanistan emerged in June 1926. The monarchy lasted until 1973.

eras.polity: Republic, Saur Revolution and Soviet intervention
eras.note: The Republic of Afghanistan was declared in 1973, the Saur Revolution followed in 1978 and the Soviet invasion in 1979. An army mutiny at Herat in March 1979 was followed by reprisals that killed an estimated 3,000 to 24,000 people, and Soviet forces withdrew in 1989.

eras.polity: Civil war and the Taliban Islamic Emirate
eras.note: The Taliban controlled most of the country by 1996 and held the Islamic Emirate from 1996 to 2001.
The United States invaded in 2001, and the Taliban returned to power in 2021, forming an interim government in September 2021.

regions.label: Kabul, Ghazni, Jalalabad and the Hazarajat
regions.sub: Kabul, Ghazni, Jalalabad, Gardez, Khost, Bamyan

eras.note: Before registers.
Ahmad Shah Durrani founded the Durrani Empire in 1747. Timur Shah died in 1793, after which his sons fought over the succession.

eras.polity: Emirate of Afghanistan - the Barakzai Emirs
eras.note: The Emirate is dated from 1823, and Dost Mohammad Khan's wars of unification ran from 1823 to 1863. The First Anglo-Afghan War lasted from 1838 to 1842.

eras.polity: Emirate of Afghanistan under British influence
eras.note: The Second Anglo-Afghan War lasted from 1878 to 1880. The Durand Line agreement of 12 November 1893, signed with Emir Abdur Rahman Khan, set the limits of British and Afghan spheres of influence, and a joint survey of about 1,300 km of the line followed in 1894-1896.
The Treaty of Rawalpindi of 8 August 1919 ended the Third Anglo-Afghan War, and Afghanistan accepted the Indo-Afghan frontier. The Kingdom emerged in June 1926 and the monarchy ended in 1973.

eras.polity: Republic, Saur Revolution and Soviet intervention
eras.note: The Republic ran from 1973 to 1978, followed by the Saur Revolution of 1978 and the Soviet invasion of 1979; Soviet forces withdrew in 1989.

eras.polity: Civil war and the Taliban Islamic Emirate
eras.note: The Taliban held the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan between 1996 and 2001.
The Taliban took Kabul in 2021 and formed an interim government in September 2021.

regions.label: Afghan Turkestan: Mazar-e Sharif, Balkh and Maymana
regions.sub: Mazar-e Sharif, Balkh, Maymana, Shibirghan, Andkhoy, Aibak

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Durrani realm and the Uzbek khanates
eras.note: The territory was part of Ahmad Shah Durrani's realm, then of his son Timur Shah's. In the early 19th century it belonged to Bukhara, with Uzbek chiefs governing separate khanates, and Dost Mohammad Khan began his campaigns there in the 1830s, including the Afghan Turkestan campaign of 1838-1839.

eras.polity: Turkestan Province of the Emirate of Afghanistan
eras.note: The Afghans retook Balkh and Tashkurgan in 1850, and Akcha and the four western khanates (Sar-e Pul, Shibirghan, Andkhoy, Maymana) came under Afghan control in 1855. An Anglo-Russian agreement of 1873 settled disputes over Andkhoy, Shibirghan, Sar-e Pul and Maymana in Afghanistan's favour; Turkestan Province was created with Mazar-e Sharif as capital, with no exact year given.
Afghanistan accepted the Indo-Afghan frontier in the Treaty of Rawalpindi of 8 August 1919, and the Kingdom emerged in June 1926.

eras.polity: Republic, Saur Revolution and Soviet intervention
eras.note: The Republic ran from 1973 to 1978, with the Saur Revolution in 1978 and the Soviet invasion in 1979; Soviet forces withdrew in 1989.

eras.polity: Civil war and the Taliban Islamic Emirate
eras.note: The Taliban controlled most of the country by 1996 and held the Islamic Emirate until 2001.
The United States invaded in 2001, and the Taliban returned to power in 2021.

regions.label: Kunduz, Takhar and Badakhshan
regions.sub: Kunduz, Taloqan, Fayzabad, Pul-e Khumri, Baghlan, Khanabad

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Emirate of Badakhshan and the Khanate of Kunduz
eras.note: The Emirate of Badakhshan became independent in 1657 and was subject to the Durrani Empire from the mid-18th century. The Khanate of Kunduz was a separate power until Afghanistan conquered it in 1859.

eras.polity: Emirate of Afghanistan - Qataghan and Badakhshan
eras.note: Badakhshan was formally abolished as an emirate and incorporated into Afghanistan in 1873, linked to the Great Game and the demarcation of the northeastern frontier. The Wakhan Corridor dates from the same period, as a buffer between British India and the Russian Empire. Abdur Rahman Khan abolished the Kunduz khanate in 1888, and Qataghan-Badakhshan was split off as its own province in 1890.
Badakhshan was established as a province in 1965 under the 1964 constitution.

eras.polity: Republic, Saur Revolution and Soviet intervention
eras.note: The Soviet invasion of 1979 made Badakhshan a mujahideen base; Soviet forces withdrew in 1989.

eras.polity: Civil war and the Taliban Islamic Emirate
eras.note: The Taliban ruled from 1996 to 2001 but never fully captured Badakhshan.
The Afghan government collapsed in August 2021 and the Taliban took control of the province.

regions.label: Bangladesh: Rajshahi, Rangpur and Khulna
regions.sub: Rajshahi, Rangpur, Khulna, Bogra, Jessore, Kushtia

eras.note: The Bengal Sultanate is dated 1352-1576, and the dynasty was founded by Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah in the 14th century.
Akbar's victory over the Sultanate is dated 1576 (the same account elsewhere says 1590), and the Bengal Subah is dated 1576-1717.

eras.polity: East India Company: Bengal after Plassey
eras.note: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757.
Crown rule replaced Company rule under the Government of India Act 1858, which took effect on 2 August 1858.
The Partition of Bengal in 1905 created the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, which existed from 1905 to 1912.

The Radcliffe award, published on 17 August 1947, gave Khulna to East Pakistan (a marginal 51 percent Hindu majority) and Murshidabad to India despite a 70 percent Muslim majority. Most of Malda district, including Malda town, also went to India.

eras.polity: Pakistan - East Bengal, East Pakistan from 1956
eras.note: The 1956 Constitution renamed East Bengal as East Pakistan. The Bengali language movement is dated 1948-1956.
Independence was proclaimed on 26 March 1971 and Pakistani forces surrendered on 16 December 1971.

regions.label: Bangladesh: Dhaka, Barishal and Chattogram
regions.sub: Dhaka, Chattogram, Mymensingh, Barishal, Cox's Bazar, Narayanganj

eras.note: Chittagong was conquered by Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah in 1340. The Kingdom of Mrauk U (1530-1666) and a Portuguese settlement (1528-1666) are both dated on the coast.
The Subah is dated 1576-1717 here; the date of the Mughal conquest is contested between 1576 and 1590.

eras.polity: East India Company: Dacca and the delta
eras.note: The Battle of Plassey in 1757 began the Company's control of Bengal.
Baptisms, marriages and burials of Christians in the Presidency were returned to London and are in the British Library's India Office ecclesiastical returns (1698-1968), indexed by FIBIS.
Dhaka was the capital of the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam, formed in 1905 and dissolved in 1912.
The Radcliffe award of 17 August 1947 gave the Chittagong Hill Tracts to Pakistan although about 97 percent of the population was non-Muslim.

eras.polity: Pakistan - East Bengal, East Pakistan from 1956
eras.note: East Bengal was renamed East Pakistan by the 1956 Constitution, and Dhaka was declared a second capital in 1962. The 1970 election gave the Awami League a landslide in East Pakistan, and a crackdown began on 26 March 1971.
Independence was declared at Dhaka on 26 March 1971, and East Pakistan became Bangladesh when Pakistani forces surrendered on 16 December 1971.

regions.label: Bhutan and the Duars: Thimphu, Paro, Jaigaon and Dinhata
regions.sub: Thimphu, Paro, Phuntsholing, Jaigaon, Dinhata, Dhubri

eras.note: Ngawang Namgyal consolidated Bhutan from 1616 and died in 1651, although his death was kept secret for years. Bhutanese raids into Cooch Behar in 1862 helped lead to the Duar War of 1864-1865.

eras.polity: British India - the Duars; Bhutan under the Sinchula subsidy
eras.note: By the Treaty of Sinchula of 11 November 1865 Bhutan gave up the Assam Duars, the Bengal Duars and about 83 square kilometres of Dewangiri, and Britain agreed to pay up to 50,000 rupees a year. Ugyen Wangchuck was enthroned as the first hereditary king in December 1907.

eras.polity: British India and Bhutan - Treaty of Punakha
eras.note: The Treaty of Punakha of 8 January 1910 replaced the Sinchula treaty and stayed in effect until 1947.
Bhutan and India signed a Treaty of Friendship on 8 August 1949. An all-weather road joined Phuntsholing and Thimphu in 1962.
Thimphu became the year-round capital in 1966 (the seat of government has been at Tashichho Dzong since 1952 according to one account). Bhutan joined the United Nations in 1971.

regions.label: Nepal: the Kathmandu Valley, Pokhara and the hills
regions.sub: Kathmandu, Pokhara, Bharatpur, Hetauda, Butwal, Birendranagar

eras.polity: Malla kingdoms and the Gorkha hill states
eras.note: Malla rule in the Kathmandu valley began about 1201, and the valley divided about 1484 into the kingdoms of Kathmandu, Bhaktapur, Patan and Banepa. Gorkha forces took Nuwakot in 1744.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Nepal - the Gorkha conquest
eras.note: Gorkhali forces entered Kathmandu on 25 September 1768 and Bhaktapur fell on 25 November 1769.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Nepal after the Sugauli treaty
eras.note: The Anglo-Nepalese War of 1814-1816 ended with the Treaty of Sugauli (1816), which ceded large territories to the British. Parts of the western Terai were restored to Nepal in 1860.
Rana rule began about 1846 after the Kot massacre. Britain and Nepal signed a treaty of perpetual peace and friendship in December 1923.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Nepal - after the Rana revolution
eras.note: A revolution against the Ranas in 1951 led to the Delhi Accord that year. King Mahendra's coup of 1960 and the constitution of 16 December 1960 began the Panchayat system, which ran to about 1990.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Nepal - multiparty monarchy and civil war
eras.note: The 1990 Jana Andolan forced the monarchy to accept a multiparty parliament. The civil war is dated about 1996-2006, and parliament voted to abolish the monarchy in June 2006.
A federal republic was declared in 2008.

regions.label: The Maldives: Male and the atolls
regions.sub: Male, Kulhudhuffushi, Naifaru, Thinadhoo, Hithadhoo, Fuvahmulah

eras.note: The last Buddhist king converted to Islam in 1153, or 1193 according to some copper plates, and took the name Sultan Muhammad al Adil.
The Portuguese established a colony in 1558, and a revolt led by Muhammad Thakurufaanu expelled them in 1573.
Muhammad Thakurufaanu became sultan after the expulsion of the Portuguese.

eras.polity: Dutch Ceylon hegemony, then British Ceylon
eras.note: The Dutch exercised hegemony through Dutch Ceylon from about 1658. They withdrew in 1796, and the British, who expelled the Dutch from Ceylon, designated the Maldives a protected area.

The protectorate was formalised on 16 December 1887, with the sultan keeping internal self-government. Britain leased Gan in Addu Atoll in 1956, and the United Suvadive Republic seceded in the southern atolls from 1959 to 1963 (dated 1958-1963 in some accounts).
Independence from Britain was achieved on 26 July 1965.
A referendum on 15 March 1968 was followed by the declaration of a republic on 11 November 1968. British forces left Gan in 1976 (1975 in another section of the same account).

regions.label: Mumbai and the Konkan coast
regions.sub: Mumbai, Thane, Virar, Palghar, Ratnagiri, Vapi

eras.note: Before registers.

Portugal acquired the islands of Bombay under the Treaty of Bassein signed on 23 December 1534, and Bassein and the seven islands were surrendered on 25 October 1535. Bombay passed to England as part of Catherine of Braganza's dowry under the marriage treaty of 8 May 1661.

eras.polity: East India Company: Bombay and the Peshwa's Konkan
eras.note: A royal charter of 27 March 1668 gave Bombay to the East India Company, and the Company moved its western headquarters there from Surat in 1687. The Treaty of Bassein of 1802 gave the Company its first mainland territory, in the Konkan, and the Peshwa was defeated at Kirkee on 5 November 1817.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Bombay Presidency
eras.note: Peshwa territories were annexed in stages up to 1818, and Thane and Ratnagiri are among the Konkan Division districts of the Presidency.

The Bombay Municipal Corporation was established in 1872, and the Presidency was renamed the Province of Bombay in 1937. Church baptisms, marriages and burials of the Presidency are among the India Office ecclesiastical returns in the British Library.
Bombay Province became Bombay State on 26 January 1950, and the Bombay City and Bombay Suburbs districts merged into the Greater Bombay District in April 1950.
Maharashtra was formed with Bombay as capital on 1 May 1960. The city was renamed Mumbai on 6 March 1996.

regions.label: Madras: Chennai and the Chingleput coast
regions.sub: Chennai, Tiruvottiyur, Alandur, Mahabalipuram, Pallikaranai, Covelong

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: East India Company: Fort St George
eras.note: The Company bought the village of Madraspatnam in 1639 (1640 in another section of the same account) and set up Fort St George. It was a Presidency from 1652, an agency again in 1655, and a Presidency again from 1684.

eras.polity: East India Company: Madras and the Chingleput jaghire
eras.note: The Chingleput jaghire, obtained in 1763, was the Presidency's first district. The Carnatic Treaty of 1801 brought the Carnatic under British rule, and the first census of the Presidency was taken in 1822.

The first organised census of India was taken in 1871. The Presidency was renamed the Province of Madras in 1937. The India Office ecclesiastical returns in the British Library hold copies of Madras church registers.
The Province became Madras State on 26 January 1950.

regions.label: Delhi's eastern bank and the Upper Doab: Meerut, Ghaziabad and Dehradun
regions.sub: Meerut, Ghaziabad, Noida, Faridabad, Dehradun, Roorkee

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Ceded and Conquered Provinces
eras.note: General Lake took the Meerut and Agra divisions and the districts around Delhi in 1803, and the Provinces were administered under the Bengal Presidency from 1805 to 1836. The Treaty of Sugauli of 1816 added Dehradun, which Gorkha forces had held since 1804.

eras.polity: East India Company: the North-Western Provinces
eras.note: The North-Western Provinces were created in 1836 with Charles Metcalfe as first Lieutenant-Governor. The Delhi Territory was part of the province until 1858.

eras.polity: British Raj: North-Western Provinces; Delhi Territory in the Punjab
eras.note: The Delhi Territory was transferred to the Punjab in 1858, so the Delhi-side districts and the Meerut-side districts of this strip fall under different provincial series. Allahabad was the provincial capital from 1858.

eras.polity: British Raj: United Provinces of Agra and Oudh
eras.note: The North-Western Provinces were reorganised as the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh in 1902 and renamed Agra Province in 1904 in one account.

eras.polity: India: United Provinces/Uttar Pradesh and East Punjab
eras.note: The Dehradun side stayed in the United Provinces, later renamed Uttar Pradesh. The Punjab-side districts went to East Punjab on partition in 1947.
Haryana was formed on 1 November 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act, with Gurgaon among the districts that joined it.

eras.polity: India: Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Uttarakhand
eras.note: Uttarakhand, first named Uttaranchal, was created in 2000 from the north-western districts of Uttar Pradesh, with Dehradun as its interim capital.

regions.label: Mewat and the Chambal: Alwar, Bharatpur, Morena and Bhind
regions.sub: Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Karauli, Morena, Bhind

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: East India Company: treaties with the Rajput states
eras.note: The first agreements with the Rajputana rulers were made in 1817 and the treaties completed by the end of 1818. The Rajputana Agency was established at Ajmer in 1832, and the Central India Agency was created in 1854, with the Gwalior Residency placed under it.

eras.polity: British Raj: Eastern Rajputana States and Central India
eras.note: Bharatpur, Karauli and Dholpur were handled by the Eastern Rajputana States Agency at Bharatpur, and Alwar by its own Agency. Gwalior Residency was separated from the Central India Agency, whose headquarters was Indore, in 1911, and Datia fell under the Bundelkhand states.
Alwar, Bharatpur, Dholpur and Karauli were merged into the Matsya Union on 18 March 1948. The western part of the Central India Agency became Madhya Bharat.
The Matsya Union merged into Greater Rajasthan on 15 May 1949 and the state of Rajasthan was formed on 26 January 1950.
Madhya Bharat, Vindhya Pradesh and Bhopal merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

regions.label: Hadoti and western Malwa: Kota, Mandsaur and Pratapgarh
regions.sub: Kota, Mandsaur, Rawatbhata, Pratapgarh, Jhabua

eras.note: Rao Deva conquered Bundi in 1241 and Kota was captured in 1264; the region takes its name from the Hada branch of the Chauhan Rajputs.

eras.polity: East India Company: Kotah-Jhalawar and Bundi
eras.note: Treaties with the Rajput states were completed by the end of 1818. The Kotah-Jhalawar Agency was based at Kota and the Haraoti-Tonk Agency, covering Bundi, at Deoli; the Malwa side was brought into the Central India Agency created in 1854.

eras.polity: British Raj: Rajputana and Central India
eras.note: The Southern States Agency was renamed the Malwa Agency in 1934. Records of the princely states are separate from the provincial series.
The western part of the Central India Agency became Madhya Bharat in 1947, while the Hadoti districts lie in present-day Rajasthan.
Madhya Bharat merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.

regions.label: Bundelkhand's northern edge: Mahoba, Atarra and Nowgong
regions.sub: Mahoba, Atarra, Nowgong, Datia, Chitrakoot

eras.note: The Chandela dynasty fell in 1182. Khangars held parts of the region from the late 12th to the mid-14th century, and Bundelas emerged in the 14th century and replaced them.
The Bundelas renounced Mughal authority after Aurangzeb died in 1707. Orchha, Datia and Samthar existed as states before British rule, and the Rani of Jhansi lived from 1828 to 1858.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Central India Agency
eras.note: The Central India Agency, headquartered at Indore, was created in 1854.

eras.polity: British Raj: Bundelkhand states and the North-Western Provinces districts
eras.note: The Bagelkhand Agency was split from Bundelkhand in 1871. The present Uttar Pradesh districts of Bundelkhand are Jhansi, Jalaun, Lalitpur, Mahoba, Banda, Hamirpur and Chitrakoot, and the Madhya Pradesh ones are Sagar, Damoh, Panna, Chhatarpur, Tikamgarh and Datia.
The eastern part of the Central India Agency became Vindhya Pradesh in 1947.
Vindhya Pradesh merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956; the Uttar Pradesh districts of Bundelkhand stayed in that state.

regions.label: Hisar to Ganganagar: the Bagar and the Punjab-Rajasthan border
regions.sub: Sri Ganganagar, Hanumangarh, Nohar, Narnaul, Bhadra, Mahendragarh

eras.note: Bikaner state was founded in 1465, though 1488 is the year of Rao Bika's title.

eras.polity: East India Company: Bikaner under British protection
eras.note: Bikaner became a British protectorate on 9 March 1818.

eras.polity: British Raj: Bikaner State and the Punjab's Delhi division
eras.note: The Ganga Canal extension into Hanumangarh and Mirzawala tehsils in 1901-1911 drew Sikh settlers. Most of present-day Haryana lay in the Delhi division of the Punjab, alongside princely states such as Jind and Loharu.
The Maharaja of Bikaner signed the accession on 7 August 1947, and the state came to share a border with Pakistan. The Haryana side was in East Punjab.
Haryana was formed on 1 November 1966, with Hisar and Mahendragarh among the districts that joined it.

regions.label: Western Odisha and Bastar: Jagdalpur, Balangir and Jharsuguda
regions.sub: Jagdalpur, Balangir, Bargarh, Jharsuguda, Nowrangapur, Medininagar

eras.polity: Bastar kingdom and the Chauhan chiefdoms
eras.note: Bastar was founded in 1324, traditionally by Annamaraja, a brother of the Kakatiya Prataparudra II, and Rajapala Deva became king in 1709. The north end of this strip (Garhwa, Medininagar, Sasaram) lies in Jharkhand and Bihar and is not covered by these sources.
The Bhonsle of Nagpur conquered Sambalpur in 1800, and the British returned it to the Chauhan king Jayant Singh in 1817 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Nagpur Province
eras.note: Nagpur was annexed under the doctrine of lapse in 1853 after Raghoji III died without heirs.
The Central Provinces were formed in 1861 by merging the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories with Nagpur Province, and Bastar became part of them.

eras.polity: British Raj: Sambalpur in Bengal; Chhattisgarh in the Central Provinces
eras.note: In 1905 most of Sambalpur and several states moved to Bengal, and Chhattisgarh states moved from Bengal to the Central Provinces. The Odisha Division became part of Bihar and Odisha in 1912.
Odisha became a separate province in April 1936, adding Ganjam and Koraput from the Madras Presidency. The Chhattisgarh princely states moved to the Eastern States Agency in 1933.
The western Odisha princely states acceded in January 1948 and joined Odisha. Bastar acceded on 1 January 1948 and became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956.
Chhattisgarh was split from Madhya Pradesh as a new state in 2000, and Bastar became a district of it.

regions.label: Khandesh and the Tapi valley: Nandurbar, Shirpur and Burhanpur
regions.sub: Nandurbar, Shirpur, Shahada, Chopda, Burhanpur, Sendhwa

eras.note: Khandesh became independent in the late 14th century under the Farooqui dynasty founded by Malik Raja.
Akbar's army overran Khandesh in 1599 and captured Asirgarh. About 1640 Shah Jahan introduced Todar Mal's revenue system, which lasted until 1818.
The Marathas captured Asirgarh in 1760 and the Peshwa ousted the Mughal ruler to gain control of Khandesh.
Baji Rao II surrendered to the British in June 1818, though sporadic fighting continued in Khandesh.

eras.polity: British Raj: East and West Khandesh
eras.note: Khandesh district was split in 1906 into East Khandesh, headquartered at Jalgaon, and West Khandesh, headquartered at Dhule.
The Bombay Province became Bombay State on 26 January 1950.
East Khandesh became Jalgaon district and West Khandesh became Dhule district in 1960. West Khandesh was further divided in the 1990s to create Nandurbar district.

regions.label: Eastern Vidarbha: Wardha, Chandrapur and Adilabad
regions.sub: Wardha, Chandrapur, Adilabad, Hinganghat, Warora, Pandhurna

eras.note: Akbar took Berar in 1596 after Chand Bibi ceded it to the imperial forces under Prince Murad. In 1636 the Mughal Deccan possessions were divided into four subahs, with Ellichpur as the capital of Berar.

eras.polity: Nizam of Hyderabad and the Nagpur kingdom
eras.note: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah declared independence in 1724 and Berar became part of the Nizam's state, though only nominally. Maratha rulers overran Berar in 1680 and 1698, and the Peshwa obtained the right to collect chauth and sardeshmukhi there in 1720.
Nagpur was annexed in 1853 under the doctrine of lapse after Raghoji III died without heirs.
The Central Provinces were formed in 1861 from the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories and Nagpur Province.

eras.polity: British Raj: Central Provinces and Berar
eras.note: Berar, leased by the Nizam, was placed under the Central Provinces administration, and the merger was proclaimed on 17 September 1903. The province became Central Provinces and Berar after a full merger with Berar Division on 24 October 1936.
The province was reorganised as the state of Madhya Pradesh under the new Constitution in 1950.
The Berar and Nagpur divisions were transferred to Bombay State in 1956, and Bombay State was split into Maharashtra and Gujarat in 1960.

regions.label: Bombay Karnataka: Belagavi, Bagalkot and Gokak
regions.sub: Belagavi, Bagalkot, Gokak, Mudhol, Ilkal, Manvi

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: East India Company: Belgaum and Dharwad
eras.note: Peshwa territories were annexed in stages up to 1818, among them Belgaum and Dharwad, which joined the Bombay Presidency.

North Canara was transferred from Madras to Bombay in 1862. The Presidency was renamed the Province of Bombay in 1937. The Kannada-speaking areas were split among Bombay, Madras, Kodagu, Mysore and Hyderabad.
Hyderabad State was taken over in the police action that ended on 17 September 1948, and Bombay Province became Bombay State on 26 January 1950.
The States Reorganisation of 1956 created a Karnataka state that was called Mysore.
Mysore State was renamed Karnataka on 1 November 1973.

regions.label: Gorakhpur's east and West Champaran: Kushinagar, Padrauna and Bagaha
regions.sub: Kushinagar, Padrauna, Bagaha, Siswa Bazar, Nichlaul, Maniar

eras.note: Before registers.
The Nawab of Awadh ceded the region to the British East India Company in 1801 and Gorakhpur was made a district; the cession of 1801 also included Rohilkhand.

In 1829 Gorakhpur became the headquarters of a division comprising the Gorakhpur, Ghazipur and Azamgarh districts. The Treaty of Sugauli of 1816 had fixed the nearby frontier with Nepal, and parts of the western Terai were restored to Nepal in 1860.

eras.polity: British Raj: North-Western Provinces and United Provinces; Bihar
eras.note: The North-Western Provinces became the United Provinces of Agra and Oudh in 1902. The new province of Bihar and Odisha was formed in 1912 out of Bengal.
India became independent on 15 August 1947.

regions.label: Rameswaram and the Palk Strait coast
regions.sub: Rameswaram, Pamban, Mandapam, Vedaranyam, Velankanni

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: East India Company: the Madras Presidency
eras.note: The Carnatic Treaty of 1801 brought the Carnatic region under British rule, and the first census of the Madras Presidency was taken in 1822.
The first organised census of India was taken in 1871, and the Presidency was renamed the Province of Madras in 1937.

eras.polity: India: Madras State and Tamil Nadu
eras.note: Madras State came into being on 26 January 1950.

regions.label: Northern Thailand: Lan Na, Chiang Mai and Chiang Rai
regions.sub: Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lampang, Lamphun, Phrae, Nan, Mae Hong Son

eras.polity: Lan Na kingdom, capital Chiang Mai
eras.note: Before registers. Mangrai founded Chiang Mai in 1296 and made it the capital; the kingdom was strongest under Tilokaraj (1441-1487).

Mekuti surrendered to Bayinnaung in 1558 and Lan Na became a Burmese vassal. Chiang Mai revolted in the 18th century and was again made a vassal in 1757; Kawila captured it on 15 January 1775, ending about 200 years of Burmese rule.

eras.polity: Lan Na as a Siamese vassal
eras.note: Lan Na became an autonomous vassal of Thonburi Siam in 1774-1775. Burmese attempts to retake it in 1775-76, 1785-86 and 1797 failed.

Siam reorganised Lan Na as Monthon Phayap under direct control in 1874 (another account dates the formal incorporation to about 1874), and the thesaphiban system brought central administration in 1899. By 1909 Lan Na no longer existed as a separate polity.
Genealogy records in Thailand are kept at province level, so a northern family's papers sit with the province and district offices of Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai, Lampang and the other northern provinces.

regions.label: Central Thailand: Bangkok and the Chao Phraya plain
regions.sub: Bangkok, Ayutthaya, Nakhon Pathom, Kanchanaburi, Chonburi, Phitsanulok

eras.note: Ayutthaya was founded in 1351 by King Uthong and fell to Burmese forces in 1767, when the city was sacked and burned. Before registers.
Taksin re-established a Siamese state with its capital at Thonburi after the fall of Ayutthaya; the period runs 1767 to 1782.

eras.polity: Rattanakosin Kingdom, Chakri dynasty, capital Bangkok
eras.note: Chao Phraya Chakri, a Thonburi commander, founded the Rattanakosin Kingdom in 1782 after Taksin was deposed. Population recording in the 19th century served taxation and conscription and is described as fragmented and incomplete until about 1920.

The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica dates a first census of the rural population to 1905 and of Bangkok and its suburbs to 1909, while other accounts date a census to 1909-1910; sources differ on its extent. Thai surnames date mostly from after 1913, so earlier records often carry none.
The revolution of 1932 ended the absolute monarchy under Prajadhipok (Rama VII) and set up a constitutional monarchy.

The country was formally renamed Thailand in 1939. Civil registration runs under the Civil Registration Act B.E. 2534 (1991), administered by the Bureau of Registration Administration of the Ministry of Interior, and vital records are requested at district offices.

regions.label: Isan: the Khorat Plateau
regions.sub: Nakhon Ratchasima, Khon Kaen, Udon Thani, Ubon Ratchathani, Nong Khai, Roi Et

eras.polity: Lan Xang and the Lao muang of the plateau
eras.note: Before registers. The Khmer Empire built the sanctuaries of Phimai and Phanom Rung here; the kingdom of Lan Xang, founded about 1353, later dominated Isan, and the first Lao muang of the Chi valley, Suwannaphum (now Roi Et), was founded in 1718 under Champasak.

eras.polity: Siamese suzerainty over the Lao principalities
eras.note: Siam took Vientiane in 1778-1779 and imposed a suzerainty that lasted until 1893. In the 18th and 19th centuries Siam moved people from the left bank of the Mekong to the right bank.
After Anouvong's rebellion failed in 1826-1828, Siam destroyed Vientiane and Khorat was repopulated with forcibly moved Mekong Lao, alongside Chinese migrants.

eras.polity: Siam and French Laos: the Mekong frontier
eras.note: The Franco-Siamese crisis of 1893 ended with Siam ceding its Lao territories east of the Mekong to France, and Isan became the border region facing French Laos. The railway from Bangkok reached Khorat in 1900 and Ubon in 1928.

The railway reached Khon Kaen in 1933 and Nong Khai in 1955, and the US-built Friendship Highway of the 1960s served the northeastern bases. State-backed Thaification in the mid-20th century promoted integration into Thai national identity.

regions.label: Southern Thailand: Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Songkhla and Phuket
regions.sub: Surat Thani, Nakhon Si Thammarat, Hat Yai, Songkhla, Phuket, Trang, Satun

eras.polity: Nakhon Si Thammarat, a tributary of Ayutthaya
eras.note: Before registers. Nakhon Si Thammarat, the main city of the peninsula, became a tributary of Ayutthaya, whose kingdom dates from 1351; its precursor was probably Tambralinga.

eras.polity: Rattanakosin Siam and the peninsular cities
eras.note: The Chakri kings ruled from Bangkok from 1782. The Malay sultanates of Pattani and Kedah held the far south.

Britain and Siam signed a boundary treaty on 20 June 1826 covering the Tenasserim frontier. In the late 19th century the thesaphiban reforms brought Nakhon Si Thammarat under central control and divided the south into five monthon.
The Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 9 July 1909 fixed the border with British Malaya and excluded Setul (Satun) from the jurisdiction of Kedah.

regions.label: Patani: Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat
regions.sub: Pattani, Yala, Narathiwat, Sungai Kolok, Betong

eras.note: Before registers. Patani was established about 1400 (the date is uncertain, between 1350 and 1450) and was most prosperous in 1584-1688 under four successive queens. By the early 17th century Kelantan was subject to Patani.

eras.polity: Siamese conquest and the small principalities
eras.note: A Siamese army under Prince Surasi took and destroyed Patani in 1786. The territory was later divided into small principalities, and by the Burney Treaty of 1826 Britain recognised Siamese ownership of Patani.
Siam deposed the last raja, Abdul Kadir, in 1902 after he refused administrative reform, ending Patani as an independent state.

eras.polity: Anglo-Siamese Treaty: Pattani stays with Siam
eras.note: When the Anglo-Siamese Treaty of 1909 fixed the Malaysian border, Kedah went to British control while Pattani remained with Siam. The former sultanate covered today's Pattani, Yala and Narathiwat provinces and part of Kelantan, so a family may span both sides of the border.
During the Japanese occupation Thailand annexed Kedah on 18 October 1943 and was given Kelantan in 1943; both returned to Malayan control in 1945.

regions.label: Lower Burma: Yangon, Bago and the Irrawaddy delta
