regions.sub: Yangon, Bago, Pathein, Pyay, Taungoo, Hinthada, Hpa-an

eras.polity: Small kingdoms: Hanthawaddy (Mon), Ava, Arakan and the Shan states
eras.note: Before registers. After the Pagan kingdom collapsed, rival states including the Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy fought constantly from about 1297 to the 1550s.
Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung reunified the country under the Toungoo dynasty, which ruled 1510 to 1752; a restored Toungoo kingdom was smaller and more prosperous.

Alaungpaya reunified the country in 1752 and founded the Konbaung dynasty, whose westward expansion led to war with Britain. Lower Burma stayed Burmese through the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824-1826).

eras.polity: British Burma: Pegu and Lower Burma
eras.note: The Second Anglo-Burmese War of 1852 led to the annexation of Lower Burma (Pegu). In 1862 the annexed territories became a chief commissioner's province known as British Burma.

eras.polity: Burma as a province of British India
eras.note: All of present-day Myanmar became a province of British India on 1 January 1886. Baptisms, marriages and burials in Burma to 1936 sit within the Bengal ecclesiastical returns (series N/1) of the India Office Records, most of them digitised on Findmypast; birth registration was not compulsory, so few births were recorded.

eras.polity: Crown colony of Burma and Japanese occupation
eras.note: Burma was separated from British India as a Crown colony on 1 April 1937; ecclesiastical returns for 1937-1957 form a separate series (N/10). Japan invaded in December 1941 and British-led forces retook Rangoon in May 1945; independence followed on 4 January 1948.
Military rule lasted from 1962 to 2010 and has returned since 2021.

regions.label: Tenasserim: Mawlamyine, Dawei and Myeik
regions.sub: Mawlamyine, Dawei, Myeik, Kawthaung, Ye

eras.note: Before registers. After the fall of Bagan in 1287 the coast passed to the Siamese kingdoms of Sukhothai and then Ayutthaya.
Bayinnaung of the Toungoo dynasty brought the region back under Burmese rule in 1564.

Ayutthaya reclaimed the southern half in 1593 and the whole peninsula in 1599; in 1614 Anaukpetlun recovered the northern coast up to Dawei, while Tavoy and the south stayed Siamese. Mergui was a major trading port between Siam and Europeans.
Burma and Siam fought repeatedly for the coast from 1751; Alaungpaya retook it up to Dawei in 1760 and Hsinbyushin conquered the whole coastline in 1765.

The Treaty of Yandabo of 1826 ceded the region south of the Salween to Britain, and Britain and Siam signed a boundary treaty on 20 June 1826. Moulmein (Mawlamyine) was the capital of the Tenasserim Division; in 1852 Britain took the rest of Lower Burma.

eras.polity: Province of British India, then Crown colony of Burma
eras.note: Burma became a province of British India on 1 January 1886 and a separate Crown colony on 1 April 1937. Japan occupied much of the country from December 1941 until 1945, and independence came on 4 January 1948.

At independence in 1948 the north-eastern districts were placed in the new Karen State, and Mon State was created in 1974 from the northern part of the remaining region, with the capital of the Tenasserim division moving to Dawei. The English name Tenasserim was officially changed to Tanintharyi in 1989.

regions.label: Arakan (Rakhine): Sittwe and Mrauk U
regions.sub: Sittwe, Mrauk U, Kyaukphyu, Maungdaw, Thandwe, Taungup

eras.note: Before registers. Narameikhla regained the throne in 1430 with Bengali help and the capital moved to Mrauk U in 1431; the kingdom held Chittagong from 1459 until the Mughal conquest of 1666. Accounts differ on whether it was a Bengal protectorate until 1531 or independent from 1437.

eras.polity: Mrauk U after the loss of Chittagong
eras.note: Historians usually mark the loss of Chittagong in 1666 as the end of the kingdom's golden age. Its last king, Maha Thammada, reigned 1782-1785.
The Konbaung dynasty conquered Arakan on 2 January 1785 (1784 in some accounts), and up to 35,000 people reportedly fled to the Chittagong and Cox's Bazar areas.
The Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War and Britain annexed Arakan with Tenasserim. From 1862 the annexed territories formed the chief commissioner's province of British Burma.

eras.polity: Province of British India, then Crown colony of Burma
eras.note: Burma was a province of British India from 1 January 1886 and a separate Crown colony from 1 April 1937; independence came on 4 January 1948.
Military rule lasted from 1962 to 2010 and has returned since 2021.

regions.label: Upper Burma: Mandalay, Sagaing and Magway
regions.sub: Mandalay, Sagaing, Monywa, Meiktila, Magway, Pakokku, Naypyidaw

eras.note: Before registers. Anawrahta unified the region for the first time under the Pagan kingdom, which ran from 849 to 1297 and collapsed after Mongol invasions and Shan pressure.

eras.polity: Small kingdoms: Ava and the Shan states
eras.note: Rival states including Ava fought constantly from about 1297 until the Toungoo dynasty rose in 1510.
The Toungoo dynasty (1510-1752) reunified the country under Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung, then ruled a smaller restored kingdom.
Alaungpaya founded the Konbaung dynasty in 1752; its wars with Siam and China ended in stalemate. British forces entered Mandalay on 28 November 1885.

eras.polity: Upper Burma in the Province of Burma, British India
eras.note: All of present-day Myanmar became a province of British India on 1 January 1886. The Galon rebellion of Saya San, which began as a tax protest, ran from 1930 to 1932.

eras.polity: Crown colony of Burma and Japanese occupation
eras.note: Burma became a Crown colony on 1 April 1937; Japan occupied much of the country from December 1941, and the Aung San-Attlee Agreement of 27 January 1947 preceded independence on 4 January 1948.
Military rule lasted from 1962 to 2010 and has returned since 2021.

regions.label: Kachin State: Myitkyina and Bhamo
regions.sub: Myitkyina, Bhamo, Mogaung, Putao

eras.polity: Dali, Mong Mao and the Kachin hills
eras.note: Before registers. After Nanzhao fell, the Dali Kingdom administered the lands where Kachin people lived from the 12th century, and Mong Mao used the territory to raid Yunnan in the 14th century.
The Qing briefly controlled the area during the Sino-Burmese War of the 1760s and later exercised some control over the north-east.

eras.polity: Kachin Hills in the Province of Burma
eras.note: The British accepted tribal autonomy in the Kachin Hills, sent expeditions in 1892 and 1896, and occupied Hpimaw (Pianma) in 1910.

The Government of Burma Act of 1935 divided the Frontier Areas into Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas. At Panglong on 12 February 1947 Aung San's government agreed in principle to full internal autonomy for the Frontier Areas and a Kachin State.

eras.polity: Kachin State in the Union of Burma
eras.note: Burma became independent on 4 January 1948 and Kachin State, formed from the Bhamo, Myitkyina and Putao districts, was announced on 10 January 1948.

eras.polity: Myanmar: Kachin State and the Kachin Independence Organization
eras.note: After the 1962 coup the Kachin forces left the Burmese army to found the Kachin Independence Army (1960 or 1961 by different accounts); the state was largely self-governing from the mid-1960s until 1994. A ceasefire of 1994 lasted until fighting resumed in June 2011.

regions.label: Shan and Kayah States: Taunggyi, Lashio and Kengtung
regions.sub: Taunggyi, Lashio, Kengtung, Loikaw, Tachileik, Hsipaw

eras.note: Before registers. A Confederation of Shan States ruled Upper Burma from 1527 to 1555, until the Toungoo dynasty conquered the Shan States in 1557.
The Shan rulers, called saophas or sawbwa, kept a large degree of autonomy under the Burmese kings.

eras.polity: Shan states as princely states under British India
eras.note: After the British occupation of 1885 the Shan States became nominally sovereign princely states bound by a subsidiary alliance.

The Shan states were joined as the Federated Shan States in 1922 under the Burma Frontier Service, and the Frontier Areas were split into Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas in 1935. The Panglong Conference followed on 12 February 1947.

eras.polity: Shan State and Kayah State in the Union of Burma
eras.note: In 1948 the Federated Shan States became Shan State and the southern portion became Kayah State, with a right to secede. The Shan States are listed as fully annexed into Burma in 1959.
In 1962 Ne Win's military government removed the Shan States and the saophas' hereditary rights.

regions.label: Tonkin: Hanoi, Haiphong and the Red River delta
regions.sub: Hanoi, Haiphong, Nam Dinh, Lao Cai, Dien Bien Phu, Ha Long, Lang Son

eras.polity: Later Le dynasty, capital Thang Long
eras.note: Before registers. Le Loi overthrew Ming rule and made Thang Long, now Hanoi, his capital; he reigned 1428-1433.

eras.polity: Dang Ngoai under the Trinh lords
eras.note: From 1527 the Mac dynasty and rival lords split the country, and Westerners used Tonkin for the northern domain, Dang Ngoai, ruled by the Trinh lords. The name comes from Dong Kinh, the Eastern Capital of the Le dynasty.
Nguyen Phuc Anh was crowned at Hue as Gia Long on 1 June 1802. Minh Mang centralised the state and expanded provincial administration between 1820 and 1841.

France gained control of northern Vietnam in 1884-1885 after the Sino-French War, and Tonkin entered the Indochinese Union formed on 17 October 1887. Hanoi became the capital of French Indochina in 1901 (1902 in another account).

eras.polity: Democratic Republic of Vietnam and the First Indochina War
eras.note: A Japanese coup overthrew French rule on 9 March 1945 and Tonkin suffered famine in 1944-1945 under Japanese occupation. Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945, and the First Indochina War began on 19 December 1946.
After the Geneva Accords of 21 July 1954 Tonkin became part of North Vietnam.

Vietnam was reunified under a communist government in 1976. FamilySearch lists civil registration from 1858 with coverage of about 20 percent, and household registers from 1945 to the present, with the Ministry of Justice in Hanoi listed as the office to contact.

regions.label: Annam: Thanh Hoa, Vinh, Hue and Da Nang
regions.sub: Thanh Hoa, Vinh, Ha Tinh, Dong Hoi, Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An

eras.polity: Dai Viet under the Later Le and Mac
eras.note: Before registers. The Later Le dynasty ruled 1428-1527 and the Mac dynasty and rival lords then divided the country.

eras.polity: Dang Trong under the Nguyen lords
eras.note: Le Anh Tong appointed Nguyen Hoang to govern Thuan Hoa in 1558. The Trinh-Nguyen split became official with the first war in 1627, and Nguyen Phuc Lan made Phu Xuan (Hue) his residence in 1636.
The Tay Son-Nguyen war ran from 1771 to 1802; Nguyen Phuc Anh was crowned at Hue on 1 June 1802 and the Tay Son fell by 20 July 1802.
Gia Long was crowned at Hue on 1 June 1802, and the capital stood at Phu Xuan. Minh Mang abolished the viceroy system and expanded provincial administration between 1820 and 1841.
The Treaties of Hue of 1883-1884 created the French protectorates of Annam and Tonkin; local rulers remained as figureheads. Bao Dai abdicated on 25 August 1945.

A Japanese coup on 9 March 1945 ended French rule, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam was proclaimed on 2 September 1945, and France returned to fight the First Indochina War from 1946. The State of Vietnam was created within the French Union on 8 March 1949.

The Geneva Accords of July 1954 set a provisional demarcation line approximately along the Ben Hai River at the 17th parallel, which crossed this region. The line remained until reunification on 2 July 1976.
The country was reunified in 1976 and the Doi Moi reforms began in 1986.

regions.label: South-central Vietnam: Quy Nhon, Nha Trang, Phan Thiet and the Central Highlands
regions.sub: Quy Nhon, Nha Trang, Phan Rang, Phan Thiet, Da Lat, Pleiku, Buon Ma Thuot

eras.note: Before registers. Vijaya was the Cham capital from 982 to 1471; Vietnamese forces under Le Thanh Tong devastated it in 1471 and Chams fled, many to Cambodia.

eras.polity: Champa reduced to Panduranga and Kauthara
eras.note: Early in the 16th century what remained of Champa was split into the principalities of Panduranga and Kauthara, near Nha Trang and Phan Rang.

eras.polity: Nguyen lords and the Tay Son
eras.note: Vietnam annexed Kauthara in 1653. Panduranga became a vassal state in 1697 by one account, and the Nguyen lords took the last remnants of Champa in 1693 by another.

eras.polity: Nguyen dynasty and the vassal of Panduranga
eras.note: From 1799 to 1832 the Vietnamese court chose Panduranga's kings instead of hereditary succession.

Minh Mang annexed Panduranga, the last Cham polity, in 1832 (August in the text of one account, November in another), and the Ja Thak Wa uprising of 1833-1835 was crushed. About 40,000 Chams remained in the old Panduranga in 1885.
The Treaties of Hue of 1883-1884 placed Annam under French protection, and Annam was one of the territories joined in the Indochinese Union of 17 October 1887.
A Japanese coup on 9 March 1945 ended French rule, and the State of Vietnam was created within the French Union by the Elysee Accords of 8 March 1949.
After the Geneva Accords of 1954 this ground lay south of the demarcation line, in the State of Vietnam and then the Republic of Vietnam. The fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 ended the war.
The country was reunified in 1976.

regions.label: Cochinchina: Saigon, Dong Nai and the Mekong Delta
regions.sub: Ho Chi Minh City, Can Tho, My Tho, Bien Hoa, Vung Tau, Rach Gia, Ca Mau

eras.polity: Nguyen lords' Dang Trong expands into the Mekong
eras.note: Portuguese traders coined the name Cochin-China in 1516. From about 1600 the Nguyen lords governed the south and gradually expanded into the Mekong region.

eras.polity: Trinh capture, Tay Son and Nguyen Anh
eras.note: The Trinh captured the Nguyen capital in 1774 and the Tay Son took Gia Dinh in 1777; Nguyen Phuc Anh reunified the country as Gia Long in 1802.
The Nguyen dynasty ruled the empire from Hue and fought Siam over Cambodia. French forces captured Saigon on 17 February 1859.

The Treaty of Saigon of 5 June 1862 ceded three eastern provinces and Poulo Condore to France, and in 1867 France took three more, completing the Mekong Delta. The ceded provinces were constituted a colony in 1864 by one account and 1871 by another.

Cochinchina was ruled directly as a colony within the Union of 17 October 1887, while Annam, Tonkin, Cambodia and Laos were protectorates. French colonial civil-status registers are generally held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence, with later registers at the Foreign Ministry's civil-status service in Nantes.
After the Japanese occupation and the Viet Minh uprising of 1945 France restored its control of the region.

eras.polity: State of Vietnam and South Vietnam
eras.note: Cochinchina merged into the State of Vietnam in 1949 and into South Vietnam in 1955; Saigon fell on 30 April 1975.
The country was reunified in 1976.

regions.label: Cambodia: Phnom Penh, Siem Reap and Battambang
regions.sub: Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, Battambang, Kampong Cham, Sihanoukville, Poipet

eras.note: Before registers. Jayavarman II claimed royal legitimacy at Mount Kulen in 802; Angkor Wat was built under Suryavarman II (1113-1150), and a Cham invasion sacked Angkor in 1177.

eras.polity: Post-Angkor kingdom: Chaktomuk, Longvek and Oudong
eras.note: A Siamese intervention at Angkor about 1431 began the Middle Period, and the population shifted south towards Chaktomuk, Longvek and Oudong. Siam conquered Longvek in 1594.
Oudong became the last royal residence of the period in 1601, and Siamese and Vietnamese dominance grew through the 17th and 18th centuries.

eras.polity: Joint Siamese-Vietnamese suzerainty; Battambang under Siam
eras.note: Siam annexed Battambang in 1795 and renamed it Phra Tabong, and in the early 19th century Cambodia came under joint Siamese-Vietnamese suzerainty.
King Norodom signed the French protectorate on 11 August 1863, and Cambodia joined the Indochinese Union in 1887. Battambang and the rest of Monthon Burapha stayed under Siam until 1907.

A Franco-Siamese agreement of 1907 returned Battambang and the rest of Monthon Burapha to Cambodia, and Battambang gained provincial status on 6 December 1907. Thailand took Battambang and Angkor provinces in 1940-1941 and returned them under the agreement of 16 November 1946; a Japanese coup on 9 March 1945 proclaimed a Kingdom of Kampuchea.

Sihanouk declared independence in October 1953 after a partial agreement with France, and the Geneva Conference of 1954 secured the withdrawal of Viet Minh troops. Lon Nol's coup of 18 March 1970 ousted Sihanouk.

The monarchy was abolished and the Khmer Republic proclaimed on 9 October 1970. The Khmer Rouge took Phnom Penh on 17 April 1975, beginning Democratic Kampuchea, which lasted until Vietnamese forces captured the city on 7 January 1979.

eras.polity: People's Republic of Kampuchea and the Kingdom of Cambodia
eras.note: The People's Republic of Kampuchea followed in 1979. The Paris Peace Agreements of 1991-1993 led to UN administration and an election in 1993.

regions.label: Laos: Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Savannakhet and Pakse
regions.sub: Vientiane, Luang Prabang, Savannakhet, Pakse, Thakhek, Phonsavan

eras.note: Before registers. Lan Xang was founded about 1353 (the date is given as 1353, 1354 or 1357 in different places).
Lan Xang split into Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champasak in 1707; Champasak is dated 1713 in some accounts.
Siam took Vientiane in 1778-1779 and imposed a suzerainty that lasted until 1893.
Anouvong's rebellion failed in 1826-1828, and Siam destroyed Vientiane and forcibly moved its population.

The Franco-Siamese crisis of 1893 led Siam to cede its Lao territories east of the Mekong to France; the protectorate of Laos was established in 1893 or 1899 depending on the account. The Franco-Thai War ran from 1940 to 1941.

eras.polity: Japanese-backed state, Lao Issara and the Kingdom of Laos
eras.note: A Japanese-backed state under King Sisavangvong was set up in 1945 and the Lao Issara government was declared in October 1945. The Franco-Lao General Convention of 1949 created a quasi-independent Kingdom of Laos, and the treaty of 22 October 1953 transferred the remaining French powers; the Archives nationales d'outre-mer hold the files of the French commissariats for 1945-1954.

eras.polity: Royal Lao Government and civil war
eras.note: The Laotian Civil War ran from 1959 to 1975.
The king abdicated and the Lao People's Democratic Republic was established on 2 December 1975.

regions.label: Northwest Malaysia: Kedah, Perlis, Penang and Perak
regions.sub: Alor Setar, George Town, Ipoh, Taiping, Kangar, Langkawi, Butterworth

eras.polity: Malay sultanates of Kedah and Perak
eras.note: Before registers. The Perak Sultanate was established about 1528 by a son of the last ruler of Malacca, and the Dutch East India Company won exclusive tin-trade rights in a treaty of 1653 with Perak and Aceh.

eras.polity: Penang and Province Wellesley under the East India Company
eras.note: Francis Light took formal possession of Penang for the East India Company on 11 August 1786, and a treaty of 7 July 1800 gave Britain Province Wellesley (Seberang Perai) on the mainland. Penang became a separate presidency of British India in 1805.

eras.polity: Penang in the Straits Settlements; Kedah under Siam; Perak a Malay sultanate
eras.note: Siam invaded and annexed Kedah in November 1821 and the sultan was restored in 1842. Penang, Malacca and Singapore formed the Straits Settlements in 1826, the year Perak ceded Dindings and Pangkor to Britain after an attack from Ligor.

eras.polity: Perak under a British Resident; the Federated Malay States
eras.note: The Pangkor Treaty of 20 January 1874 introduced a British Resident in Perak, and the Resident, J.W.W. Birch, was assassinated in 1875, prompting the Perak War of 1875-1876. Perak joined the Federated Malay States in 1895 or 1896, while Kedah and Perlis remained under Siam until 1909.

eras.polity: Kedah and Perlis under British advisers; Perak in the FMS; Penang a Crown colony settlement
eras.note: On 9 July 1909 the Anglo-Siamese Treaty made Kedah a British protectorate, and the Straits Settlements, including Penang, had been a Crown colony since 1 April 1867.
Japan invaded in December 1941 and occupied Penang until British forces returned in September 1945. Kedah was annexed by Thailand on 18 October 1943.

eras.polity: Malayan Union and Federation of Malaya
eras.note: The Straits Settlements were dissolved on 1 April 1946 and Penang joined the Malayan Union; the Federation of Malaya followed in 1948 and became independent on 31 August 1957.

Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963. FamilySearch dates civil registration here from 1859, with coverage of about 10 percent before 1980; registration became compulsory in 1961 for everyone except Muslims, and the National Registration Department holds the records in each state.

regions.label: Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Negeri Sembilan and Malacca
regions.sub: Kuala Lumpur, Klang, Shah Alam, Seremban, Malacca, Port Dickson

eras.note: Before registers. Selangor was under the Malacca Sultanate in the 15th century.
Portugal held Malacca from 1511 to 1641, and Selangor came under the Johor Sultanate after the fall of Malacca.
The Dutch East India Company took Malacca on 14 January 1641 with Johor's help. In 1766 Raja Salehuddin founded the present Selangor Sultanate at Kuala Selangor.

eras.polity: British occupation, Dutch restoration, transfer to Britain
eras.note: Britain administered Malacca from 1795 and Dutch rule was fully regained in 1818; the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 permanently ceded Malacca to Britain, effective 1 March 1825.

eras.polity: Malacca in the Straits Settlements; Selangor civil war
eras.note: Malacca joined the Straits Settlements in 1826, which became a Crown colony on 1 April 1867. The Selangor Civil War of 1867-1874 was fought partly over tin revenue.

eras.polity: British Residents and the Federated Malay States
eras.note: Selangor accepted a British Resident in 1874; Klang was the colonial capital from 1875 until 1880, when it moved to Kuala Lumpur. The Federated Malay States, with Kuala Lumpur as capital, took effect on 1 July 1896.
Japan invaded in December 1941 and occupied the Federated Malay States by January 1942 until its surrender in September 1945.

eras.polity: Malayan Union and Federation of Malaya
eras.note: The FMS was dissolved on 1 April 1946 into the Malayan Union, which included Malacca after the Straits Settlements were dissolved. The Federation of Malaya followed in 1948 and independence on 31 August 1957.
Malaysia was formed in 1963. Selangor ceded Kuala Lumpur to the federal government in 1974, and Shah Alam became the state capital.

regions.label: Johor
regions.sub: Johor Bahru, Muar, Batu Pahat, Kluang, Segamat, Pontian

eras.note: Before registers. The Johor Sultanate was founded in 1528 after the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511.

eras.polity: Johor after the Dutch capture of Malacca
eras.note: Johor and the Dutch East India Company captured Malacca from the Portuguese in 1641.
The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 set the borders of the modern peninsula.

eras.polity: Johor under the 1885 treaty with Britain
eras.note: The Anglo-Johor Treaty of 1885 formalised close ties with Britain and gave the state its present boundary. The Johor State Constitution of 1895 was the first written constitution among the Malay states.

eras.polity: Unfederated Malay State with a British Adviser
eras.note: Johor accepted a resident British Adviser in 1914 and was one of the five Unfederated Malay States.
Japanese forces occupied Johor in 1942 during the Second World War.

eras.polity: Malayan Union and Federation of Malaya
eras.note: Johor joined the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948; Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957.
Malaysia was formed on 16 September 1963 with Johor as a state.

regions.label: East coast: Kelantan, Terengganu and Pahang
regions.sub: Kota Bharu, Kuala Terengganu, Kuantan, Kuala Lipis, Temerloh, Pekan

eras.polity: Kelantan, a trading centre and Malacca vassal
eras.note: Before registers. Kelantan was an important trading centre around 1411 and became a vassal of the Malacca Sultanate in 1499.
After Malacca fell in 1511 local chieftains ruled Kelantan, and by the early 17th century they were subject to Patani.

eras.polity: Kelantan sultanate; Siamese rights over Kelantan and Terengganu until 1909
eras.note: Long Yunus unified Kelantan about 1760, Long Muhammad became Sultan Muhammad I in 1800, and Kota Bharu was built from 1844 under Muhammad II. Siam held rights over Kelantan and Terengganu until it transferred them to Britain in 1909.

eras.polity: Pahang in the Federated Malay States
eras.note: Pahang joined the Federated Malay States, formed by treaty effective 1 July 1896, while Kelantan and Terengganu remained under Siamese rights.

eras.polity: Kelantan and Terengganu under British advisers
eras.note: Under the Bangkok Treaty of 1909 Siam transferred its rights over Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis to Britain, and Kelantan became an Unfederated Malay State with a British adviser.
Japanese forces landed in Kelantan on 8 December 1941, and in 1943 Japan transferred the state to Thailand; it returned to Malayan control in 1945.

eras.polity: Malayan Union and Federation of Malaya
eras.note: Kelantan joined the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948; independence came on 31 August 1957.
Malaysia was formed in 1963.

regions.label: Singapore
regions.sub: Singapore, Jurong, Changi, Tuas, Woodlands

eras.note: Raffles arrived on 28 January 1819 and the Treaty of Singapore was signed on 6 February 1819. A second treaty of 7 June 1823 extended British possession over most of the island, and in 1824 it was ceded in perpetuity to the East India Company; the first census that year counted 10,683 people.
Singapore joined Penang and Malacca as the Straits Settlements in 1826, and the capital moved from George Town to Singapore in 1832. Control passed to the British Raj in 1858.

eras.polity: Crown colony of the Straits Settlements
eras.note: The Straits Settlements became a separate Crown colony on 1 April 1867; their population was about 572,000 in 1901 and reached about 1.37 million by 1939.
Allied forces surrendered to Japan on 15 February 1942 and the occupation lasted until 1945.
The Straits Settlements were dissolved on 1 April 1946 and Singapore became a separate Crown colony. The People's Action Party won the elections of May 1959 under Lee Kuan Yew.
The Malaysia Agreement was signed on 9 July 1963, and the federation formed on 16 September 1963 included Singapore until 1965.
Singapore became an independent republic on 9 August 1965.

regions.label: Brunei Darussalam
regions.sub: Bandar Seri Begawan, Kuala Belait, Seria, Tutong, Muara

eras.note: Before registers. Spanish forces captured Brunei in April 1578 and held it for 72 days before returning to Manila on 26 June.

eras.polity: Sultanate and the Brooke Rajahs of Sarawak
eras.note: James Brooke was made Rajah of Sarawak in September 1841 after helping the sultan against a rebellion, and open conflict in 1843 ended in the sultan's defeat. Sarawak expanded along the coast, taking Bintulu in 1861 and Trusan in 1884.
The Protectorate Agreement was signed on 17 September 1888, and in 1890 Charles Brooke annexed Limbang from Brunei to Sarawak.
The Supplementary Treaty of 1905-1906 established a British Resident with substantial authority. Crude oil was first found in 1909 and major strikes followed in 1927.
Japan occupied Brunei from 1941, the sultan's role became largely symbolic, and Australian forces liberated Brunei in June 1945.
The first oil platform was built at Seria in 1952.
Brunei's first written constitution was signed and proclaimed on 29 September 1959, ending British control over internal affairs; independence came on 1 January 1984.
Brunei became independent on 1 January 1984.

regions.label: Sarawak
regions.sub: Kuching, Sibu, Miri, Bintulu, Sri Aman, Limbang

eras.polity: Brunei sultanate and a short-lived Sarawak sultanate
eras.note: Before registers. Brunei conquered Santubong in 1512, and a Sarawak sultanate under a Bruneian prince ran from 1599 to 1641 before it was absorbed back into Brunei. Iban people migrated from the Kapuas region into Sarawak from the 1750s.
In September 1841 Brunei's Pengiran Muda Hashim gave James Brooke the title of Rajah. The Brookes ruled Sarawak until 1946 and added Bintulu in 1861 and Trusan in 1884.

eras.polity: British protectorate under the Brooke Rajahs
eras.note: Sarawak became a British protectorate in 1888, and the Brookes added Limbang in 1890 and Lawas in 1905.
Japan invaded in December 1941 and occupied Sarawak for about three years and eight months; the Japanese surrendered in September 1945.
Charles Vyner Brooke ceded Sarawak to Britain and it became a Crown colony on 1 July 1946, which sparked an anti-cession movement. Self-government came on 22 July 1963.
Sarawak joined the Federation of Malaysia on 16 September 1963. A communist insurgency ran from 1960 to 1990, ending in a peace agreement in October 1990.

regions.label: Sabah and Labuan
regions.sub: Kota Kinabalu, Sandakan, Tawau, Lahad Datu, Kudat, Labuan

eras.polity: Territory claimed by the Sultanates of Brunei and Sulu
eras.note: Before registers. In 1877-1878 Gustav Overbeck obtained land concessions here from the Sultanates of Brunei and Sulu.

Overbeck passed the concessions to Alfred Dent, whose North Borneo Provisional Association received a royal charter in 1881 and was replaced by the Chartered Company in 1882. The capital was Kudat from 1881 to 1884, then Sandakan.
Spain's claim was settled by the Madrid Protocol of 1885 and Britain made North Borneo a protectorate in May 1888. Labuan joined the Straits Settlements in 1907.
Japan invaded in January 1942 and held the territory until Allied liberation in 1945, followed by a British Military Administration.
The Chartered Company ceded North Borneo to the Crown on 15 July 1946; Jesselton (now Kota Kinabalu) became the capital, and Labuan was attached to North Borneo.
North Borneo became part of Malaysia in 1963 as Sabah; the new federation was formed on 16 September 1963.

regions.label: Timor-Leste
regions.sub: Dili, Baucau, Lospalos, Maliana, Suai, Same

eras.note: Portuguese traders first arrived about 1512-1515 and Dominican friars began missionary work in 1556, settling in Solor.
The Portuguese administration moved from Lifau to Dili in 1769.

eras.polity: Portuguese Timor and the Dutch border
eras.note: The Treaty of Lisbon of 1859 set the border between Portuguese Timor and the Dutch East Indies, and the Hague arbitration of 1914 drew the definitive border that is still Timor-Leste's boundary with Indonesia.

eras.polity: Japanese occupation and the end of Portuguese rule
eras.note: Japan occupied Timor in February 1942 and Portuguese rule resumed after Japan's surrender. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974 Portugal abandoned the colony, and Fretilin declared independence on 28 November 1975.
Indonesia invaded on 7 December 1975, and East Timor became its 27th province on 17 July 1976.
A UN-sponsored referendum on 30 August 1999 produced a 78.5 percent vote for independence, and the UN Transitional Administration was established on 25 October 1999.
Timor-Leste became formally independent on 20 May 2002.

regions.label: The Gambia — Banjul and the river
regions.sub: Banjul, Serekunda, Brikama, Farafenni, Bakau

eras.polity: Mali Empire vassal states on the Gambia; Portuguese traders
eras.note: Before registers. Mali expanded into the Gambia valley in the 13th century and its vassal Kaabu was founded; Portuguese ships reached the river mouth in 1455.

eras.polity: Courland, Dutch and then English forts at James Island; Royal African Company
eras.note: The Duke of Courland obtained St Andrew's Island in 1651 and the Dutch West India Company took over in 1659; the English under Robert Holmes seized the fort in 1661 and renamed it James Fort. Senegambia was a British colony administered from St Louis from 1766 to 1783, when Britain ceded St Louis and Gorée to France.

Bathurst, now Banjul, was founded in 1816 by Alexander Grant after a treaty with the King of Kombo. The Colonial Office correspondence for the Gambia, 1828 to 1951, is series CO 87 at The National Archives, Kew.

eras.polity: Colony and Protectorate of the Gambia
eras.note: The Gambia became a separate colony in 1888, an 1889 agreement delimited the Gambia, Senegal and Casamance, and the Colony and Protectorate was established in 1894. A Protectorate Ordinance followed in 1902.

eras.polity: Independent Gambia, a Commonwealth monarchy then a republic
eras.note: Independence came on 18 February 1965 and the country became a republic on 24 April 1970. Births and deaths are now registered through the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare in Banjul and marriages through the Registrar General's Department.
The 1982 Treaty of Confederation joined the Gambia with Senegal; the Gambia withdrew in 1989.

regions.label: Senegal — Dakar, Saint-Louis, Kaolack and the interior
regions.sub: Dakar, Saint-Louis, Thiès, Touba, Kaolack, Tambacounda

eras.polity: Jolof Empire and its tributaries Kajoor, Baol and Waalo
eras.note: Before registers. The Jolof Empire dates from the 14th century and reportedly collapsed around 1550; the Portuguese reached Gorée in 1444 and built a chapel there in 1481.

eras.polity: French trading posts at Saint-Louis and Gorée
eras.note: Saint-Louis was founded in 1659. Gorée passed from the Dutch West India Company (which bought it in 1627) to France in 1677; Britain took Saint-Louis in 1758, France retook it in 1779, the 1783 Treaty of Versailles confirmed French possession, and Britain occupied it again from 1809 to 1816.

eras.polity: Colony of Senegal and the Four Communes
eras.note: The Four Communes (Saint-Louis, Dakar, Gorée, Rufisque) had residents with French citizenship rights from 1848, and the originaires received full voting rights in 1916. The colony of Senegal is dated 1817 to 1946, and Blaise Diagne became the first African deputy in 1914.

eras.polity: Senegal in French West Africa, federal capital Saint-Louis then Dakar
eras.note: French West Africa was formed on 27 October 1895 with Saint-Louis as capital; Dakar replaced it in 1902. Civil registration for Senegal is dated from 1730, with registration offices in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and copies of much of the colonial-period registration are at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

eras.polity: Senegal as an overseas territory; Mali Federation
eras.note: The 1946 Loi Lamine Guèye granted limited citizenship rights to natives of the African colonies. Senegal and French Sudan formed the Mali Federation in 1959, which became independent on 20 June 1960 and dissolved on 20 August 1960.
Independence is commemorated on 4 April 1960, the date of the transfer-of-power agreement; the Republic of Senegal was formally proclaimed on 5 September 1960.

regions.label: Casamance — Ziguinchor, Kolda and Sédhiou
regions.sub: Ziguinchor, Kolda, Sédhiou, Bignona, Vélingara

eras.polity: Bainuk Kasa kingdom and Jola chiefdoms; Portuguese traders
eras.note: Before registers. A Portuguese trading station was set up in the 15th century, dealing with Jola chiefs and the king of Kasa; the Bainuk Kasa kingdom was the dominant state of Lower Casamance from the 15th to the 18th century.

eras.polity: Portuguese Ziguinchor (Portuguese Guinea); French Carabane from 1836
eras.note: The Portuguese founded Ziguinchor in 1645 and France acquired Carabane in 1836. Negotiations after the Berlin Conference (1885) fixed the boundary between French Senegal and Portuguese Guinea, dated 1888, and Portugal lost Casamance.

eras.polity: Casamance as part of French Senegal
eras.note: Casamance lay inside French Senegal from 1888 and inside French West Africa from its formation in 1895. Civil registration for Senegal is dated from 1730, and copies of much of the colonial-period registration are at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.

eras.polity: Republic of Senegal — Casamance independence movement
eras.note: The Movement of Democratic Forces of Casamance (MFDC) was founded in 1982 and its armed wing in 1985; a low-level insurgency against the government dates from 1990.

regions.label: Guinea-Bissau — Bissau, Bafatá and Gabú
regions.sub: Bissau, Bafatá, Gabú, Cacheu, Bolama

eras.polity: Portuguese Guinea, a dependency of Cape Verde
eras.note: Cacheu was founded in 1588 and Bissau in 1687; the territory was a dependency of Portuguese Cape Verde until 1879. Bolama was the capital from 1852, and Britain and Portugal went to arbitration over it in 1868 to 1870, when President Grant awarded it to Portugal.

It became a separate colony in 1879 and Bissau replaced Bolama as capital in 1942. Negotiations with France after 1885 settled the boundaries and Casamance went to France; the Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino in Lisbon holds a Guinea series, including correspondence sent to Guinea in 1892 to 1910.
It was renamed an overseas province in 1951. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 and adopted guerrilla tactics in 1961.

eras.polity: Republic declared by the PAIGC at Madina do Boé
eras.note: The PAIGC declared independence at Madina do Boé on 24 September 1973; the Algiers accord followed the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974.
Portugal recognised the PAIGC government on 26 August 1974 and independence is dated 10 September 1974.

regions.label: Guinea — Conakry, Futa Jallon and Upper Guinea
regions.sub: Conakry, Kindia, Labé, Kankan, Siguiri, Faranah

eras.note: Before registers. The Fulani imamate of Futa Jallon is dated 1735 to 1898, with a written constitution and alternating rulers.
Rivières du Sud was established as a colony in 1882 and was first administered as part of the colony of Senegal.

eras.polity: French Guinea colony; conquest of Samori Touré's Wassoulou Empire
eras.note: French Guinea was established as a colony in 1891 and French West Africa was formed in 1895. Samori Touré's Wassoulou Empire, dated 1878 to 1898, held the Malinké area of Upper Guinea.

eras.polity: French Guinea in French West Africa
eras.note: French control was secured by the defeat of Samori's armies in 1898. French overseas civil registration for Guinea, 1867 to 1915, is online as index and images from the Archives nationales d'outre-mer.

eras.polity: Republic of Guinea under Sékou Touré
eras.note: Guinea voted overwhelmingly for independence in a referendum on 28 September 1958 and proclaimed it on 2 October 1958. Sékou Touré ruled until his death on 26 March 1984.
Mayors are the registration authority for births, marriages and deaths.

regions.label: Southern Mali — Bamako, Ségou, Sikasso and Kayes
regions.sub: Bamako, Sikasso, Ségou, Kayes, Koutiala, Kati

eras.note: Before registers. The Mali Empire is dated from 1230 or about 1235, and the Battle of Kirina was in 1235; Songhai under Sunni Ali asserted independence in the 15th century and lost to Moroccan forces at Tondibi on 13 March 1591.

eras.polity: Bambara kingdoms of Ségou and Kaarta
eras.note: Before registers. The Bambara Empire at Ségou is dated 1712 to 1861; the Kingdom of Kaarta was founded in 1753 and was defeated by Umar Tall in 1854.
Umar Tall's forces took Ségou on 10 March 1861 and the Toucouleur Empire is dated from 1864. Kénédougou moved its capital to Sikasso in 1876.

eras.polity: French military posts of the Upper River; French Sudan
eras.note: The Upper River military posts date from 1880, Kayes fort from 1881, and the territory was named French Sudan on 18 August 1890. The Toucouleur Empire's rule ended with the French conquest in 1890, Kénédougou fell to the French in 1898, and Samori Ture's Wassoulou Empire (1878 to 1898) ended the same year; the colony was reorganised as Senegambia and Niger in 1902.
The colony was renamed Upper Senegal and Niger in 1904 and its capital moved from Kayes to Bamako in 1908.

eras.polity: French Sudan in French West Africa
eras.note: The name French Sudan returned in 1921. When Upper Volta was dissolved in 1933 its northern territory was added to French Sudan; Upper Volta was re-established in 1947 and French Sudan's borders then became those of present-day Mali.

eras.polity: Sudanese Republic and the Mali Federation
eras.note: The Sudanese Republic was declared on 24 November 1958 with internal autonomy. The Mali Federation with Senegal was formed in April 1959 and became independent on 20 June 1960; it was dissolved on 20 August 1960.

The Republic of Mali was proclaimed after Senegal withdrew, dated after 22 September 1960. French-period registers for 1864 to 1917 are indexed and imaged online by the Archives nationales, and the National Directorate of Civil Status is at Kati.

regions.label: Northern Mali — Mopti, Timbuktu, Gao and Kidal
regions.sub: Mopti, Timbuktu, Gao, Djenné, Kidal, Douentza

eras.note: Before registers. Timbuktu became part of the Mali Empire in the early 14th century and Mansa Musa's visit is dated to about 1325; Tuareg control in the first half of the 15th century was brief.
Before registers. The Songhai Empire absorbed Timbuktu in 1468, with Gao as its capital, until the Moroccan victory at Tondibi on 13 March 1591.

eras.polity: Moroccan occupation and the Arma of Timbuktu
eras.note: Moroccan forces controlled Gao, Timbuktu and Djenné after 1591; the Arma ruling class became virtually independent of Morocco after 1612, and Moroccan control waned in the late 18th century.

eras.polity: Massina state and the Toucouleur Empire
eras.note: An uprising in the Inner Niger Delta established the Massina state in 1818, which the Toucouleur Empire defeated in 1862. The Toucouleur Empire ruled most of present-day Mali until the French conquest in 1890, and the French took over Timbuktu in 1893.

eras.polity: French Sudan (Upper Senegal and Niger 1904 to 1921)
eras.note: Timbuktu was incorporated into French Sudan, which was renamed Upper Senegal and Niger in 1904 and French Sudan again in 1921. Independence came as the Republic of Mali, dated after 22 September 1960.
The Tuareg insurgency in the north was suppressed in 1962 to 1964, and another rebellion in 1990 to 1991 ended with a peace accord in January 1991.

eras.polity: Republic of Mali — northern occupation and retaking
eras.note: Tuareg rebels (MNLA) and Ansar Dine captured Timbuktu on 1 April 2012, and French and Malian troops retook it on 28 January 2013.

regions.label: Burkina Faso — Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso and the Mossi plateau
regions.sub: Ouagadougou, Bobo-Dioulasso, Koudougou, Ouahigouya, Fada N'gourma

eras.note: Before registers. The Mossi Kingdoms were founded from about the 11th century and ruled the central region until the end of the 19th century.

The French claimed the area in 1896 and Mossi resistance ended with the capture of Ouagadougou in 1901. French overseas civil registration for 1897 to 1914 is online as index and images from the Archives nationales.
Provinces of Ivory Coast were united as French Upper Volta in 1919; another account dates the separation from French Sudan to 1921.

eras.polity: Upper Volta divided between neighbouring colonies
eras.note: The colony was split up in 1932 for economic reasons and its territory was parcelled out to neighbouring colonies; French Sudan received the northern part, a transfer dated 1933 in one account. Records of these years may sit in a neighbouring colony's series.
Upper Volta became a territory of French West Africa again on 4 September 1947 and an autonomous republic in the French Community on 11 December 1958.
France agreed to full independence on 11 July 1960 and the Republic of Upper Volta declared it on 5 August 1960.

The country was renamed Burkina Faso on 2 August 1984, confirmed by the National Assembly on 4 August. Civil registration is run through the Directorate of Civil Registration in Ouagadougou and the mayors.

regions.label: Niger — Niamey, Maradi, Zinder and Agadez
regions.sub: Niamey, Maradi, Zinder, Tahoua, Agadez, Dosso

eras.polity: Sultanate of Agadez; Songhai Empire in the west
eras.note: Before registers. The Sultanate of Agadez was founded in 1449 and conquered by the Songhai Empire in 1500; Songhai controlled parts of Niger in the 15th and 16th centuries.

eras.polity: Sultanate of Damagaram at Zinder; Sokoto Caliphate over Hausa lands
eras.note: Zinder was made capital of the Sultanate of Damagaram in 1736. The Fulani Empire of Sokoto gained control of much of the Hausa territory in the late 18th century, and the Bornu Empire ended in 1893.

Lt. Pallier of the Voulet-Chanoine mission occupied Zinder in July 1899. The first French post at Niamey was set up in 1901, Niamey became the territorial capital in 1903, and the capital returned to Zinder in 1911.

eras.polity: Colony of Niger in French West Africa
eras.note: Niger became a colony in 1922 and the capital moved from Zinder to Niamey on 28 December 1926. French-period civil registers are held at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence.
Niger declared independence on 3 August 1960 under Prime Minister Hamani Diori, who was elected first President in November 1960. Mayors are responsible for civil registration in their areas.

regions.label: Mauritania — Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, Rosso and the Hodhs
regions.sub: Nouakchott, Nouadhibou, Rosso, Kaédi, Kiffa, Atar

eras.polity: Berber confederations of the Almoravid movement; gum arabic trade
eras.note: Before registers. The Almoravid movement arose among Berber confederations in the 11th century, and trade in gum arabic dominated from the 15th to the 19th century.

eras.polity: French sovereignty over the Senegal River and Mauritanian coast
eras.note: France's sovereignty over the Senegal River and the Mauritanian coast was recognised at the Congress of Vienna in 1815; conquest of the interior began in 1900.
Mauritania became part of French West Africa in 1904. French-period births, marriages and deaths for 1895 to 1917 are held as images at Geneanet.

eras.polity: Colony of Mauritania, administered from Saint-Louis
eras.note: Saint-Louis in Senegal was the capital of the colony of Mauritania from 1920 to 1957, so the colony was run from outside the present border.

France agreed to independence on 28 July 1960 and Mauritania declared it on 28 November 1960. Nouakchott was founded around independence on the site of a colonial-era village, the Ksar; civil registration is run by the National Agency for the Register of Population and Secure Documents in Nouakchott.

regions.label: Western Sahara — Laayoune, Dakhla and Smara
regions.sub: Laayoune, Dakhla, Smara, Boujdour, Aousserd

eras.polity: Spanish protectorate of Río de Oro
eras.note: Spain declared a protectorate over Río de Oro, Cape Blanc and Angra de Cintra in December 1884, ratified at the Berlin Conference. Villa Cisneros (today's Dakhla) was the capital from 1884 to 1940, and the Treaty of Paris of 27 June 1900 defined the border with French Mauritania.
Spain occupied Daora on 1 May 1934 and Smara on 15 May 1934. El Aaiún was founded in 1940 and was the capital until 1976; Spanish West Africa (with Cape Juby and Ifni) is dated 1946 or 1947.
Río de Oro and Saguia el-Hamra became the Province of the Sahara in 1958; Cape Juby was ceded to Morocco that year and Ifni in 1969. The Polisario Front formed in 1973.

eras.polity: Spanish withdrawal; Moroccan and Mauritanian control
eras.note: Spain signed the Madrid Accords on 14 November 1975 and withdrew; Morocco and Mauritania took control in 1976 and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 27 February 1976. Mauritania annexed the southern third as Tiris al-Gharbiyya in 1975.

eras.polity: Disputed territory — Morocco and the Polisario Front
eras.note: Mauritania relinquished its claim in 1979. A UN-negotiated ceasefire came in 1991 and a referendum has not been held.

regions.label: Benin — Cotonou, Porto-Novo, Abomey and Parakou
regions.sub: Cotonou, Porto-Novo, Abomey, Ouidah, Parakou, Natitingou

eras.polity: Allada and Hueda (Whydah); early Dahomey on the Abomey plateau
eras.note: Before registers. Dahomey was founded about 1600 on the Abomey plateau by Aja settlers from Allada; King Agaja conquered Allada in 1724 and Whydah (Ouidah) in 1727. A French trading lodge was set up at Savi, the Hueda capital, in 1671 and the English Royal African Company moved its base there in 1682.

Dahomey was a tributary of the Oyo Empire from the 1730s (the start is dated between 1728 and 1748 depending on the source) until Ghezo broke Oyo's control (dated 1823 or 1827). Porto-Novo, a Dahomean tributary, became a French protectorate in 1863; Dahomey lost the First Franco-Dahomean War in 1890, ceding Porto-Novo and Cotonou, and Béhanzin surrendered in 1894 after the second war.

eras.polity: French protectorate, then colony of Dahomey
eras.note: The kingdom was disestablished in 1904 and became the French colony of Dahomey; French Dahomey is dated from 1894 in some accounts. Civil registration began in 1933, mainly for French citizens and foreigners; French overseas civil registration for Dahomey, 1889 to 1918, is held by the Archives nationales d'outre-mer with images online.

In 1946 Dahomey became an overseas territory with its own parliament and representation in the French national assembly. It became the Republic of Dahomey on 4 December 1958 and independent on 1 August 1960; by 1950 registration covered most residents within about 24 km of a registration centre.
Military coups took place in 1963 and 1972.
The country was renamed the People's Republic of Benin in 1975, and the People's Revolutionary Party held power until the early 1990s.

A national conference in 1990 introduced a democratic constitution and the Republic of Benin was established. Death registration is indexed for 1891 to 2014 with images, and the Archives Nationales du Bénin are at Porto-Novo.

regions.label: Togo — Lomé, Kpalimé, Sokodé and Kara
regions.sub: Lomé, Aného, Kpalimé, Sokodé, Kara, Dapaong

eras.polity: Slave Coast; Ewe, Mina and Guin settlements
eras.note: Before registers. Portuguese explorers sailed the coast in 1471 to 1473, and for about 200 years afterward it was a major European slave-trading centre, the Slave Coast.

Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty with Mlapa III on 5 July 1884 and the capitals were Bagida (1884 to 1887), Sebe (1887 to 1897) and Lomé from 1897. It became the colony of Togoland in 1905, when the Lomé to Aného railway opened.
Anglo-French forces invaded on 7 August 1914 and the colony surrendered on 26 August 1914. On 27 December 1916 the territory was split into British and French zones.

eras.polity: French Togoland, a League of Nations mandate
eras.note: A League of Nations Class B mandate took effect on 20 July 1922; French Togoland was about two-thirds of the former colony, and Lomé was transferred to France on 1 October 1920.

eras.polity: French Togoland, an autonomous republic from 1955
eras.note: A 1955 statute made French Togoland an autonomous republic and a 1956 referendum approved its constitution. British Togoland voted in a May 1956 plebiscite to join Ghana and was integrated in 1957, so the western part of the former German colony is Ghanaian.

Togo became independent on 27 April 1960, ending the UN trusteeship. Vital events are declared to mayors or delegates in municipalities, and the Ministry of Justice and Legislation in Lomé is the office to contact.

regions.label: Southern Côte d'Ivoire — Abidjan, Grand-Bassam and the Agni kingdoms
regions.sub: Abidjan, Grand-Bassam, Bingerville, Agboville, Abengourou, Aboisso

eras.polity: Agni kingdoms of Sanwi and Indénié
eras.note: Before registers. The Agni kingdoms of Sanwi and Indénié were established in the mid-18th century by Akan groups fleeing the Ashanti Empire.

eras.polity: French protectorate at Grand-Bassam and Assinie
eras.note: In 1843 to 1844 Admiral Bouët-Willaumez signed treaties with the kings of Grand-Bassam and Assini, and the first French posts were at Assinie and Grand-Bassam. Civil registration for Côte d'Ivoire is dated from 1843.

eras.polity: Colony of Côte d'Ivoire — capital Grand-Bassam, then Bingerville
eras.note: Côte d'Ivoire became a French colony on 10 March 1893 with Louis-Gustave Binger as first governor. The capital was Grand-Bassam (1893 to 1896) and then Bingerville.

eras.polity: Colony of Côte d'Ivoire — capital Abidjan
eras.note: Abidjan was the capital from 1934 to 1960. Civil status acts were drawn up in duplicate, one for the commune and one for the tribunal, and a third copy went to the colonial depot whose holdings are now at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence; French overseas registration for 1843 to 1918 is online as images.

France agreed to independence on 11 July 1960 and it took effect on 7 August 1960 in one account (13 August in another). Death records for 1931 to 2014 are indexed with images, and civil registration now falls under the Ministry of the Interior and Decentralization.

eras.polity: Republic of Côte d'Ivoire — divided by rebellion from 2002
eras.note: A rebellion that began on 19 September 2002 divided the country, and the UN established UNOCI in February 2004; fighting over the 2010 presidential election ended in April 2011.

regions.label: Central and northern Côte d'Ivoire — Bouaké, Yamoussoukro, Korhogo and Odienné
regions.sub: Bouaké, Yamoussoukro, Korhogo, Odienné, Séguéla, Bouna

eras.polity: Gyaman, the Baoulé kingdom and the Kong state
eras.note: Before registers. Gyaman was founded around 1690; Seku Watara took power at Kong in the early 1700s and died around 1745; and Akan groups fleeing the Ashanti Empire founded a Baoulé kingdom in the mid-18th century.
Samori Touré built an empire from 1878 over parts of present-day Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso and Ivory Coast, and was captured in 1898.

Provinces of the colony were united as Upper Volta in 1919 and that colony was dissolved in 1932, so interwar records for the north should be checked in both colonies' series. The Archives nationales d'outre-mer in Aix-en-Provence hold copies of much of the 1843 to 1960 registration.
Houphouët-Boigny became first president in 1960 and led the ruling PDCI until his death on 7 December 1993.

eras.polity: Republic of Côte d'Ivoire — divided by rebellion
eras.note: A rebellion that began on 19 September 2002 divided the country, and the UN established UNOCI in February 2004.
Fighting that followed the 2010 presidential election ended on 11 April 2011.

regions.label: Western Côte d'Ivoire — Daloa, Gagnoa, San-Pédro and Man
regions.sub: Daloa, Gagnoa, San-Pédro, Man, Soubré, Sassandra

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: French treaties on the east coast
eras.note: The French treaties of 1843 to 1844 were made with the kings of Grand-Bassam and Assini, on the east coast.
The colony was proclaimed on 10 March 1893. Samori Touré's empire, which extended over parts of present-day Ivory Coast, ended with his capture in 1898.

eras.polity: Colony of Côte d'Ivoire — capital Abidjan
eras.note: Abidjan was the capital from 1934 to 1960.

eras.polity: Republic of Côte d'Ivoire — divided by rebellion from 2002
eras.note: A rebellion that began on 19 September 2002 divided the country; fighting after the 2010 presidential election ended in April 2011.

regions.label: Além São Francisco - the Bahia lands on the middle São Francisco
regions.sub: Casa Nova, Remanso, Pilão Arcado, Santa Rita de Cássia, Formosa do Rio Preto, Buritirama

eras.polity: Captaincy of Pernambuco - the São Francisco sertão
eras.note: An arraial at Pilão Arcado is dated to the late 17th century and was founded by order of the viceroy D. João de Lencastre, against attacks by the Mocoazes and Acoroazes on cattle ranches.

eras.polity: Pernambuco - Comarca do Rio de São Francisco
eras.note: The Vila do Pilão Arcado was created in 1810 in the lands of the Captaincy of Pernambuco, within the Comarca do Rio de São Francisco.

eras.polity: Minas Gerais (provisional) - Comarca do Rio de São Francisco
eras.note: After the Confederação do Equador in 1824 the comarca was separated from Pernambuco and provisionally placed under the province of Minas Gerais. The trap: three years of this ground's paper belong to a third province, neither Pernambuco nor Bahia.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - Province of Bahia (Além São Francisco)
eras.note: From 1827 all of Além São Francisco, the lands beyond the river, was administered by Bahia. In 1857 Pilão Arcado was extinguished as a municipality and absorbed into the Vila de Nossa Senhora do Remanso de Pilão Arcado; Casa Nova (São José do Riacho de Casa Nova, grown on the salt trade) was created out of Remanso by provincial law, with 20 June 1879 given as its date.

Pilão Arcado was separated from Remanso again in 1890 (emancipation dated 15 January 1890 in one listing, elevation to city on 31 October 1890 in the text). A law of 1850 required civil registration of births and deaths nationally, and Catholic parish registers continue alongside the civil books, so search both.

eras.polity: Brazil - State of Bahia, the Sobradinho reservoir
eras.note: In 1974 Decreto-lei 1.316 made Casa Nova a municipality of national-security interest, with an appointed mayor until 1985. The town of Casa Nova was relocated in 1976 because of the Sobradinho dam.

regions.label: Ceará's north-west coast - Acaraú and Itarema, Tremembé country
regions.sub: Acaraú, Itarema, Almofala

eras.note: Before registers. The Tremembé held the Acaraú delta before the Portuguese arrived.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Ceará, a dependency of Pernambuco
eras.note: In 1690 Jesuits settled Tremembé people at the river mouth, and the mission was later moved east to Almofala, now in Itarema. Portuguese settlement began in the 17th century with refugees from the Dutch wars in Pernambuco, Paraíba and Rio Grande do Norte, and grew with cattle ranching and dried-meat (charque) production in the 18th. Ceará was a dependency of Pernambuco from 1680.

eras.polity: Captaincy of Ceará, independent of Pernambuco from 1799
eras.note: The Captaincy of Ceará became independent of Pernambuco in 1799. On 22 September 1799 the settlement became the district of Acaracu under the vila of Sobral, so its paper sits under Sobral.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - Province of Ceará, district of Acaracu in Sobral
eras.note: Ceará became a province in 1822. A general decree of 5 September 1832 created the parish, moving its seat from the Almofala church, a former Tremembé mission, to Barra do Acaraú.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - Vila do Acaracu, then município of Acaraú
eras.note: Law 480 of 31 July 1849 raised it to a vila separate from Sobral (installed 5 February 1851), and provincial law 2.019 of 19 September 1882 gave it município status under the name Acaraú. Ceará was the first Brazilian province to abolish slavery, on 25 March 1884.

Tremembé people still live in the municipality in three areas: Córrego João Pereira, described as the first recognised Indigenous land in Ceará, and Queimadas and Aroeira, whose recognition is still being sought. FamilySearch's guide notes that a law of 1850 required registration of births and deaths nationally, with the Church recording in parallel.

regions.label: The Gurupi - Viseu, Carutapera and the Pará-Maranhão border
regions.sub: Viseu, Carutapera, Cachoeira do Piriá

eras.polity: Governorate General of Brazil - the Gurupi coast
eras.note: The Portuguese navigator Diogo Leite reached this coast in 1531 (historians disagree whether the inlet he named is at the mouth of the Gurupi or of the Turiaçu). The French settled in Maranhão around 1594 and were expelled in 1615.

eras.polity: State of Maranhão, later Maranhão and Grão-Pará
eras.note: The State of Maranhão was created on 13 June 1621 apart from the Governorate General of Brazil, extinguished in 1652 and reconstituted as Maranhão and Grão-Pará in 1654. A royal charter of 9 February 1622 granted the Captaincy of the Gurupi (Caeté to Turiaçu) to Gaspar de Sousa, and the village of Vera Cruz on the Gurupi was founded in April 1627.

eras.polity: State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão, capital Belém
eras.note: The state was renamed Grão-Pará and Maranhão in 1751 and its capital moved from São Luís to Belém. In 1758 a district named Viseu was created and three parishes were founded in the Vera Cruz area.

eras.polity: Grão-Pará and Rio Negro; Maranhão and Piauí
eras.note: The old state was divided into two, Grão-Pará and Rio Negro and Maranhão and Piauí (dated 1772-1775). Viseu, in Pará, borders Carutapera, in Maranhão, so the two jurisdictions' records meet on this ground; the official foundation of Viseu is recorded on 13 January 1781.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - Provinces of Pará and Maranhão
eras.note: Provincial Law 301 of 22 December 1856 raised the Viseu district to a vila, separating it administratively from Bragança.

eras.polity: Brazil - States of Pará and Maranhão
eras.note: State Law 324 of 6 July 1895 made Viseu a city. A law of 1850 required civil registration of births and deaths nationally, and the Catholic parish books run alongside.

regions.label: Dom Eliseu and Itinga do Maranhão - the PA-70 and Belém-Brasília frontier
regions.sub: Dom Eliseu, Itinga do Maranhão

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Brazil - the PA-70 settlement of Quilômetro Zero
eras.note: Settlement began in the 1960s when the BR-010 highway was opened and the Pará government built PA-70 (now BR-222). The first settler, Leopoldo Cunha, arrived in 1961, and under the 1964 military government's incentives families from Piauí, Maranhão, Bahia, Goiás and Minas Gerais received land titles; the village was called Quilômetro Zero or Vila do Zero.

eras.polity: Brazil - the village of Filinto Müller, Pará
eras.note: After a July 1973 air crash killed the president of the Senate, Filinto Müller, the settlers renamed the village for him. A timber boom had begun around 1970. Itinga do Maranhão lies across the line in Maranhão.

On 14 September 1983 Filinto Müller became a district of Paragominas, and it was then renamed Dom Eliseu after the bishop of the Diocese of Bragança, so these years' registers are filed under Paragominas.

eras.polity: Brazil - município of Dom Eliseu, Pará
eras.note: The municipality was created by state law 5.450, dated 1 May or 10 May 1988 depending on the source. The first municipal election was held on 15 November 1988 and the first mayor took office on 1 January 1989.

regions.label: Carolina and the Tocantins - Maranhão's southern frontier
regions.sub: Carolina, Goiatins

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Settlement on the Tocantins - São Paulo de Alcântara
eras.note: In 1809 Manoel Coelho Paredes and Elias Ferreira Barros set up cattle pens on the Tocantins. In 1810 Pinto Magalhães, claiming the land for the prince, named the place São Paulo de Alcântara and stayed until 1816; Barros resettled it in 1820.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - the village of Carolina
eras.note: In 1823 Padre Camargo Gleury named the village Carolina, for Brazil's first empress.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - disputed between Maranhão and Goiás
eras.note: The village was raised to a vila in 1831, and the Goiás government had it moved to São Pedro de Alcântara, putting it under Goiás. Maranhão and Goiás disputed control from 1831 to 1854, so registers of these years may be filed under either province.

eras.polity: Empire of Brazil - Province of Maranhão
eras.note: Decree no. 773 of 23 August 1854 ended the dispute and returned the village to Maranhão under the name Carolina. The foundation and political emancipation of the municipality are dated 8 July 1859.
A law of 1850 required civil registration of births and deaths nationally; Catholic parish books exist alongside the civil books and can differ, so search both.

regions.label: The Mato Grosso do Sul-Paraguay frontier - Bela Vista, Iguatemi, Itaquiraí and Eldorado
regions.sub: Bela Vista, Iguatemi, Itaquiraí, Eldorado, Japorã

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Itatín missions and the Colônia Militar de Iguatemi - the Spanish-Portuguese frontier
eras.note: In the 1630s Jesuits set up short-lived missions among the Guaraní in the Itatín region of present Mato Grosso do Sul, destroyed by bandeirantes and by Indigenous revolts. The Colônia Militar de Iguatemi, the first settlement of European origin here, was destroyed by Spanish forces under the governor of Paraguay, Agostinho Fernandes de Pinedo; no date is given for either event.
The Guarani-Kaiowá, the first peoples of the area, were first contacted by non-Indigenous people in the 1800s.

eras.polity: Brazil - State of Mato Grosso, Ponta Porã and Amambai
eras.note: A new settlement, Vila Sacarón, was laid out around a spring of the Sacarón stream in 1909. Federal decree-law 9.055 of 12 March 1946 created the district of Iguatemi under Ponta Porã, and state law 370 of 31 July 1954 transferred it to Amambai.

eras.polity: Brazil - State of Mato Grosso, município of Iguatemi
eras.note: State law 1.951 of 11 November 1963 raised Iguatemi to a municipality, split from Amambai, with the districts of Iguatemi, Eldorado and Morumbi; it was installed on 8 May 1965. Eldorado was split off as its own municipality by law 3.692 of 13 May 1976.

eras.polity: Brazil - State of Mato Grosso do Sul
eras.note: Complementary Law 31 of 11 October 1977 divided Mato Grosso and created Mato Grosso do Sul, a full state from 1 January 1979, so records before 1979 for this ground sit under Mato Grosso. Itaquiraí became a municipality by state law 76 of 12 May 1980.

regions.label: Southern Rondônia - Colorado do Oeste and the Guaporé Territory
regions.sub: Colorado do Oeste

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Brazil - Amazonas and Mato Grosso, the Madeira-Mamoré railway
eras.note: The Treaty of Petrópolis (1903) obliged Brazil to build the Madeira-Mamoré railway, which spurred development in the region once Acre became a Brazilian territory that year.
Decree-Law 5.812 of 13 September 1943 created the Federal Territory of Guaporé from parts of Amazonas and Mato Grosso, so earlier records for this ground sit under those two states.
A law of 17 February 1956 renamed the territory Rondônia. From the 1970s tax incentives, federal investment, highways and colonisation centres drew migrants, mainly from the Center-South.
The territory became a state in 1982 (1982; some sources differ), with 13 municipalities, the capital being Porto Velho.

regions.label: Ashland, Kentucky - Poage's Landing on the Ohio
regions.sub: Ashland, Flatwoods, Poage's Landing

eras.note: Before registers.

A Virginia Assembly act of 31 December 1776 created Kentucky County, effective early 1777 (the county is dated 1777-1780). In 1786 the Poage family came from the Shenandoah Valley through the Cumberland Gap and built a homestead on the Ohio River called Poage's Landing.
Kentucky became the 15th state on 1 June 1792. Poage's Landing remained largely an extended-family community until the mid-19th century.

eras.polity: Commonwealth of Kentucky - the city of Ashland
eras.note: In 1854 the settlement was renamed Ashland, after Henry Clay's estate at Lexington, and the General Assembly chartered the Kentucky Iron, Coal, and Manufacturing Company; the city was formally incorporated in 1856 (1854 in some accounts).

eras.polity: Commonwealth of Kentucky - Ashland and its steel town
eras.note: The American Rolling Mill Co. (ARMCO) opened its Ashland Works steel mill in 1922. The city government changed from council-manager to commissioner-manager in 1950.

regions.label: Owensboro - Yellow Banks on the Ohio
regions.sub: Owensboro, Yellow Banks

eras.note: Before registers.

Kentucky became a state on 1 June 1792. The frontiersman William Smeathers (also spelled Smothers) is the first European descendant recorded as settling here, in 1797, at a place called Yellow Banks for the colour of the land beside the Ohio.
Yellow Banks was formally established as Owensborough in 1817, named for Col. Abraham Owen.

eras.polity: Commonwealth of Kentucky - the city of Owensborough
eras.note: The city was incorporated in 1850.
The spelling was shortened from Owensborough to Owensboro in 1893, so older records and indexes may file the town under either spelling. Owensboro is the county seat of Daviess County.

regions.label: The Outer Banks - Roanoke, Hatteras and Kill Devil Hills
regions.sub: Outer Banks, Kill Devil Hills

eras.polity: English Roanoke colonies, then colonial North Carolina
eras.note: English attempts to colonise Roanoke began in 1584. Roanoke Island and the banks later lay within Currituck, Tyrrell and Hyde counties.

eras.polity: State of North Carolina - Currituck, Hyde and Carteret counties
eras.note: The Thirteen Colonies declared independence on 4 July 1776. Currituck, Hyde and Carteret are among the counties that hold parts of the banks.

eras.polity: State of North Carolina - the Hatteras forts attacked in 1861
eras.note: On 27 August 1861 Commodore Silas Stringham and General Benjamin Butler decided to attack two Confederate forts at Cape Hatteras; the assault took about two days.

eras.polity: State of North Carolina - Dare County
eras.note: Dare County was formed in 1870 from parts of Tyrrell, Currituck and Hyde counties and named for Virginia Dare, so county records before 1870 for the islands sit with those parent counties.

eras.polity: State of North Carolina - Dare County, Kill Devil Hills
eras.note: The first controlled, powered flight took place at Kill Devil Hills on 17 December 1903.

regions.label: The lower Ohio and Mississippi shore - the Jackson Purchase, Cape Girardeau and Metropolis
regions.sub: Paducah, Cape Girardeau, Metropolis, Caruthersville, Charleston

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Louisiana - Lorimier's Cape Girardeau post under Spanish grant
eras.note: In 1793 the Spanish government granted Louis Lorimier, a French-Canadian, a trading post and a large tract at Cape Girardeau, and he became commandant of the district. Baron Carondelet also granted land near Cape Girardeau to the Black Bob Band of the Hathawekela Shawnee.

eras.polity: Louisiana Territory, then Missouri Territory - and Chickasaw country to the east
eras.note: The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 passed the west bank to the United States; Louisiana Territory dates from 1804 and Missouri Territory from 4 June 1812, and Cape Girardeau was incorporated in 1808. Across the Mississippi, the land claimed by Kentucky since its 1792 statehood was not under US control until 1818.

eras.polity: The Jackson Purchase - Kentucky and Tennessee
eras.note: The Treaty of Tuscaloosa of 19 October 1818, signed by Andrew Jackson and Isaac Shelby, bought the Chickasaw land for $300,000 paid over 15 years; the region was annexed to Kentucky and Tennessee in 1819.

eras.polity: State of Missouri; Commonwealth of Kentucky - the Purchase counties
eras.note: Missouri became a state on 10 August 1821. In the Purchase, Paducah was incorporated in 1838, Hickman in 1841, Murray in 1844 and Mayfield in 1846; Cape Girardeau was reincorporated as a city in 1843.

regions.label: Manitowoc and Two Rivers - Wisconsin's Lake Michigan shore
regions.sub: Manitowoc, Two Rivers

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Menominee country and the fur trade
eras.note: French fur traders first arrived in 1673 and the Northwest Fur Company set up a trading post in 1795. The Menominee ceded the land to the United States in the 1836 Treaty of the Cedars.

eras.polity: Territorial legislature: Brown County, then Manitowoc County
eras.note: Land sales were authorised in 1835 before the Menominee transfer, and the first recorded buyers were William Jones and Louis Fizette on 3 August 1835. The county dates from 1836 in one source and from 1838, when the territorial legislature separated it from Brown County, in another; it was organised in 1848.
Manitowoc was chartered as a village on 6 March 1851 and replaced Manitowoc Rapids as county seat in 1853. German, Norwegian, British, Irish and Canadian immigrants were among the early settlers.

eras.polity: State of Wisconsin - city of Manitowoc
eras.note: Manitowoc was incorporated as a city on 12 March 1870. In the 2000 census 53.7 percent of county residents reported German ancestry.

regions.label: La Costa - Mar del Tuyú and the Atlantic shore of Buenos Aires province
regions.sub: Mar del Tuyú, Santa Teresita, Mar de Ajó, San Clemente del Tuyú, Pinamar

eras.polity: Spanish Río de la Plata - the Tuyú coast
eras.note: In 1580 Hernando Arias de Saavedra led an overland expedition from Asunción; the Guaraní with him called the region Tuyú, meaning mud. Father Tomás Falkner drew a chart of the coast in 1744, and the first settlers, among them Ángel Fulco and the Saenz Valiente family with the establishment El Tuyú, arrived at the end of the 18th century.

eras.polity: United Provinces - Buenos Aires province, partido of Monsalvo
eras.note: Argentina declared independence from Spain on 9 July 1816. The ground lay in the partido of Monsalvo until Rosas carved a new partido out of it in 1839.

eras.polity: Province of Buenos Aires - partido del Rincón de Ajó
eras.note: A decree of Juan Manuel de Rosas of 20 December 1839 created the partido del Rincón de Ajó from lands of Monsalvo.

eras.polity: Province of Buenos Aires - partido of General Lavalle
eras.note: The partido was renamed General Lavalle on 19 October 1891. The resort towns were founded late: San Clemente del Tuyú, La Margarita (now Mar de Ajó) and Jagüel del Medio in 1935, San Bernardo in 1944, Mar del Tuyú on 24 October 1945, Santa Teresita on 3 March 1946, and Aguas Verdes and Costa del Este in 1966. A national law of 1886 began civil registration, with provinces starting at different times; Buenos Aires province's registry is in La Plata.

eras.polity: Province of Buenos Aires - municipio and partido de La Costa
eras.note: On 1 July 1978 an urban-municipalities law created La Costa, with Mar del Tuyú as its seat, on the same day as the urban municipalities of Monte Hermoso, Villa Gesell and Pinamar. Pinamar, inside this ring, is a separate municipality and not part of La Costa. La Costa became a partido on 23 May 1983 (1 July 1983 in some accounts), and its first elected government came from the elections of 30 October 1983.

regions.label: Eastern Entre Ríos - Concepción del Uruguay and the Uruguay river
regions.sub: Concepción del Uruguay, Chajarí, Mocoretá

eras.polity: Spanish Río de la Plata - the Jesuit Concepción
eras.note: A Jesuit settlement called Concepción existed around 1619 and had no formal founding.

eras.polity: Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata - Villa de la Concepción del Uruguay
eras.note: The villa was founded on 25 June 1783 by Tomás de Rocamora, then commandant general of the Entre Ríos partidos, on the orders of Viceroy Vértiz. In 1814 the Supreme Director Gervasio Antonio Posadas declared it the capital of the province of Entre Ríos.

eras.polity: Province of Entre Ríos - Concepción del Uruguay
eras.note: Argentina declared independence on 9 July 1816. Urquiza created the Colegio del Uruguay, the first lay school in the country, dated 28 July 1849 in one section of the source and 1848 in another; in 1851 he pronounced against Rosas in the Plaza Ramírez, which led to the battle of Caseros on 3 February 1852.

eras.polity: Province of Entre Ríos - capital at Concepción del Uruguay
eras.note: The provincial convention of 1860 declared the city capital again, a function it kept until 1883. The municipality was formally created on 1 January 1873.

eras.polity: Province of Entre Ríos - capital at Paraná
eras.note: The provincial capital moved to Paraná in 1883. Argentina's civil registration began with a law of 1886 and the provinces started at different times; the Catholic Church kept recording after that, so search both.

regions.label: San Francisco - Santa Fe's colony on the Córdoba plain
regions.sub: San Francisco, Freyre

eras.note: Before registers.
Argentina declared independence from Spain on 9 July 1816. The town's documented history begins with the colony of 1886.

eras.polity: Colonia San Francisco, a Santa Fe colonisation plan
eras.note: San Francisco was founded on 9 September 1886 by José Bernardo Iturraspe under a colonisation plan promoted by the government of Santa Fe, on a site about 8 km north of today's centre. The plan came from Santa Fe, yet the town lies in the province of Córdoba, so the 1880s papers may be in either province's archives.

eras.polity: Province of Córdoba - San Francisco at the railway
eras.note: The Ferrocarril Central Córdoba reached the town in 1888 and it moved to its present site. Piedmontese immigrants predominated from the early 20th century to the 1960s, and the first communal governments were formed by foreigners.

eras.polity: Province of Córdoba - city of San Francisco
eras.note: San Francisco became a ciudad between 1911 and 1920, with official proclamation in 1915. Argentina's civil registration began with a law of 1886, with provinces starting at different times.

regions.label: The Neuquén lakes - San Martín de los Andes and Villa La Angostura
regions.sub: San Martín de los Andes, Villa La Angostura

eras.note: The zone was the territory of the Mapuche Curruhuinca, linked to the cacique Valentín Sayhueque. Before registers.

eras.polity: Argentina - the last town of the Campaña del Desierto
eras.note: San Martín de los Andes was founded on 4 February 1898 as the last Patagonian town of the campaign. It was officially attributed to Colonel Rohde, but recent research credits Lieutenant Colonel Celestino Pérez.

An arbitral award of Edward VII in 1902, favouring Perito Moreno's thesis of the high peaks, left the zone in Argentina. Administration was military until 1907, and settlers came from Syria and Lebanon, the Netherlands, Switzerland, France, Italy and Germany, many by way of Chile.
The Lanín National Park was founded in 1937 and restricted the timber industry in the 1960s; the economy shifted from timber and cattle to tourism.

The Chapelco winter centre opened in 1973, the Sol de los Andes hotel in 1974 and the gondola system in 1983. Ash from the Puyehue-Cordón Caulle eruption in 2011 and from the Calbuco volcano in 2015 covered the town. Argentina's civil registration began with a law of 1886 and the provinces started at different times.

regions.label: Río Bravo, Tamaulipas - the lower Río Grande haciendas
regions.sub: Ciudad Río Bravo, Colombres

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Hacienda lands on the lower Río Grande
eras.note: A hacienda was founded here in 1774. The district was then known as Colombres.

eras.polity: Mexico - State of Tamaulipas, La Sauteña estate
eras.note: The El Nacional railway opened in 1882 from Estación Cuevas to Matamoros, through the station of Ébano that became Río Bravo, and the La Sauteña estate was founded in 1888, its main partner the Asturian landowner Íñigo Noriega. Civil registration began on 28 July 1859 under Benito Juárez but was not vigorously enforced until 1867, and parish registers remain essential.

eras.polity: Mexico - Revolution on the Río Bravo
eras.note: On 10 May 1913 General Lucio Blanco took Reynosa and then Colombres, and the revolutionaries destroyed the town.
