Irrigation works in northern Mexico revived the region; colonies such as 18 de Marzo and Magüelles were settled by displaced workers and by repatriates from the United States.

eras.polity: Mexico - municipality of Río Bravo, Tamaulipas
eras.note: The municipality of Río Bravo was created on 4 December 1961, and in 1962 it was granted city status.

regions.label: Agua Prieta - the Sonora border at Douglas
regions.sub: Agua Prieta, Naco

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Mexico - railroad camp on the Douglas-Nacozari line
eras.note: The town arose in 1899 as railroads were built between Douglas, Arizona, and Nacozari, Sonora; its first settlers worked for the US mining company Phelps Dodge, based in Douglas.

eras.polity: Mexico - commissary of the municipality of Fronteras, Sonora
eras.note: A contract of 1903 between officials and private citizens, under the name Camou, made the area a commissary of Fronteras, so registers of these years are filed under Fronteras. Carranza's government had its seat at the Hotel Central in 1914, and in 1915 Pancho Villa's night attack was repelled by forces under Plutarco Elías Calles.

eras.polity: Mexico - municipality of Agua Prieta, Sonora
eras.note: Agua Prieta became an independent municipal seat on 28 August 1916, with Rodolfo L. Márquez as its first president.

eras.polity: Mexico - municipality of Agua Prieta, Sonora
eras.note: The Plan de Agua Prieta was signed on 23 April 1920 by Adolfo de la Huerta and Plutarco Elías Calles in support of Álvaro Obregón. Civil registration began on 28 July 1859 under Juárez but was not vigorously enforced until 1867.

regions.label: Tecate - Rancho Tecate and the Kumiai valley
regions.sub: Tecate

eras.note: Kuuchamaa Mountain is sacred to the Kumeyaay, called Kumiai in Mexico. Before registers.
The Mexican governor José María de Echeandía granted the valley as the 4,439-acre Rancho Tecate to Juan Bandini in 1829.

eras.polity: Mexico - abandoned rancho resettled by farmers
eras.note: Kumeyaay people raided and plundered the rancho in 1836; Bandini abandoned it and was compensated with Rancho Jurupa in 1838. Farmers and ranchers resettled the area in the late 19th century.

eras.polity: Mexico - the town of Tecate, in the municipality of Tijuana
eras.note: The town was founded on 2 April 1888 and incorporated as a city on 12 October 1892; Governor Esteban Cantú ordered its first urban plan in 1919. Civil registration began on 28 July 1859 under Juárez but was not vigorously enforced until 1867.

eras.polity: Mexico - municipality of Tecate, Baja California
eras.note: Tecate Municipality was separated from Tijuana Municipality in 1953, so earlier municipal records sit with Tijuana.

regions.label: Putumayo - Orito, Puerto Asís and the Sibundoy approaches
regions.sub: Orito, Puerto Asís, Villagarzón

eras.polity: Spanish rule - missions linked to Popayán
eras.note: The Spanish invaded in 1542 and Catholic missions administered the region from 1547; under colonial rule it was linked to Popayán. The southwest was Cofán territory, the northwest Kamentxá, the centre and south Tukanoan peoples such as the Siona, and the east Witoto-speaking peoples.
In the early republic the territory was part of the Azuay Department, which took in areas now in Ecuador and Peru. The junta of Santa Fe was created on 20 July 1810.

eras.polity: Province of Popayán, then the Federal State of the Cauca
eras.note: Popayán Province dates from 1831 and the Federal State of the Cauca from 1857.
Under the 1886 reorganisation the territory belonged to the Cauca Department.
The Intendencia del Putumayo was created in 1905 and the Intendencia del Caquetá in 1909.
The Comisaría Especial del Putumayo dates from 1912; in 1953 the territory was attached to the Department of Nariño, and the comisaría was reinstated in 1957, so the 1950s papers may sit with Nariño.
The area became the Intendencia Especial del Putumayo in 1968.
Putumayo was established as a department in 1991.

regions.label: Machiques and the Perijá foothills
regions.sub: Machiques

eras.note: Before registers.
Machiques was established by the Spanish in 1750.
Venezuela declared independence on 5 July 1811.
Machiques was raised to a civil parish on 18 November 1841, the date taken as its official founding.

eras.polity: Venezuela - seat of the Guzmán Blanco department
eras.note: On 27 July 1872 Machiques became the seat of the municipality then called Departamento Guzmán Blanco.

eras.polity: Venezuela - Machiques, an ecclesiastical parish of the diocese of Mérida
eras.note: On 8 April 1890 Bishop Román Lovera of Mérida raised it to an ecclesiastical parish. The civil parish (1841) and the ecclesiastical parish (1890) are separate foundations, so church and civil books start on different dates.

regions.label: Guasdualito - the Apure plains on the Colombian border
regions.sub: Guasdualito

eras.polity: Spanish rule - cattle hatos on the Apure plains
eras.note: A hato (cattle estate) is recorded around Guasdualito about 1750, and by 1765 it counted as a settled centre.

The foundation is dated 8 December 1770 and attributed to Fray Jerónimo José de Lucena; José Ignacio del Pumar refounded it in 1771-1772. A record of 1787 counts nine hatos, about 728 inhabitants and about 15,000 head of cattle.

eras.polity: Venezuela - the war of independence at Guasdualito
eras.note: Venezuela declared independence on 5 July 1811. In 1815 the patriot officer Francisco Olmedilla attacked royalist forces at Guasdualito.

eras.polity: Venezuela - the move to the Sarare
eras.note: The inhabitants began to move to the banks of the Río Sarare, founding a hamlet called Periquera; the Casa Cural archives date this to 16 July 1845, while other historians place it in 1830 or 1832.

In 1866 the population moved to Corozal but returned to the original site after a year. In the time of Guzmán Blanco the town was raised to the rank of Departamento, with over 3,000 people in 586 houses; the exact date is uncertain.

regions.label: Tumeremo and El Dorado - the Guayana gold country and the Esequibo claim
regions.sub: Tumeremo, El Dorado

eras.polity: Spanish rule - Provincia de Nueva Andalucía y Paria, then Guayana
eras.note: The territory belonged to the Provincia de Nueva Andalucía y Paria from 1568 to 1777 and to the Provincia de Guayana from 1585 to 1864.

eras.polity: Captaincy General of Venezuela - Provincia de Guayana
eras.note: In 1777 the territory became part of the Capitanía General de Venezuela. The foundation of Tumeremo is dated 26 January 1788.
Venezuela declared independence on 5 July 1811. Part of the territory was included in the Cantón Upata from 1840 to 1875.
The Provincia de Guayana ended in 1864; the Cantón Upata ran to 1875.
The Paris arbitral award of 1899 began a long-running dispute with Guyana over the eastern frontier (the Guayana Esequiba); Venezuela declared the award null and void.
Tumeremo became part of Bolívar State in 1901. In 2023 it was designated the provisional capital of the Guayana Esequiba state that Venezuela claims, a territory Guyana administers.

regions.label: Tambopata - Puerto Maldonado and the Madre de Dios rubber frontier
regions.sub: Puerto Maldonado, Tambopata

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Peru - the Madre de Dios, explored
eras.note: Faustino Maldonado of Tarapoto explored the Madre de Dios in 1861 and drowned in rapids on the Mamoré. Peru's independence was proclaimed on 28 July 1821.

eras.polity: Peru - the rubber boom on the Madre de Dios
eras.note: Rubber workers brought diseases that caused epidemics among Indigenous peoples along the Manu River from 1889 to 1892, with another outbreak in 1896. The rubber baron Carlos Fermín Fitzcarrald died in 1897 when his ship sank at the point where Puerto Maldonado was later founded.

eras.polity: Peru - the station of Puerto Maldonado
eras.note: Puerto Maldonado was officially founded on 10 July 1902, at the meeting of the Tambopata and Madre de Dios rivers; the founder is spelled Juan Villalta or Villata.

eras.polity: Peru - Department of Madre de Dios
eras.note: The Department of Madre de Dios was created by law on 26 December 1912, with Puerto Maldonado as its capital; the city was formally recognised in 1985.

regions.label: Rurrenabaque, Reyes and Ixiamas - the Beni and La Paz lowlands
regions.sub: Rurrenabaque, Reyes, Ixiamas

eras.note: Jesuits, Carmelites and Franciscans arrived from 1560, and the missions introduced cattle. In 1656 the town of Reyes stood at Los Arenales, near today's airport, and in 1810 it was moved to its present site by order of Pedro Pablo de Urquizo. The Arawak, Tacana and Araona peoples lived here before.

Bolivia's declaration of independence is dated 6 August 1825. Tradition gives the founding of Rurrenabaque to the priest Giovani Gianelli on 2 February, but the documented date is 15 November 1844; a law of 17 November 1844 under President José Ballivián ordered the name Ciudad Ballivián, which was not carried out.
Around 1880 the rubber boom turned Rurrenabaque into an important shipping port.

eras.polity: Bolivia - province of General José Ballivián
eras.note: The province of General José Ballivián was created on 3 December 1937 from cantons of the Yacuma province, so earlier records sit under Yacuma.
Since 1995 Rurrenabaque has been the capital of the municipality of the same name in the province of General José Ballivián.

regions.label: Lebu and the Arauco coast
regions.sub: Lebu

eras.polity: Spanish rule - Fuerte de Santa Margarita de Austria
eras.note: The Fuerte de Santa Margarita de Austria was founded in the valley of Lebu in 1604.

The government junta of Chile was established on 18 September 1810. The Lebu river was the natural frontier between the unconquered territories and Chilean penetration until the mid-19th century; the first coal seams were found in 1852 (1854 in another source).

eras.polity: Chile - the new town of Lebu
eras.note: The city of Lebu was founded on 8 October 1862, with the first stone of Fuerte Varas (2 December 1862 in the Asta-Buruaga dictionary); European immigrants, mainly Basque, British and French, followed.
In 1869 Lebu became the capital of the department of Lebu.
In 1875 Lebu became the capital of the province of Arauco. Coal later ceased to be the main economic driver.

regions.label: Presidente Franco - the first town of Alto Paraná
regions.sub: Presidente Franco

eras.note: Before registers.
Paraguay's independence is dated 14 and 15 May 1811.
Vicente Matiauda founded the town on 13 October 1929, near Ciudad del Este, naming it for Manuel Franco, president of Paraguay in 1918. It was the first city founded in Alto Paraná.

eras.polity: Paraguay - municipality of the third category
eras.note: In 1974 it became a municipality of the third category.
In 1979 it became a first-class municipality and later headed nearby river ports including Puerto Indio, Hernandarias and Marangatú, and a major commercial centre.

regions.label: Cornwall - the Loyalists' Royal Town on the upper St Lawrence
regions.sub: Cornwall

eras.polity: Before registers - Mohawk and Ojibwe lands
eras.note: French explorers called the site Pointe Maligne; it was not a settlement or trading post. The Mohawk territory of Akwesasne lies to the south. Before registers.

eras.polity: British North America - Loyalist 'Royal Town No. 2'
eras.note: United Empire Loyalists led by Lieutenant-Colonel Sir John Johnson founded the first documented European settlement in 1784, first called Royal Town No. 2, then Johnson or New Johnstown.
In 1791 the British divided the province into Upper and Lower Canada. The settlement was later renamed Cornwall, for the Duke of Cornwall; the date is not given.
Cornwall was among the first incorporated municipalities in Upper Canada in 1834, and the Cornwall Canal was built from 1834 to 1842. Its population was about 1,600 in 1846.
The Dominion of Canada was established on 1 July 1867.

regions.label: Orito - the oil frontier of the Putumayo border
regions.sub: Orito

eras.note: Catholic missions administered the region from 1547, and under colonial rule it was linked to Popayán.

eras.polity: Early republic - Azuay Department, then Popayán Province
eras.note: The territory was part of the Azuay Department, which included areas in Ecuador and Peru, and then of Popayán Province from 1831.

eras.polity: Federal State of the Cauca; Department of the Cauca
eras.note: The Federal State of the Cauca dates from 1857 and the Cauca Department from 1886.

eras.polity: Intendencia and Comisaría of the Putumayo
eras.note: An Intendencia del Putumayo was created in 1905 and a Comisaría Especial in 1912; in 1953 the area was listed under the Department of Nariño.

eras.polity: Comisaría, then Intendencia Especial del Putumayo
eras.note: The Comisaría Especial was reinstated in 1957 and became the Intendencia Especial del Putumayo in 1968.
Putumayo Department was established in 1991, so records of Orito before that year sit with the territorial authorities listed above.

regions.label: Mariveles and Limay, southern Bataan
regions.sub: Mariveles, Limay, Cabcaben, Corregidor

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Pampanga and the corregimiento of Mariveles
eras.note: Spanish missionaries founded the coastal Bataan villages in the 1570s. The corregimiento of Mariveles then also took in Morong, Bagac and Maragondon across Manila Bay, while the northern Bataan towns belonged to Pampanga.

Bataan was created as a province on 11 January 1757 by Governor-General Pedro Manuel Arandia, out of Pampanga towns and the corregimiento of Mariveles. Limay was a barrio of Orion (Udyong) until it became a town in 1917.

eras.polity: United States rule: Bataan military reservation
eras.note: Before the 1941 invasion Bataan was a military reservation for the defence of Corregidor, and the US Navy had a small base at Mariveles. The Treaty of Paris of 1898 was made between Spain and the United States.

Japanese forces invaded in December 1941; the siege of Bataan began on 7 January 1942 and the all-out assault on 3 April 1942. American and Filipino forces surrendered on 9 April 1942, and the prisoners were marched more than 100 km to Capas, Tarlac (the Bataan Death March).
The Philippines became independent in 1946.

regions.label: Marilao to Rodriguez, Bulacan and Rizal edge
regions.sub: Marilao, Bagong Silang (Caloocan), Rodriguez (Montalban)

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Bulacan and the province of Tondo
eras.note: Spanish forces under Martín de Goiti reached Malolos and Calumpit in November 1571. Bulakan was officially established on 30 April 1578 (15 August 1578 is also given as the province's founding date, and the exact date is undocumented). Marilao is in Bulacan.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Bulacan, Manila province and the Morong district
eras.note: In 1853 a new district with Morong as capital was formed from Tondo and Laguna towns, and was renamed the Politico-Military District of Morong four years later. The province of Tondo was renamed Manila province in a later reorganisation, dated 1859 or 1860 depending on the source; Caloocan was a Manila-province municipality.

eras.polity: United States rule: Bulacan, Manila and Rizal
eras.note: In 1901 Manila province was dissolved: the city of Manila absorbed six small municipalities and the rest merged with the Morong district to form Rizal province (11 June 1901 is given as its founding date). Montalban (now Rodriguez) went to Rizal, while Caloocan became part of Metro Manila. The seat of Bulacan's government moved to Malolos in 1901.
The Japanese Imperial Army occupied Bulacan in 1942; Filipino, American and guerrilla forces liberated it in 1945.
Caloocan, a former Manila-province municipality, now lies in Metro Manila; Rodriguez is in Rizal and Marilao in Bulacan, so a family here may be filed under three different provincial series.

regions.label: Northern Mindoro and the Lubang Islands
regions.sub: Calapan, Puerto Galera, Lubang

eras.polity: Before registers. Borneans and Sulus were still extracting tribute from Mindoro's people as late as 1574.
eras.note: Before registers. Borneans and Sulus were still extracting tribute from Mindoro's people as late as 1574.

Spanish conquest was followed by wars with Moro raiders from Mindanao and depopulation of the coasts. By the end of the 1700s Mindoro had 3,165 native families and four Spanish Filipino families; by 1818 the Spanish Filipino families numbered 47.
Mindoro joined the revolution against Spain in 1898. From 1920 to 1950 it was a single province with Calapan as its capital; Allied forces captured Calapan on 24 January 1945.
Calapan remained the capital of the undivided province.

The island was divided on 13 June 1950 under Republic Act No. 505 (15 November 1950 is also given as the new province's founding date). Calapan is in Oriental Mindoro, but the Lubang Islands belong to Occidental Mindoro.

regions.label: Aurora, Infanta and the Polillo Islands, Luzon Pacific coast
regions.sub: Baler, Casiguran, Infanta, Polillo

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Pampanga, Kalilayan (Tayabas) and Nueva Ecija
eras.note: Juan de Salcedo is the first European recorded in the region (1572). In 1591 Baler and Casiguran, previously part of Pampanga, became part of Kalilayan, renamed Tayabas in 1749. Franciscans established missions at Baler and Casiguran in 1609, with later missions at Dipaculao (1719) and Casiguran (1753). Nueva Ecija became a regular province on 25 April 1801 and took in Baler from Tayabas.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Nueva Ecija, Tayabas and El Principe
eras.note: In 1818 Nueva Ecija annexed Baler, Casiguran, Infanta and the Polillo Islands from Tayabas. A military district of Tayabas was separated from Nueva Ecija in 1853; El Principe was a military comandancia with its capital at Baler from 1855 (a cited reference says 1856) to 1885, and Binangonan de Lampon and Polillo were attached to Infanta in 1858.
On 12 June 1902 the El Principe district was moved from Nueva Ecija to Tayabas. In 1905 the northern area, including parts of Dilasag and Casiguran, was transferred from Nueva Vizcaya to Tayabas.
In 1942 the Japanese authorities moved Baler and Casiguran from Tayabas to Nueva Ecija; this was reversed in 1945.

Tayabas was renamed Quezon in 1946. Aurora became a sub-province of Quezon on 14 June 1951 under Republic Act No. 648 and an independent province by Batas Pambansa Blg. 7 (dated 21 November 1978 or 13 August 1979 depending on the source, with a plebiscite in May 1979).

regions.label: Camarines Norte, Daet to Paracale
regions.sub: Daet, Vinzons, Labo, Paracale, José Panganiban

eras.note: Before registers.
Juan de Salcedo explored the area in 1571 and visited the gold towns of Mambulao and Paracale. The Bicol province was founded in 1573 and Camarines created in 1636.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Camarines Norte and Ambos Camarines
eras.note: Camarines was split in 1829 into Camarines Norte (capital Daet) and Camarines Sur; Camarines Norte then had Talisay, Indan (now Vinzons), Labo, Paracale, Mambulao (now José Panganiban), Capalonga and others. The two were merged as Ambos Camarines in 1854-1857, separated in 1858 and merged again in 1893, so records of the period may be filed under either name. The Daet revolt took place on 14-17 April 1898.

eras.polity: American Philippines: Ambos Camarines, then Camarines Norte
eras.note: Ambos Camarines was divided again in 1917. Act 2809 of 3 March 1919 formally separated Camarines Norte from Camarines Sur, and Executive Order No. 22 of 20 March 1920 set up the province (15 April 1920 is cited as the date it began to function).

The first guerrilla engagement in the Philippines in the Second World War took place at Laniton, Basud, on 18 December 1941. US forces returned in 1945 and helped local troops and guerrillas liberate the province.

regions.label: Mapun and the Sibutu Islands, outer Tawi-Tawi
regions.sub: Mapun (Cagayan de Sulu), Sitangkai, Sibutu

eras.polity: Before registers: Sama-Bajau islands trading with Sulu and Labuan
eras.note: Sama-Bajau people occupied Mapun in the late 1700s. An East India Company ship traded here for a month in 1783, and rice grown in the 1790s was exported to the Tausug in Sulu.

In 1872, while conquering Jolo, the Spanish issued a regulation aimed at destroying Tausug shipping, but trading boats from Cagayan de Sulu kept sailing to the British settlement at Labuan. The islands lay outside the boundary drawn in the Treaty of Paris of 1898; the Treaty of Washington of 7 November 1900 included Cagayan de Sulu and Sibutu in Philippine territory, and they stayed under Spanish sovereignty until cession on ratification on 23 March 1901.
The municipality of Cagayan de Sulu was established on 11 February 1904 under Act No. 38.
The municipality was renamed Cagayan de Tawi-Tawi on 7 March 1984 (Batas Pambansa Blg. 647) and Mapun on 5 September 1988 (Republic Act No. 6672), so older records use the earlier names.

regions.label: Antique, west coast of Panay
regions.sub: San Jose de Buenavista, Sibalom, Patnongon, Belison, San Pedro

eras.polity: Before registers: Hantik, Akean and Irong-Irong
eras.note: Before the Spanish arrived Antique was one of three districts (sakups) of Panay: Hantik, Akean and Irong-Irong.
Spanish settlement is dated to 1569, when the area was recorded as Hantique, later Antique. Watchtowers were built along the coast against Moro raiders.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: politico-military province of Antique
eras.note: Antique became a politico-military province in 1790, with the town of Antique (now Hamtic) as its first capital; the seat later moved to Bugason (now Bugasong) and then to San Jose de Buenavista.
The province's founding date is given as 10 March 1917.
The Imperial Japanese Army landed in Antique in 1942; Commonwealth forces and local guerrillas retook the province in 1944-1945.

regions.label: Northern Aklan and Boracay
regions.sub: Boracay (Malay), Caticlan, Buruanga

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Spanish Philippines: Aklan in the province of Capiz
eras.note: Miguel López de Legazpi landed in Batan in 1565 and claimed the island for Spain. A census of 1818 recorded Spanish-Filipino families in Kalibo (167), Batan (56), Ibajay (30), Malinao (11) and Banga (8); Aklan was then politically united with Capiz.
Aklan stayed part of Capiz until 1956, so records before then are filed under Capiz.
Japanese forces invaded Aklan in 1942; combined Filipino and American forces, with Aklanon guerrillas, liberated it in 1945.
Republic Act No. 1414, signed on 25 April 1956, created Aklan as a separate province, which was inaugurated on 8 November 1956.

regions.label: Dinagat Islands, Surigao Strait
regions.sub: San Jose, Loreto, Dinagat

eras.note: Before registers.

The municipality of Dinagat was formally established in 1855 and at first covered the whole island. Loreto became a Spanish pueblo on 4 September 1890; between 1890 and 1990 the municipality's territory was divided into the seven current municipalities.
Loreto was created in 1918 under the province of Surigao. American forces landed at Loreto on 17 October 1944.

eras.polity: Philippines: Surigao del Norte, First District
eras.note: Before it became a province the Dinagat Islands formed part of the First District of Surigao del Norte.

The province was created on 2 December 2006 under Republic Act No. 9355. The Supreme Court declared its creation void on 11 February 2010 (final 18 May 2010) and reversed itself on 12 April 2011, so records of 2010-2011 may sit under either province.

regions.label: Jembrana and the Banyuwangi tip, Bali Strait
regions.sub: Negara, Gilimanuk, Wongsorejo

eras.note: Blambangan, a vassal of Majapahit and the last Hindu kingdom of Java, lost its independence to Balinese kingdoms; Mataram later gained control and renamed the territory Banyuwangi. The palace of the kingdom of Jembrana was built in the early 17th century.
Banyuwangi was part of the Mataram territory controlled by the VOC from 1770.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies: Jembrana regency in Banyuwangi Residency
eras.note: A friendship agreement was signed between the royal government of Jembrana and the Dutch East Indies government on 30 June 1849. The traditional royal bureaucracy lasted until 1855, and from 1856 to 1882 Jembrana was a regency (regentschap) in the Banyuwangi Residency.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies: Residency of Bali and Lombok
eras.note: By Staatsblad 123 of 1882 Bali and Lombok became a separate residency, and by Staatsblad 124 Jembrana became a district (afdeling) with Singaraja as capital, so Jembrana records before and after 1882 sit under different residencies. On 1 July 1938 the Balinese regions were made self-governing territories (Zelfbestuurlandschapen).
Jembrana passed through the Republic of Indonesia (1946-1950) and the State of East Indonesia, then the unitary republic from 1950; the regency was established on 14 August 1958.

regions.label: Oecusse and Kefamenanu, the Timor enclave
regions.sub: Pante Macassar (Oecusse), Lifau, Kefamenanu

eras.note: The Portuguese first landed on Timor at Lifau in 1515.

eras.polity: Portuguese Timor: Lifau as colonial capital
eras.note: Lifau became the colonial capital in 1702, when it received its first governor from Goa.

eras.polity: Portuguese Timor: capital moved to Dili
eras.note: The governor's capital was transferred from Lifau to Dili in 1769.

eras.polity: Portuguese Oecusse enclave in Dutch and Indonesian West Timor
eras.note: The Treaty of Lisbon of 1859 divided Timor between Portugal and the Netherlands and left Oecusse an enclave in Dutch territory; the definitive border was drawn by The Hague in 1916. The Bobometo crossing lies on the road to Kefamenanu, which is on the Indonesian side.
Indonesian forces invaded Oecusse on 6 June 1975.

Oecusse became part of independent Timor-Leste on 20 May 2002 and the Special Administrative Region of Oecusse Ambeno was created by Law 03/2014. West Timor surrounds it on all sides except the north.

regions.label: Nunukan and Sebatik, Indonesia-Sabah border
regions.sub: Nunukan, Sebatik

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Dutch East Indies: Bulungan; British North Borneo across the line
eras.note: The Anglo-Dutch treaty of 20 June 1891 set the boundary between British North Borneo and the Dutch East Indies, and its Article IV ran the line across Sebatik along 4 degrees 10 minutes north, so the island has always been split between two jurisdictions. Boundary pillars were set up in 1912-1913 and a further agreement was made in 1915.

Nunukan Regency was created on 4 October 1999 from the northern districts of Bulungan Regency. The northern half of Sebatik belongs to Malaysia, and a re-demarcation in 2019 replaced the boundary marks laid in 1915.

regions.label: Asahan coast, Tanjung Balai
regions.sub: Tanjung Balai, Teluk Nibung

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Sultanate of Asahan (a princely state of the East Coast of Sumatra Residency)
eras.note: The Malay sultanate of Asahan is dated from about 1630 to 1946, with Tanjung Balai as its capital. Its founder was a son of Sultan Iskandar Muda of Aceh and the state remained tributary to Aceh until the early nineteenth century.

The East Sumatra revolution began in early March 1946, with the worst violence at Tanjung Balai, where crowds besieged the sultan's palace. The Dutch set up the State of East Sumatra after reoccupying North Sumatra in July 1947, and it merged with the former Tapanuli Residency to form the province of North Sumatra on 15 August 1950.
Tanjung Balai was the capital of Asahan Regency until it became an independent city in 1984. Batubara Regency was carved out of Asahan on 15 June 2007.

regions.label: Ulleungdo, East Sea
regions.sub: Dodong, Jeodong

eras.note: The Samguk sagi records the conquest of the island, then called Usan-guk, by the Silla general Kim Isabu in 512.

eras.polity: Goryeo, then Joseon: the empty-island policy
eras.note: Goryeo annexed the island in 930. Under Joseon the government adopted an empty-island policy that proved impossible to enforce; it was officially rescinded in 1881. A fishing-rights dispute with Japan arose in the 1690s.
American whaleships hunted off the island from 1848 to 1892.

regions.label: Awaji Island
regions.sub: Sumoto, Minamiawaji, Fukura

eras.note: Awaji was a province (Awaji Province) of the Nankaido from about the 7th to the 19th century.
Edo-period population registers (shumon jinbetsu aratamecho) combined household registration with religious affiliation.

The Family Registration Law of 1871 took effect in 1872 and was based on actual residence. From 1898 the registered domicile (honseki) was separated from where a person lived, so the koseki of an Awaji family may sit in a different municipality.

The Family Register Act of 1947 took effect in 1948; closed registers (joseki) are kept for 150 years. The Great Hanshin earthquake of 1995 had its epicentre on the island and killed over 5,500 people, worst in the north; the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge to Kobe opened on 5 April 1998.

regions.label: Seto Inland Sea, Okayama coast to Suō-Ōshima
regions.sub: Tamano, Ikuchijima, Ōshima, Hirao

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Edo period: Inland Sea coasts and islands
eras.note: Edo-period population registers (shumon jinbetsu aratamecho) combined household registration with religious affiliation.

eras.polity: Meiji and Imperial Japan: Inland Sea
eras.note: The Family Registration Law of 1871 took effect in 1872. From 1898 the registered domicile (honseki) was separated from actual residence, so the koseki of an islander may be kept by the municipality the family came from.
The Family Register Act of 1947 took effect in 1948 and centres the koseki on a married couple and their children; closed registers (joseki) are kept for 150 years.

regions.label: Uonuma and the Mikuni mountains, Echigo
regions.sub: Muikamachi, Shiozawa, Yuzawa

eras.note: The Uonuma area was part of Echigo Province.
Edo-period population registers (shumon jinbetsu aratamecho) combined household registration with religious affiliation.
The village of Muikamachi was established in 1889. The Family Registration Law of 1871 took effect in 1872, and from 1898 the registered domicile (honseki) was separated from actual residence.
The city of Minamiuonuma was formed in 2004 by a merger involving Muikamachi and Yamato, and Shiozawa joined in 2005, so older records stay under the former town and village names.

regions.label: Hachijō-jima, Izu Islands
regions.sub: Hachijō, Mitsune, Nakanogo

eras.note: Under the early ritsuryo system the island belonged to Suruga Province and moved to Izu Province when Izu separated from Suruga in 680. Its volcano, Nishi-yama, erupted in 1487 and 1518-1523.

Hachijō was a place of exile for convicts, among them the daimyo Ukita Hideie after Sekigahara; from 1704 the grounds for banishment were broadened, and exiles were never told how long their sentences would last.
After a general amnesty in 1868 most residents moved to the mainland; the policy of banishment was not officially abolished until 1881.

Settlers from Hachijō were the first inhabitants of the Daito Islands in 1900. The island was a strategic point for defending the sea approaches to Tokyo, with a base for kaiten suicide submarines on the south coast near the war's end.
From the end of the war through the 1960s the island was promoted for tourism as the Hawaii of Japan.

regions.label: Gagra, Abkhazia coast
regions.sub: Gagra, Ipnari

eras.note: The Ottoman Empire conquered western Georgia, including Gagra, in the 16th century. Earlier names of the site are Triglite (Greek) and Nitica (Roman).

Russia built a small fort in 1833, destroyed during the Crimean War. A census of 1866 recorded 616 residents. Turkish troops destroyed the town and expelled its population in 1877-1878, and Russia rebuilt it after winning the war.

eras.polity: Russian Empire: Black Sea Governorate, resort of Gagra
eras.note: Duke Alexander of Oldenburg developed Gagra as a resort in 1904, the year the area was transferred to the Black Sea Governorate. A local uprising of 1905 produced a short-lived Republic of Gagra.
The Bolsheviks took over in 1917 and the town was incorporated within the Georgian SSR. Lenin's decree of 1919 nationalised Oldenburg's resort as a workers' resort; the population was 26,636 in 1989.

Gagra was at the centre of the war in Abkhazia in 1992-1993 and suffered heavy damage; many ethnic Georgians were expelled and the town came under Abkhaz control. The population was estimated at 12,002 in 2018.

regions.label: Jiaodong tip, Penglai and Rongcheng
regions.sub: Penglai (Dengzhou), Changdao, Yatou, Rongcheng

eras.note: The Ming built the Water Fortress at Penglai in 1376. In 1398 Weihai became a military stronghold (wei) named Weihaiwei, with fortifications built in 1403, under the Ming-era Deng Prefecture.
Rongcheng's county seat was at Chengshanwei from 1735.

In 1858 Yantai became one of the first ports on the Shandong Peninsula open to foreigners, through Penglai; the harbour proved inadequate for traders, so Zhifu, about 48 km away, was developed as Yantai's port. Japan occupied Weihai in 1895 in the Battle of Weihaiwei.
The core of Weihai was ruled by the British from 1 July 1898 under a lease from the Chinese empire, with Port Edward as its capital.
The leased territory of Weihaiwei returned to the Republic of China on 1 October 1930; Liugong Island stayed leased to the United Kingdom until 1940.
The Japanese occupation of Weihai is dated 1938-1945, and Japan occupied Liugong Island in 1940.

eras.polity: People's Republic of China: Yantai and Weihai
eras.note: Weihai was separated from Yantai in 1987. Changdao County, the islands of the Bohai Strait, was merged into Penglai, which became a district, in 2020.

regions.label: Lüshun (Port Arthur) and the Changhai islands, Kwantung
regions.sub: Lüshun, Changhai islands

eras.note: The Beiyang Fleet established a naval base and coaling station at Lüshunkou in 1882.

eras.polity: Qing: Japanese occupation and the Triple Intervention
eras.note: Japan occupied the region in 1894-1895 and the Treaty of Shimonoseki gave it sovereignty, but Germany, France and Russia forced its return to China within weeks.

eras.polity: Russia: leased territory of Port Arthur and Dalny
eras.note: Russian naval vessels entered the harbour in December 1897 and Russia leased the region from China for 25 years in March 1898. Russia founded Dalniy, later Dairen or Dalian, in 1899.

The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred the lease to Japan in 1905; Port Arthur became Ryojun and Dalniy became Dairen. The territory was administered by the Kwantung Governor-General, later the Kanto Bureau, with civil affairs bureaus at Dairen, Ryojun, Kinshu (Jinzhou) and Furanten (Pulandian); the Kwantung Garrison became the separate Kwantung Army in 1919. The lease was extended to 99 years under the Twenty-One Demands, and the 1935 census recorded 1,034,074 residents, 168,185 of them Japanese nationals.

The Soviet Union occupied the territory after Japan's surrender on 2 September 1945 and its navy used the Ryojun base; it handed Kwantung and the Lüshun base to the People's Republic of China on 16 April 1955.

regions.label: Hekou and Lào Cai, the Red River border
regions.sub: Hekou (Yunnan), Mường Khương, Bát Xát, Si Ma Cai

eras.polity: Vietnam: Hưng Hóa (Lê dynasty); Yunnan across the river
eras.note: In 1463 the Lê dynasty made Lào Cai the capital of its northernmost region, then called Hưng Hóa. Hekou, on the Chinese side, is in Yunnan.

eras.polity: Black Flag Army at Lào Cai
eras.note: Jean Dupuis's map of Tonkin of 1879 labels the site as the residence of the chief of the Black Flags.

eras.polity: French Indochina: Tonkin protectorate; Lào Cai military post
eras.note: Tonkin became a French protectorate, which China recognised in 1884 after the Sino-French War. French troops set up customs posts at Lào Cai and other crossings into Yunnan and Guangxi between April 1885 and April 1886, and French colonial rule at Lào Cai is dated from 1889.

The narrow-gauge Yunnan-Vietnam Railway linking Kunming with Haiphong was opened by the French in 1910 and crosses the border at Hekou. In March 1945 Emperor Bảo Đại rescinded the Patenôtre Treaty, ending the protectorates over Annam and Tonkin; the Geneva Accords of 21 July 1954 ended French Indochina.
Lào Cai became the official spelling in November 1950, replacing the French Lao-Kay.

eras.polity: Border closed after the Sino-Vietnamese war
eras.note: Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia prompted a Chinese invasion of northern Vietnam in 1978-1979, and the border was closed for years.

eras.polity: Vietnam: Lào Cai; China: Hekou border zone
eras.note: The border town reopened in 1993; Hekou Border Economic Cooperation Zone was established in 1992, a highway to Lào Cai opened in 2008 and the Mengzi-Hekou rail section was completed in 2014. Yen Bai Province was merged into Lào Cai Province on 12 June 2025.

regions.label: Tonga
regions.sub: Nuku'alofa (Tongatapu), Vava'u, Ha'apai, 'Eua

eras.note: Before registers. The title of Tu'i Kanokupolu was created in 1610, and its holders gradually gained power over Tonga; civil wars are recorded in the 15th and 17th centuries.
The first recorded European contact was by Schouten and Le Maire in April 1616; Abel Tasman visited Tongatapu in January 1643, and James Cook visited in 1773, 1774 and 1777.
The first London missionaries arrived in 1797 and the Wesleyan Methodist Walter Lawry in 1822. The murder of Tuku'aho in 1799 began about fifty years of civil war.
Taufa'ahau unified the islands as King George Tupou I in 1845, and Tonga was declared a constitutional monarchy in 1875.
A Treaty of Friendship with the United Kingdom signed on 18 May 1900 made Tonga a British protected state.
Protected-state status ended and Tonga became independent on 4 June 1970.

regions.label: Tuvalu (Ellice Islands)
regions.sub: Funafuti, Nanumea, Nukulaelae, Vaitupu

eras.note: Before registers.
Álvaro de Mendaña sighted Nui on 16 January 1568, the first recorded European contact.

eras.polity: Peruvian labour raids and the first missions
eras.note: Peruvian blackbirding ships took islanders for labour in 1862-1863, about 180 from Funafuti and about 200 from Nukulaelae in 1863. The Cook Islands deacon Elekana landed at Nukulaelae in 1861 and the London Missionary Society's Rev. Archibald Wright Murray became the first European missionary in 1865.
The Ellice Islands were declared a British protectorate between 9 and 16 October 1892.

The protectorate was incorporated into the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony in 1916. US Marines landed on Funafuti on 2 October 1942 and US forces built airfields there. A referendum in 1974 favoured separate status from the Gilbert Islands.

eras.polity: Tuvalu as a separate British dependency
eras.note: The Tuvaluan Order took effect on 1 October 1975, with separate administrations from 1 January 1976.
Tuvalu became independent on 1 October 1978.

regions.label: Turks and Caicos Islands
regions.sub: Providenciales, Grand Turk, Cockburn Town, Grace Bay

eras.note: Columbus is recorded as first landing on Grand Turk in 1492, and the first recorded European sighting of the islands is dated 1512. The Lucayan population declined sharply from slavery and disease. Bermudians began raking salt here in the 16th century.
Bermudian salt collectors built the first permanent settlement on Grand Turk in 1681. Spanish and French forces captured the islands from Bermuda in 1706 and Bermuda retook them in 1710.
The islands became part of the Bahamas colony in 1766. Bahamian and Bermudian authorities disputed jurisdiction and taxation from 1773 to 1786, with repeated seizures of Bermudian vessels.

eras.polity: Separate colony under a council president
eras.note: The islands separated from the Bahamas in 1848 and became a colony under a council president, supervised by the governor of Jamaica.
An Act of Parliament annexed the islands to Jamaica in 1873 (the same page also says 1874). They got their own administrator in 1959, with Jamaica's governor still overseeing them.

After Jamaica's independence in 1962 the islands became a Crown colony. In the 1960s-1980s American investors funded an airstrip and the first hotel on Providenciales, and Club Med opened a resort at Grace Bay.

regions.label: British Virgin Islands
regions.sub: Road Town (Tortola), Virgin Gorda, Jost Van Dyke, Anegada

eras.note: Before registers.

Joost van Dyk organised the first permanent settlement at Soper's Hole, and Spanish records noted it by 1615. Dutch company interest effectively ended in the 1650s, when Tortola was sold to Willem Hunthum.
Colonel William Burt took control of Tortola for England no later than 13 July 1672. Slavery was abolished on 1 August 1834.

eras.polity: British Virgin Islands in the Leeward Islands
eras.note: Denmark sold St Thomas, across the boundary, to the United States in 1917, so its records are Danish and then American.
The Leeward Islands Federation was abolished in 1956, which raised the Territory's political status. A constitution took effect by order-in-council in 1967, with elections that year.

regions.label: Ascension Island
regions.sub: Georgetown, Wideawake Airfield, Green Mountain

eras.note: João da Nova is credited with discovering the island in 1501 and Afonso de Albuquerque named it Ascension in 1503. HMS Roebuck was wrecked there in 1701 and a Dutch sailor was exiled there in 1725, but neither led to a settlement. The island has never had an indigenous population.

Britain claimed the island on 22 October 1815, partly to guard against escape attempts by Napoleon on nearby Saint Helena, and the Royal Navy treated it as a stone frigate, HMS Ascension. A Royal Marines garrison was established in 1823 and the Eastern Telegraph Company laid a submarine cable in 1899.

Admiralty control ended in 1922, when letters patent made Ascension a dependency of Saint Helena and the Eastern Telegraph Company took over administration on 20 October. The US built the Wideawake airbase in 1941-1942.

A British administrator replaced the Eastern Telegraph Company's head as the island's administrator in 1964. An elected Island Council began in 2002 and a new constitution of 2009 made Ascension a constituent part of the territory. The 2016 census recorded 806 residents.

regions.label: Sunraysia, Mildura and the Murray border
regions.sub: Mildura, Irymple

eras.polity: Latje Latje and Ngintait country: New South Wales
eras.note: The Latje Latje and Ngintait peoples were the original inhabitants of the Mildura area, and the Jarijari are also named among local tribes. Port Phillip was separated from New South Wales on 1 July 1851.

eras.polity: Colony of Victoria: Mildura sheep station
eras.note: The 1851 Act described the new colony as running along the Murray River to South Australia's eastern boundary, so Mildura (on the Victorian side) and the New South Wales towns across the river file in different colonies. Mildura was the name of an early sheep station covering most of the area.

eras.polity: Colony of Victoria: Chaffey irrigation settlement
eras.note: After a drought from 1877 to 1884, Alfred Deakin visited California's irrigation areas and met George and William Chaffey. In 1886 George Chaffey chose the derelict Mildura station for his first irrigation settlement; the settlement of Mildura was established in 1887 and its post office opened on 23 January 1888.
Federation of Australia took place on 1 January 1901. A Carnegie library opened in Mildura in 1908.
Mildura was proclaimed a city in 1934. After the Second World War migrants from Italy, Greece and other Mediterranean countries came for work in fruit picking.

regions.label: Otago coast, Dunedin and the Otago Peninsula
regions.sub: Dunedin (St Kilda), Port Chalmers, Otago Peninsula

eras.polity: Maori and Ngai Tahu: Otago Peninsula
eras.note: Maori settled the region first, mostly along the coast and centred on the Otago Peninsula; most of the Maori population today belongs to Ngai Tahu, with the Otago runanga at Otakou, Moeraki and Puketeraki.
The Weller Brothers established a European settlement on Otago Harbour in 1831, which gave the area its old European name.

The Scottish Presbyterian settlement of Dunedin was founded in March 1848 as an offshoot of the Free Church of Scotland, when the John Wickliffe and Philip Laing arrived from Greenock. Otago Province was created in 1853 (1852 in some accounts), and gold was found at Gabriel's Gully in 1861. Southland split off in 1861 and was re-absorbed in 1870.
Provincial governments were abolished under the Abolition of the Provinces Act, effective 1 November 1876.

regions.label: Rouergue — Rodez, Millau and the Aveyron
regions.sub: Rodez, Millau, Decazeville, Saint-Affrique

eras.polity: Counts of Rouergue, who also took Toulouse
eras.note: Before registers. Charles the Bald detached Rouergue from the Duchy of Aquitaine and made it a county; in 852 its counts took Toulouse and founded the Raimondin dynasty.

eras.polity: Counts of Toulouse and the separate County of Rodez
eras.note: Before registers. In 1112 the Raimondins ceded the County of Rodez to Richard, viscount of Millau. Simon IV de Montfort ravaged towns including Millau between 1208 and 1214.

Rouergue was incorporated into the French crown in 1271 after the death of Countess Jeanne of Toulouse; the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) is among its changes of ruler. In 1349 sixteen vigueries are recorded and in 1579 Rouergue was attached to the généralité of Guyenne. Copies of pre-1792 church registers are usually in the departmental archives.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — royal domain, généralité of Montauban
eras.note: Rouergue was attached to the royal domain in 1607 under Henri IV. In 1716 the Montauban généralité was restricted to the Rouergue and Quercy elections, and in 1779 Rouergue was merged with Quercy as Haute-Guyenne.

The Aveyron department was created in 1790 with Rodez as chef-lieu. The canton of Saint-Antonin-Noble-Val was transferred to Tarn-et-Garonne in 1808, so a family from the old province's western edge may be filed under that department. Civil registration began in 1792: one register stays at the mairie and the second goes to the departmental archives once it is 100 years old.

regions.label: Haute-Auvergne — Aurillac and Saint-Flour (Cantal)
regions.sub: Aurillac, Saint-Flour, Arpajon-sur-Cère

eras.polity: County of Auvergne under Alphonse de Poitiers — bailliage des Montagnes d'Auvergne
eras.note: The distinction between the high and low country dates from about 1250, when Alphonse de Poitiers created the bailliage des Montagnes d'Auvergne. After Alphonse's death in 1271 Auvergne reverted to the royal domain.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — Haute-Auvergne, diocese of Saint-Flour
eras.note: The diocese of Saint-Flour was created in 1317. In 1328 the Montagnes bailliage counted 215 parishes and 27,382 hearths. The gentlemen of the high country were mustered at Aurillac on 15 May 1533.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — vice-bailliage of the Montagnes d'Auvergne
eras.note: A vice-bailli of the Montagnes d'Auvergne was created in 1573 to suppress disorder and the post was suppressed in 1720. Historians treat the Haute-Auvergne before the Revolution as mainly a droit écrit area.

Cantal was one of the original departments created on 4 March 1790, with Aurillac as prefecture and Saint-Flour and Mauriac as sub-prefectures. The Civil Constitution of the Clergy abolished the diocese of Saint-Flour, whose bishop refused the oath. Civil registration began in 1792.

The bishopric of Saint-Flour was reinstated after the Concordat of 1801 with the borders of the Cantal department. Registers older than 100 years are in the departmental archives; the more recent ones stay at the mairie.

regions.label: Gévaudan, Velay and the Brivadois — Mende, Le Puy and Brioude
regions.sub: Le Puy-en-Velay, Mende, Brioude, Ambert, Yssingeaux, Marvejols

eras.polity: Gévaudan (under the Count of Toulouse) and Velay
eras.note: Before registers. In the early 10th century Mende replaced Javols as capital of Gévaudan and Le Puy replaced Saint-Paulien as capital of Velay.

eras.polity: Bishop-counts of Mende and Le Puy; Gévaudan under the Crown of Aragon from 1166
eras.note: In 1096 the Count of Toulouse transferred his rights over eastern Gévaudan to the Bishop of Mende, and in 1166 Alfonso II of Aragon inherited Gévaudan. Velay is first named a county in 1142 and became an independent county in 1162 with its bishop as count; it had eighteen baronies and Gévaudan eight.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — Languedoc (Gévaudan, Velay) and Auvergne (Brivadois)
eras.note: The Bishop of Mende was granted the title of count of Gévaudan in 1307. Gévaudan and Velay were nominally part of Languedoc but kept their own Estates until 1789; Brioude is listed among the territories of the diocese of Saint-Flour (created 1317), so it belongs with Auvergne, not Languedoc. The religious wars ruined the country in the 16th century.

On 4 March 1790 Gévaudan ceased to exist and the Lozère department was created; Haute-Loire was created from Velay with parts of Auvergne, Gévaudan and Vivarais, and Auvergne was divided into Puy-de-Dôme, Cantal, Haute-Loire and Allier. A family moving between Mende, Le Puy and Brioude therefore crosses departmental archives. Civil registration began in 1792.

regions.label: Alençon and the Orne — Alençon, Argentan, La Ferté-Macé
regions.sub: Alençon, Argentan, La Ferté-Macé

eras.polity: Lords of Bellême, then the County of Alençon
eras.note: Before registers. The Bellême line held Alençon from the 10th to the early 13th century.

eras.polity: County of Alençon — appanage of Charles of Valois
eras.note: Charles of Valois was given the county in appanage in 1291 (the same source also gives 1293).

The county was raised to a duchy in 1414. Duke Jean I was killed at Agincourt on 25 October 1415; Jean II was dispossessed at Verneuil on 17 August 1424 and reconquered the domain in 1449. The duchy reverted to the crown on the death of the childless Charles IV (dated 1524 in the text and 1525 in the list of dukes).

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — Alençon held as dower and appanage
eras.note: Marguerite, Charles IV's widow, held the title until 1549; it went to Catherine de' Medici as jointure in 1559 and became an appanage in 1566 (François, Duke of Anjou), 1646 (Gaston, Duke of Orléans), 1710 (the Duke of Berry) and 1774 (the Count of Provence).

Civil registration began in 1792. Registers older than 100 years are in the departmental archives and those of Alençon also in the municipal archives; pre-1792 church registers are usually in the departmental archives.

regions.label: Longwy and the Pays-Haut — Longwy, Mont-Saint-Martin, Longuyon
regions.sub: Longwy, Mont-Saint-Martin, Longuyon

eras.polity: Upper Lorraine and the Duchy of Bar
eras.note: Before registers. Longwy first belonged to Lotharingia, then to Upper Lorraine and the Duchy of Bar. It was ceded to Wenceslaus I of Luxembourg in 1368 and returned to Bar in 1378; Bar was annexed to the Duchy of Lorraine in 1480.
Longwy was part of the Kingdom of France from 1648 to 1660 and then returned to Lorraine.

eras.polity: Kingdom of France — fortress town of Louis XIV
eras.note: Longwy became French again in 1670 and the Treaties of Nijmegen (1678) confirmed it; Vauban fortified the town. The Revolutionary civil registration began in 1792. Before 1871 Longwy belonged to the Moselle department.

eras.polity: France — Longwy a frontier town of Meurthe-et-Moselle
eras.note: After the Treaty of Frankfurt only one fifth of Moselle, including Longwy, escaped annexation by Germany. Longwy is now in Meurthe-et-Moselle, so records before and after 1871 may lie with different departmental archives.
After the Battle of the Ardennes the town was occupied by the German army from August 1914 until the Armistice of 1918; Lieutenant Colonel Darche held the German 5th Army for three weeks.
The Longwy "ville neuve" was listed in 2008 as part of the Fortifications of Vauban.

regions.label: Crotone and the Marchesato — Cotrone, Cirò, Cutro
regions.sub: Crotone, Cirò Marina, Isola di Capo Rizzuto, Cutro

eras.polity: Byzantine rule, Norman conquest and the Ruffo marquisate of Cotrone
eras.note: Before registers. Totila besieged the city unsuccessfully about 550; it passed to the Byzantine Empire, was sacked by Saracens about 870 and later conquered by the Normans (undated). A seal of 1401 styles Niccolò Ruffo "Marquess of Cotrone"; he was Viceroy and Justiciar of the Calabrias.
Alfonso V conquered the Kingdom of Naples in 1442 and reunited Naples and Sicily under Aragon.
The viceroyalty is dated 1504 to 1714. The Castle of Charles V in Crotone is of the 16th century.
The Treaty of Rastatt (7 March 1714) gave Naples to Charles VI.
A Spanish army conquered Naples and Sicily in 1734 and Charles, Duke of Parma, was king from 1735.

Joseph Bonaparte was installed as king in 1806 and Murat followed. The British occupied and sacked Crotone in 1806 and the French later occupied it. Civil registration began in southern Italy in 1809.
Ferdinand was restored in 1815 and the Two Sicilies were formed on 8 December 1816. The Kingdom of Naples kept registering births, marriages and deaths without interruption after 1815.

The Kingdom of Sardinia conquered the Two Sicilies in 1860 and the territory joined Italy in 1861. The town was called Cotrone from the Middle Ages until 1928, so search both names. The Province of Crotone was created in 1992. Many state-archive civil registers are on the Antenati portal.

regions.label: Western Riviera — Ventimiglia, Bordighera and Sanremo
regions.sub: Ventimiglia, Bordighera, Vallecrosia, Sanremo

eras.polity: County of Ventimiglia under Genoa; Sanremo under Genoese bishops, the Doria and De Mari
eras.note: Genoa forced Ventimiglia to surrender in 1139 and the count kept the city as a Genoese vassal; the Lascaris dynasty of Tenda began in 1269. Sanremo was first under the County of Ventimiglia, then under the Genoese bishops, and was sold to the Doria and De Mari families in 1297; it became a free town in the second half of the 15th century.

eras.polity: Republic of Genoa (Ventimiglia); Sanremo independent of Genoa
eras.note: Ventimiglia was annexed to the Genoese Republic in 1505. Sanremo stayed independent of Genoa and rose against Genoese attempts at control in 1753, after which Genoa built the Santa Tecla fortress.
Napoleon took Genoa in May 1797 and the Ligurian Republic was founded in June 1797.

eras.polity: French Empire — departments of Apennins, Gênes and Montenotte
eras.note: France annexed the Ligurian territory in June 1805 as the departments of Apennins, Gênes and Montenotte.
After the Savoy restoration in 1814 Sanremo was annexed to the Kingdom of Sardinia; the Liguria territory was awarded to Piedmont-Sardinia on 3 January 1815 after the Congress of Vienna.
National civil registration began in 1866 in northern and central Italy; many state-archive civil registers are on Antenati.

regions.label: South coast of Sicily — Pozzallo, Scicli, Pachino and Niscemi
regions.sub: Pozzallo, Scicli, Ispica, Pachino, Santa Croce Camerina, Niscemi

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily — County of Modica
eras.note: Frederick III conceded the County of Modica to Manfredi I Chiaramonte on 25 March 1296; it was re-created in 1392 for Bernat IV de Cabrera after Andrea Chiaramonte was beheaded on 1 July 1392. The Compromise of Caspe (1412) added Sicily permanently to the Crown of Aragon. The towns named for the county under the Cabreras include Scicli, Spaccaforno (today's Ispica) and the port of Pozzallo, but not Niscemi or Pachino.

eras.polity: Spanish Sicily — County of Modica under the Enríquez-Cabrera
eras.note: Spanish domination dates from 1479; the Enríquez-Cabrera counts held Modica from 1530. The 1693 earthquake killed over 60,000 people in Sicily and was followed by Late Baroque rebuilding in the Val di Noto.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sicily under the House of Savoy
eras.note: The Treaty of Utrecht gave Sicily to the House of Savoy in 1713.
Savoy exchanged Sicily for Sardinia in 1720 (Treaty of The Hague) and Austria ruled until 1735.
Britain occupied the island from 1806 to 1814 and the Sicilian Constitution of 1812 is linked to the end of feudalism; the County of Modica is dated 1296 to 1812.
Ferdinand merged Sicily with Naples in 1816. Civil registration in Sicily began in 1820 in a format almost identical to the Napoleonic registers.
The Two Sicilies became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861; many state-archive civil registers are on Antenati.

regions.label: Lake Maggiore and the Ticino — Varese shore and the Novara frontier
regions.sub: Sesto Calende, Somma Lombardo, Luino, Laveno, Galliate

eras.note: The Duchy of Milan of 1395 lay between the Adda and Ticino rivers.
The Spanish viceroys governed Milan from 1535; France recognised Philip II's possession in 1559 (Cateau-Cambrésis).
Austrian rule dates from 1707 and the Treaty of Baden (1714) ceded the duchy to the Austrian Habsburgs.

The Treaty of Vienna (1738) left Novara and Tortona to Charles Emmanuel III of Savoy-Sardinia. A place near Novara therefore changed registers in 1738 while those on the Varese side of Lake Maggiore stayed in Austrian Milan.

eras.polity: Transpadane, Cisalpine and Napoleonic republic and kingdom
eras.note: The French set up the Transpadane Republic in 1796; it merged with the Cispadane Republic in 1797 to form the Cisalpine Republic, capital Milan. Napoleonic civil registration ran roughly 1806 to 1814 in Lombardy and 1804 to 1814 in Piedmont.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia (Lombard side); Kingdom of Sardinia (Novara side)
eras.note: The decisions of the Congress of Vienna of 9 June 1815 created the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia as an Austrian land. Piedmont resumed civil records in 1839.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Sardinia, then Kingdom and Republic of Italy
eras.note: Lombardy was ceded to Piedmont-Sardinia in 1859 and the Kingdom of Italy followed in 1861. Civil registration became national in 1866 in northern and central Italy.

regions.label: Eastern Seville and the Sierra Sur — Osuna, Marchena and Estepa
regions.sub: Osuna, Marchena, Estepa, Palma del Río, Rute, Olvera

eras.note: Ferdinand III of Castile conquered Osuna from the Almohads in 1239.

eras.polity: Order of Calatrava — Encomienda of Osuna
eras.note: Osuna was handed to the Order of Calatrava in 1264, which created the Encomienda of Osuna.
Don Pedro Girón appropriated Osuna in 1445. The collegiate church dates from 1534 and the University of Osuna was founded in 1549.

Philip II conferred the title of Duke of Osuna on Pedro Téllez in 1562. The university was suppressed in 1820. The other towns in this ring (Marchena, Estepa, Palma del Río, Rute, Olvera) had their own lords.
Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837. The records are held in each municipality's archive.

regions.label: The Valencia–Castile frontier — Villajoyosa, Benidorm, Castalla and Utiel
regions.sub: Benidorm, Villajoyosa, Castalla, Ayora, Utiel

eras.polity: Kingdom of Valencia — Treaty of Almizra frontier
eras.note: James I of Aragon signed the Treaty of Almizra on 26 March 1244: the lands south of a line from Biar to Villajoyosa, through Busot, were reserved to Castile. James nevertheless conquered Caudete, Villena and Sax, which technically belonged to Castile.

eras.polity: Crown of Aragon after the conquest of Murcia
eras.note: In 1296 James II of Aragon conquered the Kingdom of Murcia.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Valencia — Crown of Aragon
eras.note: Medio Vinalopó, Bajo Vinalopó, L'Alacantí and the Vega Baja del Segura were incorporated into Valencia by the treaties of Torrellas (1304) and Elche (1305).

eras.polity: Spain — after the Nueva Planta decree for Valencia
eras.note: The abolition of the Valencian institutions was promulgated on 29 June 1707; the Furs of Valencia were repealed completely and the Courts abolished.
Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837; the records are kept in each municipality's archive.

regions.label: Spanish Cerdanya — Puigcerdà and Llívia
regions.sub: Puigcerdà, Llívia

eras.note: Before registers. Cerdanya became a Frankish vassal about 785 under Carolingian pressure; Wilfred the Hairy was count from 870 to 897 and the line of the counts ended in 1117.

eras.polity: Counts of Barcelona and kings of Aragon
eras.note: The county passed to the counts of Barcelona, later kings of Aragon, in 1117. Puigcerdà replaced Hix as capital of Cerdanya in 1178.
The Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) split Cerdanya between France in the north and Spain in the south; Llívia stayed Spanish. Records of the French half are filed in France.

eras.polity: Spain — Catalonia after the Nueva Planta
eras.note: The Nueva Planta decree for Catalonia was dispatched on 16 January 1716 (issued 9 October 1715); the Generalitat and General Court were abolished.
Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837; the records are kept in each municipality's archive.

regions.label: La Rioja — Haro and Calahorra
regions.sub: Haro, Calahorra

eras.note: Before registers. Sancho I of Pamplona reconquered most of the territory in 923; the Kingdom of Viguera existed from 970 to about 1005, after which the area was part of Pamplona. The name La Rioja first appears in 1099.
After Sancho IV's murder in 1076 Navarre was divided and Castile obtained La Rioja. From 1134 García Ramírez and Sancho VI fought Castile for former Pamplonese lands.
The region was annexed by Castile in 1177 after a judgement by Henry II of England. A province of Logroño was created in January 1822 under the Liberal Triennium, but Ferdinand VII annulled it.

eras.polity: Spain — province of Logroño, renamed La Rioja in 1980
eras.note: The province of Logroño was formed again in 1833 within Castilla la Vieja and temporarily enlarged in 1841; it was renamed La Rioja in 1980. Spanish civil registration began in 1871, with some municipalities from 1837.

eras.polity: Spain — autonomous community of La Rioja
eras.note: The Statute of Autonomy took effect on 9 June 1982.

regions.label: Baix Empordà coast — Palafrugell, Palamós and Platja d'Aro
regions.sub: Palafrugell, Palamós, Castell-Platja d'Aro

eras.note: Before registers. The County of Empúries is dated 812 (Ermenguer's separate county forms about 813); it was merged with the County of Roussillon from 817 until 989 and its dynasty ended in 1322. It corresponds to the historic comarca of Empordà.

eras.polity: County of Empúries — Crown of Aragon
eras.note: Hugh VI sold the county to Peter IV of Ribagorza in 1325 and it became an apanage of the Crown of Aragon in 1341.
The county is listed as annexed into the Principality of Catalonia in 1402; Empúries escheated to the crown between 1410 and 1436.

eras.polity: Spain — Catalonia after the Nueva Planta
eras.note: The Nueva Planta decree for Catalonia was dispatched on 16 January 1716; the Generalitat, General Court and Consell de Cent were abolished.

eras.polity: Spain — civil registration; Baix Empordà comarca
eras.note: Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837. The Empordà was divided into Alt Empordà and Baix Empordà in the comarcal division of 1936.

regions.label: Baza, Huéscar and the Vélez country — north-eastern Granada
regions.sub: Baza, Huéscar, Vélez-Rubio, Pulpí

eras.note: Ibn al-Ahmar was declared emir at Arjona on 16 July 1232 and took Granada in April 1238. Baza was under Islamic rule from 713 until 1489, and its bishopric was restored in 1306.

eras.polity: Crown of Castile — Kingdom of Granada
eras.note: Baza fell to Isabella I in 1489 after a seven-month siege. The Treaty of Granada was signed on 25 November 1491 and Boabdil surrendered Granada on 2 January 1492. On 21 May 1492 the see of Baza was merged with Guadix as the Diocese of Guadix-Baza. A Mudéjar uprising took place in 1500. The conquest dates of Huéscar, Vélez-Rubio and Pulpí differ from Baza's.
The Morisco revolt began in 1568 and lasted about three years; a decree of 1609 ordered the expulsion of the Moriscos. The union of the Guadix and Baza sees ended in 1851.
Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837; the records are kept in each municipality's archive.

regions.label: Southern Galicia — Ponteareas, O Porriño, Nigrán and Baiona
regions.sub: Ponteareas, O Porriño, Nigrán, Baiona, Mondariz

eras.note: Before registers. Portugal separated from Galicia in 1128 (the Battle of São Mamede).

eras.polity: Kingdom of Galicia — Crown of Castile
eras.note: Ferdinand III's accession in 1230 brought Galicia under the Crown of Castile. Ferdinand I of Portugal was a rival claimant in 1369. Galicia is dated as administered within the Crown of Castile from 1490 to 1715.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Galicia — Crown of Spain
eras.note: Galicia was under Napoleonic occupation from January to July 1809. The kingdom is dated as dissolved in 1833 or 1834 depending on the passage.
Ponteareas, O Porriño, Nigrán and Baiona are municipalities of the province of Pontevedra today.
Spanish civil registration began in 1871, although some municipalities have records from 1837; the records are kept in each municipality's archive.

regions.label: Great Yarmouth and Lowestoft — the Norfolk–Suffolk coast
regions.sub: Great Yarmouth, Gorleston, Caister-on-Sea, Lowestoft, Hemsby

eras.note: The Domesday Book places Lowestoft in the king's holding in the hundred of Lothingland (Suffolk). Great Yarmouth is in Norfolk.

eras.polity: Borough of Great Yarmouth (Norfolk) and Lowestoft (Suffolk)
eras.note: King John granted Great Yarmouth a charter in 1208. The Battle of Lowestoft against the Dutch was fought on 13 June 1665; the town's Royalist sympathies in 1643 were partly tied to its rivalry with Yarmouth.

eras.polity: Great Yarmouth enlarged to include Little Yarmouth
eras.note: A charter of Charles II in 1668 extended the borough to include Little Yarmouth (Southtown), which lay in the Suffolk parish of Gorleston. Queen Anne's charter of 1703 replaced the two bailiffs with a mayor.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Great Britain — a borough straddling Norfolk and Suffolk
eras.note: Until 1 April 1891 the borough of Great Yarmouth straddled Norfolk and Suffolk for ceremonial and judicial purposes, so check both county record offices.

The Municipal Corporations Act 1835 reformed Great Yarmouth as a municipal borough in 1836 with its boundaries enlarged to include all of Gorleston parish; Lowestoft became a municipal borough in 1885. Civil registration in England and Wales began on 1 July 1837.

eras.polity: County borough of Great Yarmouth; Lowestoft in East Suffolk
eras.note: Great Yarmouth became a county borough in 1889 and Lowestoft joined the administrative county of East Suffolk that year. On 1 April 1891 the county boundary was adjusted so the whole Yarmouth borough lay in Norfolk.

eras.polity: Borough of Great Yarmouth (Norfolk) and Waveney (Suffolk)
eras.note: On 1 April 1974 the Local Government Act 1972 took effect: the Great Yarmouth county borough and parish were abolished and Lowestoft became part of the Waveney district.

regions.label: West Pembrokeshire — Haverfordwest and Milford Haven
regions.sub: Haverfordwest, Milford Haven, St Davids, Fishguard

eras.note: Before registers. Normans and Flemings arrived between 1067 and 1111 and built castles such as Pembroke Castle.

Pembrokeshire was declared a county palatine in 1138, followed by a wave of Flemish settlement. The Landsker Line divides the English-speaking south ("Little England beyond Wales"); George Owen of Henllys remarked on the distinction in 1603.

eras.polity: England and Wales — county of Pembroke
eras.note: The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 reorganised the county into seven hundreds. Civil registration in England and Wales began on 1 July 1837.

eras.polity: United Kingdom — two districts of Dyfed
eras.note: The county was abolished under the Local Government Act 1972 (in force from 1 April 1974) and Pembrokeshire became two districts of Dyfed.
Pembrokeshire was restored as a unitary authority on 1 April 1996.

regions.label: The Epirote coast — Parga, Preveza and Igoumenitsa
regions.sub: Preveza, Parga, Igoumenitsa, Lefkada

eras.polity: Venetian Parga; Preveza Ottoman and Venetian by turns
eras.note: Parga passed to Venice in 1401 as an exclave of Corfu; the Ottomans held it for two years from 1452 and Barbarossa burned its fortress in 1537. Preveza was refounded by the Ottomans in the late 15th century (dated 1477 or about 1486-87 depending on the source), was captured by Venice in September 1684 and returned in 1699, and Venice retook it in November 1717 and held it until 1797.

eras.polity: French rule, Ali Pasha and British protection
eras.note: Venetian rule ended in 1797 and Parga passed to France; its citizens revolted in 1815 and sought British protection. In Preveza the French were overwhelmed by Ali Pasha at the Battle of Nicopolis on 12 October 1798, and Ali Pasha ruled it until 1820.

In 1819 Britain handed Parga to Ali Pasha for a monetary settlement and the town was abandoned by its inhabitants. After Ali Pasha died in 1822, Constantinople controlled Preveza more directly, and in 1863 it became the seat of the Sanjak of Preveze. Igoumenitsa and the town of Lefkada fall inside this ring but are not described here.

The Greek Army took Preveza on 21 October 1912 and the Treaty of London (1913) made southern Epirus part of Greece. In 1924 about 1,500 Albanian-speaking Muslims were transferred from Parga to Turkey.

regions.label: The Balkan Mountains — Troyan, Teteven, Tryavna and Kotel
regions.sub: Troyan, Teteven, Tryavna, Kotel

eras.note: Ottoman Bulgaria is dated from 1396 (the Battle of Nicopolis); the Bulgarian National Revival runs from about 1762 to 1878, with the April Uprising in 1876. Troyan was named a town in 1868 as a craft centre.

eras.polity: Principality of Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia
eras.note: The Principality of Bulgaria was established on 13 July 1878. The Treaty of Berlin created Eastern Rumelia, an autonomous province with Plovdiv as capital, lying between the Balkan Mountains, the Rhodope Mountains and Strandzha. Kotel was a canton of the Sliven department of Eastern Rumelia, so check which side of the mountains a place lay.

eras.polity: Principality of Bulgaria — united with Eastern Rumelia
eras.note: Eastern Rumelia was united with the Principality on 6 September 1885 in a bloodless revolution.
Bulgaria declared its independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908.

regions.label: Bergisches Land — Gummersbach, Wipperfürth, Wiehl
regions.sub: Gummersbach, Wipperfürth, Wiehl, Hückeswagen, Nümbrecht

eras.note: Before registers. The counts of Berg appear in 1101 as a junior line of the Ezzonen and moved their court from Schloss Burg to Düsseldorf in 1280.

eras.polity: Duchy of Berg — Jülich-Berg, then the United Duchies
eras.note: Wenceslaus raised the counts to dukes in 1380. Berg and Jülich were joined under one ruler (dated 1348 or 1423 depending on the source) and ruled with Cleves as the United Duchies from 1521; the last duke died in 1609.

eras.polity: Duchy of Berg under Palatinate-Neuburg, the Palatinate and Bavaria
eras.note: The Treaty of Xanten (1614) gave Berg to Palatinate-Neuburg, which inherited the Palatine electorate in 1685. Berg was united with Bavaria in 1777 and separated again in 1803 under a junior Wittelsbach branch.

Raised to a grand duchy on 15 March 1806 (Murat, then Napoleon, then Napoléon Louis, with French officials administering); the grand duchy itself ended in 1813. Civil registration was kept here from 1806 until 1815, after which parishes went back to church registers.

eras.polity: Prussia — Province of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, from 1822 the Rhine Province
eras.note: After the Congress of Vienna, Berg joined the Province of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, which merged into the Rhine Province in 1822.

eras.polity: Prussia — Rhine Province in the German Empire
eras.note: Standesamt registration started in Prussia in October 1874 and became general in Germany on 1 January 1876. Registers stay with the local Standesamt, with older ones in city or state archives.

regions.label: Bremen-Verden — Stade, Buxtehude and Jork
regions.sub: Stade, Buxtehude, Jork, Neu Wulmstorf

eras.note: Before registers. The Peace of Westphalia secularised the archbishopric, and the Prince-Bishopric of Verden, in 1648.
Sweden held the duchies of Bremen and Verden in personal union; Stade was the seat of government chosen in the 1648 reorganisation.
Denmark-Norway occupied the duchies in the Great Northern War and sold them to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715.
The Treaty of Stockholm (1719) settled Sweden's compensation for the loss of the duchies.

Added to the Kingdom of Westphalia on 1 March 1810 and annexed by France effective 1 January 1811. Parts of Hanover kept civil registers in 1811-1815 before going back to church registers, so check whether a given parish did.
Restored to Hanover in 1813; Hanover became a kingdom in 1814. In 1823 the two duchies were merged into the High-Bailiwick of Stade.

eras.polity: Prussia after the annexation of Hanover
eras.note: Prussia annexed the Kingdom of Hanover in 1866. Prussia introduced civil registration in October 1874; the rest of Germany followed from 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Jülich land — Jülich, Erkelenz and Wegberg
regions.sub: Jülich, Erkelenz, Wegberg, Inden

eras.note: Before registers. Gerhard III is the first to style himself count of Jülich in 1081, and Jülich received town privileges in 1234.
Charles IV raised the count to duke in 1356. Jülich was united with Guelders from 1393 to 1423.

eras.polity: Jülich-Berg, from 1521 the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg
eras.note: Jülich merged with Berg in 1423 and joined Cleves in the United Duchies in 1521. The last duke died in 1609, starting the War of the Jülich Succession.

eras.polity: Duchy of Jülich under Palatinate-Neuburg, then Palatinate-Sulzbach
eras.note: The Treaty of Xanten (1614) gave Jülich and Berg to Palatinate-Neuburg. Charles Theodore of Palatinate-Sulzbach inherited both in 1742.

France occupied and annexed the duchy in 1794 and the Treaty of Lunéville (1801) recognised the cession; it lay in the Roer department. French civil registration began in 1798 west of the Rhine and continued after 1815.

eras.polity: Prussia — Province of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, from 1822 the Rhine Province
eras.note: Jülich became a Prussian province in 1815; it joined the Rhine Province in 1822. Sittard and Tegelen went to the United Kingdom of the Netherlands in 1815.

regions.label: Paderborn land and the Upper Weser — Höxter, Warburg, Beverungen
regions.sub: Höxter, Warburg, Borgentreich, Beverungen

eras.note: Before registers. The bishop received the regalia in 1281, giving the bishopric imperial immediacy; Protestantism gained ground in the diocese in 1502-32 and the Augsburg Confession was allowed in 1577-85.

Dietrich IV of Fürstenberg (1585-1618) restored Catholic practice and founded the University of Paderborn in 1614. Corvey Abbey was a separate imperial abbey, so check whether a parish near Höxter fell to Corvey or to the bishopric.
The bishopric was secularised in 1802 and became Prussian.
Part of the Kingdom of Westphalia, 1807-13. Civil registration was kept in the kingdom from 1807 until 1815, then parishes returned to church registers.
Prussian again from 1813, in the Province of Westphalia. The Catholic Diocese of Paderborn was recreated in 1821.

eras.polity: Prussia — Province of Westphalia in the German Empire
eras.note: Civil registers (Standesamt) exist from October 1874 in Prussia, with national coverage from 1 January 1876. The Diocese of Paderborn was raised to an archdiocese in 1930.

regions.label: Waldeck — Korbach and Bad Arolsen
regions.sub: Korbach, Bad Arolsen, Medebach

eras.note: Before registers. A branch of the Schwalenberg family took its name from Waldeck Castle in 1180.
The county gained imperial immediacy in 1349, inherited Pyrmont in 1625-26 and moved its residence from Waldeck to Arolsen in 1655.
Raised to a principality in January 1712.
Waldeck joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1807.

eras.polity: Principality of Waldeck under Prussian administration
eras.note: From 1 January 1868 Prussia ran Waldeck's internal administration, courts and schools, while the principality stayed nominally independent. Civil registration covered all Germany from 1 January 1876.
The monarchy was abolished on 13 November 1918 and Waldeck became a free state; Pyrmont left for Prussia in 1921.
The free state was abolished on 1 April 1929 and joined the Prussian Province of Hesse-Nassau; a Waldeck district with Korbach as capital was formed in 1942.
The territory became part of Greater Hesse in 1945-46 and then the state of Hesse.

regions.label: Birkenfeld and the upper Nahe — Idar-Oberstein, Nohfelden
regions.sub: Idar-Oberstein, Birkenfeld, Nohfelden, Freisen

eras.polity: Several small sovereigns, including Pfalz-Birkenfeld and Palatine Zweibrücken
eras.note: Before registers. The land later gathered in the French Sarre department came from seven sovereigns.
French civil registration began in 1798 in the Rhineland west of the Rhine and continued after Napoleon's defeat.
In 1815 Prussia agreed to cede land from the former Sarre department to compensate Oldenburg; the division was settled in 1816.

eras.polity: Principality of Birkenfeld — an Oldenburg exclave
eras.note: Oldenburg took possession on 16 April 1817. The Napoleonic Code stayed in force until the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch replaced it in 1900; the neighbouring Lichtenberg district was sold to Prussia in 1832.

eras.polity: Oldenburg's Birkenfeld under French occupation, then the Weimar Republic
eras.note: A 'Birkenfeld Republic' was proclaimed on 14 July 1919 under French occupation; French troops withdrew in 1930.

eras.polity: Nazi Germany — Landkreis Birkenfeld in Prussia's Rhine Province
eras.note: On 1 April 1937 the Greater Hamburg Act made the territory a Landkreis in Prussia's Rhine Province. Most of the former Nohfelden court district now lies in Saarland.

regions.label: East Frisia — Norden, Borkum and Norderney
regions.sub: Norden, Norderney, Borkum, Hage

eras.note: Emperor Frederick III made a Cirksena a count in 1465; the emperor accepted Count Edzard and his descendants in 1517.

eras.polity: Principality of East Frisia — seat at Aurich
eras.note: The counts were raised to princes in 1654, though their power stayed limited.
Prussia took over East Frisia in 1744 after the last Cirksena prince died without issue, under a contract made beforehand.

eras.polity: Napoleonic Kingdom of Holland, then the French Empire
eras.note: Annexation by the Kingdom of Holland is dated 1806 or 1807 depending on the source, and the French Empire followed. East Frisians registered family names after 1811.
Prussia ceded East Frisia to the Kingdom of Hanover in 1815.

eras.polity: Prussia after the annexation of Hanover
eras.note: Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866. The Prussian civil registers begin in October 1874, and a German-wide system took over on 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Upper Lusatia — Weißwasser and Niesky
