regions.sub: Weißwasser, Niesky

eras.polity: Upper Lusatia in the Bohemian Crown
eras.note: Before registers. King John of Bohemia incorporated Görlitz into the Bohemian Crown in 1329, and the Lusatian League of towns formed in 1346.
Ferdinand I inherited the lands after Louis II died at Mohács in 1526. Maximilian II officially implemented the Confessio Augustana here in 1564.
The Peace of Prague (1635) transferred the Margraviate of Upper Lusatia to Saxony.

In 1815 the north-eastern part of Upper Lusatia, including the districts of Hoyerswerda, Rothenburg, Görlitz and Lauban, moved from Saxony to Prussian Silesia, so neighbouring villages can sit on different sides of the 1815 line. After 1874 (October, in Prussia) civil registers run alongside church books; all Germany was covered from 1 January 1876.

eras.polity: Soviet zone, then the GDR (founded 7 October 1949)
eras.note: The Oder-Neisse line fixed the border with Poland in 1945 and split Upper Lusatia between East Germany and Poland.
East Germany joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.

regions.label: Passau and the Inn-Danube corner of Lower Bavaria
regions.sub: Passau, Plattling, Fürstenzell, Bad Griesbach, Untergriesbach

eras.note: Before registers. Lower Bavaria was first created in 1255; Bavaria-Straubing and Bavaria-Landshut were created in 1353 and Bavaria was permanently reunited in 1505.

eras.polity: Bavaria around the Prince-Bishopric of Passau
eras.note: The city of Passau and its lands were a prince-bishopric until 1803. The Diocese of Vienna was cut from Passau territory in 1469, and Joseph II's reforms created the dioceses of Linz and St. Pölten from it in 1784.

Bavarian forces entered Passau on 22 February 1803: the city and the lands on the left bank of the Inn and right bank of the Ilz went to Bavaria, while the lands on the left bank of the Danube and the Ilz went to Ferdinand of Habsburg-Lorraine (Salzburg, later Austria). Bavaria was divided into Kreise modelled on French départements in 1808.
In 1837 the Unterdonaukreis, whose capital had been Passau, was renamed Lower Bavaria and its capital moved to Landshut. The Diocese of Passau was reconstituted in 1818 with 136 parishes.

eras.polity: Bavaria in the German Empire and after
eras.note: Civil registration covered all Germany from 1 January 1876. Lower Bavaria and the Upper Palatinate were administered as one district from 1932.
Lower Bavaria and the Upper Palatinate were separated again in 1954.

regions.label: Tecklenburg land — Ibbenbüren
regions.sub: Ibbenbüren, Tecklenburg

eras.note: Before registers. Bentheim annexed the county in 1263 after the Tecklenburg counts died out in 1262; the Counts of Schwerin ruled from 1327-28 to 1557 (end date given as 1557 or 1562).
The counts introduced Calvinism in 1588. In 1686 the Reichskammergericht split the territory between Bentheim-Tecklenburg and Solms-Braunfels, which ceded its claim to Brandenburg-Prussia in 1696.
Solms-Braunfels sold the county to Prussia in 1707, which the Aulic Council declared illegal. A Berlin treaty of 1729-30 paid Bentheim-Tecklenburg 750,000 Reichstaler and Prussia annexed the county.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Berg, then France
eras.note: Mediatised to the Grand Duchy of Berg in 1808 and annexed by France in 1810. The grand duchy kept civil registers from 1806 to 1815, after which parishes returned to church registers.

Tecklenburg went back to Prussia at the Congress of Vienna (1815 or 1816, depending on the source). State civil registration reached Prussia in October 1874 and the whole of Germany on 1 January 1876.

regions.label: Eastern Lüneburg — Winsen, Bleckede, Dannenberg and Lüchow
regions.sub: Winsen, Bleckede, Dannenberg, Hitzacker, Lüchow

eras.note: Before registers. The principality was created in 1267 or 1269 when Brunswick-Lüneburg was split; the dukes ruled from Celle from 1378, and the Welfs secured it after the Battle of Winsen in 1388.
Duke Ernest the Confessor introduced Lutheranism from 1520 and signed the Augsburg Confession in 1530. A Dannenberg side line existed from 1569 and reverted to Celle in 1671.
George of Hanover inherited the principality in 1705 and merged it into the Electorate of Brunswick-Lüneburg. By 1815 Hanover was a kingdom.

eras.polity: Prussia after the annexation of Hanover
eras.note: Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866. Standesamt registers begin in October 1874 for Prussian ground, and in 1876 for the whole of Germany.

regions.label: Canton of Geneva — Vernier and Le Grand-Saconnex (communes added in 1815)
regions.sub: Vernier, Le Grand-Saconnex, Les Avanchets

eras.polity: Outside the Republic of Geneva — French and Savoyard villages
eras.note: The communes added to Geneva by the treaties of 1815 and 1816 were not part of the Republic of Geneva, so their parish registers before then belong to their French or Savoyard parishes.

Geneva became the capital of the French département of Léman in April 1798. Civil registration began in Geneva in 1798, and the canton's civil records are online to 1880 from the Archives d'État de Genève.

eras.polity: Canton of Geneva — Treaty of Paris communes
eras.note: Geneva joined the Swiss Confederation in 1815 as the 22nd canton. The 1815 Treaty of Paris added Versoix, Collex-Bossy, Pregny-Chambésy, Vernier, Meyrin and Grand-Saconnex.

eras.polity: Canton of Geneva — Treaty of Turin communes
eras.note: The 1816 Treaty of Turin with Sardinia added further communes (Carouge, Veyrier, Laconnex, Soral and Onex, among others); the two treaties together added 159 km2 and over 16,000 inhabitants.

Federal civil registration began on 1 January 1876. Local civil registry offices keep the registers, with a duplicate for the cantonal authority; records over 100 years old may have moved to archives.

regions.label: Basel-Landschaft — Liestal, Muttenz and Pratteln
regions.sub: Liestal, Muttenz, Pratteln, Frenkendorf

eras.polity: City of Basel and its countryside
eras.note: Basel joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. Most of the land now in Basel-Landschaft belonged to the city of Basel.

eras.polity: Basel countryside under the Helvetic and Mediation constitutions
eras.note: The countryside gained equality with the city in 1798. the Arlesheim district in 1792 and annexed it in 1793.
The Arlesheim district joined Basel at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Civil registration began in Basel-Landschaft in 1827.
The canton separated from the city on 26 August 1833, after the Battle of the Hülftenschanz near Frenkendorf.
Federal civil registration began on 1 January 1876. Laufental joined Basel-Landschaft on 1 January 1994.

regions.label: Bern and its hinterland — Muri, Ittigen, Belp and Bolligen
regions.sub: Muri bei Bern, Ittigen, Belp, Bolligen

eras.polity: Republic of Bern — Old Swiss Confederacy
eras.note: Bern joined the Confederacy in 1353. The Reformation took hold in Bernese lands, and Interlaken Monastery was secularised in 1528.
Under the Helvetic Republic Bern was split and the Oberland and Léman cantons were detached.

eras.polity: Canton of Bern in the Mediation Confederation
eras.note: Bern was one of six directorial cantons of the Napoleonic Swiss Confederation, 1803-14.
In 1815 Bern gained the Bernese Jura and Biel/Bienne from the Bishopric of Basel. Bern civil registration records for 1792-1876 are indexed with images on FamilySearch.
Federal civil registration began on 1 January 1876. In 2010 the 26 districts were merged into 10.

regions.label: Upper Valais — Brig, Visp, Naters and Zermatt
regions.sub: Brig, Visp, Naters, Zermatt

eras.note: Before registers. King Rudolph III of Burgundy gave the Bishop of Sion temporal rights in 999; settlers from Hasli in the 13th century made the upper valley German-speaking.

eras.polity: The Seven Zenden under the Prince-Bishop
eras.note: Charles IV confirmed the liberties of seven Zenden (including Visp, Brig, Raron and Conches) in 1354. The Morge stream was recognised as the border with Savoyard Lower Valais in 1384, and Valais became an associate member of the Swiss Confederation in 1529.
The prince-bishop gave up secular power permanently in 1634 (after a first, temporary withdrawal in 1613), and the Upper Valais governors formed the Republic of the Seven Tithings.
Lower Valais, ruled as subject territory, revolted and gained equal status in 1798.
Valais became a separate Rhodanic Republic in 1802.
France annexed Valais as the Simplon department in 1810-13; Austrian troops occupied it in late 1813.
Valais entered the Swiss Confederation on 4 August 1815.

Cantonal civil registration began in 1853 and federal registration on 1 January 1876. The language border runs from Sierre/Salgesch along the ridge, so Upper Valais records are in German and Lower Valais in French.

regions.label: Lower Austria — St. Pölten, Krems, Tulln and the Industrieviertel edge
regions.sub: St. Pölten, Krems, Tulln, Neunkirchen, Berndorf, Hollabrunn

eras.polity: Duchy of Austria below the Enns
eras.note: Before registers. The area was known as the Principality below the Enns from the mid-13th century; the Habsburgs rose after the Battle on the Marchfeld on 26 August 1278.
The Diocese of Vienna was created from Passau territory in 1469. Joseph II's reforms created the Diocese of St. Pölten in 1784 from former Passau territory.
Napoleon fought the Austrian army at Aspern and Wagram in 1809. Vienna was separated from Lower Austria as a state of its own in 1921.
Civil marriage registration began on 1 August 1938, and births and deaths were registered from 1 January 1939.
Occupation ended with the State Treaty in 1955. St. Pölten has been the provincial capital since 1986.

regions.label: East Tyrol — Lienz and the Drau valley
regions.sub: Lienz, Sillian, Matrei

eras.note: Before registers. The Counts of Gorizia held the area from Lienz in the 12th century and inherited the County of Tyrol in 1253; when Tyrol passed to the Habsburgs in 1363 they kept Lienz.
The Gorizian line died out in 1500 and Maximilian I incorporated the area into Austrian Tyrol.
The Italian Army occupied all Tyrol in November 1918. The Treaty of Saint-Germain (1919) ceded South Tyrol to Italy, and East Tyrol stayed Austrian but cut off from North Tyrol.
After the Anschluss East Tyrol was attached to Carinthia. Civil marriage registration began on 1 August 1938 and births and deaths from 1 January 1939.
East Tyrol lay in the British zone after the war and was returned to Tyrol in 1947.

regions.label: Belgian Gaume — Athus, Aubange and Messancy
regions.sub: Aubange, Athus, Messancy

eras.note: The duchy passed to the Habsburgs in 1477 (1482 in some accounts). France under Louis XIV held it from 1684 until the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.
Luxembourg was confirmed as part of the Austrian Habsburgs' Southern Netherlands by the Treaty of Utrecht (1713-15).
Revolutionary France annexed Luxembourg in 1795; the Peasants' War of 1798 was a short-lived uprising against French rule.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg in union with the Netherlands
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna made Luxembourg a Grand Duchy in personal union with the Netherlands and a member of the German Confederation. The Conference of London carried out a Third Partition of Luxembourg in 1830-31.

William I agreed to the partition in 1839 and the western, predominantly French-speaking part went to Belgium, with Arlon as the provincial capital. The Gaume is the southernmost part, around Virton, and the Arlon area has historically spoken Luxembourgish alongside Walloon.

regions.label: Luxembourg City — the fortress quarters (Bonnevoie, Gare, Hollerich, Merl)
regions.sub: Bonnevoie, Gare, Hollerich, Merl

eras.note: Before registers. Count Siegfried I acquired the fort Lucilinburhuc from the Abbey of St. Maximin of Trier in 963; the House of Luxembourg produced emperors and kings of Bohemia in the 14th-15th centuries.
The duchy passed to the Habsburgs in 1477 (1482 in some accounts).
Louis XIV invaded in 1684 and held the duchy until the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.
Luxembourg became part of the Austrian Southern Netherlands, confirmed by the Treaty of Utrecht (1713-15).
Revolutionary France annexed Luxembourg in 1795; a Peasants' War broke out against French rule in 1798.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Luxembourg — German Confederation fortress
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna made Luxembourg a Grand Duchy in personal union with the Netherlands, and Prussia garrisoned the fortress. The 1839 Treaty of London ceded the western part to Belgium.

A second Treaty of London in 1867 guaranteed independence and neutrality, and the fortress walls were demolished. The grand duchy passed to the House of Nassau-Weilburg in 1890; Germany occupied it in 1914-18.
Germany invaded in 1940 and de facto incorporated Luxembourg into the Reich in 1942.

regions.label: North Zealand — Hillerød, Helsinge and Gilleleje
regions.sub: Hillerød, Hørsholm, Helsinge, Gilleleje

eras.note: The Lutheran Church of Denmark dates from 1536. Some pastors began registers before the royal order.
Christian IV ordered a church book in every parish on 20 May 1645, first to the Bishop of Sjælland.
A resolution of 1812 required two books per parish, kept in different buildings, which most parishes had adopted by 1814-15. From 1851 a couple could choose a civil marriage in some circumstances.
The 1970 reform cut the counties from 24 to roughly 14. Frederiksborg County had its seat at Hillerød and 19 municipalities, among them Hillerød, Helsingør and Frederikssund.
Frederiksborg County was abolished on 1 January 2007 and merged into the Capital Region.

regions.label: Copenhagen County — Ballerup, Albertslund and Ishøj
regions.sub: Ballerup, Albertslund, Ishøj, Vallensbæk, Måløv

eras.note: Parish ground west of the capital was Lutheran from 1536; some pastors kept registers before the royal order, the earliest noted being at Nakskov from 1572.
The royal order for parish registers was issued to the Bishop of Sjælland on 20 May 1645, and to the other bishoprics in 1646.
From 1814 the second copy of each parish book was kept apart from the first, so a lost original may survive as a duplicate.
Copenhagen County had its seat at Glostrup and took in the metropolitan municipalities other than Copenhagen and Frederiksberg, which had county status of their own.
The counties were abolished on 1 January 2007 and replaced by five regions.

regions.label: Bornholm — Rønne and the island
regions.sub: Rønne, Nexø, Allinge

eras.note: Frederick I pawned Bornholm to Lübeck for 50 years from 1525. The Lutheran Church of Denmark dates from 1536.
Swedish forces conquered the island in 1645 and the Second Treaty of Brömsebro returned it. Royal orders for parish registers went to the bishoprics in 1645-46.
The Treaty of Roskilde ceded Bornholm to Sweden in 1658. The islanders revolted on 8 December 1658 and handed it back to the Danish king; the Treaty of Copenhagen confirmed Danish rule in 1660.
Bornholm was a county from 1660 until 2002 (the end is given as 2002 or 2003).
Duplicate parish books were kept separately from 1814-15.
Soviet aircraft bombed Rønne and Nexø on 7-8 May 1945 and Soviet troops landed on 9 May; they left on 5 April 1946.
The 21 municipalities were reorganised on 1 April 1970; Bornholm Regional Municipality was formed on 1 January 2003.

regions.label: Orava (Árva) — Námestovo and Trstená
regions.sub: Námestovo, Trstená, Zákamenné

eras.note: Árva was first mentioned in 1349 and became a county with its own administration in 1370; the seat moved from Orava Castle to Alsókubin (now Dolný Kubín) in 1683.
Árva merged with Turóc into Árva-Turóc county on 13 September 1850, within the military district of Preßburg.
Hungary's pre-1850 counties were restored in 1860. Hungarian civil registration began in 1895.

The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) gave the whole county to Czechoslovakia; some north-eastern villages were later exchanged with Poland. Civil registration by civil authorities was enacted across Czechoslovakia in 1921, and the county became part of Váh County on 1 January 1923.
The Slovak State governed the area in 1939-45.
Czechoslovakia was restored after the war.
Slovakia became independent in 1993.

regions.label: Zemplín and the Uh border — Trebišov, Snina and Sobrance
regions.sub: Trebišov, Snina, Sobrance

eras.note: Before registers. Zemplén was a county of the Kingdom of Hungary from the 11th century.
The county belonged to the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom in 1544-70 and to the Principality of Transylvania in 1621-29 and 1645-48.

Back under the Kingdom of Hungary from 1648; the seat moved to Sátoraljaújhely (dated 1685 or 1748). Hungarian civil registration began in 1895. Villages at the eastern edge of this ring may have belonged to a neighbouring county, so check each village.

The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) put the northern part of Zemplén under Czechoslovakia and left the southern part in Hungary. In November 1938 the First Vienna Award returned a further part to Hungary. Civil authorities took over registration across Czechoslovakia in 1921.
The Slovak State of 1939-45 included this ground.
The Czechoslovak state returned in 1945.
About 4,506 km2 of the old county is in Slovakia (the Zemplín region) and 1,776 km2 in Hungary.

regions.label: The Váh valley and Kysuce — Považská Bystrica, Čadca, Piešťany
regions.sub: Považská Bystrica, Čadca, Piešťany, Partizánske, Bánovce

eras.polity: Trencsén County and neighbouring counties — Kingdom of Hungary
eras.note: Trencsén County existed from the 11th century to 1920, with its seat at Trenčín Castle and from about 1650 in the town. It bordered Moravia, Galicia, Silesia and the counties of Árva, Turóc and Nyitra, and the Váh ran through it; towns at the ring's southern edge may lie in a neighbouring county.
Hungarian civil registration was introduced in 1895.

The Treaty of Trianon (4 June 1920) placed Trencsén County in Czechoslovakia, where it continued as Trenčianska župa until 1922 with different powers. Civil authorities took over registration across Czechoslovakia in 1921.
The county was recreated in 1940 with a slightly extended territory.
The area returned to Czechoslovakia after the Second World War.
The area became part of Slovakia in 1993.

regions.label: Southern Posen — Ostrów, Krotoszyn and Rawicz
regions.sub: Ostrów Wielkopolski, Krotoszyn, Rawicz

eras.note: The Second Partition of 1793 passed this ground to Prussia.
Prussian South Prussia, until the Treaties of Tilsit of 1807.
Under the Treaties of Tilsit the territory became part of the French client state, the Duchy of Warsaw, in 1807.

eras.polity: Prussia — Grand Duchy of Posen, from 1848 the Province of Posen
eras.note: The Congress of Vienna returned the western part to Prussia as the Grand Duchy of Posen in 1815; a cabinet order of 1848 established the Province of Posen.

Posen was incorporated into the German Empire in 1871. Civil registration in Prussia dates from October 1874; it was national from 1 January 1876. Towns appear under German names: Ostrowo, Krotoschin, Rawitsch.
The Treaty of Versailles took effect on 10 January 1920 and most of the province became the Poznań Voivodeship.
Nazi Germany annexed the former province into the Reichsgau Wartheland in 1939.
All historical parts of the province came under Polish control by 1947.

regions.label: Głogów and Żagań — the Silesian duchies on the Oder and Bóbr
regions.sub: Głogów, Żagań

eras.note: Before registers. Konrad I received the northern Głogów territory in 1251, and the Duchy of Żagań was split off in 1273.

King John of Bohemia seized Głogów as a fief in 1331; in 1349 half went to the Duchy of Żagań and half into the Crown of Bohemia. Matthias Corvinus conquered Głogów in 1488, and it became an immediate dominion of the Bohemian Crown in 1506.
The duchy passed to the Habsburgs through Ferdinand I after Louis II died in 1526.
Prussia took Głogów with most of Silesia in 1742-48; the Treaty of Aachen (1748) confirmed it.
The duchy was dissolved into the Province of Silesia in 1815. From October 1874 Prussian parishes were joined by civil registrars, and from 1 January 1876 the rule held across Germany.
Prussian Silesia east of the Oder-Neisse line was granted to Poland after the Second World War (Potsdam Agreement).

regions.label: Sieradz land — Sieradz and Zduńska Wola
regions.sub: Sieradz, Zduńska Wola, Poddębice, Kłodawa

eras.note: Before registers. Sieradz was the capital of its own duchy from 1263 to 1339.
Sieradz was the capital of the Sieradz Voivodeship from 1339 to 1793.
Prussia annexed Sieradz in 1793.
Sieradz joined the Duchy of Warsaw in 1807.
Sieradz became part of Congress Poland under the Russian Empire in 1815; Polish insurgents fought Russian troops here in the January Uprising of 1863-64.
Poland regained the town in 1918.
German forces occupied the town in 1939 and renamed it Schieratz.
Soviet forces arrived in January 1945. Sieradz was again a voivodeship seat from 1975 to 1998.

regions.label: Masuria and the Osterode uplands — Szczytno, Olsztynek and Iława
regions.sub: Szczytno, Olsztynek, Iława

eras.note: Before registers. The Order held the region from 1224 to 1525 and was defeated by Polish-Lithuanian forces at Grunwald in 1410.

eras.polity: Teutonic Order as a fief of the Polish Crown
eras.note: The Second Peace of Thorn (1466) restored the Order's authority over the region as a fief of the Polish Crown.
The Order was secularised in 1525 and Albert of Prussia turned Lutheran, bringing the region into Protestantism.
The region became part of the Kingdom of Prussia when Frederick I was crowned at Königsberg in 1701.
Polish-language lessons were removed from schools in 1872. The Standesamt system began in Prussia in October 1874 and applied across Germany from the start of 1876.
In the plebiscite of 11 July 1920 about 99.32% of voters in Masuria proper chose to remain in East Prussia.

The region passed to Poland under the Yalta and Potsdam decisions in 1945; most Germans were expelled and the remaining Masurians underwent a nationality verification. Szczytno appears as Ortelsburg in German records.

regions.label: Narva and Ivangorod
regions.sub: Narva, Ivangorod

eras.polity: Danish Estonia — Narvia and its castle
eras.note: Before parish registers. Narva appears as the village Narvia in the Danish Census Book of 1241, the castle dates from the second half of the 13th century, and the town received Lübeck law from Valdemar IV of Denmark in 1345.

eras.polity: Livonian Order — Narva, with Muscovite Ivangorod opposite from 1492
eras.note: The castle and town became a possession of the Livonian Order in 1346. Ivan III of Moscow founded the Ivangorod fortress across the river in 1492, which made the river a state frontier.

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia — Livonian War occupation
eras.note: Muscovy held Narva from 1558 to 1581.
Sweden conquered Narva in 1581. A Russian attempt to retake it in 1590–1595 failed, and Charles XII defeated Peter I at the battle of Narva in 1700.

Peter I's forces took Narva in 1704. The town stayed on the Russian fortress list until 1863 and was administratively part of the Saint Petersburg Governorate until 1917. From the 17th century until 1945 Ivangorod was administratively part of Narva.

A referendum in July 1917 attached the Narva district to Estonia, and the town became part of the independent Republic of Estonia in 1918. Bolshevik troops held it from 28 November 1918 to 19 January 1919.
The German invasion came in 1941 and German forces evacuated the city in January 1944.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Narva in the Estonian SSR; Ivangorod in Leningrad Oblast
eras.note: In January 1945 Soviet authorities separated Ivangorod from Narva and Estonia and transferred it to the Leningrad Oblast of the Russian SFSR, where it became a town in its own right.
Estonia regained independence in 1991, so the two banks of the river are now in different states and different archive systems.

regions.label: Karelian Isthmus — the Finnish south shore
regions.sub: Primorsk (Koivisto), Roshchino (Raivola), Kamenka, Sosnovo, Vaskelovo

eras.note: Sweden held the whole isthmus after gaining it in the 17th century. Russia held it from 1721, after the Great Northern War.

eras.polity: Grand Duchy of Finland — the north-western half of the isthmus attached in 1812
eras.note: The Grand Duchy of Finland was created in 1809 as an autonomous part of the Russian Empire, and in 1812 the north-western half of the isthmus was transferred to it as part of Old Finland. The border therefore ran across the isthmus, and a place in this ring must be checked against which side of that line it lay.
Finland declared independence in 1917 and kept the isthmus, except the area roughly matching the present Vsevolozhsky District and some St Petersburg districts, which stayed Russian.

Finland ceded the isthmus in the Moscow Peace Treaty of 12 March 1940. Most of it entered the Karelo-Finnish SSR on 31 March 1940, and the whole Karelian population of the ceded areas, about 422,000 people, was evacuated to other parts of Finland.

eras.polity: Finland — regained in the Continuation War
eras.note: Finland regained the territory in 1941 and about 260,000 Karelian evacuees returned. The Soviet Vyborg Offensive began on 9 June 1944 and the returning Karelians were evacuated again.

The Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944 made the whole isthmus Soviet, and the ceded areas were incorporated into Leningrad Oblast. Finland recognised the 1940 border in the Paris Peace Treaties of 1947.

regions.label: Pechenga (Petsamo) and the Arctic frontier
regions.sub: Nikel, Zapolyarny, Zaozyorsk, Pechenga

eras.polity: Russia — Pechenga monastery and the Sámi lands
eras.note: Pechenga Monastery was founded in 1533 and the settlement counts as part of Russia from then. The area was inhabited by Sámi and resettled by Pomors and other Russians.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — the Norwegian border fixed
eras.note: The present Norway–Russia border was settled in 1826.

Soviet Russia ceded Pechenga (Petsamo) to Finland by the Treaty of Tartu in 1920. Nickel deposits found in 1921 were mined from 1935. The Soviets briefly occupied Petsamo in the Winter War of 1939–1940, and the Moscow Peace Treaty ceded the Rybachy Peninsula to the USSR.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Murmansk Oblast, Pechengsky District
eras.note: In the Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944 Finland ceded the area, 8,965 km2 in all. Pechengsky District, centred on Nikel, was created in Murmansk Oblast by decree of 21 July 1945. Finland exchanged the Jäniskoski-Niskakoski territory in 1947.

regions.label: Faroe Islands
regions.sub: Tórshavn, Klaksvík

eras.note: Before registers. Norse settlers arrived in the 9th and 10th centuries, and the islands were officially converted to Christianity about 1000.
The islands became part of the Kingdom of Norway in 1035.

eras.polity: Kalmar Union — a possession of the Norwegian crown
eras.note: Norwegian rule gave way to the Kalmar Union in 1380 and the islands remained a possession of the Norwegian crown. In the 1390s Henry I Sinclair, Earl of Orkney, took them as a vassal of Norway.

eras.polity: Denmark–Norway — administered by the central government
eras.note: Denmark–Norway returned the islands and the trade monopoly to the central government in 1708, after the period of Gabel rule.

The Treaty of Kiel of 1814 ended the Denmark–Norway union and the islands came under Denmark. The Løgting was abolished in 1816 and replaced by a Danish judiciary, then re-established in 1852 as a county council with an advisory role. British forces occupied the islands in the Second World War, and the last British troops left in September 1945.

eras.polity: Home Rule within the Danish Realm
eras.note: The Home Rule Act of 1948 granted extended self-governance.

regions.label: Vorkuta and the Polar Urals
regions.sub: Vorkuta, Vorgashor

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Pechora coal basin and the Vorkuta camps
eras.note: Coal was found on the Vorkuta River in 1930. A settlement began in 1931, with most workers inmates of the Ukhta-Pechora Camp, and Vorkutlag was set up in 1932. The northern part of the field, Vorkuta included, lay in the Nenets Autonomous Okrug of Arkhangelsk Oblast, and only the southern part in the Komi ASSR.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — the town of Vorkuta
eras.note: Vorkuta received town status on 26 November 1943. A prisoner-built railway linked it with Konosha, Kotlas and Inta in 1941, and the camp uprising took place in 1953. The 1989 census recorded the peak population of 115,646.

eras.polity: Russia — Komi Republic, Vorkuta Urban Okrug
eras.note: Vorkuta is a town of republic significance in the Komi Republic. The settlement of Sovetsky became part of Vorkuta in 2002, and the 2021 census recorded 56,985 people.

regions.label: Berezovo and the Northern Sosva (western Yugra)
regions.sub: Igrim, Sovetskiy, Yugorsk, Pionerskiy

eras.note: Tobolsk Governorate was formed in 1782 as part of the Tobolsk Viceroyalty.

The governorate was re-formed by decree of 12 December 1796. It joined the Siberian General Governorate in 1802 and the West Siberian General Governorate in 1822, and its uyezds were called okrugs from 1822 until 1898. In 1920 it was renamed Tyumen Governorate.
Tobolsk Governorate was renamed Tyumen Governorate by decree of 21 April 1920.
The Ostyak-Vogul National Okrug was established on 10 December 1930 and renamed the Khanty-Mansi National Okrug in October 1940.
In 1977 the national okrugs of the Russian SFSR became autonomous okrugs.
Yugra was added to the official name in 2003.

regions.label: Tobolsk–Urals border strip (Kurgan and Turinsk)
regions.sub: Kurtamysh, Kargapolye, Mishkino, Yurgamysh, Turinskaya Sloboda

eras.polity: Tobolsk Governorate, on its western edge
eras.note: Tobolsk Governorate was formed in 1782 and re-formed in 1796. The strip lies along the western edge of the governorate, so the uyezd of a place must be checked before choosing an archive.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Chelyabinsk and Omsk regions, with Turin in Tyumen Governorate
eras.note: A decree of 27 August 1919 moved Kurgan from Tobolsk Governorate to Chelyabinsk, and Turin returned to the governorate on 6 October 1919. The governorate was renamed Tyumen Governorate in 1920.
Kurgan Oblast was formed by decree of 6 February 1943 from 32 districts of the eastern Chelyabinsk region and 4 districts of the Omsk region.

regions.label: Evenkia and the Vilyuy diamond country
regions.sub: Tura, Mirny, Aykhal, Udachny, Chernyshevsky

eras.polity: Tsardom of Russia — Lensky Ostrog and the Yakutsk lands
eras.note: Pyotr Beketov founded Lensky Ostrog, the future Yakutsk, in 1632, and in August 1638 Moscow created a new administrative unit centred on it.
Irkutsk Governorate was created in 1782 in an administrative reform.

Yakutsk Oblast was split from Irkutsk Governorate in 1805. The ring crosses the old boundary between Yakutsk lands and the lands to their west, so the place decides which jurisdiction recorded a family.

eras.polity: Yakut ASSR; Evenk National Okrug from 1930
eras.note: The former Yakutsk Oblast was proclaimed the Yakut ASSR on 27 April 1922. The Evenk National Okrug, with Tura as its centre, was established on 10 December 1930.
A kimberlite pipe was found in 1955 by an expedition led by Yury Khabardin and Mirny was founded. Mirny received town status in 1959, and its population was 38,793 at the 1989 census.

eras.polity: Russia — Sakha Republic; Evenkia within Krasnoyarsk Krai
eras.note: The Yakut ASSR became the Republic of Sakha (Yakutia) on 27 December 1991. A referendum on 17 April 2005 approved merging the Evenk Autonomous Okrug into Krasnoyarsk Krai, which took effect on 1 January 2007.

regions.label: Landskrona and the Scanian sound coast
regions.sub: Landskrona

eras.note: Landskrona was chartered in 1413, with a first mention about 1405, and its citadel was completed in 1559. Scania was Danish until it was ceded to Sweden in 1658.
Scania passed to Sweden in 1658.
Danish forces took the citadel after a siege from 8 July to 2 August 1676 and held Landskrona until 1679.
The fortifications were condemned in 1822 and the garrison was abolished in 1869.

regions.label: Stockholm archipelago (Värmdö and Södertörn coast)
regions.sub: Gustavsberg, Nynäshamn, Värmdö

eras.polity: Sweden — the provinces of Uppland and Södermanland
eras.note: Before Stockholm County existed this coast lay in the historic provinces of Uppland (Roslagen) and Södermanland (Södertörn).
Stockholm County was established in 1714. The City of Stockholm stood outside it as a separate administrative entity under the Governor of Stockholm, though it was the county seat.

eras.polity: Sweden — Stockholm County, united with the City of Stockholm
eras.note: On 1 January 1968 the county was united with the City of Stockholm and its borders were redrawn.

regions.label: Jiu Valley (Valea Jiului)
regions.sub: Petroşani, Lupeni, Vulcan, Uricani

eras.note: Transylvania became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002.
The Principality of Transylvania was created by the Treaty of Speyer in 1570. The Habsburgs gained possession in 1690 and the Ottomans recognised the loss at Karlowitz in 1699.

eras.polity: Habsburg monarchy — Principality, then Grand Principality of Transylvania
eras.note: Habsburg control was consolidated by the Peace of Szatmár in 1711, and the Grand Principality of Transylvania was reintroduced in 1765.

Transylvania was reincorporated into the Kingdom of Hungary in 1867. Coal mining began in the Jiu Valley in the mid-19th century, with workers brought from across the Habsburg lands. Civil registration began in Transylvania and the Banat in 1895.

Transylvania united with Romania on 1 December 1918 and the Treaty of Trianon placed it in the Kingdom of Romania in 1920. In the Lupeni strike of 1929 the army killed 23 workers. Records under 100 years old stay with local civil registration offices and older ones go to the National Archives.
Private mines were nationalised in 1948. About 35,000 miners protested in Lupeni on 1 August 1977, and the number of miners reached about 179,000 in 1979.
Coal production fell sharply after 1989. The Petrila mine closed in 2015 and the Uricani and Paroșeni mines in 2017.

regions.label: Háromszék (Trei Scaune) and the Brașov foothills
regions.sub: Sfântu Gheorghe, Covasna, Săcele, Predeal, Tărlungeni

eras.note: Transylvania became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in 1002. Saxon colonists settled in the south-east of Transylvania in the 12th and 13th centuries, and Burzenland (Țara Bârsei) is the Saxon area around Brașov. The Székely lived mainly in the east.
The Principality of Transylvania was created by the Treaty of Speyer in 1570 and the Habsburgs gained possession in 1690.
Habsburg control was consolidated in 1711 and the Grand Principality of Transylvania was reintroduced in 1765.

Transylvania was reincorporated into the Kingdom of Hungary in 1867. Háromszék County, with Sfântu Gheorghe as its seat, was mostly identical with the later Trei Scaune County. Civil registration began in Transylvania in 1895.

The Treaty of Trianon transferred the territory to Romania in 1920 and Trei Scaune County was established in 1925. The 1930 census recorded 136,122 inhabitants, 80.4% of them Hungarians. The southern part of this ring, around Săcele, Tărlungeni and Predeal, is Brașov ground rather than Trei Scaune.
Nearly all of Trei Scaune County was transferred back to Hungary in 1940 under the Second Vienna Award. Romanian forces recaptured it in September and October 1944.
The Paris Peace Treaties of 1947 confirmed Romanian rule. Trei Scaune County was disbanded on 6 September 1950 in the administrative reform and was not re-established in 1968.

regions.label: Maramureș — the Vișeu valley and Seini
regions.sub: Vișeu de Sus, Vișeu de Jos, Seini, Poienile de sub Munte, Rozavlea

eras.note: Maramureș became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in the 11th century and was reorganised as Máramaros County in the 14th.

eras.polity: Principality of Transylvania, then Habsburg administration
eras.note: In the 16th century Maramureș came under the Principality of Transylvania, and in the late 17th century under Habsburg administration.
Maramureș was transferred to the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary in 1732, and the monarchy became the Austrian Empire in 1804.
The county lay in the Hungarian part of Austria–Hungary from 1867. Civil registration began in Transylvania in 1895.
After the First World War the historic county was divided between Romania and the Carpathian Ruthenia of Czechoslovakia. This ring holds the Romanian share.
Hungary annexed Northern Transylvania, including southern Maramureș, in August 1940. Hungarian control ended in 1944.

The southern section returned to Romania after the Second World War and the Treaty of Paris of 1947 confirmed the return of Northern Transylvania. The northern section was incorporated into the Ukrainian SSR.

regions.label: Hutsul Carpathians and the Pokuttya hills
regions.sub: Nadvirna, Yaremche, Verkhovyna, Kosmach, Delyatyn

eras.note: Casimir III moved to incorporate the region into the Kingdom of Poland in 1340. In 1388 Władysław II Jagiełło pledged it as loan collateral and the Moldavian prince Petru II gained economic rights over it, but it stayed within Poland.

eras.polity: Moldavia — Stephen the Great holds Pokuttya
eras.note: Stephen the Great took control in 1485 under the Colomeea oath to Casimir IV, while Poland still claimed sovereignty. The Muha Rebellion of 1490–1492, with Cossacks and Hutsuls, captured several Pokuttya towns.
Poland retook the region at the Battle of Obertyn in 1531, and minor clashes continued for about 15 years.
After the Partitions of Poland the region fell under the Habsburg Monarchy in 1772.
In May 1919 Polish and Romanian forces occupied Pokuttya, and in August the Romanian army handed eastern Pokuttya to Poland. It remained Polish after the Polish–Soviet War.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Ukrainian SSR, Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast
eras.note: The area was attached to the Ukrainian SSR in 1939 after the Soviet–German partition of Poland, came under German control after the invasion of 1941 until 1944, and was then incorporated into the Ivano-Frankivsk oblast.

regions.label: Yedisan coast — Chornomorsk (Illichivsk)
regions.sub: Chornomorsk (Illichivsk), Odesa Gulf coast

eras.note: The Crimean Khanate occupied the southern coastal edge of Yedisan from the 1520s. The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774 gave Russia the region east of the Southern Bug, and the Treaty of Jassy of 1792 extended the Russian frontier to the Dniester, ending Yedisan.
Odesa was founded in 1794 after the Russian takeover. Before the port was built, the site of Chornomorsk held only scattered farmsteads, the Buhovi khutory, on land of a landowner named Buhovyi.
The settlement was renamed Illichivskyi Khutir in 1927. A port was established in 1952 and the surrounding territory was urbanised into the city of Illichivsk.

The city council voted on 12 November 2015 to rename Illichivsk as Chornomorsk, and the Verkhovna Rada confirmed the change on 4 February 2016. Records before 2016 are filed under Illichivsk. The municipality was abolished in July 2020 and merged into Odesa Raion.

regions.label: Tavria steppe coast — Skadovsk and Henichesk
regions.sub: Skadovsk, Henichesk, Novooleksiyivka, Novofedorivka

eras.note: Russia annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783 and Taurida Oblast was set up soon afterwards. It was abolished in the reign of Paul I.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Taurida Governorate (Dnieper and Melitopol uyezds)
eras.note: Taurida Governorate was established in 1802, when the oblast was re-established as a governorate. Its mainland uyezds were Berdyansk, Dnieper (Oleshky) and Melitopol, and the peninsula held the rest. References date the end of the governorate to 1917 or 1918.
The Crimean People's Republic was proclaimed on 13 December 1917 and the Crimean ASSR existed from 1921 to 1945, but this ring lies on the mainland north of the isthmus.

regions.label: Starobilsk and the Aidar valley
regions.sub: Aydar, Markivka, Milove, Bilokurakyne, Troitske, Chertkovo

eras.polity: Sloboda Cossack lands — the Ostrohozk Regiment
eras.note: Starobilsk was repopulated in 1686 by servicemen of the Ostrohozk Sloboda Cossack Regiment.

eras.polity: Russian Empire — Kharkov Governorate, Starobelsk uyezd
eras.note: The sloboda of Staro-Bila was renamed Starobelsk on 1 May 1797 and became the centre of Starobelsk uyezd in Kharkov Governorate. The ring crosses the present Ukrainian–Russian border, so the east and north of it belong to other governorates and archives.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Donets Governorate, then the Ukrainian SSR and the RSFSR
eras.note: In 1919 Starobilsk was administratively part of the Donets Governorate of Ukraine, and it received city status in 1938.

eras.polity: Ukraine (Luhansk Oblast) and Russia (Rostov and Belgorod oblasts)

regions.label: The Zbruch frontier — Galicia, Podolia and Volhynia
regions.sub: Volochysk, Pidvolochysk, Husiatyn, Borshchiv, Zdolbuniv

eras.note: After 1569 Volhynia was organised as a voivodeship within Lesser Poland Province.

eras.polity: Poland-Lithuania and the Habsburg monarchy meet on the Zbruch
eras.note: From 1772 to 1793 the Zbruch was the border between Poland-Lithuania and the Habsburg monarchy.

eras.polity: Austria–Russia frontier — Austrian Galicia west, Imperial Russia east
eras.note: From 1793 to 1807 and from 1815 to 1918 the Zbruch separated Austrian Galicia from Imperial Russia. The crossing between Pidvolochysk and Volochysk was a major border checkpoint. Eastern and central Volhynia, where Zdolbuniv lies, passed to Russia in 1795 as the Volhynian Governorate.

eras.polity: Poland — frontier with the Soviet Union on the Zbruch
eras.note: Volhynia became part of the Polish-controlled Volhynian District in 1919. The Peace of Riga of 1921 divided Volhynia between Poland and the Soviet Union and the Volhynian Voivodeship was established. The Polish–Soviet border ran along the Zbruch until 1939.
The Soviet Union invaded and occupied the Polish part of Volhynia in 1939 after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact.

regions.label: Western Volhynia — the Novovolynsk coal strip
regions.sub: Novovolynsk

eras.note: Poland took western Volhynia and Lithuania eastern Volhynia in 1352–1366.
After 1569 Volhynia was organised as a voivodeship within Lesser Poland Province.
The Third Partition annexed eastern and central Volhynia to the Russian Empire in 1795 as the Volhynian Governorate.
Volhynia became part of the Polish-controlled Volhynian District in 1919. The Peace of Riga of 1921 divided it between Poland and the Soviet Union and the Volhynian Voivodeship was established.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — Ukrainian SSR; Novovolynsk built as a mining town
eras.note: The Soviet Union occupied the Polish part of Volhynia in 1939. Novovolynsk was built in 1950 as a mining town (1951 in some listings) and received city status in 1957.

regions.label: Wallachian Carpathian foothills
regions.sub: Râmnicu Sărat, Nehoiu, Buşteni, Rucăr, Brezoi

eras.note: The founding of Wallachia is dated by tradition to 1290 and its independence to 1330.
Wallachia accepted Ottoman suzerainty in 1417, and the tribute was raised in 1462.

eras.polity: Wallachia — Phanariot rule and the Russian protectorate
eras.note: Phanariot rule began in 1715 under Nicholas Mavrocordatos and ended after the events of 1821. The Treaty of Adrianople of 1829 placed Wallachia under Russian military rule and the Organic Statute dates from 1834–1835. At the western end of the ring, Oltenia was under Habsburg rule from the Treaty of Passarowitz until 1739.
Wallachia and Moldavia united on 5 February 1859 and the name Romania was adopted in 1866. National civil registration began in Wallachia and Moldavia in 1865.
The Kingdom of Romania dates from 1881. Records under 100 years old stay with local civil registration offices, and older registers go to the National Archives county branches.

regions.label: Oltenia — the Danube plain (southern Dolj)
regions.sub: Băileşti, Maglavit

eras.note: The founding of Wallachia is dated by tradition to 1290 and its independence to 1330.
Wallachia accepted Ottoman suzerainty in 1417.
The Ottomans ceded Oltenia to Charles VI of Austria after the war of 1716–1718 (Treaty of Passarowitz), and it was returned to Wallachia in 1739 by the Treaty of Belgrade.

eras.polity: Wallachia — Phanariot rule and the Russian protectorate
eras.note: Phanariot rule ran from 1715 until the events of 1821, Russia held military rule from the Treaty of Adrianople of 1829, and the Organic Statute dates from 1834–1835.
Wallachia and Moldavia united on 5 February 1859. National civil registration began in Wallachia in 1865.
The Kingdom of Romania dates from 1881.

regions.label: Memelland — Šilutė (Heydekrug) and the Nemunas delta
regions.sub: Šilutė (Heydekrug)

eras.note: The Teutonic Order built Memel Castle where the Dangė flows into the Neman in 1252.

eras.polity: Duchy of Prussia — border with Lithuania fixed by the Treaty of Melno
eras.note: The Treaty of Melno of 1422 set a Prussia–Lithuania border that lasted until 1918. The Duchy of Prussia was a fief of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth from 1525 to 1618.

eras.polity: Kingdom of Prussia, then the German Empire
eras.note: The Kingdom of Prussia held the region from 1701, and it was part of the German Empire from 1871 to 1918.

eras.polity: League of Nations territory under French administration
eras.note: The Treaty of Versailles separated the northern part of East Prussia from Germany, effective 10 January 1919. French troops arrived and a temporary French military administration began on 15 February 1920, and a French civilian administration followed in 1921. The Klaipėda Revolt took place in January 1923.

Lithuania annexed the territory on 19 January 1923. The Klaipėda Convention of 8 May 1924 made it an autonomous part of Lithuania with its own parliament, two official languages and separate institutions.
Lithuania ceded the Memel Territory to Germany on 23 March 1939 after a German ultimatum.
Lithuania regained independence on 11 March 1990, and the region returned to it without its former autonomy.

regions.label: Moscow–Tver border country
regions.sub: Taldom, Zavidovo, Verbilki, Zaprudnya, Bogorodskoye

eras.note: Moscow Governorate was established on 29 December 1708 (18 December Old Style).

eras.polity: Moscow and Tver governorates meet here
eras.note: Tver Viceroyalty was established on 25 November 1775 and Tver Governorate on 12 December 1796. Moscow Governorate's uyezds included Dmitrovsky and Klinsky, and Tver's included Korchevskoy (added in 1803), Zubtsovsky and Vyshnevolotsky. The ring lies across the line between the two, so a place has to be matched to its uyezd.

eras.polity: Moscow Oblast and the Western Oblast
eras.note: Moscow Governorate was abolished on 14 January 1929 when modern Moscow Oblast was created. Tver Governorate was abolished on 12 August 1929 and split between Moscow and Western oblasts.
The former Tver Governorate is now split between Tver and Moscow oblasts.

regions.label: Gus-Khrustalny and the Moscow–Vladimir–Ryazan seam
regions.sub: Gus-Khrustalny, Roshal

eras.note: Vladimir Province was formed in 1719 as part of Moscow Governorate. The Gus crystal works, around which Gus-Khrustalny grew, was founded in 1756.

The independent Vladimir Viceroyalty was formed in 1778 with 14 uyezds and became Vladimir Governorate on 1 November 1796, with 13 uyezds and unchanged borders from 1881 to 1917. Gus-Khrustalny is catalogued under Melenkovsky uyezd. The ring touches the Moscow and Ryazan governorates, so the villages near Roshal may be filed under a neighbouring governorate.

eras.polity: Ivanovo Industrial Oblast, then Vladimir Oblast
eras.note: Vladimir Governorate was abolished on 1 October 1929 and the Ivanovo Industrial Oblast, formed from the Ivanovo-Voznesensk, Vladimir, Yaroslavl and Kostroma governorates, took its place. Gus-Khrustalny received town status in 1931.
Gus-Khrustalny stands in Vladimir Oblast, about 63 km south of Vladimir.

regions.label: Kostroma, Vetluga and the Gorokhovets Volga
regions.sub: Shar'ya, Manturovo, Vetluga, Yuryevets, Gorokhovets

eras.note: The Vladimir Viceroyalty was formed in 1778 with 14 uyezds. Kostroma Governorate was preceded by a Kostroma Viceroyalty.

eras.polity: Kostroma Governorate, with Vladimir Governorate at the Gorokhovets end
eras.note: Kostroma Governorate was established in 1796 with 12 uyezds, among them Chukhlomskoy, Makaryevsky, Vetluzhsky and Yuryevetsky. Vladimir Governorate was formed on 1 November 1796. The ring also takes in ground outside the Kostroma uyezds, so the uyezd of a place must be identified.

eras.polity: Ivanovo Industrial Oblast and successor oblasts
eras.note: Kostroma Governorate was disestablished in 1929, and the Ivanovo Industrial Oblast was formed from the Ivanovo-Voznesensk, Vladimir, Yaroslavl and Kostroma governorates.

regions.label: Tikhvin and Ustyuzhna uplands
regions.sub: Pikalevo, Boksitogorsk, Babayevo, Ustyuzhna, Chagoda

eras.note: Novgorod Governorate was established in 1727 from parts of Saint Petersburg Governorate. Tikhvin was a city of Novgorod Province, and Tikhvinsky uyezd was established in 1773.
Catherine II abolished the governorate in 1776 and created the Novgorod and Tver viceroyalties.

eras.polity: Novgorod Governorate — Tikhvinsky and Ustyuzhensky uyezds
eras.note: The governorate was restored in 1796. Tikhvinsky uyezd, with Tikhvin as its centre, existed from 1859 to 1917, and Ustyuzhensky uyezd was one of the governorate's uyezds.
In June 1918 the Beloozersky, Kirillovsky, Tikhvinsky, Ustyuzhensky and Cherepovetsky uyezds were split off from Novgorod Governorate into Cherepovets Governorate.

Novgorod Governorate became part of Leningrad Oblast on 1 August 1927. The ring today spans parts of Leningrad, Novgorod and Vologda oblasts, so a town's present oblast decides where its modern files are held.

regions.label: Vychegda — Koryazhma
regions.sub: Koryazhma

eras.polity: Russia — Koryazhemsky Nikolaevsky Monastery on the Vychegda
eras.note: The Koryazhemsky Nikolaevsky Monastery was founded in 1535 at the mouth of the Bolshaya Koryazhemka River and gave the town its name. It was abolished in 1917 after the October Revolution.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — the Koryazhma paper-mill town
eras.note: Construction of a large paper mill began in 1953, the first brick houses went up in 1954, and the mill settlement became an urban-type settlement in 1957. The mill started work in 1961, the population was about 42,000 in 1975, and Koryazhma received town rights on 15 August 1985.

regions.label: Tambov–Penza border strip
regions.sub: Kirsanov, Zemetchino

eras.note: The Tambov Viceroyalty was organised in 1779.
Tambov Governorate was created in 1796 from the viceroyalty and had 12 uyezds, including Kirsanovsky. In 1926 its northern half was split between Penza and Ryazan governorates.
The governorate was abolished in 1928 and became the Tambov, Kozlov and Borisoglebsk okrugs. Tambov Oblast was formed in 1937.
The strip lies on the boundary between the two oblasts.

regions.label: Upper Tisza — Rakhiv and Ruske Pole (Ukrainian Maramureș)
regions.sub: Rakhiv, Ruske Pole, Hlybokyi Potik

eras.note: Maramureș became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in the 11th century and was reorganised as Máramaros County in the 14th.

eras.polity: Principality of Transylvania, then Habsburg administration
eras.note: In the 16th century Maramureș came under the Principality of Transylvania, and in the late 17th century under Habsburg administration.
Maramureș was transferred to the Habsburg Kingdom of Hungary in 1732, and the monarchy became the Austrian Empire in 1804.
The county lay in the Hungarian part of Austria–Hungary from 1867.
After the First World War the historic county was divided between Romania and the Carpathian Ruthenia of Czechoslovakia. This ring holds ground on the Czechoslovak side.
Hungary annexed Carpathian Ruthenia in March 1939 and Hungarian control ended in 1944.
After the Second World War the northern section of Maramureș was incorporated into the Ukrainian SSR.

regions.label: Balta and the Kodyma borderland
regions.sub: Balta, Teplyk

eras.note: Balta is first mentioned in 1526 on the right bank of the Kodyma. In the 18th century Józef Aleksander Lubomirski founded Józefgród on the left bank, opposite Ottoman-ruled Balta, and Józefgród received town rights in 1776. Russian troops burned the town in 1768, which led to the Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774.
Russia annexed Balta in 1791 and Józefgród in 1793, and the two towns merged under Balta's name in 1797.

eras.polity: Soviet Union — capital of the Moldavian ASSR
eras.note: Balta was the capital of the Moldavian Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic from 1924 to 1929.
The occupation began in August 1941 and the Red Army recaptured Balta on 29 March 1944.
Balta became a city of oblast significance in 2016, and in 2020 the municipality was merged into Podilsk Raion.

regions.label: Ngamiland and Chobe
regions.sub: Maun, Kasane, Shakawe, Gumare, Okavango Delta

eras.note: Before registers. The Yeyi moved from the upper Chobe into the Okavango Delta in the 18th century.

eras.polity: Bechuanaland Protectorate - extended north to Ngamiland
eras.note: The protectorate was extended north to include Ngamiland on 30 June 1890, reaching the Chobe River; Germany recognised this the next day. Administration passed to the High Commissioner for Southern Africa on 9 May 1891, and British officials did not arrive in Ngamiland until 1894.

eras.polity: Bechuanaland Protectorate - Batawana capital at Maun
eras.note: Maun was founded in 1915 as the capital of the Batawana and is the administrative centre of Ngamiland, in the North-West District. The protectorate was governed from Mafeking, outside its own borders, until 1965.
Gaborone was declared the capital in 1965, the new constitution took effect, and the BDP won the first general election.

eras.polity: Republic of Botswana - North-West and Chobe Districts
eras.note: Independence came on 30 September 1966. Civil registration records for Botswana are listed from 1939 to the present, held in national, provincial and district archives.

regions.label: Ghanzi and the Kgalagadi
regions.sub: Ghanzi, Tshabong, Kang, Hukuntsi, Charles Hill

eras.note: Before registers. Hendrik van Zyl, described as the first Afrikaner to settle at Ghanzi, began hunting and ivory trading there around 1870.

An Order-in-Council of 27 January 1885 placed the Kalahari south of the 22nd parallel under British control, and the Bechuanaland Protectorate was established on 31 March 1885 with the 22nd parallel as its northern limit; it was extended north on 30 June 1890.
The High Commissioner for Southern Africa administered the protectorate from 9 May 1891, from Mafeking outside its borders. The first substantial Boer migration into Ghanzi began about 1897-1898.
Gaborone became the capital in 1965, the constitution took effect and the BDP won the general election.

eras.polity: Republic of Botswana - Ghanzi and Kgalagadi Districts
eras.note: Botswana became independent on 30 September 1966. The Botswana National Archives and Records Services are at the Government Enclave, Gaborone.

regions.label: Central and North-East Botswana
regions.sub: Francistown, Serowe, Selebi-Phikwe, Letlhakane, Tonota, Bobonong

eras.note: Before registers. The Kalanga kingdom of Butua fell in 1840, and the Tati Goldfields gold rush began in 1868.

The Bechuanaland Protectorate was established on 31 March 1885. The Tati area was first claimed by Matabeleland, and in 1887 Samuel Edwards, working for Cecil Rhodes, obtained a mining concession there.

eras.polity: Bechuanaland Protectorate - Bamangwato under Khama III
eras.note: Khama III founded Serowe in 1902 as the capital of the Bamangwato. In 1895 Khama III, Sebele I and Bathoen I travelled to Britain and blocked the transfer of the protectorate to the British South Africa Company.

The Tati Concessions Land Act of 21 January 1911 transferred the eastern Tati territory to the protectorate, where it later formed the North-East District. Seretse Khama, born at Serowe, was banished from the protectorate in 1950 and returned in 1956.
Gaborone was declared the capital in 1965 and the BDP, under Seretse Khama, won the first general election on 1 March 1965.

eras.polity: Republic of Botswana - Central and North-East Districts
eras.note: Extensive diamond deposits were found in 1969 and Debswana was created in 1978. Civil registration records are listed for Botswana from 1939.

regions.label: Southern Botswana: Kweneng and the Southern District
regions.sub: Molepolole, Kanye, Lobatse, Ramotswa, Mogoditshane, Jwaneng

eras.note: Before registers. The Ngwaketse regent Sebogo expelled Kololo attackers in 1826, Livingstone established the Kolobeng Mission in 1845, and in 1853 the Kwena chief Sechele asked for a British protectorate and was refused.

The Bechuanaland Protectorate was established on 31 March 1885 after treaties with several chiefs. The Tswana country south of the Molopo was proclaimed the separate Crown colony of British Bechuanaland in September 1885.

Britain ran the protectorate from Mafeking, outside its borders. In 1895 Sebele I and Bathoen I travelled to Britain with Khama III to oppose absorption by the British South Africa Company; the railway was built in 1897 and the protectorate joined the Southern African Customs Union in 1910.
Gaborone, on the eastern edge of this ground, was declared the capital in 1965 when the constitution took effect.

eras.polity: Republic of Botswana - Kweneng and Southern Districts
eras.note: Botswana became independent on 30 September 1966. The Botswana National Archives and Records Services are at the Government Enclave, Gaborone.

regions.label: Mafikeng and the Molopo
regions.sub: Mafikeng, Mmabatho, Ramatlabama

eras.note: Before registers.

The Boer-led states of Stellaland and Goshen seceded from the Tswana country in 1882; the London Convention of 1884 made Stellaland a British protectorate, and British forces under Charles Warren restored order in early 1885.
British Bechuanaland existed from 30 September 1885 to 16 November 1895, with Vryburg as capital and Mafeking laid out as an administrative centre.

British Bechuanaland was annexed to the Cape Colony on 16 November 1895. Civil registration of Cape births and deaths began about 1895 (approximate). The Bechuanaland Protectorate to the north was governed from Mafeking.

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province, Mafeking
eras.note: The Cape Colony became the Cape Province of the Union in 1910. Mafeking remained the seat of the Bechuanaland Protectorate administration until 1965.

Bophuthatswana had self-government from 1 June 1972 and nominal independence on 6 December 1977, recognised only by South Africa and Transkei. Mafeking was incorporated into it in 1980 after a local referendum, and it was reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994.
Mmabatho merged with Mafikeng, which is the capital of North West Province.

regions.label: Western Transvaal along the Vaal
regions.sub: Schweizer-Reneke, Wolmaransstad, Christiana, Delareyville, Sannieshof, Itsoseng

eras.note: Before registers.
The Sand River Convention of 17 January 1852 recognised Boer independence north of the Vaal River; the Vaal is the southern edge of this ground.
Britain annexed the republic in 1877; the Boers revolted in the First Boer War of 1880-81, and the Pretoria Convention followed.
The London Convention of 1884 restored full independence. Britain occupied the republic during the Second Boer War of 1899-1902.

The Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 ended the republic, which became the Transvaal Colony. Civil registration of births and deaths in the Transvaal is listed from 1901 and of marriages from 1870 (approximate dates).

eras.polity: Union and Republic of South Africa - Transvaal Province
eras.note: The Transvaal became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910.
The old republic's territory now comprises most of Gauteng, Limpopo, Mpumalanga and North West provinces; the Vaal towns here are in North West.

regions.label: The Transkei, Griqualand East and Pondoland
regions.sub: Mthatha, Kokstad, Matatiele, Dutywa, Mount Frere, Lusikisiki

eras.note: Before registers. Pondoland runs from the Mthatha River to the Mtamvuna River, and King Faku allowed Wesleyan missionaries to set up a mission in 1820.
Griqualand East (New Griqualand) was a Griqua state from about 1862 to 1879, with Kokstad its capital from 1872. Britain took control of it in 1874.

eras.polity: Cape annexations of the Transkeian Territories
eras.note: The Transkei, Pondoland, Tembuland and Griqualand East were incorporated into the Cape Colony between 1879 and 1894. The annexation act for Griqualand East was passed in 1877 and took effect on 17 September 1879.
Britain annexed the Mpondo region in 1894 despite resistance. Civil registration of Cape births and deaths began about 1895 (approximate).

eras.polity: Union of South Africa - Cape Province
eras.note: Griqualand East became part of the Cape Province in 1910.

Transkei was given nominal self-government in 1963 and declared nominally independent on 26 October 1976 with Umtata (now Mthatha) as capital; only South Africa recognised it. Pondoland became part of the Transkei in 1963, and Griqualand East was partly incorporated in the 1980s. Transkei was reincorporated on 27 April 1994.
Transkei became part of the Eastern Cape; Griqualand East, including Kokstad, joined KwaZulu-Natal in 1994.

regions.label: Natal South Coast
regions.sub: Port Shepstone, Margate, Port Edward

eras.note: Before registers.

eras.polity: Natal, a British colony run from the Cape
eras.note: Natal was proclaimed a British colony on 4 May 1843 and was administered from the Cape Colony until 1856.

Natal became a separate colony in 1856. Port Shepstone was founded in 1867 after marble was found near the mouth of the Mzimkhulu, and 246 Norwegian immigrants settled there in 1882 and founded Marburg. Civil registration in Natal is listed from 1868 for births, 1845 for marriages and 1888 for deaths (approximate dates).
Responsible government began in 1893, the year Port Shepstone was declared a full fiscal port. Zululand was annexed to Natal in 1897, and the railway reached Port Shepstone in 1901.

eras.polity: Union and Republic of South Africa - Natal Province
eras.note: On 31 May 1910 Natal became a province of the Union of South Africa.
Port Shepstone is in KwaZulu-Natal province.

regions.label: Cape West Coast and the Southern Peninsula
regions.sub: Saldanha, Vredenburg, Langebaan, Muizenberg, Simon's Town, Constantia

eras.note: Before registers. A ship under António de Saldanha called at the bay in 1503; the name passed to Saldanha Bay in 1601, when Table Bay received its present name.

eras.polity: Dutch East India Company - the Cape
eras.note: Jan van Riebeeck founded the VOC supply station in 1652; former employees leased farms as free burghers, with slaves brought from Madagascar, Mozambique and Asia. The Merestein was wrecked near Jutten Island on 3 April 1702, and in 1781 a British squadron seized six Dutch East Indiamen sheltering in Saldanha Bay.

eras.polity: First British occupation of the Cape
eras.note: Britain occupied the Cape in 1795. The Martello tower at Simon's Town dates from the British works of 1795-96.
Britain returned the Cape to the Batavian Republic in 1803 under the Peace of Amiens.

Britain occupied the Cape again in 1806 after the Battle of Blaauwberg, and the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814 confirmed British sovereignty. Civil registration of Cape births and deaths began about 1895 (approximate), and the Saldanha Bay Canning Company was founded in 1905.

eras.polity: Union and Republic of South Africa - Western Cape
eras.note: Simon's Town has been a naval base for over two centuries, first for the Royal Navy and now for the South African Navy; Saldanha Bay was developed as the port for iron ore railed from the Northern Cape.

regions.label: Lowveld: Nkomazi and Komatipoort
regions.sub: Komatipoort, Kamaqhekeza, Emtfuntini, Kamhlushwa

eras.note: Before registers.
The republic was recognised north of the Vaal by the Sand River Convention of 17 January 1852.
Britain annexed the republic in 1877 and the Boers revolted in 1880-81.

eras.polity: South African Republic - Delagoa Bay railway
eras.note: Komatipoort was a rough railway construction camp in the 1890s, the last stop on the Pretoria-Delagoa Bay line; the first train crossed the border there in 1891 by one account. From 1900 to 1902 it was a base for Steinaecker's Horse, recruited by the British to fight Boer guerrillas.
The Treaty of Vereeniging of 31 May 1902 turned the republic into the Transvaal Colony. Transvaal civil registration of births and deaths is listed from 1901 (approximate).

eras.polity: Union and Republic of South Africa - Transvaal Province
eras.note: The Nkomati Accord was signed at Komatipoort in 1984.
Komatipoort lies in the Nkomazi Local Municipality of Mpumalanga, where the Crocodile and Komati rivers meet.

regions.label: Lesotho Lowlands
regions.sub: Maseru, Mafeteng, Mabote, Mapoteng

eras.note: Before registers. Moshoeshoe I sought British protection during the conflict with the Orange Free State.
Britain declared the territory British in 1868.
The Cape Colony ruled Basutoland from 1871. Cape rule was unpopular and led to the Basuto Gun War of 1880-81.
From 1884 the territory came under the direct authority of the Crown, administered by British Resident Commissioners. It joined a customs union in 1891 and a national council was formed in 1903.
Basutoland became independent as the Kingdom of Lesotho on 4 October 1966.

regions.label: Southern Namibia coast and the Orange River
regions.sub: Lüderitz, Oranjemund, Warmbad, Aussenkehr

eras.note: Before registers.

Adolf Lüderitz placed his settlement at Angra Pequena under German protection in 1884; the flag was raised on 7 August 1884. In 1908 the Atlantic coast around the area was declared a restricted zone, the Sperrgebiet, because of alluvial diamonds.

eras.polity: South African occupation and the League mandate
eras.note: Allied forces including South African troops captured the colony in 1915; Germany ceded it in the Treaty of Versailles of 1919, and it became South West Africa under a League of Nations mandate administered by South Africa.

eras.polity: South West Africa - Oranjemund diamond town
eras.note: After diamonds were found south of the Orange River in 1927, rich deposits were found on the north side; mining began in 1935 and the town of Oranjemund was formally settled in 1936. Access to the town was limited to employees and their relatives.
Namibia became independent in 1990. Oranjemund was proclaimed a town in 2011 and is governed by a town council.

regions.label: Annobon
regions.sub: San Antonio de Pale, Aual

eras.note: The Portuguese reached the island on New Year's Day 1473, which gave it the name ano bom (good year). Most residents speak a Portuguese-based creole, Annobonese.
Spain received the island under the Treaty of El Pardo of 1778, and Spanish authority was re-established in the late 19th century.
The Spanish colonies in the Gulf of Guinea were administratively united in 1926.

The territory became a province of Spain in 1956 and in 1959 was reclassified as the Equatorial Region, split into the provinces of Fernando Poo and Rio Muni; a referendum approved the Regime of Autonomy in 1963.
Spain handed power to the new government on 12 October 1968 (13 October in some accounts). Annobon is the country's smallest province, with its capital at San Antonio de Pale.

regions.label: Lebombo Frontier: Ressano Garcia and Namaacha
regions.sub: Ressano Garcia, Namaacha

eras.note: Before registers.

The railway from Lourenco Marques to Pretoria crosses the border at Ressano Garcia, facing Komatipoort; one account dates the first train across the border to 1891. Portugal granted charters in 1891 to the Mozambique and Niassa companies, which held the centre and north of the colony.
The colony was renamed an overseas province in 1951; FRELIMO began its guerrilla campaign in September 1964.

eras.polity: People's Republic of Mozambique and the civil war
eras.note: Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975. The civil war between FRELIMO and RENAMO ran from 1977 to the Rome General Peace Accords of 4 October 1992.
Ressano Garcia is a border town in Maputo Province next to Komatipoort, on the Pretoria-Maputo railway.

regions.label: Niassa: Lake Niassa shore and Mandimba
regions.sub: Metangula, Mandimba

eras.note: Before registers.

The Niassa Company held a Portuguese charter from 1891 over present-day Cabo Delgado and Niassa provinces; French and British investors took it over in 1892-93 and moved its headquarters to London, and it founded Porto Amelia (now Pemba) in 1904. The concession was abolished on 27 October 1929.
The Niassa Company's concession ended on 27 October 1929 after Portugal refused to extend it.
The colony was renamed an overseas province in 1951, and FRELIMO began its guerrilla campaign in September 1964.
Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975; the civil war of 1977-1992 ended with the Rome General Peace Accords of 4 October 1992.

regions.label: Lake Mweru and Kaputa
regions.sub: Nchelenge, Kaputa, Mwansabombwe, Chiengi

eras.note: Before registers. When Livingstone visited in 1867-68 the capital of Mwata Kazembe was further north, at what is now Kanyembo; the Kazembe capital has been at Mwansabombwe since the 1890s.

eras.polity: Northern Rhodesia under the British South Africa Company
eras.note: Northern Rhodesia was formed in 1911 by merging Barotziland-North-Western Rhodesia and North-Eastern Rhodesia, administered by the Company on behalf of the British government.
Administration passed to the British government in 1924; the capital was Livingstone until 1935, when it moved to Lusaka.
Northern Rhodesia was part of the Federation from 1953 to 1963.

eras.polity: Republic of Zambia - Luapula and Northern Provinces
eras.note: Zambia became independent on 24 October 1964. Mwansabombwe, the seat of Mwata Kazembe, lies in Luapula Province.

regimeNote: Five of these carry a Wikidata id and the dates Wikidata holds for them. The rest do not, and that is deliberate: fuzzy matching offered Circassia for Croatia, Audhali for Australia and Basutoland for Poland, and several of the labels here — «Aquileia · Gorizia · Frankopan», «German occupation» — are this project's own shorthand for a situation rather than the name of a state. An honest blank beats a plausible lie. data/polities-wikidata.json holds 1,857 former countries with dates as a REFERENCE for whoever authors the next region, not as something a machine should match automatically.
regimeArchivesNote: `archives` is WHICH MODERN STATE HELD THIS GROUND under that regime — the country whose flag flew over it, and whose archive inherited the paper. Habsburg is AT and HU because the Dual Monarchy filed in both capitals; Galicia is PL and UA because the border of 1945 cut it and its archives in half. It is NOT a claim about who owns the ground today, and it is not a border: it is the answer to «whose archive do I write to for these years, and whose flag was over the parish when the entry was made». A regime that left no single successor state — the Aquileia/Gorizia/Frankopan feudal centuries — carries an empty list on purpose, because a guess at which modern capital inherited a patriarchate is exactly the inference this atlas refuses elsewhere. Read by abroadFor() for the «also governed from» sources, and by eraFlagsHtml() for the flags over the selected era.
countriesNote: Derived from each ring — the vertices, the edge midpoints and the centre — rather than from the places walked inside it. A region is a piece of ground and which countries it covers is a fact about the ground, not about whether anybody has walked a parish in it yet. A country claimed by a single sampled point is dropped as a corner clipping a neighbour.
